rows.summary: Live-cell imaging of mRNA encoding secretome proteins and translated nascent peptide markers show that secretome translation occurs at endoplasmic reticulum junctions near lysosomes, requires lunapark protein and is modulated by nutrient status.

rows.title: Assessing phylogenetic confidence at pandemic scales
rows.summary: A method using subtree pruning and regrafting-based tree assessment (SPRTA), which considers evolutionary relationships between lineages, enhances interpretability of phylogenetic analyses such as those of SARS-CoV-2 variants.

rows.title: Vector-stimuli-responsive magnetorheological fibrous materials
rows.summary: Vector-stimuli-responsive magnetorheological fibrous materials can be mass-produced, which can be assembled into yarns and woven into a variety of fabrics with actuation and stiffening abilities.

rows.title: The new frontier in understanding human and mammalian brain development
rows.summary: Recent studies integrating multi-omics data with cell atlases across development for brains of humans and model organisms are revealing conserved and divergent patterns of brain development at the molecular and cellular levels, and linking these to complex behavioural and neuropsychiatric phenotypes.

rows.title: Lymph node environment drives FSP1 targetability in metastasizing melanoma
rows.summary: Targeting FSP1 in lymph nodes has considerable potential for blocking melanoma progression.

rows.title: Fair human-centric image dataset for ethical AI benchmarking
rows.summary: The Fair Human-Centric Image Benchmark (FHIBE, pronounced ‘Feebee’)—an image dataset that implements best practices for consent, privacy, compensation, safety, diversity and utility—can be used responsibly as a fairness evaluation dataset for many human-centric computer vision applications.

rows.title: Global satellite survey reveals uncertainty in landfill methane emissions
rows.summary: High-resolution satellites reveal major uncertainties in methane emissions from global waste sites, highlighting the need to reconcile observed and reported data, with actionable insights to improve estimates and guide targeted mitigation efforts.

rows.title: Synthetic α-synuclein fibrils replicate in mice causing MSA-like pathology
rows.summary: Synthetic fibril strain 1B is a pathogen that is capable of self-replication and inducing glial cytoplasmic inclusions in vivo in mice, and the structural features of 1B may underlie the pathology of individuals with multiple-system atrophy.

rows.title: Lymphoid gene expression supports neuroprotective microglia function
rows.summary: PU.1 low CD28-expressing microglia may act as suppressive cells in Alzheimer’s disease, mitigating its progression by reducing neuroinflammation and amyloid plaque load, indicating potential immunotherapeutic approaches for treatment.

rows.title: Atomically accurate de novo design of antibodies with RFdiffusion
rows.summary: The combination of computational design, laboratory-based screening and biophysical validation enables the de novo generation of variable heavy-chain antibody fragments and antibodies that precisely target chosen disease-related molecules.

rows.title: Lineage-resolved atlas of the developing human cortex
rows.summary: Lineage tracing in human tissue samples from gestational weeks 16 to 24 provides insight into lineage relationships between cortical cell types and shows a switch in progenitor output from glutamatergic to GABAergic neurons.

rows.title: Continuous cell-type diversification in mouse visual cortex development
rows.summary: A high-resolution transcriptomic and epigenomic cell-type atlas of the developing mouse visual cortex from embryonic to postnatal development is presented, providing a real-time dynamic molecular map associated with individual cell types and specific developmental events.

rows.title: Structural snapshots capture nucleotide release at the μ-opioid receptor
rows.summary: Structures of GDP-bound MOR–G i conformational states combined with pharmacological assays show an inverse correlation between ligand efficacy and GDP affinity, where agonists decrease GDP affinity, promoting GTP exchange, and antagonists increase GDP affinity, dampening activation, thus providing structural and mechanistic insights into G protein activation.

rows.title: Conservation and alteration of mammalian striatal interneurons
rows.summary: An analysis of cell-type diversity in brain samples from a variety of mammalian species, both during development and in adult animals, reveals that the TAC3 initial class of striatal interneurons is conserved across placental mammals and is homologous to Th striatal interneurons in rodents.

rows.title: Two residues reprogram immunity receptors for nitrogen-fixing symbiosis
rows.summary: An investigation of plant receptor-like kinases identifies regions of these proteins that control whether immune or symbiotic signalling pathways are activated, with minimal changes to specific residues in one of these regions being sufficient to alter signalling specificity.

rows.title: Eight millennia of continuity of a previously unknown lineage in Argentina
rows.summary: A previously unsampled deep lineage in central Argentina was discovered that had distinctive genetic drift by 8,500 bp and persisted as the main Native American ancestry component in the region up to the present day.

rows.title: Anti-progestin therapy targets hallmarks of breast cancer risk
rows.summary: Results of an early-phase breast cancer prevention trial demonstrate the potential for breast cancer prevention in premenopausal women with anti-progestin therapy by inducing epithelial–stromal remodelling and suppression of luminal progenitors.

rows.title: A probabilistic histological atlas of the human brain for MRI segmentation
rows.summary: NextBrain is an open source, probabilistic atlas of the entire human brain, assembled using artificial-intelligence-enabled registration and segmentation methods to reconstruct the multimodal serial histology of five human half brains, and which can be used to automatically segment brain MRI scans into 333 regions.

rows.title: Spatial dynamics of brain development and neuroinflammation
rows.summary: A tri-omic atlas of the mouse brain from postnatal day 0 to P21 reveals that layer-specific projection neurons have a role in coordinating axonogenesis and myelination.

rows.title: The importance of past rifting in large igneous province development
rows.summary: Seismic data from the Turkana Depression in East Africa show that areas of thinned lithosphere are not necessarily persistent weak zones where extension and magmatic provinces will develop.

rows.title: Specificity, length and luck drive gene rankings in association studies
rows.summary: Genetic association tests prioritize candidate genes based on different criteria.

rows.title: Millisecond lifetimes and coherence times in 2D transmon qubits
rows.summary: A materials platform using tantalum as a base layer and silicon as the substrate to construct superconducting qubits enables device performance improvements such as millisecond lifetimes and coherence times, as well as high time-averaged quality factors.

rows.title: Transcriptomic and spatial organization of telencephalic GABAergic neurons
rows.summary: Long-distance migration and dispersion is a common characteristic of nearly all classes of telencephalic GABAergic neurons, which diversify extensively after birth in the cortex and striatum, but show limited postnatal changes in the septum, preoptic area and pallidum.

rows.title: Adenosine signalling drives antidepressant actions of ketamine and ECT
rows.summary: Adenosine signalling is identified as the central mechanism of action of the antidepressant effects of ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy, and newly developed analogues of ketamine exhibit improved antidepressant efficacy with reduced side effects.

rows.title: Safeguards for virology must be designed in partnership with the public
When will Africa have a Nobel prize in medicine?
Can AI predict and limit online hate?
China should undertake more risky research to close the Nobel gap
Single video camera tells the story of deadly Myanmar quake
rows.summary: Footage from a lone camera incidentally located metres from a fault provides data on slippage duration and motion.

rows.title: From the archive: Do sunspots affect the price of corn?
rows.summary: Crop prices correlate with an 11-year solar period, and a meteor detonates over Ireland, in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

rows.title: Biggest black-hole outburst ever seen records death throes of a star
rows.summary: A ‘superflare’ 10 trillion times brighter than the Sun is confirmed as the record-holder for luminosity.

rows.title: Japan’s first female prime minister doesn’t call herself a feminist — but the country needs her to tackle sexism in science
rows.summary: Sanae Takaichi has pledged to make the country ‘strong and prosperous’ again; success hinges on breaking barriers for women in science.

rows.title: The ‘implementation COP’: why the Belém summit must ratchet up climate action
rows.summary: Delegates to the climate conference in Brazil must accelerate commitments to rapidly developing a low-carbon economy. There is no Planet B.

rows.title: Climate change is devastating mining of minerals needed to fight it
rows.summary: Extreme weather threatens the extraction of critical minerals required to produce clean energy.

rows.title: How the rush for critical minerals is neglecting human needs
rows.summary: A focus on national security alone is limiting people’s access to key materials.

rows.title: COVID-19 is spreading again — how serious is it and what are the symptoms?
rows.summary: Limited COVID-19 surveillance data are hampering vaccination and health strategies, researchers say.

rows.title: Daily briefing: A guide to global climate change action
rows.summary: How the world can fight climate change without the help of the United States. Plus, the benefits of walks long and short and whether attitudes to controversial ‘CRISPR babies’ are changing.

rows.title: How I’m helping to cultivate science entrepreneurship in Brazil
rows.summary: A course on disruptive innovation, and a supportive professional network, helped to unleash João Paulo Longo’s entrepreneurship skills.

rows.title: Antibodies unleashed against pancreatic cancer
rows.summary: Blocking the mechanism that cancer cells exploit to avoid destruction by the immune system could spur new treatments for the disease.

rows.title: From pangolins to primates: how I use zoo facilities to treat wild animals
rows.summary: Charlene Yeong works as a veterinarian with animals from zoos and those native to Singapore.

rows.title: Sex, drugs and the conscious brain: Francis Crick beyond the double helix
rows.summary: A thoroughly researched account of the history and relationships that shaped the scientist who co-discovered the structure of DNA.

rows.title: How to fight climate change without the US: a guide to global action
rows.summary: With the US government absent from the COP30 global climate summit, it will be up to others to avert catastrophe.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Custom-made gene-editing therapy for children to enter clinical trial
rows.summary: Researchers are preparing to trial the personalized base-editing therapy that saved a baby boy last year in at least five more children. Plus, get to know the real Francis Crick and what tree rings reveal about ancient coffins.

rows.title: PhD training needs a reboot in an AI world
rows.summary: As machines get better at data analysis and writing tasks, doctoral training must evolve to make the most of artificial-intelligence outputs.

rows.title: Alzheimer’s decline slows with just a few thousand steps a day
rows.summary: A modest increase in physical activity can delay cognitive decline by three years — or more.

rows.title: Insiders warn how dismantling federal agencies could put science at risk
rows.summary: From NASA to the National Institutes of Health, federal agencies conduct research that universities cannot. Agency scientists speak out about the irreplaceable facilities, institutional knowledge and training opportunities that the country is losing.

rows.title: ‘Memory foam’ skeleton in cells helps them to navigate
rows.summary: Cells change shape to move efficiently in a range of spatial environments. This response can be informed by the cell’s memory of past deformation.

rows.title: My funding applications are taking up too much time. How can I stay focused on my research?
rows.summary: A young academic in China worries that the grant-application lottery is wasted effort.

rows.title: ‘Biotech Barbie’ says the time has come to consider CRISPR babies. Do scientists agree?
rows.summary: A company’s plan to edit the genomes of human embryos worries some researchers — but it might reflect the changing attitudes towards the controversial approach.

rows.title: Independent mechanisms of inflammation and myeloid bias in VEXAS syndrome
rows.summary: UBA1 -mutant macrophages exposed to inflammatory stimuli undergo aberrant apoptotic and necroptotic cell death mediated by CASP8 and RIPK3–MLKL, offering insights into the mechanisms underlying VEXAS syndrome.

rows.title: Accelerating the discovery of multicatalytic cooperativity
rows.summary: A pooling–deconvolution algorithm identifies cooperative catalyst behaviours with low experimental cost while accommodating potential inhibitory effects between catalyst candidates.

rows.title: By the time you hear these bats, it’s too late
rows.summary: The fringe-lipped bat ambushes its prey, helping to make it an exceptionally efficient hunter.

rows.title: Artificial brains with less drain
rows.summary: Biologically inspired electronic neurons could boost the efficiency of artificial-intelligence systems.

rows.title: Forests’ misty breath sustains crops in distant lands
rows.summary: The moisture emitted by forests travels across national borders to provide precipitation to far-away fields.

rows.title: Longer walks beat shorter strolls for heart health
rows.summary: People who rack up most of their daily steps in walks lasting less than five minutes have a higher risk of cardiovascular disease than do those who amass their steps in big blocks.

rows.title: Secret route to warm cosmic ‘inflation’: the nuclear force
rows.summary: Modelling shows how the infant Universe might have stayed warm and dense during its primoridal expansion.

rows.title: Personalized gene editing helped one baby: can it be rolled out widely?
rows.summary: In a world first, a bespoke gene-editing therapy benefited one child. Now researchers plan to launch a clinical trial of the approach.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Wildlife wonders and a Super Heavy — the month’s best science images
rows.summary: An illuminated swell shark egg and a SpaceX launch are among the month’s most striking science shots. Plus, a ‘teen T. rex ’ is actually a totally different dinosaur and chatbots trained on social-media junk get ‘brain rot’.

rows.title: Powerful new antibiotic that can kill superbugs discovered in soil bacteria
rows.summary: Surprise discovery could pave the way for new treatments against drug-resistant infections.

rows.title: Why India’s controversial ‘cloud seeding’ trial failed to make it rain
rows.summary: According to the Indian government, the experiment helped to reduce air pollution — but researchers attribute that to the weather.

rows.title: Please stay out of the abandoned buildings
rows.summary: Learning by example.

rows.title: Too much social media gives AI chatbots ‘brain rot’
rows.summary: Large language models fed low-quality data skip steps in their reasoning process.

rows.title: Hotly debated dinosaur is not a tiny T. rex after all
rows.summary: A key fossil suggests that the controversial Nanotyrannus is its own species, not a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex .

rows.title: Author Correction: Reciprocal signalling by Notch–Collagen V–CALCR retains muscle stem cells in their niche
T. rex debate settled: contested fossils are smaller rival species, not juveniles
rows.summary: New evidence answers the question about whether some fossils are Tyrannosaurus rex juveniles or a different species, with implications for decades of published science.

rows.title: Can IVF save the northern white rhino from extinction? — October’s best science images
rows.summary: The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature ’s photo team.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The bowhead whale’s secret to living to 200
rows.summary: A cold-activated protein protects the bowhead whale’s DNA from dangerous mutations. Plus, an elephant-inspired bioprinter and a new way to test the progress of artificial intelligence.

rows.title: ‘Teenage T. rex’ fossil is actually a different species
rows.summary: The discovery of smaller predator Nanotyrannus could prompt a rethink of tyrannosaur evolution.

rows.title: Nanotyrannus and Tyrannosaurus coexisted at the close of the Cretaceous
rows.summary: A well-preserved skeleton of a nearly mature tyrannosaur from the Hell Creek Formation in Montana, USA supports the existence of a second Nanotyrannus species, Nanotyrannus lethaeus sp. nov., and validates the recognition of Nanotyrannus as a genus separate from Tyrannosaurus .

rows.title: Experiments reveal extreme water generation during planet formation
rows.summary: In the high-pressure environments in which rocky planets form, their molten interiors can interact with their hydrogen atmospheres to release water.

rows.title: Single antivenom protects against 17 different snakebites
rows.summary: Researchers immunized an alpaca and a llama with snake venoms, and combined some of the antibodies produced into a potent cocktail.

rows.title: Bowhead whales can live for more than 200 years — this protein might be why
rows.summary: Cold-induced RNA-binding protein was shown to enhance DNA repair — plus, a more universal snakebite venom.

rows.title: 7 basic science discoveries that changed the world
rows.summary: Ozempic, MRI machines and flat screen televisions all emerged out of fundamental research decades earlier — the very types of study being slashed by the US government.

rows.title: World’s smallest 3D bioprinter could rebuild tissue during surgery
rows.summary: Flexible device inspired by an elephant’s trunk can deliver healing hydrogels.

rows.title: Why we should limit the autonomy of AI-enabled weapons
rows.summary: In the rush to adopt autonomous systems, countries risk overlooking crucial safeguards, warns international law professor Nehal Bhuta.

rows.title: ‘A real risk’: the rise of weapons that can act alone
rows.summary: A weapons specialist answers Nature ’s questions on the future of technology and conflict.

rows.title: Reply to: On anisotropy in cubic Cu 2 O photoelectrodes
Ultrasound-driven artificial muscles can grasp, flex and swim
rows.summary: Soft materials filled with microbubbles flex when exposed to ultrasound — forming the basis of wireless devices that can be made to pass through organs such as the intestine.

rows.title: Daily briefing: How the plastics-treaty breakdown could pave the way for something better
rows.summary: Three perspectives on how to fix the plastic-pollution problem. Plus, glowing sperm helped to reveal secrets of mosquito sex and seven times that basic science changed the world.

rows.title: Reply to: Carbon implications of wood harvesting and forest management
Wildfire smoke and its harmful effects will worsen with climate change
rows.summary: Pollution from wildfire smoke is increasing in the United States. Climate change is projected to exacerbate the problem, leading to 70,000 premature deaths each year by 2050. If no extra measures are taken, wildfire smoke could become one of the country’s worst climate disasters.

rows.title: From MRI to Ozempic: breakthroughs that show why fundamental research must be protected
rows.summary: In these financially straitened times, funders must recognize that great discoveries often arise from work that was looking for something completely different.

rows.title: This ‘impressive’ AI model predicted Hurricane Melissa’s perilous growth
rows.summary: An artificial-intelligence tool is helping to crack the challenge of forecasting hurricane intensity.

rows.title: Molecular ‘glues’ and ‘bumpers’ on receptors can bias signalling inside the cell
rows.summary: Compounds that bind to the intracellular core of G-protein-coupled receptors can encourage interactions with some G proteins and prevent them with others, leading to a switch in downstream signalling pathways. Rational design of such core-targeted compounds could be used to find small molecules that modulate this diverse superfamily of receptors.

rows.title: Treatment made that is effective against a wide range of snake venoms
rows.summary: Improved therapies to treat snakebite are needed. A new approach might lead to the development of more-effective treatments for use in the clinic.

rows.title: Retraction Note: sFRP2 in the aged microenvironment drives melanoma metastasis and therapy resistance
To make water, exoplanets might just need some pressure
rows.summary: A reaction between hydrogen and magma at high pressure can produce water, which might explain evidence for ‘wet planets’ in places where water can’t condense.

rows.title: Atomically resolved edges and defects in lead halide perovskites
rows.summary: A majority methylammonium and iodine edge termination is observed by electron ptychography in the perovskite methylammonium lead iodide, and the stability of its edges and internal defects depends on the concentration and type of vacancies present.

rows.title: How nanobots are accelerating cancer-targeting therapies
rows.summary: The near-invisible robots have yet to make it to a clinical trial, but scientists are already using them as a way to diagnose and treat various cancers.

rows.title: We need a new Turing test to assess AI’s real-world knowledge
rows.summary: A fresh set of benchmarks could help specialists to better understand artificial intelligence.

rows.title: Komorebi
rows.summary: A search for meaning.

rows.title: On anisotropy in cubic Cu 2 O photoelectrodes
Electronic paper could enable virtual reality with human-eye resolution
rows.summary: Shrinking conventional visual displays for use closer to the eye causes problems with colour mixing and requires a trade-off between resolution and brightness. An innovative technology called retina E-paper brings ultrahigh resolution to reflective displays, reaching the limits of human vision when scaled to pupil-sized screens.

rows.title: Carbon implications of wood harvesting and forest management
This whale lives for centuries: its secret could help extend human lifespan
rows.summary: A cold-activated protein that mends damaged DNA could play a part in keeping the bowhead whale in tip-top shape.

rows.title: Policed and censored: professors in the southern US feel under siege
rows.summary: Politics trumps salary as the main reason academics are looking for jobs in other states, a survey of university educators shows.

rows.title: What changing energy flows reveal about Africa’s ecosystems
rows.summary: As the giants of the animal kingdom dwindle in numbers, a new way to assess ecosystem function sheds light on animals’ changing ecological contributions.

rows.title: Nanobody-based recombinant antivenom for cobra, mamba and rinkhals bites
rows.summary: A recombinant antivenom composed of eight nanobodies provides broad protection against venom-induced lethality and dermonecrosis in mice challenged with venoms from cobras, mambas and rinkhals snakes.

rows.title: A ductile solid electrolyte interphase for solid-state batteries
rows.summary: A ductile inorganic-rich solid–electrolyte interphase that retains its structural integrity and allows easy ion diffusion enables a long cycle life under practical conditions for lithium metal batteries.

rows.title: Evidence for improved DNA repair in the long-lived bowhead whale
rows.summary: Analysis of the longest-lived mammal, the bowhead whale, reveals an improved ability to repair DNA breaks, mediated by high levels of cold-inducible RNA-binding protein.

rows.title: Thiorphan reprograms neurons to promote functional recovery after spinal cord injury
rows.summary: Thiorphan is identified as a new and effective drug treatment for spinal cord injury that can be adopted across nervous system disease states in the development of new therapies for human neurological disorders.

rows.title: Building wet planets through high-pressure magma–hydrogen reactions
rows.summary: Experimental evidence shows that hydrogen–silicate reactions can generate abundant water in sub-Neptunes, suggesting hydrogen-rich planets have the potential to reach water-rich compositions.

rows.title: Many-body interference in kagome crystals
rows.summary: Experimental evidence of coherent charge transport in the normal state of the kagome metal CsV 3 Sb 5 is presented, revealing the nature of correlated order in kagome metals and new directions for exploring quantum coherence in correlated electron systems.

rows.title: Plug-in strategy for resistance engineering inspired by potato NLRome
rows.summary: A catalogue of nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) genes in wild and cultivated potato genomes enables the identification of genes that confer protection against late blight, and provides a transgene-free strategy for engineering disease resistance in potato.

rows.title: Ocean warming threatens the viability of 60% of Antarctic ice shelves
rows.summary: The viability of Antarctic ice shelves under low rates and high rates of global warming is modelled to estimate when it will become unfeasible for the ice shelves to maintain their present-day shape.

rows.title: Helicase-mediated mechanism of SSU processome maturation and disassembly
rows.summary: Structural studies of 16 native yeast ribosomal small subunit processome structures provide insights into the mechanisms governing the transformation into a pre-40S particle.

rows.title: A pangenome and pantranscriptome of hexaploid oat
rows.summary: A pangenome of oat, assembled from 33 wild and domesticated oat lines, sheds light on the evolution and genetic diversity of this cereal crop and will aid genomics-assisted breeding to improve productivity and sustainability.

rows.title: Mechanism of conductance control and neurosteroid binding in NMDA receptors
rows.summary: Ion-channel conductance levels are controlled by the bending patterns of pore-forming transmembrane helices in the heterotetrameric neuronal channel GluN1a-2B N -methyl- D -aspartate receptor.

rows.title: Ultrasound-driven programmable artificial muscles
rows.summary: A soft artificial muscle with programmable actuation is achieved using microbubble arrays and targeted ultrasound activation, with potential applications in soft robotics, wearable technologies, haptics and biomedical instrumentation.

rows.title: Sensory expectations shape neural population dynamics in motor circuits
rows.summary: Experiments with human volunteers and macaques show that expectations produced by probabilistic cueing of future sensory inputs shape motor circuit dynamics in order to increase the efficiency of movement responses.

rows.title: Multi-omic profiling reveals age-related immune dynamics in healthy adults
rows.summary: This multi-omic longitudinal analysis of the healthy human peripheral immune system constructs the Human Immune Health Atlas and assembles data on immune cell composition and state changes with age, including responses to cytomegalovirus infection and influenza vaccination.

rows.title: Energy flows reveal declining ecosystem functions by animals across Africa
rows.summary: An ecosystem energetics approach, quantifying trophic energy flows across species, offers a unified framework for linking animal biodiversity loss to changes in ecosystem function and Earth system processes.

rows.title: Multiple LDLR family members act as entry receptors for yellow fever virus
rows.summary: The low-density lipoprotein receptor family members LRP1, LRP4 and VLDLR are entry receptors for yellow fever virus.

rows.title: Magnetotelluric evidence for a melt-rich magmatic reservoir beneath Mayotte
rows.summary: Magnetotelluric data provide evidence of a large melt-rich magmatic reservoir beneath Mayotte island that might be connected to the system that fed the large submarine eruption of Fani Maoré in 2018–2019.

rows.title: Technological pathways for cost-effective steel decarbonization
rows.summary: A model has been developed to identify the least-cost technology pathway for global individual iron and steel plants over 2020–2050 in alignment with national carbon-neutrality targets.

rows.title: Origins of chromosome instability unveiled by coupled imaging and genomics
rows.summary: Coupling live-cell imaging, machine learning and genomic sequencing, the MAGIC platform enables investigation of the cellular context, mutation rates and triggers of spontaneous chromosomal abnormality formation, shedding light on fundamental determinants of chromosomal instability.

rows.title: Electromagnetic interference shielding using metal and MXene thin films
rows.summary: Embedding non-porous MXene film into metal thin films can achieve unprecedented shielding performance, which can be used to protect electronic components and equipment from electromagnetic noise.

rows.title: Don’t overlook the plastic footprint of fireworks
A limerick competition celebrates science through rhyme
rows.summary: Submissions of scientifically inspired verse, and footsteps glow in a dark field, in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

rows.title: Universities can harness AI to make learning intuitive
Treat children as citizen co-researchers in health technology
Ethics must keep pace with embryo research
What now for the global plastics treaty?
rows.summary: Ending plastic pollution will mean embracing the complexity of political and economic realities.

rows.title: Environmental treaties are paralysed — here’s how we can do better
rows.summary: The collapse of talks about a UN plastics treaty is the wake-up call we didn’t need. It’s time to study what is going wrong and why.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The secret language of plants
rows.summary: Scientists are only now starting to understand the full role of the plant cell wall. Plus, the risks of a less-familiar form of avian influenza virus and how tides impact the development of urbanization.

rows.title: Taiwan invests in genetic resource for health
rows.summary: A large biobanking effort captures genetic and health data from half a million people in Taiwan, widening the diversity of genomes used to predict disease risk.

rows.title: Open-source protein structure AI aims to match AlphaFold
rows.summary: The developers of OpenFold3 have released an early version of the tool, which they hope will one day perform on par with DeepMind’s protein-structure model.

rows.title: Plants have a secret language that scientists are only now starting to decipher
rows.summary: Signals from the plant cell wall help to orchestrate growth, reproduction and immune function. Can harnessing this molecular cross talk help in creating better crops?

rows.title: Glowing sperm helps to reveal secrets of mosquito sex
rows.summary: Female Aedes mosquitoes signal that copulation can proceed by subtly extending their genitalia.

rows.title: Trust and science: the essential elements missing from plastics treaty talks
rows.summary: A plan to limit plastics pollution globally is in crisis. But disagreements can be resolved with a more formal role for science and more informal spaces for delegates.

rows.title: Preserving Pompeii’s past, one step at a time
rows.summary: Art conservator and restorer Ludovica Alesse works to safeguard Ancient Roman remains unearthed in the latest excavations to ensure the city’s story will never fade.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Surprise illnesses had a role in the demise of Napoleon’s army
rows.summary: ‘No one epidemic’ ravaged Napoleon’s troops on their retreat from Moscow, researchers say. Plus, large language models are sycophants and the art restorer working to preserve the history of Pompeii.

rows.title: AI can supercharge inequality — unless the public learns to control it
rows.summary: Understanding prediction algorithms and engaging in decisions about their use is crucial to curbing concentrated power and rising inequality.

rows.title: How to understand exoplanets — space scientists call on lab-based chemists to help
rows.summary: Stronger links between researchers who work on Earth’s and other planets’ atmospheres, and between the experimental, modelling and observational communities, will help to interpret the astronomical data now at our fingertips.

rows.title: How do you know what I know you know? Steven Pinker on common knowledge
rows.summary: From using words to overthrowing regimes, shared awareness is necessary for people to coordinate. The cognitive scientist explains to Nature how it works.

rows.title: This ‘minor’ bird flu strain has potential to spark human pandemic
rows.summary: Experiments suggests H9N2 has adapted to human cells, but cases of person-to-person transmission haven’t been reported yet.

rows.title: Direct deaminative functionalization with N -nitroamines
rows.summary: A safe, versatile deaminative method converts aromatic amines into diverse C–X and C–C bonds via N -nitroamine intermediates, enabling broad one-pot cross-couplings without hazardous diazonium salts.

rows.title: A matrix-confined molecular layer for perovskite photovoltaic modules
rows.summary: A matrix-confined molecular layer of compact surface coverage and good conductivity is developed as charge transport substrate to fabricate perovskite solar-cell devices with high efficiencies, which shows application potential for scalable production.

rows.title: All-perovskite tandem solar cells with dipolar passivation
rows.summary: A dipolar-passivation strategy enables all-perovskite tandem solar cells with a power conversion efficiency of over 30%.

rows.title: How to grow crystals when and where you want them
rows.summary: Scientists ‘draw’ crystal patterns using laser light.

rows.title: Audio long read: How to get the best night’s sleep — what the science says
rows.summary: Lessons learnt from research into the body’s internal clock could be key to unlocking blissful slumber.

rows.title: Sugarcane genomes offer sweet surprise: mystery ancestor
rows.summary: A previously unknown strain left a stamp on modern varieties of the world’s most popular sugar source.

rows.title: Ancient graffiti and brain complexities: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: China seeks self-reliance in science in next five-year plan
rows.summary: Beijing wants to double down on advanced semiconductor technologies, artificial intelligence and basic research.

rows.title: Chen-Ning Yang obituary: intuitive physicist whose work was inspired by the beauty of symmetry
rows.summary: Nobel prizewinner who helped to improve scientific relations between China and the United States.

rows.title: AI chatbots are sycophants — researchers say it’s harming science
rows.summary: Nature asked researchers who use artificial intelligence how its propensity for people-pleasing affects their work — and what they are doing to mitigate it.

rows.title: How Napoleon’s army met its doom: DNA reveals surprise illnesses had a role
rows.summary: Remains of some of the 300,000 soldiers who died on the retreat from Moscow reveal two bacterial diseases that probably added to the death count.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Key coral species are functionally extinct after record-breaking heatwave
rows.summary: Efforts to conserve Florida corals must now shift towards trying to develop heat-resistant strains, scientists say. Plus, what gives civet coffee its flavour and what we can learn from Brazil about saving rainforests.

rows.title: Paper or plastic?
rows.summary: The real thing.

rows.title: The sci-fi films that physicists love to watch — from Interstellar to Spider-Man
rows.summary: Nature surveyed scientists about their favourite cinematic moments to celebrate the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology.

rows.title: This AI method could turbocharge the hunt for new medicines
rows.summary: A deep-learning design sidesteps the need for time-consuming drug-screening.

rows.title: Google Scholar-based tool gives extra credit to first and last authors
rows.summary: Researchers welcome the initiative, but say it doesn’t go far enough to capture the nuance of researcher productivity and impact.

rows.title: Daily briefing: People with cancer lived longer if they’d had a COVID-19 vaccine
rows.summary: mRNA vaccines seem to ‘rev up’ the immune system to boost immunotherapy. Plus, a rare meteorite has been recovered from the Moon and the mysterious transition between wakefulness and sleep.

rows.title: Does gravity produce quantum weirdness? Proposal divides physicists
rows.summary: A theoretical study suggests that gravity could have quantum effects without itself being a quantum theory. Other researchers aren’t so sure.

rows.title: These iconic corals are nearly extinct due to heatwaves: can they be saved?
rows.summary: Florida’s primary reef-building corals have been declared ‘functionally extinct’ — prompting a shift in conservation strategies.

rows.title: This luxury ‘cat poo’ coffee has a unique flavour: what’s behind it?
rows.summary: Civets enrich coffee beans they eat and excrete with two fatty acids often used in dairy products, study finds.

rows.title: Honey, I ate the kids: how hunger and hormones make mice aggressive
rows.summary: Researchers unpick the neural mechanisms of how hunger and hormones lead to aggressive behaviours in mice — plus, what gen-AI could mean for universities and students’ education.

rows.title: We need more than good science to fight infectious disease
rows.summary: Vaccine research will fall behind if funding and public support continue to wane.

rows.title: Author Correction: Structures of α-synuclein filaments from multiple system atrophy
Four game-changing immunology tools to watch
rows.summary: Researchers are getting an unprecedented look at the human immune system through emerging techniques.

rows.title: Copper-free chips generate robust ‘combs’ of multicoloured light
rows.summary: A stable ‘frequency comb’ of photons with discrete colours has been generated on a microscale chip by removing copper contaminants from the circuit.

rows.title: Pancreatic cancer relies on opposing signalling pathways to drive its cellular diversity
rows.summary: Communication between epithelial and mesenchymal cells in pancreatic cancer leads to a poor prognosis. The molecular basis for this signalling has now been revealed.

rows.title: Google claims ‘quantum advantage’ again — but researchers are sceptical
rows.summary: The firm says it has solved a problem on a quantum processor faster than a classical computer, and is optimistic about future scientific applications.

rows.title: People with some cancers live longer after a COVID vaccine
rows.summary: mRNA vaccines seem to boost the effectiveness of an immune therapy for skin and lung cancer ― in an unexpected way.

rows.title: Google AI aims to make best-in-class scientific software even better
rows.summary: An artificial-intelligence-guided software-evolution system tweaks tools to boost performance.

rows.title: Tumours might be sensitized to immune therapy by COVID mRNA vaccines
rows.summary: Commercially available mRNA vaccines against COVID have been shown to train patients’ immune systems to kill cancer cells. Combining these vaccines with standard-of-care immune therapy overwhelms tumour defences and is associated with improved survival, both in animal models and in large cohorts of people with cancer.

rows.title: What makes PhD students happy? Good supervision
rows.summary: Supervisors who invest in positive mentoring relationships with their PhD candidates also reap the benefits for their own research.

rows.title: A guide to the Nature Index
rows.summary: A description of the terminology and methodology used in this supplement, and a guide to the functionality that is available free online at natureindex.com.

rows.title: Sex differences in depression revealed by large genetics study
rows.summary: A comprehensive genome analysis suggests that women have more genetic risk variants for major depressive disorder than do men, with stronger links to metabolic traits.

rows.title: Evolutionary history of stony corals suggests that some could be resilient to climate change
rows.summary: Climate change is threatening coral reefs worldwide. A comprehensive tree-like representation of evolutionary relationships between stony coral species captures the group’s spectrum of traits. It shows that shallow-water species that have mutually beneficial relationships with microalgae have been more vulnerable and less resilient than their deep-water counterparts across past adverse environmental events.

rows.title: Uncertain climate effects of anthropogenic reactive nitrogen
AI discovers learning algorithm that outperforms those designed by humans
rows.summary: An artificial-intelligence algorithm that discovers its own way to learn achieves state-of-the-art performance, including on some tasks it had never encountered before.

rows.title: Measles, polio, tuberculosis: what’s causing spikes in infectious diseases?
rows.summary: The huge power of vaccines is being diluted by hesitancy, funding cuts and conflict.

rows.title: How to spot fake scientists and stop them from publishing papers
rows.summary: Journals are considering doing identity checks to expose fake authors — but there are downsides.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Stinkbugs nurture fungi in a newly discovered organ
rows.summary: Female stinkbugs rub fungal symbionts onto their eggs to shield them from parasitic wasps. Plus, how to stop fake scientists from publishing real papers and perspectives on animal-testing alternatives.

rows.title: Here there be
rows.summary: A fair fight?

rows.title: Is there a ‘smoking gun’ test for quantum gravity?
rows.summary: Quantum-entanglement experiments have been proposed as a way to test whether gravity is quantum, but getting definitive proof might be harder than previously thought.

rows.title: The search for mutations that sperm acquire as men age
rows.summary: Age-related mutations give sperm-forming stem cells a selective advantage during sperm production, shaping disease risk and genetic variation in offspring.

rows.title: Gene implicated in the heart defects associated with Down’s syndrome
rows.summary: A search for the genes responsible for the high incidence of heart defects in children with Down’s syndrome casts a light on potentially affected developmental processes.

rows.title: Reply to: Uncertain climate effects of anthropogenic reactive nitrogen
Surprise meteorite debris uncovered on Moon’s far side
rows.summary: The rare samples, collected by China’s Chang’e-6 mission, might help to uncover secrets of how the Solar System evolved.

rows.title: Classical theories of gravity produce entanglement
rows.summary: By applying the full framework of quantum field theory, it is shown that local classical theories of gravity can transmit quantum information and, thus, generate entanglement through physical, local processes.

rows.title: Optimization by decoded quantum interferometry
rows.summary: Decoded quantum interferometry is a quantum algorithm that uses the quantum Fourier transform to reduce optimization problems to decoding problems.

rows.title: Enteropathogenic bacteria evade ROCK-driven epithelial cell extrusion
rows.summary: The bacterial ubiquitin ligase NleL evades host defence mechanisms both by inhibiting pyroptosis and by preventing infected intestinal epithelial cells from being extruded into the lumen and expelled in the faeces.

rows.title: Deterministic soliton microcombs in Cu-free photonic integrated circuits
rows.summary: Copper-impurity-free Si 3 N 4 photonic integrated circuits reduce thermal absorption and enable robust, deterministic soliton generation.

rows.title: A metallic p -wave magnet with commensurate spin helix
rows.summary: A metallic p -wave magnet with commensurate spin helix and anisotropic electronic properties is experimentally realized and shows a giant anomalous Hall effect when distorted by a tiny spontaneous magnetization.

rows.title: Oxidative potential of atmospheric particles in Europe and exposure scenarios
rows.summary: Extensive oxidative potential measurements from across Europe analysed with the two most common assays, dithiothreitol and ascorbic acid, using a standardized protocol show the strong influence of site type and suggest pathways for mitigation strategies.

rows.title: Myocardial reprogramming by HMGN1 underlies heart defects in trisomy 21
rows.summary: Studies using human pluripotent stem cells and a mouse model of Down syndrome identify HMGN1 as a key contributor to congenital heart defects in individuals with Down syndrome.

rows.title: A circular economy approach for the global lithium-ion battery supply chain
rows.summary: A circular economy approach applied to the global lithium-ion battery supply chain shows that combining cross-regional cooperation on technology and trade with regionally tailored domestic circular economy policies yields the highest global emission reduction.

rows.title: Transcriptional interferences ensure one olfactory receptor per ant neuron
rows.summary: Ants evolved a transcriptional-interference-based mechanism to express a single odorant receptor from an array of Or genes with functionally similar promoters.

rows.title: Designing allosteric modulators to change GPCR G protein subtype selectivity
rows.summary: Studies of the G-protein-coupled receptor NTSR1 show that the G protein selectivity of this receptor can be modified by small molecules, enabling the design of drugs that work by switching receptor subtype preference.

rows.title: SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines sensitize tumours to immune checkpoint blockade
rows.summary: mRNA vaccines targeting SARS-CoV-2 also sensitize tumours to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

rows.title: A global coral phylogeny reveals resilience and vulnerability through deep time
rows.summary: The most recent common ancestor of the stony coral Scleractinia dates to about 460 million years ago and was probably a solitary, heterotrophic and free-living organism.

rows.title: Joint neutrino oscillation analysis from the T2K and NOvA experiments
rows.summary: The joint analysis of datasets from NOvA and T2K, the two currently operating long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments, provides new constraints related to neutrino masses and fundamental symmetries.

rows.title: Discovering state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms
rows.summary: An autonomous method discovers reinforcement learning rules from the cumulative experiences of a population of agents across a large number of complex environments, and the discovered rule achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging benchmarks.

rows.title: Mapping Plasmodium transitions and interactions in the Anopheles female
rows.summary: Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of Plasmodium falciparum and Anopheles gambiae reveal key developmental stages, processes and factors in parasite–mosquito interactions and identify potential targets for blocking malaria transmission.

rows.title: Cryogenic X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy for battery interfaces
rows.summary: Cryogenic X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, combined with immediate plunge freezing, can be used to probe the pristine solid electrolyte interphase in lithium metal batteries.

rows.title: Bottom-up design of Ca 2+ channels from defined selectivity filter geometry
rows.summary: De novo design of Ca 2+ channels with ion selectivity that can assemble appropriately and mediate Ca 2+ conductance when expressed in cells is described.

rows.title: Observation of constructive interference at the edge of quantum ergodicity
rows.summary: Experimental measurements of high-order out-of-time-order correlators on a superconducting quantum processor show that these correlators remain highly sensitive to the quantum many-body dynamics in quantum computers at long timescales.

rows.title: Non-van der Waals superlattices of carbides and carbonitrides
rows.summary: A method to make a big family of non-van der Waals superlattices of carbides and carbonitrides based on the delamination and rolling-up of multilayer MXenes is presented.

rows.title: Integration of hunger and hormonal state gates infant-directed aggression
rows.summary: Combined behavioural, circuit-level and cellular approaches are used to demonstrate how hypothalamic neurons integrate hunger and oestrous state to drive a switch in how female mice interact with pups.

rows.title: Video‐rate tunable colour electronic paper with human resolution
rows.summary: Researchers have developed retina electronic paper with electrically tunable metapixels comprising WO 3 nanodisks, achieving >25,000 pixels per inch, full-colour video and high contrast, enabling low-power immersive displays for virtual reality applications.

rows.title: Neuroendocrine control of calcium mobilization in the fruit fly
rows.summary: The peptide hormone Capa is responsible for regulating extracellular fluid Ca 2+ levels in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster.

rows.title: Hopes of realizing a dream ‘city of health’
rows.summary: Musings on manifesting a world of sanitary homes and hospitals, and thoughts on an essay that defines rhythm, in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

rows.title: ‘Gland-in-a-dish’ secretes stress hormone like the real thing
rows.summary: Lab-grown structure mimics the adrenal cortex, which produces the critical hormone called cortisol.

rows.title: Brazil must beef up its COP30 scheme to preserve tropical forests
Take the time to ensure that AI is safe
The race for deep-sea minerals could cause geopolitical and ecological harm
Genetics can give evolving societies a leg up
Stinkbug ‘ear’ actually hosts parasite-fighting fungi
rows.summary: Fungal armour keeps stinkbug eggs safe from hungry young wasps.

rows.title: Universities are embracing AI: will students get smarter or stop thinking?
rows.summary: Millions of students arriving at campuses are now using artificial intelligence. Worries abound.

rows.title: The TrumpRx website won’t slash drug prices — but this will
rows.summary: Tighter price regulation would deliver fewer new drugs but improve global health.

rows.title: Daily briefing: People with macular degeneration can read again after retinal implant
rows.summary: A wireless implant paired with camera-glasses has improved the vision of people with age-related blindness. Plus, breastfeeding boosts immune cells that protect against breast cancer and how AI tools are changing universities.

rows.title: US PhD admissions shrink as fears over Trump’s cuts take hold
rows.summary: Some doctoral programmes are admitting no students at all amid uncertainty about federal science funding.

rows.title: Cake to the rescue: how these PhD students are cooking up a sense of community
rows.summary: One treat at a time, these graduate students are helping to raise funds for charitable organizations.

rows.title: Cold plunge: how I gained hands-on experience in marine biology
rows.summary: Matthew Kim learnt how to conduct research while studying in a small Canadian town for a semester.

rows.title: What’s the cap on human energy expenditure? Elite athletes reveal ‘metabolic ceiling’
rows.summary: When athletes devote large amounts of energy to running or cycling, they unconsciously cut back on energy output elsewhere.

rows.title: John Gurdon obituary: Biologist who made cloning possible
rows.summary: He showed that specialized cells retain the genes to form an organism.

rows.title: People with blindness can read again after retinal implant
rows.summary: An electronic eye implant has restored vision in people with blindness caused by age-related macular degeneration.

rows.title: Why simply ending animal testing isn’t the answer in biomedical research
rows.summary: Animal models provide insights that alternative approaches can’t. A heated debate about which method is better is distracting researchers from doing good science.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Time to retire the Turing test?
rows.summary: Some researchers want an upgraded version of Alan Turing’s AI thought experiment; others want it scrapped entirely. Plus, why the rate of peanut allergies might have dropped in the United States and a blood test for Alzheimer’s disease.

rows.title: Disconnecting part of the brain sends it into a deep sleep
rows.summary: Study on the effects of surgical epilepsy treatment adds to researchers’ understanding of unconsciousness.

rows.title: Why we still don’t understand the Universe — even after a century of dispute
rows.summary: Despite huge breakthroughs, astronomers still can’t agree on what the cosmos is made of, much less how it came to be. A fresh account delves into the reasons.

rows.title: Breastfeeding boosts immune cells that protect against breast cancer
rows.summary: The protective, long-lived T cells can persist for decades after a woman gives birth.

rows.title: AI language models killed the Turing test: do we even need a replacement?
rows.summary: Chatbots now ace the mathematician’s famous imitation game, but imitation never equalled intelligence.

rows.title: Are these the happiest PhD students in the world?
rows.summary: Brazil, Australia and Italy have the highest satisfaction scores in Nature ’s global 2025 PhD survey — but are these nations really the best places to do a doctorate?

rows.title: Alternatives to animal testing are the future — it’s time that journals, funders and scientists embrace them
rows.summary: Biomedical research techniques that don’t involve the use of animals are gaining momentum, but those using innovative approaches still face resistance from some quarters.

rows.title: How scientists are pushing back against Trump’s funding ‘deal’ for universities
rows.summary: Seven institutions have so far rejected the administration’s list of demands over academic freedom and other concerns.

rows.title: Parity and lactation induce T-cell-mediated breast cancer protection
rows.summary: Parity induces an accumulation of CD8 + T cells, including cells with a tissue-resident-memory-like phenotype within human normal breast tissue, offering long-term protection against triple-negative breast cancer.

rows.title: Selective methylene oxidation in α,β-unsaturated carbonyl natural products
rows.summary: A modified Mn–PDP/HFIP catalyst that selectively oxidizes methylene C–H bonds in α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compounds is introduced; removing carboxylic acid additives and introducing HFIP suppresses undesired epoxidation with Mn-PDP, probably by promoting a more charged, chemoselective oxidation pathway.

rows.title: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy in mismatch-repair-proficient colon cancers
rows.summary: The results from the phase II NICHE trial on immunotherapy in mismatch-proficient colon cancer are presented.

rows.title: Would ChatGPT hire you? Your age and gender matter
rows.summary: Online stereotypes about younger women and older men could impact real-world hiring decisions.

rows.title: Author Correction: A room temperature rechargeable all-solid-state hydride ion battery
Blood tests are now approved for Alzheimer’s: how accurate are they?
rows.summary: A second blood test has been been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to assist in diagnosing Alzheimer’s disease. Will these tests change how cognitive decline is measured?

rows.title: Warning signs
rows.summary: Temptation waits.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Gene that causes obesity also shields against heart disease
rows.summary: Rare forms of the MC4R gene could explain why some people with obesity maintain good heart health. Plus, grant success is getting tougher in Europe and the solution to an iconic CIA cryptographic puzzle.

rows.title: Is academic research becoming too competitive? Nature examines the data
rows.summary: Applications for European research grants increased in 2025. Scientists say they’re feeling the competition.

rows.title: Time-resolved fluorescent proteins expand the microscopy palette
rows.summary: An innovative strategy has produced light-emitting proteins that can be differentiated both by colour and by how long the molecules remain in an excited state.

rows.title: Daily briefing: How the brain locks in long-term memories
rows.summary: Astrocyte ‘support’ cells help engrave emotional memories on the brain in mice. Plus, what’s causing mysterious dots in images of the early universe and how making poison helped toads conquer the world.

rows.title: This gene causes obesity — and shields against heart disease
rows.summary: People with certain forms of the MC4R gene have lower cholesterol levels than do other individuals with a high body-mass index.

rows.title: Parenting, illnesses and medical commitments: the private details grant reviewers shouldn’t need to know
rows.summary: Is it fair for grant reviewers — who are often our colleagues — to judge the legitimacy of career breaks due to personal circumstances?

rows.title: The problem with career planning in science
rows.summary: Having too rigid a plan could result in exciting opportunities passing you by, warns Ottoline Leyser.

rows.title: Global health is in crisis — who will step in to fix it?
rows.summary: The United States and Europe have cut billions of dollars in health aid. Can anyone fill the gap?

rows.title: Wastewater treatment produces surprising amounts of greenhouse gases
rows.summary: Emissions from the process could balloon unless efforts are made to mitigate them.

rows.title: New bird flu vaccine could tackle multiple variants with one shot
rows.summary: Evolutionary map of viral proteins used to design vaccine that provides broad immunity — plus, reviewing 25 years of carbon offsetting.

rows.title: How emotional memories are engraved on the brain, with surprising helper cells
rows.summary: Astrocytes have a more active role in stabilizing memories than once thought.

rows.title: Extreme confinement unleashes water’s hidden electrical capabilities
rows.summary: Water has extraordinary electrical properties when trapped in tiny channels — a finding that calls for a re-think about key processes in biology, climate and nanotechnology.

rows.title: Using heat to power up molecular systems
rows.summary: Synthetic DNA circuits and neural networks have previously been developed to process molecular information while consuming energy stored in kinetic traps. Now they have been re-engineered to take in energy from heat when the temperature increases, and to recharge themselves by restoring kinetic traps for subsequent computation.

rows.title: Mysterious cosmic ‘dots’ are baffling astronomers. What are they?
rows.summary: A consensus is emerging that the dots, sometimes called rubies, are an entirely new type of object in the Universe.

rows.title: The year of the Ghost Ant
rows.summary: A brief encounter.

rows.title: Photocatalytic oxygen-atom transmutation of oxetanes
rows.summary: A general photocatalytic strategy is described to convert oxetanes into other useful molecules by selectively substituting the oxygen atom with a nitrogen-, sulfur- or carbon-based moiety, simplifying the synthesis of pharmaceuticals and complex drug analogues.

rows.title: The quest to make babies with lab-grown eggs and sperm
rows.summary: Sex cells made from scratch could revolutionize human reproduction. But researchers are struggling to translate promising results in mice into benefits for humans.

rows.title: First known fossil hand of the hominin Paranthropus boisei
rows.summary: Hand bones from a human relative, found in Kenya, reveal features similar to those of living gorillas, complicating the evolutionary history of hand and tool manipulation.

rows.title: Yeast genomes show how large genomic variations affect trait diversity
rows.summary: Almost-complete genomes of more than 1,000 strains of the single-celled yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae have been assembled and integrated with phenotypic (trait) measures of growth and of RNA and protein expression. The analysis shows how large genomic variations called structural variants disproportionately shape traits.

rows.title: Scientists lose jobs and grants as US government shutdown takes a toll
rows.summary: Hundreds of people at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have received lay-off notices, and work at many federal laboratories has been suspended.

rows.title: UNESCO stands at a crossroads — researchers must back its new leader
rows.summary: Khaled El-Enany, the agency’s first director-general from an Arab state, will lead the UN’s education, science and cultural organization through one of its most severe tests.

rows.title: Ion stencils used for synthesis of patchy nanoparticles
rows.summary: Metal nanoparticles have been made with polymer patches accurately placed on their surfaces — enabling them to self-assemble into otherwise inaccessible 3D structures.

rows.title: How journals can break down barriers for Latin American scientists
rows.summary: The publishing ecosystem must do more to tackle inequities; quotas and partnerships with societies can help.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Making babies with lab-grown eggs and sperm
rows.summary: Sex cells made from scratch could revolutionize human reproduction. Plus, a conference in which all the authors and reviewers are AI systems and the impact of the government shutdown on US science.

rows.title: The astrocytic ensemble acts as a multiday trace to stabilize memory
rows.summary: Emotional experience evokes signalling in astrocytes, which form an ensemble that is reinforced by secondary astrocytic state changes resulting from repeated experience, leading to memory stabilization.

rows.title: Deaminative cross-coupling of amines by boryl radical β-scission
rows.summary: A strategy is described making use of in situ activation of radical boron chemistry to convert amines to handles for cross-coupling, enabling a range of useful chemistries to make and modify drug-like molecules.

rows.title: A vaccine central in A(H5) influenza antigenic space confers broad immunity
rows.summary: A high-resolution antigenic map of influenza A(H5) haemagglutinin (HA) enables the design of immunogenic and antigenically central vaccine HA antigens that elicit antibody responses broadly covering the A(H5) antigenic space.

rows.title: Isolation, engineering and ecology of temperate phages from the human gut
rows.summary: Human host-associated cellular products may act as induction agents for bacteriophages.

rows.title: Population-specific polygenic risk scores for people of Han Chinese ancestry
rows.summary: The Taiwan Precision Medicine Initiative recruited and genotyped more than half a million Taiwanese participants, almost all of Han Chinese ancestry, and performed comprehensive genomic analyses and developed polygenic risk score prediction models for numerous health conditions.

rows.title: The Taiwan Precision Medicine Initiative provides a cohort for large-scale studies
rows.summary: The Taiwan Precision Medicine Initiative (TPMI) has built a cohort of more than half a million individuals with Han Chinese ancestry, providing a rich resource of genetic and medical data for this group.

rows.title: In-plane dielectric constant and conductivity of confined water
rows.summary: Scanning dielectric microscopy of nanocapillaries filled with water reveals that interfacial and strongly confined water exhibits a large in-plane dielectric constant and an in-plane conductivity approaching superionic values.

rows.title: Modern sea-level rise breaks 4,000-year stability in southeastern China
rows.summary: Spatiotemporal hierarchical modelling of geological sea-level proxies and tide gauge data suggest that the modern global mean sea-level rise rate since 1900 has exceeded any century over at least the past four millennia, breaking the long-term stability observed in southeastern China.

rows.title: Patchy nanoparticles by atomic stencilling
rows.summary: An atomic stencilling method based on the co-adsorption of iodide and 2-naphthalenethiol on gold is described, yielding more than 20 different types of nanoparticle with masked and painted regions and patchy particle morphologies not reported previously.

rows.title: A conserved H3K14ub-driven H3K9me3 for chromatin compartmentalization
rows.summary: G2E3-catalysed H3K14 mono-ubiquitination is crucial for SUV39H compartmentalization and H3K9 trimethylation in pericentromeric heterochromatin, which is essential for proper euchromatin organization and transcriptional regulation in mammalian cells.

rows.title: Integrated lithium niobate photonics for sub-ångström snapshot spectroscopy
rows.summary: RAFAEL is a sub-ångström ultra-high-transmittance snapshot spectroscopic imaging sensor leveraging electro-optic reconfigurability in integrated lithium niobate photonics.

rows.title: Aboveground biomass in Australian tropical forests now a net carbon source
rows.summary: A transition from carbon sink to source for the aboveground woody biomass of moist tropical Australian forests has occurred, driven by increasingly extreme climate anomalies.

rows.title: A long-necked early dinosaur from a newly discovered Upper Triassic basin in the Andes
rows.summary: Discovery of a nearly complete skeleton of Huayracursor jaguensis , a Carnian dinosaur from the Northern Precordillera Basin in northwestern Argentina provides evidence of increased body size and early cervical elongation during the Late Triassic epoch.

rows.title: Niche-specific dermal macrophage loss promotes skin capillary ageing
rows.summary: Capillary-associated macrophages are selectively lost over time, contributing to impaired vascular repair and reduced tissue perfusion in older mice.

rows.title: New fossils reveal the hand of Paranthropus boisei
rows.summary: Analyses of newly discovered hand and foot bones of a Paranthropus boisei specimen provide insight into possible tool use and other palaeobiology characteristics among Plio-Pleistocene hominin species.

rows.title: From genotype to phenotype with 1,086 near telomere-to-telomere yeast genomes
rows.summary: A newly compiled atlas of species-wide structural variants and gene-based and graph pangenomes derived from highly complete assemblies of genomes from 1,086 natural isolates enable integrative genome-scale studies of Saccharomyces cerevisiae .

rows.title: Tin-based perovskite solar cells with a homogeneous buried interface
rows.summary: A molecular interfacial layer optimizes hole transport in tin-based perovskite solar cells, improving energy-level alignment and enhancing hole extraction efficiency.

rows.title: Hijacking a bacterial ABC transporter for genetic code expansion
rows.summary: Bacterial ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters can be utilized and engineered to transport non-canonical amino acids into Escherichia coli for highly efficient synthesis of proteins with novel functions.

rows.title: Spatial metabolic gradients in the liver and small intestine
rows.summary: Mapping of spatial metabolic gradients in the mouse liver and intestine identifies fructose-induced focal derangements in liver metabolism.

rows.title: Efficient quantum thermal simulation
rows.summary: An efficient quantum thermal simulation algorithm that exhibits detailed balance, respects locality, and serves as a self-contained model for thermalization in open quantum systems.

rows.title: The evolution of facultative symbiosis in stony corals
rows.summary: Genomic sequencing of the thermotolerant coral species Oculina patagonica , single-cell transcriptomic analyses of symbiotic and non-symbiotic specimens and comparisons with obligate symbiotic coral species reveal adaptations that provide resilience to coral bleaching.

rows.title: Gigantic black holes did not have starring role in early cosmic transition
rows.summary: Stars in young galaxies must have been responsible for stripping most intergalactic gas of its electrons.

rows.title: Red lines for religious AI
Brazil’s COP30 legacy should be to protect more of its forests
Do rats double-dip food with their tails?
rows.summary: Nature ’s pages feature evidence that rodents reach refreshment through wily means, and a review of a book that celebrates everything honey.

rows.title: Japan declares a flu epidemic — what this means for other nations
rows.summary: Researchers say that the number of infections for this time of year is unusual.

rows.title: AI’s therapeutic potential goes beyond emotional connection
Longer grant cycles would boost research in Africa
Daily briefing: Could microbe-friendly buildings help us be healthier?
rows.summary: Modern buildings might be denying us exposure to beneficial microbes. Plus, men’s brains shrink more as they age than women’s brains do and a flu epidemic in Japan.

rows.title: Faulty mitochondria cause deadly diseases: fixing them is about to get a lot easier
rows.summary: CRISPR-based tools can’t easily access the DNA in these organelles, but researchers are finding other ways in.

rows.title: The spectre of malnutrition is back and must be tackled — fast
rows.summary: Nobody should be going hungry in the twenty-first century. Scientists must determine the reasons why malnutrition is increasing so policymakers can act.

rows.title: The probiotic home: where microbes are welcome guests
rows.summary: Architects and microbiologists are exploring whether making buildings hospitable to friendly microorganisms can improve human health.

rows.title: The race to uncover snow’s many mysteries before it disappears forever
rows.summary: Historian brings icy climate warnings and warm personal memories.

rows.title: Inside our university’s mission to pivot to research
rows.summary: Innovation is key to meeting today’s global challenges. This is why the University of Botswana, originally a teaching institution, is now fostering research, and others should take the leap.

rows.title: Carbon credits are failing to help with climate change — here’s why
rows.summary: The idea that emissions can be offset through projects that claim to avoid releases or to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is fatally flawed.

rows.title: AI bots wrote and reviewed all papers at this conference
rows.summary: Event will assess how reviews by models compare with those written by humans.

rows.title: Defending Ohuira Bay, Mexico
rows.summary: Melina Maldonado Sandoval, a member of the Mayo-Yoreme Indigenous community, assists researchers in studying the risks of petrochemical manufacturing in the Sinaloa region.

rows.title: Andean peoples hunted and gathered long after they embraced farming
rows.summary: Remote-sensing data reveal hunting corrals that were used well into the eighteenth century.

rows.title: Birds’ intruder alert hints at how sounds took on new meanings
rows.summary: Diverse bird species recognize the same vocalization to rally neighbours against invading cuckoos. The finding plays into a broader debate about the emergence of language.

rows.title: Digital flocks, predators allow ecologists to simulate real-world animal behaviour
rows.summary: ‘Digital twins’ of real-world objects are moving from manufacturing to wildlife management.

rows.title: ‘Am I redundant?’: how AI changed my career in bioinformatics
rows.summary: A run-in with some artefact-laden AI-generated analyses convinced Lei Zhu that machine learning wasn’t making his role irrelevant, but more important than ever.

rows.title: Metals are key to the global economy — but three challenges threaten supply chains
rows.summary: The metals industry must confront metals’ scarcity, rising demand and climate impacts. Sustainable solutions exist that must be embraced.

rows.title: Economics Nobel prize won by researchers who showed how science boosts growth
rows.summary: Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt share economics prize for work that underlines the importance of investing in research and development.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Corals have been pushed beyond an irreversible tipping point, says report
rows.summary: ‘We have the knowledge’ to stop further tipping points, say the authors of a new climate report. Plus, how an international plastics treaty can be salvaged and the people standing up to save marine life in Mexico.

rows.title: What an academic misconduct accusation taught me about sharing research
rows.summary: Posting preliminary results on my group’s website allowed someone to plagiarize our work, but it also exonerated us.

rows.title: Men’s brains shrink faster than women’s: what that means for Alzheimer’s
rows.summary: Women’s brains age more slowly, but that doesn’t seem to protect them from a common form of dementia.

rows.title: Alchemy: discredited pseudoscience or chemistry’s worthy ancestor?
rows.summary: A spirited tour of alchemy shows how it bridged everything from chemical reactions, medicine and craft to philosophy, art and religion.

rows.title: Host cell Z-RNAs activate ZBP1 during virus infections
rows.summary: Cellular Z-RNAs generated during active virus infections are bona fide ZBP1 ligands, and position ZBP1-activated cell death as a host response to counter viral disruption of the cellular transcriptional machinery.

rows.title: Coral die-off marks Earth’s first climate ‘tipping point’, scientists say
rows.summary: A surge in global temperatures has caused widespread bleaching and death of warm-water corals around the world.

rows.title: Author Correction: Loss-of-function mutations in PLD4 lead to systemic lupus erythematosus
Current mosquitoes evolved more recently than previously thought
rows.summary: Genetic analysis reveals that most living genera of mosquitoes emerged around 73 million years ago.

rows.title: European bats capture migrating birds and eat them on the wing
rows.summary: Recordings of chewing sounds combined with altitude data bear evidence of a gruesome night-time feast.

rows.title: Portable muon beam could accelerate archaeology scans
rows.summary: Laser plasma device could be light enough to be used on the field.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Don't sideline Palestinian scientists after ceasefire, say experts
rows.summary: Efforts to rebuild Gaza must embrace Palestinian expertise, say researchers. Plus, what might help naked mole rats to live so long and a possible diagnostic blood test for a mysterious fatigue syndrome.

rows.title: Rebuilding Gaza: don’t sideline Palestinian scientists, say experts
rows.summary: Researchers warn against ‘top down’ solutions as ceasefire is agreed in the first phase of a peace deal.

rows.title: Future solitude
rows.summary: Alone but not lonely.

rows.title: Dangerous ‘nitazene’ opioids are on the rise: researchers are worried
rows.summary: This class of synthetic opioids is more potent than heroin and morphine.

rows.title: The world’s first plastics treaty is in crisis: can it be salvaged?
rows.summary: Hopes of securing a United Nations treaty on plastics pollution are fading after the final round of negotiations ended without an agreement.

rows.title: Should genetically modified wildlife be banned? Scientists weigh the risks
rows.summary: Conservationists debate the pros and cons of using synthetic-biology techniques to alter wild species.

rows.title: Naked mole rats live for decades — genetic tweaks reveal insights into ageing
rows.summary: Four subtle changes to an enzyme might explain the hairless rodents’ longevity.

rows.title: Mark Norell obituary: palaeontologist who showed that dinosaurs still walk among us — as birds
rows.summary: Through fieldwork and innovative research, he transformed how scientists and the public perceive the prehistoric world.

rows.title: More than 30% of this century’s science Nobel prizewinners immigrated: see their journeys
rows.summary: The most common destination for eventual Nobel laureates in physics, chemistry and medicine since 2000 is the United States, Nature has found.

rows.title: First proposed blood test for chronic fatigue syndrome: what scientists think
rows.summary: A blood test has achieved 96% accuracy in diagnosing the condition in a small study of individuals. What does the test detect, and is it a biomarker of the condition?

rows.title: This list of non-negotiables helped me to defeat PhD-student guilt
rows.summary: By refusing to bend the rules I set for myself, I created structure and a better environment for my mental health.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Chronic pain linked to small cluster of brain cells
rows.summary: A group of neurons in mice stay active long after an initial pain response. Plus, how AI agents might change research and the winners of this year’s ‘genius grants’.

rows.title: How to pause and restart your science career
rows.summary: Funding crises, bereavement and a supervisor’s relocation can derail your career path, but you can overcome them.

rows.title: How stereotypes shape AI – and what that means for the future of hiring
rows.summary: Images from across the web portray women as being younger than men, despite the underlying reality — plus, astronomers’ favourite exoplanets, and the 2025 Nobel prizes.

rows.title: Hippos still roamed Europe during the last ice age
rows.summary: DNA found in fossils from southwestern Germany suggests the populations survived in the region much longer than expected.

rows.title: AI models that lie, cheat and plot murder: how dangerous are LLMs really?
rows.summary: Tests of large language models reveal that they can behave in deceptive and potentially harmful ways. What does this mean for the future?

rows.title: Low-quality papers are flooding the cancer literature — can this AI tool help to catch them?
rows.summary: A large language model scans abstracts and titles for signs that an article was produced by a ‘paper mill’ company.

rows.title: Brain area linked to chronic pain discovered — offering hope for treatments
rows.summary: The newfound ensemble of neurons could lead to therapies to treat persistent pain, which affects roughly one in five people globally.

rows.title: The girl who used to be my sister
rows.summary: A voyage of self-discovery.

rows.title: Tracing the ancestry of barley in time and space
rows.summary: The genetic ancestry of domesticated barley has been mapped at high resolution, with each genome segment traced to its wild origins and the date estimated for when it entered the domesticated lineage. The findings reveal a mosaic of contributions from across western and central Asia, shaped by early cultivation and later gene flow.

rows.title: Chemistry Nobel for scientists who developed massively porous ‘super sponge’ materials
rows.summary: Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi pioneered the creation of metal–organic frameworks, which can capture and store molecules such as carbon dioxide.

rows.title: Ultra-sensitive DNA sequencing maps mutations that precede cancer
