rows.summary: Scientists have used low-error genome-sequencing methods in normal tissues from large cohorts of individuals to scan for mutations that set the stage for cancer.

rows.title: A quantum boost for ultra-precise clocks
rows.summary: The light frequency associated with changes in the energy state of atoms can be used to define the ticking of high-precision optical clocks. Experiments with ytterbium atoms have further enhanced the clocks’ precision by using a quantum amplification technique.

rows.title: Sacrificial metal speeds up synthesis of nano-alloys from multiple elements
rows.summary: An approach for making nanoscale high-entropy alloys using liquid metal provides much-needed control over the structure and composition of these remarkable materials.

rows.title: ‘Google for DNA’ brings order to biology’s big data
rows.summary: MetaGraph compresses vast data archives into a search engine for scientists, opening up new frontiers of biological discovery.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Chemistry Nobel for ‘super sponge’ MOFs
rows.summary: This year’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to the three chemists behind the world’s most porous solid materials. Plus, the risks of AI models that scheme and lie, and a warning from six former US surgeons general about the nation’s public health system.

rows.title: Drones switch payloads in mid-air using a flying toolbox
rows.summary: Close cooperation in flight between vertically stacked multirotor drones is widely regarded as dangerous, because there is persistent and intense ‘downwash’ interference. A ‘flying toolbox’ has been developed that achieves high-accuracy docking despite the downwash, enabling mid-air tool exchanges and unlocking diverse aerial manipulation tasks.

rows.title: Clues to why the weight-loss condition cachexia arises when cancer occurs
rows.summary: Analyses of RNA expression reveal molecules underpinning the cancer-associated process of skeletal-muscle wasting, a condition called cachexia.

rows.title: Distorted representations of age and gender are reflected in AI models
rows.summary: A big-data analysis shows that online content represents men as older than women in the same occupations and social roles, and that AI reproduces these warped presentations.

rows.title: A parabrachial hub for need-state control of enduring pain
rows.summary: Activity in a set of parabranchial neurons in the mouse brain is increased during chronic pain, predicts coping behaviour, and can be modulated by circuits activated by survival threats.

rows.title: Hotspots of human mutation point to clonal expansions in spermatogonia
rows.summary: A systematic statistical genetics approach discovers CES drivers as hotspots of human de novo mutation and shows that clonal expansions in germline may both modulate the prevalence of disorders and lead to false-positive disease associations.

rows.title: Enzyme specificity prediction using cross-attention graph neural networks
rows.summary: A cross-attention-empowered SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network architecture named EZSpecificity was developed for predicting enzyme substrate specificity.

rows.title: Age and gender distortion in online media and large language models
rows.summary: Stereotypes of age-related gender bias are socially distorted, as evidenced by the age gap in the representations of women and men across various media and algorithms, despite no systematic age differences in the workforce.

rows.title: A full-featured 2D flash chip enabled by system integration
rows.summary: A full-featured 2D NOR flash memory chip realized by an atomic device to chip technology combines a superior 2D electronic device as a memory core and a powerful CMOS platform to support complex instruction control.

rows.title: Somatic mutation and selection at population scale
rows.summary: A new version of nanorate DNA sequencing, with an error rate lower than five errors per billion base pairs and compatible with whole-exome and targeted capture, enables epidemiological-scale studies of somatic mutation and selection and the generation of high-resolution selection maps across coding and non-coding sites for many genes.

rows.title: Efficient and accurate search in petabase-scale sequence repositories
rows.summary: MetaGraph enables scalable indexing of large sets of DNA, RNA or protein sequences using annotated de Bruijn graphs.

rows.title: Sperm sequencing reveals extensive positive selection in the male germline
rows.summary: A combination of whole-genome NanoSeq with deep whole-exome and targeted NanoSeq is used to accurately characterize mutation rates and genes under positive selection in sperm cells.

rows.title: A ductile chromium–molybdenum alloy resistant to high-temperature oxidation
rows.summary: A single-phase chromium–molybdenum–silicon alloy is described that exhibits compression ductility at room temperature as well as resistance to oxidation, pesting, nitridation and scale spallation at temperatures up to at least 1,100 °C.

rows.title: Southward impact excavated magma ocean at the lunar South Pole–Aitken basin
rows.summary: Observations of the shape, topography, crustal thickness and surface composition of the South Pole–Aitken impact basin on the Moon suggest a southward impact trajectory and the excavation of a discontinuous remnant magma ocean from beneath the crust.

rows.title: Sex and smoking bias in the selection of somatic mutations in human bladder
rows.summary: Sex bias and association with smoking history identified in the landscape of driver mutations and clonal expansions in normal human bladder tissue may explain the higher bladder cancer risk in men and smokers.

rows.title: Quantum-amplified global-phase spectroscopy on an optical clock transition
rows.summary: The precision of determining the phase of an optical atomic clock is increased above the standard quantum limit in a new spectroscopic method.

rows.title: KCTD10 is a sensor for co-directional transcription–replication conflicts
rows.summary: KCTD10 interacts with the DNA replication machinery and the RNA polymerase complex, inducing ubiquitination and removal of the transcription machinery in the event of co-directional transcription–replication conflicts.

rows.title: Programmable on-chip nonlinear photonics
rows.summary: An optical slab waveguide with highly programmable nonlinear functionality is described, enabling the demonstration of versatile control over broadband second-harmonic generation across the spectral, spatial and spatio-spectral domains.

rows.title: Flexible perceptual encoding by discrete gamma events
rows.summary: Using a new analytical method for tracking gamma band events in mouse visual cortex, flexible encoding of visual information according to behavioural context is shown.

rows.title: Insect biodiversity monitoring must be expanded
Stop destructive fishing in marine protected areas
The 1975 discovery of long-lost letters between Albert Einstein and the astronomer Willem de Sitter
rows.summary: Lively scientific debates found in correspondence from 1916 to 1918, and Saint Patrick’s snake-banishment skills are called into question in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

rows.title: Microbe discovery holds promise for sustainable biotechnology
Incentives accelerate progress on open access in Spain
Groundbreaking quantum-tunnelling experiments win physics Nobel
rows.summary: John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis discovered quantum physics on a macroscopic scale, paving the way for quantum computing.

rows.title: The rise of ‘nightmare bacteria’: antimicrobial resistance in five charts
rows.summary: Data reveal how the global challenge to reduce deaths and infections from drug-resistant bacteria is not going according to plan.

rows.title: These immune cells won Nobel fame — can they solve autoimmune disease?
rows.summary: Regulatory T cells, which help to dampen inflammation, are being used in clinical trials against ailments such as rheumatoid arthritis.

rows.title: Customizable AI systems that anyone can adapt bring big opportunities — and even bigger risks
rows.summary: Open and adaptable artificial-intelligence models are crucial for scientific progress, but robust safeguards against their misuse are still nascent.

rows.title: The EU’s Horizon research fund needs to stay a defence-free zone
rows.summary: It is time to sound the alarm as the EU’s research priorities face an unprecedented degree of political interference.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Physics Nobel for quantum tunnelling on a macroscopic scale
rows.summary: Three researchers share this year’s Nobel Prize in Physics for demonstrating that quantum tunnelling could be observed in a special type of circuit. Plus, neurons can pass messages through tiny tubes and what a doughnut can tell us about the path to true prosperity.

rows.title: Stop treating code like an afterthought: record, share and value it
rows.summary: Scientists, research institutions, funders, libraries and publishers must all improve software practices.

rows.title: Prizes must recognize machine contributions to discovery
rows.summary: The future of science will be written by humans and machines together. Awards should reflect that reality.

rows.title: Connecting the dots: I trace the history of the East Kolkata Wetlands
rows.summary: Environmental-humanities researcher Jenia Mukherjee uncovers the complex relationship between people, canals and wetlands in Kolkata, India.

rows.title: 27 things we wish we’d known when we started our PhDs
rows.summary: Nature ’s survey of PhD candidates reveals hard-won wisdom on choosing supervisors, managing mental health and surviving academic culture.

rows.title: Jane Goodall obituary: pioneer primatologist who inspired generations of scientists
rows.summary: She was a tireless advocate for conservation, the welfare of captive chimpanzees and the protection of habitats.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Nobel Prize for discovery of ‘brake’ on immune system
rows.summary: Meet the winners of this year’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Plus, creative hobbies could slow brain ageing at the molecular level and a visit to a sewage-filtering wetland.

rows.title: The cutting-edge medical approaches that could transform ageing
rows.summary: An optimistic take on the state of the longevity field provides hope for treating a range of ageing-related diseases — but feels at odds with the current shape of US research.

rows.title: Will AI ever win its own Nobel? Some predict a prize-worthy science discovery soon
rows.summary: Other researchers question whether autonomous AI scientists are possible or even desirable.

rows.title: Wonder, empathy, life: why we called our pregnancy-diagnostic company Mirvie
rows.summary: Struggling to agree on a meaningful moniker for your start-up? This firm’s founders turned to their employees for inspiration.

rows.title: Medicine Nobel goes to scientists who revealed secrets of immune system ‘regulation’
rows.summary: Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi discovered cells that protect the body from autoimmune diseases.

rows.title: Volunteer scientists work ‘nights and weekends’ to guide vaccine advice in US
rows.summary: Medical specialists, wary of the guidance provided by Trump’s team, offer up their own advice independently of the government.

rows.title: From fossil fuels to ‘green capitalism’: the dilemmas of a just energy transition
rows.summary: Greening the global economy does not have to be done through unjust fuel extraction; societies can choose fairer paths to net-zero emissions.

rows.title: First human transplant of kidney modified to have ‘universal’ blood type
rows.summary: Recipient diagnosed with brain death received a type-O organ, which is compatible with all blood types.

‘Rogue’ planet is fastest-growing ever observed
rows.summary: Cha 1107-7626 is devouring matter during its solo drift across the Galaxy.

rows.title: Violin therapy: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: How AI agents will change research: a scientist’s guide
rows.summary: Researchers are increasingly turning to artificial-intelligence tools that can handle complex, multi-step processes.

rows.title: AI has designed thousands of potential antibiotics. Will any work?
rows.summary: Machine learning can speed up the discovery of potential antibiotics, but challenges remain.

rows.title: Creative hobbies could slow brain ageing at the molecular level
rows.summary: To keep the mind young, dance the tango.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The Nobel prizes’ most prestigious rivals
rows.summary: Several prizes are stepping up to challenge the Nobels’ place as the most coveted science award. Plus, the rise of AI-designed antibiotics and the first known wild hybrid of a blue jay and a green jay.

rows.title: Weaponizing uncertainty in science and in public health puts people in harm’s way
rows.summary: Those who cite scientific studies to support policies should take care to tell the whole story, especially when it’s complex.

rows.title: These science prizes want to rival the Nobels: how do they compare?
rows.summary: Being named as a Nobel laureate is the ultimate prize for many scientists, but how do other science prizes compare?

rows.title: The child of humanity becomes the mother of all
rows.summary: A new beginning.

rows.title: Marcus kinetics control singlet and triplet oxygen evolving from superoxide
rows.summary: The release of triplet or singlet oxygen is governed by individual Marcus normal and inverted region behaviour.

rows.title: Author Correction: EBI2 augments Tfh cell fate by promoting interaction with IL-2-quenching dendritic cells
Scooped by a cupcake business: why we called our green-cement company Sublime Systems
rows.summary: Chief executive and co-founder Leah Ellis browsed a rhyming dictionary before adapting a word that leapt out after discovering her first choice was already taken.

rows.title: These alien planets are astronomers’ favourites: here’s why
rows.summary: Space scientists look back on 30 years of exoplanet discoveries — from rows of massive ‘super-Earths‘ to worlds with perfectly synchronized orbits.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Multimodal cell maps as a foundation for structural and functional genomics
Jane Goodall’s legacy: three ways she changed science
rows.summary: The primatologist challenged what it meant to be a scientist.

rows.title: Biothreat hunters catch dangerous DNA before it gets made
rows.summary: Microsoft researchers found a biological zero-day vulnerability — and created a software patch.

rows.title: Exclusive: ex-CDC director talks about why she was fired
rows.summary: ‘I would never do that, as a scientist,‘ Susan Monarez says of being asked to approve changes to vaccine recommendations without knowing the details.

rows.title: Daily briefing: ‘A messenger of hope’ — Jane Goodall’s impact on science
rows.summary: How primatologist Jane Goodall changed what it means to be a scientist. Plus, a historic treaty to protect the world’s seas has been ratified and a parachute that’s intentionally full of holes.

rows.title: Memorable, distinctive, not too ‘sciencey’: why we named our biotech firm Anocca
rows.summary: Chief executive Reagan Jarvis describes the role a branding agency had in naming his technology company.

rows.title: Keep, lose, add: a checklist for plotting your next career move in science
rows.summary: Julie Gould learns of a career-planning framework that can help pinpoint what you love about your current role, and how that can influence future job moves.

rows.title: Model organism databases face budget cuts and closures
rows.summary: Beyond the crucial data they contain, these digital archives have provided an important space for academic communities to exchange ideas and resources.

rows.title: Research assessment: a round-up for early-career researchers
rows.summary: Confused by research evaluation and its potential impact on career progression? Here are some pointers as to how things work in different parts of the world.

rows.title: Ancient viral DNA helps human embryos develop
rows.summary: Infections particular to our genome might have helped drive human-specific traits — plus, using heat to power DNA computers.

rows.title: How research hospitals are meeting the world’s health challenges
rows.summary: Priorities for medical research depend on a country’s stage of development and the money available.

rows.title: These laser-cut discs turn into super precise parachutes
rows.summary: The kirigami-inspired design could be mass produced to deliver humanitarian aid.

rows.title: Author Correction: Prophylactic TNF blockade uncouples efficacy and toxicity in dual CTLA-4 and PD-1 immunotherapy
Trees of the Amazon are becoming even mightier
rows.summary: Forest giants are becoming bigger and more common than they once were.

rows.title: End GDP mania: how the world should really measure prosperity
rows.summary: The obsession with economic output as a measure of human development puts sustainability on the back burner. Researchers can now help to devise better indicators.

rows.title: Fixing the imbalance in cancer rates between Black and white women
rows.summary: In the United States, more Black women die of cancer than white women. This study aims to understand that disparity.

rows.title: Evolution of drug-resistant ovarian-cancer clones tracked in patients
rows.summary: After an initial treatment response, most ovarian cancers recur because of drug-resistant cell populations. Blood-based tracking, used to monitor clonal evolution in 18 patients, shows that drug-resistant clones are already present at diagnosis, expand during therapy and contain distinctive genomic alterations that have potential therapeutic relevance.

rows.title: Elaborate machinery for inserting proteins into the outer membrane of bacteria
rows.summary: Bacteria insert proteins into their outer membrane using a highly conserved apparatus known as the β-barrel assembly machinery (BAM). A large group of bacteria with particularly complex outer-membrane proteins is now shown to have a BAM apparatus with a highly unusual composition.

rows.title: A pathway that controls conversion of the amino acid cysteine into a cholesterol regulator
rows.summary: The amino acid cysteine is crucial for life but is toxic at high concentrations. Cells and tissues are exposed to high cysteine levels but maintain low intracellular concentrations through unknown mechanisms. A new technology platform has enabled the discovery of a protein that responds to cysteine fluctuations and regulates its breakdown.

rows.title: Mix-and-match fossils tell the tale of snake and lizard evolution
rows.summary: Little is known about the early history of lizards, snakes and their kin. New fossil discoveries reveal a complex evolutionary journey.

rows.title: Machine learning matches enzymes with molecular substrates
rows.summary: An approach that identifies, and predicts compatibility between, chemical and enzyme-sequence spaces can streamline and reduce risk in the discovery of enzymes that can catalyse a desired reaction. The strategy uses high-throughput experiments to generate data about enzyme-mediated reactions, and there is a tool that can predict compatible substrate–enzyme pairs.

rows.title: AI is dreaming up millions of new materials. Are they any good?
rows.summary: Critics slammed attempts by Google, Microsoft and Meta to speed up materials discovery. But behind the hype, there is progress.

rows.title: This US government shutdown is different: what it means for science
rows.summary: President Trump’s budget office lays out guidelines for mass lay-offs across the federal government.

rows.title: Features of autism can affect age of diagnosis — and so can genes
rows.summary: The age at which a person is diagnosed with autism can be partly explained by genetic factors.

rows.title: Quantum correlations enhance the sensitivity of room-temperature sensors
rows.summary: Quantum sensors based on diamond promise robustness but have limited sensitivity. Generating quantum correlations in the material might be a solution.

rows.title: Ancient viral DNA in the human genome shapes early development
rows.summary: Stem-cell models provide evidence that viral DNA sequences that entered the human genome in the past were repurposed to aid early stages of embryonic development.

rows.title: Uniting Africa’s longitudinal cohorts
rows.summary: The continent has many ongoing health studies across different countries, cultures and methodologies – this initiative aims to bring them together.

rows.title: The devourer of trust
rows.summary: How humans behave.

rows.title: A guide to the Nature Index
rows.summary: A description of the terminology and methodology used in this supplement, and a guide to the functionality that is available free online at natureindex.com.

rows.title: DNA circuits store data — with heat as their power source
rows.summary: DNA computers can use biological material to perform mathematical functions and store information, but their power sources have been fragile. Researchers now say they’ve developed a reliable source: heat.

rows.title: China’s research hospitals push for prominence
rows.summary: The country’s output in quality health research is going from strength to strength, but can it overcome questions about the integrity of its publishing practices?

rows.title: Six journal rejections and a major rethink: why I’m happy to admit to my research failures, and you should too
rows.summary: Outlining the trial-and-error processes that are involved in every research project could help others to become more efficient and paint a more honest picture of life as a researcher.

rows.title: Bacteria use a decoy defence molecule to set a trap for viruses
rows.summary: Some bacterial-infecting viruses use ‘sponges’ to mop up defence molecules, but bacteria can fight back by responding when a sponge captures decoy molecules.

rows.title: Parachutes inspired by the Japanese art of kirigami
rows.summary: Cutting a pattern into a flat disc can transform it into a parachute capable of carrying small payloads, which might be used to deliver humanitarian aid

rows.title: Early- and late-diagnosed autism are genetically distinct
rows.summary: Analyses of symptoms and genomic data indicate that autism that manifests in early childhood is distinct from autism that is diagnosed later in development.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Fireworks in space — the month’s best science images
rows.summary: Firework-like nebulae and tombs revealed by drought are among the month’s best science images. Plus, a call for virologists to unite around safety standards and accounts from the frontlines of clinical trials hobbled by US funding cuts.

rows.title: HELIOS: a microcosm of Asian health with global reach
rows.summary: Why Singapore is the perfect place for a long-term health study for Asian populations.

rows.title: Will your study change the world? This AI tool predicts the impact of your research
rows.summary: A tool called Funding the Frontier visualizes all the downstream impacts of funding — and predicts which studies will have the biggest societal impact.

rows.title: Hospitals have long been key for research, now their influence is broadening
rows.summary: Health-care systems beyond the West are providing solutions and data that can widen our medical understanding.

rows.title: Proteotoxic stress response drives T cell exhaustion and immune evasion
rows.summary: A proteotoxic stress response specific to exhausted T cells, governed by AKT signaling and accompanied by increased protein translation, represents a mechanistic vulnerability and a new therapeutic target to improve cancer immunotherapies.

rows.title: Kirigami-inspired parachutes with programmable reconfiguration
rows.summary: A thin planar disc designed with appropriately patterned cuts transforms itself, due to air flow effects, into an effective parachute exhibiting good positional stability, regardless of its initial orientation.

rows.title: Efferocytic remodelling of pancreatic islet macrophages by limited β-cell death
rows.summary: Enrichment for efferocytic macrophages in the islets of Langerhans promotes the accumulation of anergic-like CD4 + T cells and dampens autoimmune diabetes.

rows.title: Dietary cysteine enhances intestinal stemness via CD8 + T cell-derived IL-22
rows.summary: Dietary cysteine enhances intestinal stem cell-mediated intestinal repair following injury by promoting CD8 T cell-regenerative immune responses.

rows.title: A new paradigm for outer membrane protein biogenesis in the Bacteroidota
rows.summary: Structural and biochemical studies of the β-barrel-assembly machinery from Flavobacterium johnsoniae reveal a subunit composition and assembly that are distinct from those of the canonical Escherichia coli complex.

rows.title: Signal amplification in a solid-state sensor through asymmetric many-body echo
rows.summary: The experimental demonstration of many-body signal amplification in a solid-state, room-temperature quantum sensor is reported.

rows.title: Heat-rechargeable computation in DNA logic circuits and neural networks
rows.summary: Heat recharges enzyme-free DNA circuits, enabling complex logic operations and neural networks to perform multiple computations, offering a universal energy source for molecular machines and advancing autonomous behaviours in artificial chemical systems.

rows.title: Monoclonal antibodies protect against pandrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
rows.summary: Capsule-specific human monoclonal antibodies are protective against bloodstream infection by Klebsiella pneumoniae sequence type 147 in a mouse model of septicaemia, and could provide a useful strategy against pathogens with antimicrobial resistance.

rows.title: Polygenic and developmental profiles of autism differ by age at diagnosis
rows.summary: A study of several longitudinal birth cohorts and cross-sectional cohorts finds only moderate overlap in genetic variants between autism that is diagnosed earlier and that diagnosed later, so they may represent aetiologically different conditions.

rows.title: Tracking clonal evolution during treatment in ovarian cancer using cell-free DNA
rows.summary: A combined sequencing technique assesses 18 patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer over a multi-year period from diagnosis to recurrence and shows drug resistance typically arises from selective expansion of one or a few clones present at diagnosis.

rows.title: Connecting chemical and protein sequence space to predict biocatalytic reactions
rows.summary: A two-phase machine-learning-based tool making use of high-throughput experimentation is introduced to examine the connections between chemical and protein sequence space and predict productive biocatalytic reactions among substrate and enzyme pairs.

rows.title: Mosaic anatomy in an early fossil squamate
rows.summary: Breugnathair elgolensis gen. et sp. nov., an early squamate identified from a newly discovered Middle Jurassic skeleton on the Isle of Skye, provides new evidence on the origins of snakes.

rows.title: Doughnut of social and planetary boundaries monitors a world out of balance
rows.summary: A revised ‘Doughnut’ providing a visual assessment of trends in social deprivation and planetary degradation over the past two decades shows more than doubling of global GDP accompanied by accelerating ecological overshoot but only a modest reduction in human deprivation.

rows.title: A human-specific regulatory mechanism revealed in a pre-implantation model
rows.summary: Genetic manipulation of blastoids reveals the role of recently emerged transposable elements and genes in human development.

rows.title: The Panoptes system uses decoy cyclic nucleotides to defend against phage
rows.summary: The Panoptes antiphage system defends bacteria by detecting phage-encoded counter-defences that sequester cyclic nucleotide signals, triggering membrane disruption and highlighting a broader strategy of sensing immune evasion through second-messenger surveillance.

rows.title: A miniature CRISPR–Cas10 enzyme confers immunity by inhibitory signalling
rows.summary: Panoptes, an anti-phage defence system against virus-mediated immune suppression, is revealed.

rows.title: Long-distance remote epitaxy
rows.summary: Experimental evidence demonstrates long-distance remote epitaxial interactions of thin films even through thick amorphous carbon buffer layers and shows that these can be induced through dislocations in the substrate.

rows.title: Autoimmune response to C9orf72 protein in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
rows.summary: An analysis of T cell responses in people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis shows that the C9orf72 antigen is a key target of autoimmune responses in the disease, and identifies C9orf72 epitopes that are recognized.

rows.title: Spin squeezing in an ensemble of nitrogen–vacancy centres in diamond
rows.summary: An ensemble of spins from nitrogen–vacancy centres in diamonds is prepared in a spin-squeezed state.

rows.title: India and Pakistan share flood risks and must combine solutions
AI tools could reduce the appeal of predatory journals
Death of a star leaves a legacy for exoplanets
rows.summary: The elements formed from a star’s demise shape the structure of the planets that rise from the ashes.

rows.title: Early efforts to understand the processes underlying bird migration
rows.summary: Scientists try to explain bird behaviour, and a book delves into scientific paradoxes.

rows.title: Make cities more walkable, in the real world and in virtual reality
Saharan dust on the wind linked to hail in Europe
rows.summary: Satellites help scientists to document a correlation between dust travelling from Africa and hailstones falling in the Alps.

rows.title: Add a ‘speculation box’ to research papers
Daily briefing: Tiny charged bubbles of methane could explain will-o’-the-wisps
rows.summary: Spontaneous ‘microlightning’ between bubbles of gas could explain the ghostly flickering lights that can appear on marshlands. Plus, why the food system needs a revolution and how to set ourselves up for a great night’s sleep.

rows.title: Author Correction: Crystal structure of heliorhodopsin
Trust in the sea-bed mining authority is fragile — here’s how to change that
rows.summary: The authority created to safeguard the ocean floor now leans towards licensing its exploitation. Here’s how to reset the balance.

rows.title: Technology leaders should ‘pay back’ society to support the common good
rows.summary: Media technologies shape individuals’ sensitivity to the world around them. But are algorithms promoting what’s best for people?

rows.title: How to get the best night’s sleep: what the science says
rows.summary: Chuck the gadgets, the fads and the alarm. Circadian research reveals how important your body’s internal clock is to blissful slumber.

rows.title: AI uses medical records to accurately predict onset of disease 20 years into the future
rows.summary: An artificial-intelligence model trained on health-care records uses a person’s medical history to estimate whether and when any of more than 1,200 diseases might arise.

rows.title: See space fireworks and lightning spaghetti — September’s best science images
rows.summary: The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature ’s photo team.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Psilocybin’s lasting action requires pyramidal cell types and 5-HT2A receptors
Author Correction: Selenium-alloyed tellurium oxide for amorphous p-channel transistors
Little urchins, mischievous molluscs: my life as a sea champion
rows.summary: Despite being jetted by giant clams, Mei Lin Neo remains steadfast in her defence of marine species.

rows.title: How money, politics and technology are redefining the PhD experience in 2025
rows.summary: Nature ’s global survey of 3,785 doctoral students shows satisfaction has recovered from pandemic lows, but harassment and inadequate supervision remain widespread.

rows.title: NIH races to spend its 2025 grant money — but fewer projects win funding
rows.summary: Despite political obstacles, officials are on track to disburse all of the research funds allocated to US biomedical behemoth.

rows.title: Public trust in science has declined since COVID — virologists need to unite around safety standards
rows.summary: Creating international viral biosafety guidelines are key to clearing up confusion, regaining trust and ensuring that essential research continues.

rows.title: Want to do disruptive science? Include more rookie researchers
rows.summary: Papers from research teams with a substantial number of beginners are highly disruptive and innovative, study shows.

rows.title: Power and profit drive what we eat: here’s why the food system needs a revolution
rows.summary: Decades of corporate control have shaped diets, harmed farmers and strained the planet — transforming the system will take collective action.

rows.title: How to find the papers you need to read — and avoid the ones you don’t
rows.summary: With thousands of papers being published everyday, it can be a task working out which matter. Here are some tips to help you decide.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Rookie researchers boost disruptive science
rows.summary: Having a newbie in your lab might boost innovation. Plus, the global impact of China’s pledge to cut greenhouse-gas emissions and engineering education reimagined.

rows.title: Audio long read: Autism is on the rise — what’s really behind the increase?
rows.summary: Claims about what is responsible are ignoring answers from decades of research, scientists say.

rows.title: Common air pollutant has a secret weapon: bacterial toxins
rows.summary: Experiments show that the bacterial component of fine particulate matter has a highly potent inflammatory effect.

rows.title: Mitochondria expel tainted DNA — spurring age-related inflammation
rows.summary: Organelles spit out DNA contaminated with damaging components, leading to the activation of inflammatory enzymes, mouse experiments show.

rows.title: US autism research gets $50-million funding boost — amid row over Tylenol
rows.summary: An injection of funding into genetic and environmental factors underlying autism was eclipsed by Trump’s controversial claims about acetaminophen.

rows.title: China pledges to cut emissions by 2035: what does that mean for the climate?
rows.summary: The country’s plan to reduce greenhouse gases will largely determine the world’s emissions trajectory, researchers say.

rows.title: What happens if pregnant women stop taking Tylenol?
rows.summary: Untreated fevers during pregnancy can cause more harm than taking paracetamol will, scientists say.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Universities made the modern world — now they must survive it
rows.summary: A Nature special edition explores how universities can adapt to a changing world. Plus, Huntington’s disease has been treated for the first time using gene therapy and how AI could help to retain Holocaust survivors’ testimony.

rows.title: Big mother whales have more daughters than sons
rows.summary: Archival whaling data reveal a sex bias in the offspring of long female whales.

rows.title: Why is autism really on the rise? What the science says
rows.summary: As Trump blames Tylenol, Nature looks into the decades of research on the causes of autism.

rows.title: How passage through the Milky Way’s spiral arms altered our planet
rows.summary: The chemical make-up of crystals that formed from magma hint at an increase in the number of meteorites battering Earth’s surface.

rows.title: Gut microbiota keeps watch over future egg cells
rows.summary: Certain gut bacteria help to extend the reproductive lifespan of female mice, experiments show.

rows.title: Daily briefing: How to live to 117
rows.summary: The secret to living well past 100 years old seems to be a healthy lifestyle and a lucky set of genes. Plus, a machine-learning tool reveals the research that might have never happened had the US National Institutes of Health’s current grant-cutting rationale been applied in 2014.

rows.title: Mammoth challenge: why we called our de-extinction company Colossal Biosciences
rows.summary: Chief executive Ben Lamm says the name aims to capture biodiversity challenges and excite children about a flagship species.

rows.title: Swapping old immune cells in the brain with fresh ones could treat disease
rows.summary: Replacing immune cells called microglia holds promise for addressing brain conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease.

rows.title: When life gets in the way of your meticulously-planned career in science
rows.summary: Julie Gould asks two mid-career researchers to reflect on how closely their professional paths have followed their original goals and ambitions.

rows.title: US serial killer case opens door to using cutting-edge DNA data in courts
rows.summary: New York trial could set a legal precedent by admitting findings from whole-genome sequencing as evidence.

rows.title: Retractions can reshape scientists’ careers in unexpected ways
rows.summary: Institutions and publishers need to weigh context carefully and provide support when needed, says the author of a new study on the issue.

rows.title: Huntington’s disease treated for first time using gene therapy
rows.summary: Preliminary results from a small trial offer the clearest evidence yet that the brain disease’s progression can be slowed.

rows.title: Python, the movie! The programming language’s origin story comes to the silver screen
rows.summary: The creator of the NumPy and SciPy libraries reflects on their supporting role in the story of Python, now the subject of a documentary.

rows.title: How a dangerous tick-borne virus sneaks into the brain
rows.summary: Protein on the surface of brain cells appears to play a key role in disease progression — plus, a bot explores what might have happened to research if the Trump’s teams funding cuts had happened 10 years ago.

rows.title: Daily briefing: ‘Thinky think before grabby grab’ — lab tips for science success
rows.summary: Nature has compiled 99 lab hacks to make the life of a scientist easier. Plus, what Taylor Swift can tell us about how accents change and a deep dive into the medications at the centre of US President Donald Trump’s claims about autism.

rows.title: Engineered enzymes can suppress genome-editing errors
rows.summary: Genome editors are molecular machines that can rewrite the genetic code in cells, but sometimes they produce errors in the form of unintended sequence insertions or deletions, collectively known as indel errors. Genome editors have now been engineered that make up to 60-fold fewer indel errors than previous ones did.

rows.title: Trump’s $100K visa fee for foreign talent: how will it affect researchers?
rows.summary: The rollout of the H-1B visa change has sown confusion — and some fear it will be another ‘body blow’ for US science.

rows.title: Universities must move with the times: how six scholars tackle AI, mental health and more
rows.summary: Societies are evolving, and so must higher education. Researchers describe initiatives that can help to create stimulating and nurturing environments fit for today’s learning landscape.

rows.title: What research might be lost after the NIH’s cuts? Nature trained a bot to find out
rows.summary: We used machine-learning tools in an attempt to recreate the method for cutting funding, and then applied it to past US National Institutes of Health grants to reveal the broad-reaching consequences of such action.

rows.title: Robotic system takes chemistry into hyperspace
rows.summary: Exploring multidimensional ‘landscapes’ of chemical reactions provides rich insights into how they work, and might even enable the discovery of new forms of reactivity.

rows.title: Universities under fire must harness more of the financial value they create
rows.summary: Attacks on US academic institutions miss the point that they generate wealth for society. Tapping even some of that could keep innovation going.

rows.title: Climate change is reshaping fish communities in the United States
rows.summary: Rising temperatures and the introduction of non-native fishes have been linked to rapid changes in fish communities across the United States.

rows.title: Boosting immune cells to combat cancer using CRISPR engineering and large-scale in vivo testing
rows.summary: Immune cells can target cancer in the clinic. The ability to test a gene-editing technology in mice on a large scale should improve such immunotherapies.

rows.title: No lectures, exams, essays: inside a twenty-first-century university
rows.summary: Some innovative higher-education institutions are reimagining pedagogy by prioritizing local needs over research and international student recruitment. Anna McKie visits one of them.

rows.title: Arousal reframed as an organism‑wide dynamic system
rows.summary: The temporal evolution of a hidden, low-dimensional and organism-wide process, inferred from measuring the pupil of an eye, has been shown to account for complex spatio-temporal patterns of brain activity over timescales of seconds. This points to an underlying dynamic that continuously structures the unfolding of brain, body and behavioural variables.

rows.title: It’s not wokeness — it’s human rights
rows.summary: Maydianne Andrade focuses on action and support, not guilt, when helping people to recognize biases and identify ways to change unfair outcomes.

rows.title: The future of universities: a Nature special report
rows.summary: The world’s universities are under intense pressure. Nature examines the threats they face and asks how the sector can and must adapt to survive.

rows.title: Using short synthetic nucleic acids to probe genes in viruses that infect bacteria
rows.summary: Earth’s most diverse biological entities are the viruses that infect bacteria, called bacteriophages (phages). They are rich resources for discovering proteins and tools for biotechnology, but many phage–bacteria systems resist genetic manipulation. Silencing phage genes in a non-genetic way with short synthetic nucleic acids offers a solution.

rows.title: Exclusive: RFK Jr cancelled mRNA research — but the US military is still funding it
rows.summary: The Department of Defense is continuing to bankroll projects to develop vaccines against deadly pathogens.

rows.title: Universities are — and must continue to be — a force for good
rows.summary: From funding squeezes to political attacks, higher education is in trouble in many parts of the world. Fresh ideas will allow the sector to thrive and deliver value for society.

rows.title: A drug–diet combination could improve childhood cancer treatment
rows.summary: Mouse studies show that depriving neuroblastoma of certain amino acids causes a switch in protein synthesis to suppress tumour growth and promote cell differentiation.

rows.title: How a tick-borne virus enters human cells
rows.summary: Tick-borne encephalitis virus can infect the nervous system and cause life-threatening illness. Finding the cellular gateway it uses could transform prevention and treatment.

rows.title: She lived to 117: what her genes and lifestyle tell us about longevity
rows.summary: Maria Branyas Morera was the oldest person in the world when she died. Scientists analysed her genes, metabolism and more.

rows.title: Fighting climate change takes more than data — it needs wonder, love and hope
rows.summary: An informative and highly accessible book discusses climate change, its impacts and challenges to mitigating global warming through a compelling personal account.

rows.title: Electrostatic-based transfer keeps 2D materials ultra-clean
rows.summary: A technique that spontaneously detaches a 2D material from the substrate on which it was grown creates high-quality nanoscale electronic devices.

rows.title: The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing
rows.summary: More students than ever are studying across international borders, but where and what they learn is shifting.

rows.title: A common chromosome fusion in humans explained
rows.summary: A condition known as Robertsonian translocation occurs when the long arms of two chromosomes join together. The characterization of the fully sequenced and assembled fused chromosomes reveals a common fusion site and how these chromosomes are stably transmitted from cell to cell and passed on from parent to child.

rows.title: How universities came to be — and why they are in trouble now
rows.summary: What and who universities are for has changed considerably since the Second World War, leaving long-standing institutions ill-equipped to cope with current financial and political challenges.

rows.title: A press release from just before the singularity
rows.summary: Prepare for an update.

rows.title: Machine learning reveals potential consequences of cuts to US research
rows.summary: Governments have the right to decide how to spend money on science. Modelling shows that making instant cuts to grants without a plan or consultation is misconceived.

rows.title: Jazzy jaw joints: evolutionary fine-tuning reveals unexpected bone connections in ancient predecessors of mammals
rows.summary: The evolution of the jaw helped mammals to thrive. Fossil discoveries shed light on the diverse evolutionary journeys taken by joints between the skull and lower jaw.

rows.title: Tylenol is more than 130 years old — why is it still the gold-standard painkiller?
rows.summary: Acetaminophen is one of the safest drugs around, but scientists still don’t know how it reduces pain and fever.

rows.title: The geoeconomic turn in decarbonization
rows.summary: The rise of green industrial policy is transforming decarbonization efforts; the implications for policymaking and global spillovers are discussed, as well as research needs.

rows.title: Industry-compatible silicon spin-qubit unit cells exceeding 99% fidelity
rows.summary: Two-qubit operations exceeding 99% fidelity have been demonstrated by silicon devices made with standard semiconductor tooling in a 300-mm foundry environment.

rows.title: SPP1 is required for maintaining mesenchymal cell fate in pancreatic cancer
rows.summary: Mutual paracrine regulation of the cytokines GREM1 and SPP1 mediate mesenchymal and epithelial cell fate in pancreatic cancer.

rows.title: Convergent evolution of diverse jaw joints in mammaliamorphs
rows.summary: High-resolution computed tomography is used to reconstruct and analyse fossils of the herbivorous tritylodontid Polistodon and a newly named morganucodontid species called Camurocondylus , providing key insights into the evolution of the mammalian jaw joint.

rows.title: Ribonucleotide incorporation into mitochondrial DNA drives inflammation
rows.summary: Imbalanced nucleotide metabolism leads to age- and mtDNA-dependent inflammatory responses and senescence-associated secretory phenotype in senescence.

rows.title: Tailoring polymer electrolyte solvation for 600 Wh kg −1 lithium batteries
rows.summary: An in-built fluoropolyether-based quasi-solid-state polymer electrolyte enables high-capacity lithium-rich manganese-based layered oxide cathodes with stable interfaces, achieving 604 Wh kg −1 pouch-cell energy density.

rows.title: Diverging fish biodiversity trends in cold and warm rivers and streams
rows.summary: In the past three decades, fish abundance, richness and uniqueness have diverged across cold and warm streams, and the effects on native fish communities of stream warming and increases in introduced fishes have magnified each other.

rows.title: Volcanic crisis reveals coupled magma system at Santorini and Kolumbo
rows.summary: Seismological and geodetic data are used together with a machine learning earthquake catalogue to reconstruct magma migration before and during the 2025 volcano–tectonic crisis at Santorini volcano, indicating a coupling between Santorini and Kolumbo.

rows.title: Arousal as a universal embedding for spatiotemporal brain dynamics
rows.summary: Reframing of arousal as a latent dynamical system can reconstruct multidimensional measurements of large-scale spatiotemporal brain dynamics on the timescale of seconds in mice.

rows.title: Design of facilitated dissociation enables timing of cytokine signalling
rows.summary: A fresh approach to protein design that incorporates excited intermediate states enables precise control over the lifetime of protein interactions, with potential applications in cell-signalling modulation and in biosensors and synthetic circuits.

rows.title: Collective homeostasis of condensation-prone proteins via their mRNAs
rows.summary: The authors discover a homeostatic process termed interstasis, in which an increased concentration of proteins within RNA–protein condensates induces the sequestration of their own mRNAs.

rows.title: Robot-assisted mapping of chemical reaction hyperspaces and networks
rows.summary: A low-cost robotic platform using mainly optical detection to quantify yields of products and by-products allows the analysis of multidimensional chemical reaction hyperspaces and networks much faster than is possible by human chemists.

rows.title: Proximal cooperative aerial manipulation with vertically stacked drones
rows.summary: A cooperative aerial manipulation system, called FlyingToolbox, can work stably with sub-centimetre-level docking accuracy under vertical-stack flight conditions.

rows.title: Isothermal solidification for high-entropy alloy synthesis
rows.summary: Gallium is used as a sacrificial agent and mixing medium for the isothermal solidification synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanomaterials with diverse crystallinities and morphologies.

rows.title: Holliday junction–ZMM protein feedback enables meiotic crossover assurance
rows.summary: Holliday junctions maintain chromosome synapsis to enable crossover assurance in budding yeast.

rows.title: A tweezer array with 6,100 highly coherent atomic qubits
rows.summary: An array of optical tweezers trapping 6,100 neutral-atom qubits in 12,000 sites is experimentally realized, demonstrating performance exceeding present technologies and enabling the prospect of large-scale quantum computing and quantum error correction.

rows.title: Systematic discovery of CRISPR-boosted CAR T cell immunotherapies
rows.summary: CELLFIE, a CRISPR platform for optimizing cell-based immunotherapies, identifies gene knockouts that enhance CAR T cell efficacy using in vitro and in vivo screens.

rows.title: Reprogramming neuroblastoma by diet-enhanced polyamine depletion
rows.summary: Enhanced polyamine depletion in neuroblastoma models decreases translation of mRNA codons with adenosine in the third position, reprogramming the tumour proteome away from cell cycle progression and towards differentiation.

rows.title: LRP8 is a receptor for tick-borne encephalitis virus
rows.summary: LRP8, an apolipoprotein E and reelin receptor with high expression in the brain, is a receptor for tick-borne encephalitis virus.

rows.title: A haplotype-based evolutionary history of barley domestication
rows.summary: The evolutionary history of barley is analysed using ancient and modern DNA.

rows.title: The formation and propagation of human Robertsonian chromosomes
rows.summary: Analysis of human Robertsonian chromosomes originating from 13, 14 and 21 reveal that they result from breaks at the SST1 macrosatellite DNA array and recombination between homologous sequences surrounding SST1.

rows.title: Protecting double Holliday junctions ensures crossing over during meiosis
rows.summary: Conditional ablation experiments show that key components of the synaptonemal complex protect double Holliday junction recombination intermediates to ensure their resolution into crossover products, which are required for accurate chromosome segregation during meiosis.

rows.title: In vivo CRISPR screens identify modifiers of CAR T cell function in myeloma
rows.summary: In vivo loss-of-function CRISPR screens were performed to identify genes influencing CAR T cell persistence and function in human multiple myeloma, highlighting CDKN1B as a promising target.

rows.title: Electrostatic-repulsion-based transfer of van der Waals materials
rows.summary: An electrostatic-repulsion-enabled advanced transfer technique based on ammonia solution is introduced for separating van der Waals thin-film materials from their substrates, demonstrating suitability for its use in the complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) industry.

rows.title: The Biodiversity Cell Atlas: mapping the tree of life at cellular resolution
rows.summary: The Biodiversity Cell Atlas aims to create comprehensive single-cell molecular atlases across the eukaryotic tree of life, which will be phylogenetically informed, rely on high-quality genomes and use shared standards to facilitate comparisons across species.

rows.title: Low-overhead transversal fault tolerance for universal quantum computation
rows.summary: Logical operations can be performed fault-tolerantly with only a constant number of syndrome extraction rounds for a broad class of quantum error correction codes, including the surface code with magic state inputs and feedforward, to achieve ‘transversal algorithmic fault tolerance’.

rows.title: Fossil fight: how Raymond Dart countered some unfair criticism
rows.summary: A letter to the editor sets the record straight regarding the discovery of Australopithecus , and a proposal to put food on the school curriculum in this week’s pick from the Nature archive

rows.title: US investment in African food systems will have global benefits
Long-standing marine reserves need continued support
China’s private higher-education sector is at a turning point
Combat the human-made causes of Spain’s wildfires
‘Shake it off’: Taylor Swift’s changing voice shows how our accents evolve
rows.summary: An analysis of Swift’s interviews suggests her speech pattern has changed over her career.

rows.title: Ebola outbreak in the DRC: why is it so deadly?
rows.summary: ‘Spillover event’ in which an animal infected humans is likely to be the cause of 47 confirmed cases and 25 deaths.

rows.title: Daily briefing: No strong evidence backs up Trump’s claims about Tylenol and autism
rows.summary: US President Donald Trump’s claim that Tylenol (paracetamol) is linked to autism “is absolutely not grounded in the scientific findings”, say scientists. Plus, ‘Earth wind’ could be rusting the Moon.

rows.title: The meaning behind the moniker: how to choose a science-company name that delights
rows.summary: Should you have a brainstorming session, use a branding agency or go with gut feeling? In a new article series, Nature explores the art of corporate naming.

rows.title: Journals infiltrated with ‘copycat’ papers that can be written by AI
rows.summary: Tools such as ChatGPT can be used to generate almost-identical research papers that pass standard plagiarism checks. Hundreds are thought to have been published.

rows.title: Trump team backs an unproven drug for autism — but does it work?
rows.summary: Leucovorin would be available to only a minority of autistic people, and has not been tested for safety or effectiveness in a large trial. Some researchers are worried.

rows.title: How can universities train the skilled workers of tomorrow?
rows.summary: The high cost of running educational laboratories is hindering industrial progress. An innovative path forwards must be charted.

rows.title: Nerdy and easy to pronounce: why we chose Apheros as the name for our technology start-up firm
rows.summary: With a grant deadline looming, and inspired by the classics, Julia Carpenter, the company’s chief executive and co-founder, put pen to paper to capture ideas.

rows.title: The mini placentas and ovaries revealing the basics of women’s health
rows.summary: Lab-made organoids that mimic reproductive tissues could point to treatments for common conditions such as pre-eclampsia and endometriosis.

rows.title: A multimodal robotic platform for multi-element electrocatalyst discovery
rows.summary: A multimodal robotic platform is used to discover and optimize an electrocatalyst composition for formate oxidation.

rows.title: These 99 ‘lab hacks’ will make your scientific work easier
rows.summary: Nature asked contributors, editors and working researchers to share their best advice for scientists.

rows.title: Corpse flowers waft out stinky compounds as fast as landfills do
rows.summary: Gigantic plant’s stench is most powerful on the first night it blooms, all the better to draw carrion-loving pollinators.

rows.title: Is this really the world's largest mirror? Researchers put it to the test
rows.summary: Measurements show how flat this reflective lake in Bolivia really is, despite the wind blowing across it.

rows.title: I deeply scan timber to reduce wasting this precious resource
rows.summary: Johannes Huber builds an understanding of logs using medical-imaging technology, to improve future wood-harvesting methods.

rows.title: The Moon is rusting — thanks to ‘wind’ blown all the way from Earth
rows.summary: Lunar minerals generate the rust mineral haematite when bombarded with high-energy oxygen particles, experiments show.

rows.title: Gestational diabetes linked to autism in study: what scientists say
rows.summary: Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump says his administration has “found an answer to autism”.

rows.title: Author Correction: Mechanism of BRCA1–BARD1 function in DNA end resection and DNA protection
Trump links autism and Tylenol: is there any truth to it?
rows.summary: During an announcement on Monday, the US president repeatedly advised people, ‘Don’t take Tylenol’, but scientists say that strong evidence between the medication and autism is lacking.

rows.title: Real-time molecular recorders expose the inner lives of cells
rows.summary: Gene-editing tools transform cells into record-keepers, capturing hidden timelines of health and disease.

rows.title: Daily briefing: World’s first AI-designed viruses attack antibiotic-resistant bacteria
rows.summary: Scientists have used Evo1 and Evo2 to design novel genomes for viruses capable of killing E. coli . Plus, a federal research funding is trickling back into Harvard and what drove the rise of complex societies.

rows.title: What drove the rise of civilizations? A decades-long quest points to warfare
rows.summary: An ambitious analysis of a vast trove of data from 800 societies around the world concludes that there’s safety in numbers.

rows.title: Decoding the redox behaviour of copper in Ullmann-type coupling reactions
rows.summary: Here a Cu(I)/Cu(III)/Cu(II)/Cu(III)/Cu(I) redox sequence is revealed in copper-catalysed aryl iodide coupling, capturing intermediate species and redefining the mechanistic understanding of the reaction.

rows.title: Hotly anticipated US vaccine meeting ends with confusion — and a few decisions
rows.summary: Vaccine advisers chosen by US health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr vote to restrict one childhood vaccine, but delay their decision on another.

rows.title: Reviving the past and designing the future: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: Apocalypse then: how cataclysms shaped human societies
rows.summary: Science journalist Lizzie Wade joins us to talk about her new book investigating the seismic events that humans have faced through history.

rows.title: Harvard vs Trump: millions in grant money begin trickling back to scientists
rows.summary: A court ruling declared the Trump administration’s termination of the university’s research funding illegal.

rows.title: World’s first AI-designed viruses a step towards AI-generated life
rows.summary: Scientists used artificial intelligence to write coherent viral genomes, using them to synthesize bacteriophages capable of killing resistant strains of bacteria.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Functional synapses between neurons and small cell lung cancer
How a mentoring connection boosted my ambitions for a science career
rows.summary: How do you convince a teenager that a research career is within their grasp? Madeleine Cheung and her mentor, NASA scientist Charles Miller, explain.

rows.title: A Chinese AI tool can manage chronic disease — could it revolutionize health care?
rows.summary: Artificial intelligence could reduce the strain that ageing populations put on medical systems.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Device senses silent speech without an invasive brain implant
rows.summary: A wearable device senses electrical signals in the muscles used to formulate speech to detect internally articulated words. Plus, this year’s Ig Nobel prizewinners and what we can learn from octopuses.

rows.title: Atomic ‘conveyor belt’ boosts power of quantum computer
rows.summary: Array system could help to scale up technology that uses atoms to create qubits.

rows.title: Author Correction: Clonal dynamics and somatic evolution of haematopoiesis in mouse
Soft robot steers itself down the human airway
rows.summary: Device can place an emergency breathing tube in the trachea faster than medical personnel can, even those with extensive training.

rows.title: Author Correction: A Ctf4 trimer couples the CMG helicase to DNA polymerase α in the eukaryotic replisome
The ‘near-telepathic’ device that puts AI in your head
rows.summary: AlterEgo’s neural-interface device is non-invasive and is being tested in people with multiple sclerosis and motor neuron disease.

rows.title: Daily briefing: AI model can predict your risk of diseases years before you might get them
rows.summary: The first major LLM to undergo peer-review, the rise of ‘griefbots’ and a model that can make disease predictions from a person’s health records are among the latest in AI news. Plus, the World Health Organization has downgraded the international emergency status of mpox.

rows.title: Can AI chatbots trigger psychosis? What the science says
rows.summary: Chatbots can reinforce delusional beliefs, and, in rare cases, users have experienced psychotic episodes.

rows.title: Tipsy bats and perfect pasta: Ig Nobels celebrate ‘improbable’ research
rows.summary: The annual awards are a celebration of weird but thought-provoking science.

rows.title: Global warming amplifies wildfire health burden and reshapes inequality
rows.summary: Global warming will intensify wildfires, boosting emissions and increasing the number of premature deaths by about sixfold globally by 2100—shifting the health burden more evenly across regions, demanding stronger international policy responses..

rows.title: Wildfire smoke exposure and mortality burden in the USA under climate change
rows.summary: Smoke PM 2.5 could result in 71,420 excess deaths per year in the USA by 2050 under the SSP3-7.0 high-warming scenario.

rows.title: Two tools to help you achieve career success in science
rows.summary: Should you book a session with a careers advisor or go solo with an individual development plan? Here are the pros and cons of each approach.

rows.title: A plant-forward menu is linked to lower diabetes risk
rows.summary: Regimens that sideline animal products are associated with both environmental and health benefits, according to study of nearly 24,000 people.

rows.title: This AI tool predicts your risk of 1,000 diseases — by looking at your medical records
rows.summary: Trained on 400,000 medical records, the system can predict risks 20 years in advance — plus, how AIs could make you more likely to cheat.

rows.title: New Hope in Alzheimer’s Research
rows.summary: Breakthrough therapies, new diagnostics and preventive measures for fighting a devastating disease.

rows.title: Caribbean coral reefs are threatened by rising seas
rows.summary: Modelling suggests that most Caribbean coral reefs will erode by the year 2100 as sea-level rise outpaces reef growth and limits potential reef restoration.

rows.title: A surprising way to make heat in an unexpected part of fat cells
rows.summary: Organelles called peroxisomes have been found to have a role in heat generation in fat tissue, and use a mechanism independent of the known heat-producing protein UCP1. The process involves the synthesis and degradation of monomethyl branched-chain fatty acids, driven by the lipid-synthesizing enzyme FASN and the peroxisomal enzyme ACOX2.

rows.title: The parable of the doors
rows.summary: Weapon of choice.

rows.title: Controversial New Alzheimer’s Drugs Offer Hope—But at a High Cost
rows.summary: New Alzheimer’s drugs known as anti-amyloid therapies may slow disease progression—but they also carry serious risks, including brain bleeds and strokelike symptoms.

rows.title: A photonic chip enables ultrabroadband wireless communication
rows.summary: Future wireless networks should exploit the full range of telecommunications frequencies. A photonic chip that can reconfigure a broad range of frequencies enables dynamic, full-spectrum management of next-generation communications systems.

rows.title: Which diseases will you have in 20 years? This AI accurately predicts your risks
rows.summary: A modified large language model called Delphi-2M analyses a person’s medical records and lifestyle to provide risk estimates for more than 1,000 diseases.

rows.title: Bring us your LLMs: why peer review is good for AI models
rows.summary: Deepseek’s R1 model has been peer reviewed. Others should follow the firm’s example.

rows.title: My career switch from psychologist to open-science advocate
rows.summary: Kelly Cobey’s early career experiences sparked a campaigning zeal, now focused on predatory publishing and responsible research assessment.

rows.title: People are more likely to cheat when they delegate tasks to AI
rows.summary: Artificial intelligence is moving from being a mere tool to an active partner in decision-making, but when we offload misconduct to machines, who bears the blame?

rows.title: AI can learn to show its workings through trial and error
rows.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are more accurate when they output intermediate steps. A strategy called reinforcement can teach them to do this without being told.

rows.title: Secrets of DeepSeek AI model revealed in landmark paper
rows.summary: First peer-reviewed study shows how a Chinese start-up firm made the market-shaking LLM for US$300,000.

rows.title: Bespoke 3D printing adapted to features mapped using computer vision
rows.summary: Conventional 3D printers do not extract information from their environment. A ‘context-aware’ volumetric printer uses light-sheet imaging and visual processing to map objects or living cells embedded in printable materials. This enables rapid, automated fabrication of designs adapted to mapped elements, such as vasculature precisely reaching the bioprinted cells.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Can AI help us talk to animals?
rows.summary: Researchers are using AI tools to decipher the meanings of animal communications, with the hope of one day being able to talk with them. Plus, how a comb jelly orients itself and the climate scientists on a quest to digitize handwritten weather records.

rows.title: Can Diet and Exercise Really Prevent Alzheimer’s?
rows.summary: Early studies suggest that lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise and social engagement may help slow or prevent Alzheimer’s symptoms—but the evidence is inconsistent, and many doctors remain cautious.

rows.title: Pharmaceutical giants pull out of UK: why it matters for global science
rows.summary: Merck and AstraZeneca say the United Kingdom is not spending enough on medicines, but experts say it’s a symptom of underlying weaknesses in the global pharmaceutical sector.

rows.title: The Vexing Promise of New Blood Tests for Alzheimer’s
rows.summary: A new generation of Alzheimer’s blood tests could speed up diagnosis and access to care—but they also raise thorny questions about prediction, treatment and uncertainty.

rows.title: The Hidden Link between Racism and Alzheimer’s Risk
rows.summary: Black Americans face a significantly higher risk of Alzheimer’s and other dementias than white Americans. Researchers are working to find out why that is and how to intervene.

rows.title: Bioelectronic implants built from rolled-up stretchy circuits
rows.summary: Soft devices made by rolling up rubber-like sheets patterned with 2D electronics can monitor, stimulate and navigate deep tissue in animal models.

rows.title: Earth’s atmosphere took two billion years to become fully oxygenated
rows.summary: High-resolution isotope data show that a modern-like, oxygen-rich atmosphere was not established until 410 million years ago, supporting a 2-billion-year transitional oxygenation of Earth’s surface. The record also captures a dynamic co-evolution of atmospheric and oceanic reduction–oxidation states, with repeated oxygenation pulses and feedback cycles.

rows.title: Alzheimer’s Drugs Are Finally Tackling the Disease Itself. Here’s How
rows.summary: While our understanding of Alzheimer’s disease is far from complete, the latest therapies, and others in more than 100 clinical trials, offer new hope.

rows.title: Years of hits to the head prime the brain for decline
rows.summary: Repetitive head impacts trigger neuronal loss and disrupt blood vessels and immune cells long before the accumulation of neurotoxic tau protein.

rows.title: Can We Fix America’s Dementia Care Crisis before It’s Too Late?
rows.summary: More than 13.8 million Americans could have Alzheimer’s by 2060, and at the rate care facilities are closing, many of them will have nowhere to go. Regina Shih of the State Alzheimer’s Research Support Center (StARS) wants to help solve that problem.

rows.title: Three ways ex-CDC chief says that Trump team is sidelining science
rows.summary: Susan Monarez testifies at tense Senate hearing that scientific integrity is being quashed at US health agency.

rows.title: Will the public support basic science? A new non-profit aims to find out
rows.summary: The Science Foundation seeks donations to fund ten $10,000 ‘what if’ seed grants.

rows.title: Wired for growth: neuron–tumour signalling in the lung and brain increases growth of a hard-to-treat cancer
rows.summary: Signalling between neurons and tumour cells in the lung and brain promotes the growth of small-cell lung cancer. These interactions might be a therapeutic target.

rows.title: AI is helping to decode animals’ speech. Will it also let us talk with them?
rows.summary: The complexity of vocal communication in some primates, whales and birds might approach that of human language.

rows.title: Basal cell of origin resolves neuroendocrine–tuft lineage plasticity in cancer
rows.summary: Basal cells, rather than neuroendocrine cells, have been identified as the probable origin of small cell lung cancer and other neuroendocrine–tuft cancers, explaining neuroendocrine–tuft heterogeneity and offering new perspectives for targeting lineage plasticity.

rows.title: A neuronal architecture underlying autonomic dysreflexia
rows.summary: The neuronal architecture that develops after spinal cord injury and causes autonomic dysreflexia is uncovered.

rows.title: CRISPR activation for SCN2A -related neurodevelopmental disorders
rows.summary: Using SCN2A haploinsufficiency as a proof-of-concept, upregulation of the existing functional gene copy through CRISPR activation was able to rescue neurological-associated phenotypes in Scn2a haploinsufficient mice and human neurons.

rows.title: Analogue speech recognition based on physical computing
rows.summary: A temporal-signal processor based on two in-materia computing hardware platforms—reconfigurable nonlinear-processing units (RNPUs) and analogue in-memory computing (AIMC)—is used for both feature extraction and classification, advancing compactness, efficiency, and performance of heterogeneous smart edge devices.

rows.title: Repeated head trauma causes neuron loss and inflammation in young athletes
rows.summary: Repetitive head impacts from contact sports are associated with brain inflammation, vascular damage and neuron loss that are independent of hyperphosphorylated tau pathology.

rows.title: Engineered prime editors with minimal genomic errors
rows.summary: Engineered prime editor systems with reduced occurrences of unwanted insertions or deletions during genome editing are developed.

rows.title: Addressing the safety of next-generation batteries
rows.summary: Next-generation batteries will present different risks to conventional lithium-ion cells, emphasizing the need for efforts towards characterizing the abuse tolerance and hazards associated with next-generation battery materials over their life cycle and providing the data in the context of supporting affected professionals.

rows.title: Toughened self-assembled monolayers for durable perovskite solar cells
rows.summary: Cross-linkable co-SAMs improve hole-selective SAM stability, preventing defects and thermal degredation in perovskite solar cells, enabling 26.92% efficiency with high heat durability, and guiding the design of more efficient and durable solar cells.

rows.title: Transitions in dynamical regime and neural mode during perceptual decisions
rows.summary: Simultaneous recordings were made of hundreds of neurons in the rat frontal cortex and striatum, showing that decision commitment involves a rapid, coordinated transition in dynamical regime and neural mode.

rows.title: A movable long-term implantable soft microfibre for dynamic bioelectronics
rows.summary: A soft, stretchable and freely movable fibre sensor called NeuroWorm, inspired by earthworms and that can be magnetically steered through soft tissue, is described as a new platform for dynamic bioelectrical and biomechanical monitoring.

rows.title: Atomic-scale imaging of frequency-dependent phonon anisotropy
rows.summary: A new form of momentum-selective electron energy-loss spectroscopy enables the element-resolved imaging of frequency- and symmetry-dependent vibrational anisotropies with atomic resolution.

rows.title: Stratified wind from a super-Eddington X-ray binary is slower than expected
rows.summary: The XRISM Resolve spectrum of the galactic neutron star X-ray binary, GX 13+1, reveals one of the densest winds ever seen in absorption lines.

rows.title: Covariation MS uncovers a protein that controls cysteine catabolism
rows.summary: A mass spectrometry-based approach globally identifies protein regulators of metabolism and reveals the role of LRRC58 in controlling cysteine catabolism.

rows.title: Selective presynaptic inhibition of leg proprioception in behaving Drosophila
rows.summary: A study in Drosophila has identified a neural circuit that selectively suppress movement-encoding proprioceptors during self-generated movements such as walking and grooming.

rows.title: Myeloperoxidase transforms chromatin into neutrophil extracellular traps
rows.summary: Myeloperoxidase, a highly expressed neutrophil protein, disassembles nucleosomes, facilitating neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and binds stably to NETs extracellularly.

rows.title: A room temperature rechargeable all-solid-state hydride ion battery
rows.summary: A core-shell hydride 3CeH 3 @BaH 2 , which exhibits fast H − conduction at ambient temperature and becomes a superionic conductor above 60 °C, is used to construct an all-solid-state rechargeable H − battery.

rows.title: High-density soft bioelectronic fibres for multimodal sensing and stimulation
rows.summary: High-density multimodal soft bioelectronic fibres provide a platform for minimally invasive implantable electronics, where diverse sensing and stimulation functionalities can be effectively integrated.

rows.title: Reduced Atlantic reef growth past 2 °C warming amplifies sea-level impacts
rows.summary: An analysis of coral reefs in the tropical western Atlantic suggests that nearly all will be eroding by 2100 if global warming exceeds 2 °C, which will worsen the effects of sea-level rise.

rows.title: DeepSeek-R1 incentivizes reasoning in LLMs through reinforcement learning
rows.summary: A new artificial intelligence model, DeepSeek-R1, is introduced, demonstrating that the reasoning abilities of large language models can be incentivized through pure reinforcement learning, removing the need for human-annotated demonstrations.

rows.title: Structural basis for mTORC1 activation on the lysosomal membrane
rows.summary: Cryo-electron microscopy was used to study human mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) activation on lysosomal membranes, showing progressive recruitment by RAG–Ragulator, RHEB and RAPTOR, culminating in mTOR–membrane engagement and full enzyme activation.

rows.title: Delegation to artificial intelligence can increase dishonest behaviour
rows.summary: People cheat more when they delegate tasks to artificial intelligence, and large language models are more likely than humans to comply with unethical instructions—a risk that can be minimized by introducing prohibitive, task-specific guardrails.

rows.title: Learning the natural history of human disease with generative transformers
rows.summary: Delphi-2M forecasts a person’s future health, covering more than 1,000 diseases, provides insights into co-morbidity dynamics and generates synthetic data for the training of AI models that have never seen actual data.

rows.title: Co-option of an ancestral cloacal regulatory landscape during digit evolution
rows.summary: The regulatory landscape controlling Hoxd gene expression in tetrapod digit development was probably co-opted from a pre-existing cloacal regulatory mechanism, as evidenced by the effects of genetic deletion experiments in zebrafish fin, cloaca and mouse urogenital development.

rows.title: Peroxisomal metabolism of branched fatty acids regulates energy homeostasis
rows.summary: A UCP1-independent mechanism of thermogenesis involving ATP-consuming metabolism of monomethyl branched-chain fatty acids in peroxisomes is described and a previously unrecognized role for peroxisomes in adipose tissue thermogenesis is identified.

rows.title: A domed pachycephalosaur from the early Cretaceous of Mongolia
rows.summary: The pachycephalosaurian Zavacephale rinpoche , from the Early Cretaceous of Mongolia, provides crucial insights into the early evolution of dome-headed dinosaurs, including the development of the frontoparietal dome and decoupling of sociosexual and somatic maturity.

rows.title: Fertility declines are no cause for concern, history shows
Impoundment of funds endangers US investment in science and medical research
Gone with the wind: deciphering how dandelions drive seed dispersal
rows.summary: Analysis of seed attachment and the forces needed for detachment reveal how dandelion plants have evolved to spread in the same direction that the wind blows.

rows.title: A population plunge could help to mitigate the global biodiversity crisis
Mysterious mass deaths of an extinct giant deer
rows.summary: Fossil find reveals the demise of a group of enormous elks, and local birdsong dialects come under scrutiny in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

rows.title: Coordinate to combat Pakistan’s climate-driven disasters
Rare comet photobombs telescope’s view of the cosmos
rows.summary: The TESS exoplanet-hunting satellite accidentally captures images of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS.

rows.title: How did assaults on science become the norm — and what can we do?
