rows.summary: An insightful book explores attacks on science from a historical and a personal perspective.

rows.title: ‘Revolutionary’ AI tools rescue old weather data to improve climate models
rows.summary: Specialist machine-learning models are helping researchers to transcribe centuries-old handwritten records.

rows.title: How billions of hacked mosquitoes and a vaccine could beat the deadly dengue virus
rows.summary: Outbreaks of dengue are killing thousands of people in South America each year and getting worse. Brazil hopes to turn the tide with a home-grown vaccine and an army of mosquitoes infected with Wolbachia bacteria.

rows.title: Equity in science is a beautiful lie — and I’m done pretending
rows.summary: Science isn’t really moving towards equity; institutions are just perfecting the appearance of equity. We need to build an alternative system.

rows.title: Make trains great again — for the sake of people and the planet
rows.summary: As railways enter their third century of service, research must support their renaissance for more-sustainable travel that supports human development.

rows.title: Daily briefing: A ‘time crystal’ made visible to the naked eye
rows.summary: Physicists have created a form of matter once thought physically impossible. Plus, the rise of religious chatbots and the debate over ‘mirror life’ heats up.

rows.title: Mysterious changes near Earth’s core revealed by satellites in space
rows.summary: Orbiters can pick up gravitational shifts thousands of kilometres below the surface.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: TCF1 and LEF1 promote B-1a cell homeostasis and regulatory function
Delta-type glutamate receptors are ligand-gated ion channels
rows.summary: Structural and in vitro functional studies of the human delta-type ionotropic glutamate receptor GluD2 reveal that it contains an ion channel that is activated by d -serine and GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid).

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Experimental determination of partial charges with electron diffraction
Sweet like chocolate: researching in the shade of a cacao tree
rows.summary: Naailah Ali aims to support cacao farmers in the West Indies by improving the bean-fermentation process.

rows.title: Smoke-dried mummies pre-date Egypt’s embalmed bodies
rows.summary: Remains buried in Asia in a crouching position are thought to be oldest known examples of intentionally mummified burials.

rows.title: Weird ‘time crystals’ are made visible at last
rows.summary: Time crystals, a state of matter once thought physically impossible, could soon be on a banknote.

rows.title: ‘Lipstick on a pig’: how to fight back against a peer-review bully
rows.summary: Scientific societies, journals, editors and researchers are pushing back against mean-spirited peer reviews.

rows.title: Daily briefing: What’s next for gravitational-wave detectors?
rows.summary: As the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, scientists are planning the next generation of observatories. Plus, octopuses favour different arms for different tasks and what’s on the agenda at the upcoming meeting of US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr’s upcoming vaccine panel.

rows.title: How should ‘mirror life’ research be restricted? Debate heats up
rows.summary: Some researchers are calling for strict limits, while others speak out against halting basic science prematurely.

rows.title: The chatbots claiming to be Jesus: spreading gospel or heresy?
rows.summary: Jesus chatbots aren’t the only AI technologies seeping into religious practice. Some worshippers don’t agree with the use of them.

rows.title: Heroes or hoarders? The strange brains of people who collect
rows.summary: Public museums and private collections are stuffed with scientific artefacts gathered by individuals — often with highly questionable obsessions and motivations.

rows.title: GPS timekeeping is increasingly vulnerable: here’s how to deliver future-proofed time
rows.summary: With crucial infrastructure increasingly dependent on accurate, resilient clocks, outages in the dominant system for global positioning highlight the need for other ways of distributing time information.

rows.title: Mirror of the unknown: should research on mirror-image molecular biology be stopped?
rows.summary: Amid growing debates about the benefits and risks of studying looking-glass versions of life’s building blocks, there is an urgent need to bridge divergent views.

rows.title: Ready or not, the digital afterlife is here
rows.summary: Developers of griefbots say that they help people by allowing them to commune with recreations of the dead, but others say that the technology is fraught with danger.

rows.title: Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system
rows.summary: A large-scale atom-array architecture enables coherent continuous operation of more than 3,000 physical qubits, where new qubits can be introduced without destroying existing quantum information encoded in the system.

rows.title: How to help refugees thrive: have local families host them
rows.summary: Ukrainian refugees who moved into German households report greater social integration than those who lived in other settings.

rows.title: World's most energy-efficient AI supercomputer comes online
rows.summary: JUPITER, the European Union’s new exascale supercomputer, is 100% powered by renewable energy. Can it compete in the global AI race?

rows.title: LIGO is 10 years old: black-hole breakthroughs will ‘only get better’
rows.summary: A decade after the pair of observatories first detected gravitational waves, researchers are drawing up ambitious plans for its successors.

rows.title: Maintenance
rows.summary: A difficult thing to fix.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The most- and least-improved countries for chronic disease
rows.summary: Of high-income countries, when it comes to non-communicable diseases, Denmark is doing it right. Plus, a unique clinical study aims to understand HIV, and heatwaves have been linked to specific fossil-fuel producers.

rows.title: Why we launched Denmark’s second Young Academy (and what’s different about it)
rows.summary: YATSI aims to represent scientists based in academia and in industry, and to build bridges between the two sectors.

rows.title: Childhood vaccines up for review in the US: what’s at stake
rows.summary: Nature reviews the three shots under scrutiny by RFK Jr’s advisers and the data behind them.

rows.title: Is my red your red? Neuroscience has an answer
rows.summary: The age-old philosophical question of whether we see colours the same way has been explored with brain scans.

rows.title: Author Correction: A broad-spectrum lasso peptide antibiotic targeting the bacterial ribosome
Dinosaur egg dated directly for the first time
rows.summary: Laser method could help to pinpoint the age of many fossils, but some palaeontologists say further research is needed to verify the technique.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Heatwaves can be directly linked to emissions from specific companies
rows.summary: Carbon emissions from individual energy giants can be directly linked to one quarter of heatwaves between 2000 and 2023. Plus, a brain ‘dial’ that turns the desire to eat on and off in mice and the researchers fighting back against the Trump administration’s assault on US science.

rows.title: Trump team disbands controversial US climate panel
rows.summary: A report by the panel downplays the ills of global warming and was key to White House efforts to revoke federal authority to regulate climate policies.

rows.title: Tips and tricks to plan your career in science
rows.summary: Julie Gould explores some of the theories and frameworks to help identify future work goals and achieve them.

rows.title: AI tool detects LLM-generated text in research papers and peer reviews
rows.summary: Authors and peer reviewers are failing to disclose the use of LLMs despite journal policies limiting their use.

rows.title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Recovery of learning and memory is associated with chromatin remodelling
Songs of the striped mouse show who’s friend and who’s foe
rows.summary: Ultrasonic calls, too high for the human ear to detect, convey a wealth of information across the rodent’s territory.

rows.title: Feeling the heat: fossil-fuel producers linked to dozens of heatwaves
rows.summary: Attribution study suggests major energy producers play an outsized role in causing extreme heatwaves — plus, the scientists fighting back against US funding cuts.

rows.title: Jelly-filled garment keeps wearers cool when heat and humidity soar
rows.summary: Lightweight, battery-powered shirt could maintain skin at a comfortable temperature for hours.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Regenerative revolution aims to future-proof European agriculture
rows.summary: Farms across Europe are turning to regenerative agriculture to save their crops from the effects of climate change. Plus, a prototype ‘helmet’ for delivering non-invasive brain treatments and a vaccine against chlamydia for koalas.

rows.title: Heatwaves linked to carbon emissions from specific companies
rows.summary: Nearly one-quarter of heatwaves would have been ‘virtually impossible’ without global warming — and can be attributed to the emissions of individual energy producers.

rows.title: Iron-respiring microbes could have a role in sulfur cycling
rows.summary: A bacterium that uses sulfide as an energy source to metabolize solid iron oxides has been discovered, revealing a biological reaction that was previously assumed to be solely chemical. This finding uncovers a firm microbial link between sulfur and iron cycling in oxygen-free environments such as aquatic sediments.

rows.title: Synthetic data can benefit medical research — but risks must be recognized
rows.summary: Artificially generated data can help to train AI models when real data are scant, but more focus is needed on validating the results.

rows.title: AI-generated medical data can sidestep usual ethics review, universities say
rows.summary: Representatives of four medical research centres have told Nature they have waived normal ethical review because ‘synthetic’ data do not contain real or traceable patient information.

rows.title: How did the oldest star clusters form?
rows.summary: A computational model of the early-to-present-day Universe predicts that some of the first stars formed in structures that challenge conventional classification.

rows.title: Designing an alloy microstructure atom by atom to withstand extreme cold
rows.summary: Atoms are the fundamental building blocks of metallic materials, and their arrangement and distribution determine the material’s properties. Rearranging atoms from a random, disordered state into a carefully ordered dual-scale pattern enhances the mechanical performance of alloys under extremely cold conditions.

rows.title: Epigenetic clues from cancer’s past foretell its future
rows.summary: An innovative method to trace tumour evolution using patterns of fluctuating DNA modifications could be implemented in the clinic to predict cancer progression.

rows.title: ‘Brain dial’ turns food consumption on or off in mice
rows.summary: Master-control area integrates information about hunger, a food’s tastiness and more — and can even drive intake of plastic pellets.

rows.title: These scientists left the US in Trump’s first term: their tips on taking the leap
rows.summary: Nature talks to researchers about why they moved and how they relocated successfully.

rows.title: The earth will not consume our bones
rows.summary: Welcome to the garden.

rows.title: Heatwaves linked to emissions of individual fossil-fuel and cement producers
rows.summary: The emissions of leading fossil-fuel and cement producers have been systematically linked to particular heatwaves. Three scientists discuss the methodology behind the result and its potential impact on climate-liability court cases.

rows.title: A common gut fungus worsens infection with the food-borne bacterium Salmonella
rows.summary: In an intricate interaction spanning domains of life, the bacterium Salmonella hijacks the yeast Candida to make it produce and release the amino acid arginine in the gut. Arginine increases the virulence of Salmonella and downregulates the host’s immune response to Salmonella infection, leading to more-severe disease.

rows.title: Using biobanks to boost research: a how-to guide
rows.summary: From large national databases to bespoke sample collections, biobanks offer a wealth of avenues for scientific enquiry.

rows.title: Your risk of dying from chronic disease has dropped — if you live in these countries
rows.summary: A report finds that death rates from cancer and heart disease have declined since 2010 in roughly 150 countries.

rows.title: Clearest gravitational-wave detection yet confirms Hawking’s black-hole theory
rows.summary: Discovery joins a list of the greatest hits of the LIGO detector, which ten years ago became the first to detect gravitational waves.

rows.title: Climate impacts are real — denying this is self-defeating
rows.summary: The US administration is attempting to undermine efforts to curb greenhouse-gas emissions. It will ultimately leave that country, and the world, worse off.

rows.title: Scientists take on Trump: these researchers are fighting back
rows.summary: Through lawsuits, grant tracking, whistle-blowing and more, resistance to the US war on science is growing.

rows.title: Mystery Martian minerals hint at the planet’s complex geochemical past
rows.summary: The Perseverance rover on Mars has observed unusual minerals associated with organic matter — raising questions about the geochemistry of ancient Mars.

rows.title: Long-range PM 2.5 pollution and health impacts from the 2023 Canadian wildfires
rows.summary: A modelling study based on satellite observations, machine learning and a chemical transport model quantifies the global and regional exposure to particulate-matter pollution and the human health impacts related to the 2023 Canadian wildfires.

rows.title: The oldest known lepidosaur and origins of lepidosaur feeding adaptations
rows.summary: A rhynchocephalian skeleton around 3–7 million years older than the oldest currently known lepidosaur fossil provides important insight into the origin of lizards and snakes.

rows.title: Human gastroids to model regional patterning in early stomach development
rows.summary: Neural tissue is a key signalling centre for fundic–antral patterning in development of gastric organoids featuring asymmetric PDX1 patterning.

rows.title: The emergence of globular clusters and globular-cluster-like dwarfs
rows.summary: The results from a state-of-the-art suite of hydrodynamical cosmological zoom-in simulations show how globular clusters naturally emerge in the Standard Cosmology and also reveal the existence of a new class of object called globular-cluster-like dwarfs.

rows.title: Programmable antisense oligomers for phage functional genomics
rows.summary: Establishing antisense oligomers as versatile, non-genetic tools to silence phage mRNAs opens applications in basic research and biotechnology, as shown by identifying essential factors for propagation of the nucleus-forming jumbo phage ΦKZ such as the RNase H-like protein ΦKZ155.

rows.title: Stabilizing effect of amino acids on protein and colloidal dispersions
rows.summary: Amino acids possess a new and broad colloidal property: they stabilize patchy nanoscale colloids, such as proteins, by adsorbing onto their surfaces through weak interactions.

rows.title: Fluctuating DNA methylation tracks cancer evolution at clinical scale
rows.summary: Cancer evolutionary dynamics are quantitatively inferred using a method, EVOFLUx, applied to fluctuating DNA methylation.

rows.title: Loss-of-function mutations in PLD4 lead to systemic lupus erythematosus
rows.summary: PLD4 loss-of-function mutations in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus leads to excessive activation of TLR7 and TLR9.

rows.title: Amplifying antigen-induced cellular responses with proximity labelling
rows.summary: Red light- or ultrasound-controlled proximity labelling is engineered to stimulate clustering-induced receptor activation and downstream signalling amplification to promote antitumour immune responses.

rows.title: ABCA7 variants impact phosphatidylcholine and mitochondria in neurons
rows.summary: Loss-of-function variants of ABCA7 , associated with Alzheimer’s disease, result in disrupted lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, DNA repair and synaptic signalling pathways in the human brain.

rows.title: Neuronal activity-dependent mechanisms of small cell lung cancer pathogenesis
rows.summary: Glutamatergic and GABAergic (γ-aminobutyric acid-producing) cortical neuronal activity drives proliferation of small lung cell cancer via paracrine interactions and through synapses formed with tumour cells.

rows.title: Late fluid flow in a primitive asteroid revealed by Lu–Hf isotopes in Ryugu
rows.summary: Analysis of samples from the asteroid Ryugu provide evidence of late fluid flow in a carbonaceous asteroid, indicating that such bodies may have retained two to three times more water than previously thought.

rows.title: Molecular subtypes of human skeletal muscle in cancer cachexia
rows.summary: Unbiased clustering analysis of the skeletal muscle RNAome in patients with cancer identifies two molecular subtypes, one of which distinguishes individuals with cachexia and indicates potential target pathways for future research.

rows.title: Observing differential spin currents by resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
rows.summary: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering can be used to measure the spin current carried by magnons in the presence of temperature gradients across a magnetic insulator.

rows.title: Energy deficiency selects crowded live epithelial cells for extrusion
rows.summary: Crowded epithelial cells with the least energy and membrane potential are selected for extrusion.

rows.title: Systematic attribution of heatwaves to the emissions of carbon majors
rows.summary: Climate change made 213 historical heatwaves reported over 2000–2023 more likely and more intense, to which each of the 180 carbon majors (fossil fuel and cement producers) substantially contributed.

rows.title: Redox-driven mineral and organic associations in Jezero Crater, Mars
rows.summary: A geological, petrographic and geochemical survey of distinctive mudstone and conglomerate outcrops of the Bright Angel formation on Mars reveals textures, chemical and mineral characteristics, and organic signatures that warrant consideration as potential biosignatures.

rows.title: Myeloid progenitor dysregulation fuels immunosuppressive macrophages in tumours
rows.summary: An understanding of the molecular mechanisms promoting the generation of immunoregulatory and tumour-promoting monocytes and macrophages is key to breaking the cycle of tumour myelopoiesis and developing more effective myeloid-targeting therapies.

rows.title: Probing the heterogeneous nature of LiF in solid–electrolyte interphases
rows.summary: Using 19 F nuclear magnetic resonance to study LiF–LiH solid solutions revealed that it is present in the solid–electrolyte interphase of lithium metal batteries and confirms the heterogeneous nature of LiF in such interphases.

rows.title: Functional synapses between neurons and small cell lung cancer
rows.summary: Small cell lung cancer cells form functional synapses with glutamatergic neurons, receiving synaptic transmissions and deriving a proliferative advantage from these interactions.

rows.title: Structure and mechanism of the mitochondrial calcium transporter NCLX
rows.summary: Cryogenic electron microscopy structures and functional analyses reveal that NCLX functions as a H + /Ca 2+ rather than a Na + /Ca 2+ exchanger, and uncover its transport mechanism with implications for therapies treating cardiac and neurodegenerative disorders related to abnormal mitochondrial Ca 2+ .

rows.title: Probing non-equilibrium topological order on a quantum processor
rows.summary: A superconducting quantum computer is used to realize an out-of-equilibrium topologically ordered state, which hosts anyonic excitations.

rows.title: Probing the Kitaev honeycomb model on a neutral-atom quantum computer
rows.summary: Digital quantum simulations of Kitaev’s honeycomb model are realized for two-dimensional fermionic systems using a reconfigurable atom-array processor and used to study the Fermi–Hubbard model on a square lattice.

rows.title: Creativity is essential to the ethos of universities
Use computing royalties to kick-start biodiversity fund
Life scientists: educate others to help strengthen biosecurity
Bug bites convince UK doctor to support mosquito research centre
rows.summary: An encounter with blood-suckers persuades a researcher to back a new scientific institute, and an effort to standardize the printing of mathematical formulae, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Strengthen the science behind the Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies
Global geopolitics should not stall science — 5 ways to push back
rows.summary: Researchers, funders, universities and governments must work together to build scientific collaborations that are resilient to rapidly evolving international sanctions.

rows.title: These nations are wooing PhD students amid US funding uncertainties
rows.summary: Pauses to some US graduate programmes have led universities in several countries to launch initiatives to entice would-be PhD students.

rows.title: A revolution is sweeping Europe’s farms: can it save agriculture?
rows.summary: Momentum is building for regenerative agriculture, a set of approaches that could help farms to weather the changing climate and make them more profitable.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Different people’s brains process colours in the same way
rows.summary: Scans suggest that colours light up the same parts of different people’s brains. Plus, a pig-organ transplant success story and how warming water could decimate a vital phytoplankton.

rows.title: AI chatbots are already biasing research — we must establish guidelines for their use now
rows.summary: The academic community has looked at how artificial-intelligence tools help researchers to write papers, but not how they distort the literature scientists choose to cite.

rows.title: Head start: fossil clues about how bodies evolved from two-fold to five-fold symmetry
rows.summary: How the five-fold symmetrical bodies of starfish and other echinoderms evolved is a mystery. New evidence fills in a key piece of the puzzle.

rows.title: Protests are infectious: mapping rural unrest in Revolutionary France
rows.summary: Researchers have used epidemiological models to determine whether the wave of riots in 1789 known as the Great Fear spread through irrational panic or rational protest.

rows.title: Iggy bop: how I tune in to the needs of Galápagos marine iguanas
rows.summary: Zoologist Amy MacLeod supports conservation efforts by using drones to survey endangered species.

rows.title: My blue is your blue: different people’s brains process colours in the same way
rows.summary: A machine-learning tool can predict what colour a person is looking at when trained on the brain activity of others.

rows.title: The surprising ways bridges resist collapse
rows.summary: Researchers have uncovered six mechanisms that could be reinforced to prevent steel truss bridges collapsing.

rows.title: Research misconduct: how the scientific community is fighting back
rows.summary: Misconduct is rare in science, but there are worries about a detritus of fake papers in the scientific literature. In this podcast, we explore why misconduct happens and how to tackle it.

rows.title: Rainer Weiss obituary: Nobel laureate who pioneered the technique that detected gravitational waves
rows.summary: Physicist who spearheaded the construction of the LIGO observatory to detect Einstein’s predicted ripples in space-time leaves a legacy of persistence and mentorship.

rows.title: ‘Communities already have the solutions’: why I advocate for Indigenous knowledge
rows.summary: Environmental scientist and global advocate Jessica Hernandez works to secure women’s rights and to integrate Indigenous science into environmental policy.

rows.title: ‘LinkedIn is like air to me’: the scientists who’ve cracked professional networking
rows.summary: Fans of the global social-media platform explain how best to harness its career-boosting and collaboration potential.

rows.title: Can a bold ‘social contract’ make data sharing more palatable?
rows.summary: Hoarding of health data is common across Africa, owing to well-founded concerns about exploitation and misuse of biomedical information. A charter that guarantees responsible data stewardship would help to allay such fears.

rows.title: How to build nature back better — read this manual
rows.summary: By clearing the confusion, this comprehensive guide can help businesses to do more for nature.

rows.title: Can researchers stop AI making up citations?
rows.summary: OpenAI’s GPT-5 hallucinates less than previous models do, but cutting hallucination completely might prove impossible.

rows.title: ‘Amazing feat’: US man still alive six months after pig kidney transplant
rows.summary: The first six months after an organ transplant are the riskiest for recipients.

rows.title: Daily briefing: A polo-team’s worth of cloned CRISPR horses
rows.summary: Horses created with the help of the CRISPR–Cas9 gene-editing technique have sparked controversy in the world of polo. Plus, air pollution is linked to a form of dementia and a newfound immune cell in mice that could explain why inflammation spikes with old age.

rows.title: Diabetes drug shows anti-ageing effects on chromsomes
rows.summary: Treatment with henagliflozin is linked to an increase in the length of telomeres, chromosomal caps that shorten over time.

rows.title: Nature goes inside the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’ — here’s the buzz
rows.summary: Facility aims to stop deadly viruses such as Zika, dengue and chikungunya through the release of disease-fighting mosquitoes.

rows.title: How to make a ‘laser’ of neutrinos
rows.summary: Rubidium atoms that are chilled to extremely low temperatures could emit bursts of particles called neutrinos.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: In situ light-field imaging of octopus locomotion reveals simplified control
Hope for diabetes: CRISPR-edited cells pump out insulin in a person — and evade immune detection
rows.summary: Edits create cells that don’t trigger an immune response, allowing implant recipient to forego immune-suppressing drugs.

rows.title: Author Correction: PPP2R1A mutations portend improved survival after cancer immunotherapy
Daily briefing: Nine metals in two dimensions
rows.summary: Why scientists are excited about 2D MXenes, a distant relative of graphene. Plus, the low-down on a fiery Senate hearing with RFK Jr and a lyrical exploration of iconic pigments.

rows.title: First CRISPR horses spark controversy: what’s next for gene-edited animals?
rows.summary: Horses with genomic edits to make them run faster have been banned from polo, but a zoo of CRISPR-edited animals is gaining acceptance in agriculture.

rows.title: When AI rejects your grant proposal: algorithms are helping to make funding decisions
rows.summary: A Spanish foundation using an artificial-intelligence tool to screen grant applications says it makes the peer-review process more efficient, but other researchers say it’s a breakdown in trust.

rows.title: Different flames
rows.summary: A lesson learnt.

rows.title: Will a child survive? Older siblings have a powerful influence
rows.summary: Swiss birth data from 1750 to 1870 reveal that girls who had lots of older brothers close to their own age were less likely to survive than were those who did not.

rows.title: Inside a mosquito factory
rows.summary: Brazilian site could produce one kilo of mosquito eggs per week.

rows.title: Changing tides ushered in the world’s first civilization
rows.summary: Construction of tidal irrigation systems helped to drive the formation of city states some 5,000 years ago.

rows.title: Air pollution directly linked to increased dementia risk
rows.summary: Long-term exposure accelerates the development of Lewy body dementia and Parkinson’s disease with dementia in people who are predisposed to the conditions.

rows.title: RFK Jr slings accusations and defends public-health upheaval at fiery hearing
rows.summary: Senators from both parties expressed scepticism about the US health secretary’s statements on COVID-19 vaccines and more.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Is a cure for psoriasis on the horizon?
rows.summary: Some people who cease a life-long treatment remain psoriasis-free. Plus, an ant queen can clone ants of another species and Earth’s capacity to store carbon dioxide emissions could max out surprisingly soon.

rows.title: Chemists cram record nine metals into trendy 2D material
rows.summary: MXenes, distant cousins of graphene, reach new heights of complexity — opening the way for use in advanced batteries and more.

rows.title: Newfound immune cell in mice hints at why inflammation spikes with old age
rows.summary: Pathogen-consuming cells found in fat tissue also play a part in lipid balance.

rows.title: Europe’s largest paper mill? 1,500 research articles linked to Ukrainian network
rows.summary: A group of companies has flooded 380 journals with hundreds of suspect papers since 2017.

rows.title: Tiny flier could soar through the mesosphere powered only by light
rows.summary: A quirk of physics lets light power flight in low pressure environments.

rows.title: 'How is this possible?' — two species birthed by one mother
rows.summary: Two brother ants defy species borders, by sharing the same mother despite being genetically different species.

rows.title: Ultra-processed foods — it’s time for an improved definition
rows.summary: The worst excesses of industrial food production must be reined in, while ensuring people have access to adequate calories.

rows.title: ‘Almost unimaginable’: these ants are different species but share a mother
rows.summary: Ant queens of one species clone ants of another to create hybrid workers that do their bidding.

rows.title: Two ants, two species, one mother
rows.summary: Iberian harvester ants can produce males that are genetically different species — plus, new insights into preventing deadly bridge collapses.

rows.title: Cocaine-activated ion channels engineered to break the loop of addiction in rats
rows.summary: Ion channels have been created that are selectively activated by cocaine and that act to either stimulate or inhibit the electrical activity of neuronal cells in the brain. These cocaine-activated ion channels are used to engineer neural circuits in rats to respond to cocaine in a manner that reduces cocaine seeking but not food seeking.

rows.title: Damaged bridges flex and twist to prevent collapse
rows.summary: Bridges made from connected steel frameworks can sometimes survive unexpected damage by activating hidden structural responses.

rows.title: Earth’s capacity to store carbon could max out surprisingly soon
rows.summary: Around 1,460 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide can be safely stored underground, but this limit could be reached by 2200.

rows.title: Daily briefing: How bad are ultra-processed foods, really?
rows.summary: What the science says about ultra-processed foods. Plus, a microbiome in a mammoth tooth and how to keep Oceania free of bird flu.

rows.title: The diversity of microbial enzymes that turn a pollutant into an inert gas
rows.summary: Reductase enzymes catalyse the conversion of the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide (N 2 O) to environmentally benign dinitrogen gas. The discovery of a microbial N 2 O reductase reveals a previously unknown N 2 O sink and creates opportunities for innovative biotechnologies to counter the effects of N 2 O emissions.

rows.title: Ant queens produce sons of two distinct species
rows.summary: The discovery of an unusual reproductive system for one ant species solves a long-standing puzzle about a missing population of another ant species.

rows.title: Depriving brain tumours of an amino acid could enhance chemotherapy
rows.summary: Glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer, depends on the amino acid serine as a fuel source. A serine-deficient diet has been shown to slow tumour growth in mice.

rows.title: Compression causes cancer cells to start spreading
rows.summary: According to the ‘grow or go’ model, cancer cells can switch between invasive and proliferative states. A zebrafish model of skin cancer shows that the invasive switch is triggered by mechanical compression of the cancer cells by surrounding tissues. In this way, the physical environment can reprogramme the cell to dictate cancer behaviour.

rows.title: How academics and ‘big tech’ can learn from one another
rows.summary: Foreseeing clashes of cultures is the key to making industry-academic collaborations mutually beneficial.

rows.title: Ancient DNA clarifies the early history of the Slavs
rows.summary: A study examines the emergence of a group that sparked a fundamental change in lifestyle in Central and Eastern Europe in the sixth century.

rows.title: This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue
rows.summary: Raising millions upon millions of disease-fighting mosquitoes per week is no easy task, Nature learnt during its visit to the facility.

rows.title: Flies evolved a shock-absorber tissue used during embryonic development
rows.summary: The role of tissue that forms between the head and trunk of a fly embryo has been unclear. It turns out that it absorbs forces when nearby cells move and divide.

rows.title: Are ultra-processed foods really so unhealthy? What the science says
rows.summary: These foods have been linked to obesity and other health troubles, but some scientists argue the grouping is too broad to guide dietary choices.

rows.title: Heart’s desire
rows.summary: A keepsake from a former life.

rows.title: Marsquakes indicate that the inner core of the red planet is solid, not liquid
rows.summary: An analysis of seismic waves propagating through Mars finds evidence that the planet has a small, solid inner core, which challenges existing planetary models.

rows.title: A way to determine how partial charges of atoms in a molecule are distributed
rows.summary: Atomic partial charges are subtle variations in electron distribution in a molecule. They can now be measured by an innovative experimental method that exploits a phenomenon known as electron diffraction. The results provide insights into molecular interactions, potentially leading to applications in drug discovery and materials science.

rows.title: Brain tumours in mice grow more slowly when starved of key amino acid
rows.summary: Some glioblastomas steal serine from their environment — a weakness that opens the door to treatment.

rows.title: How the brain’s amygdala reacts when making decisions to avoid losses
rows.summary: Humans explore unfamiliar options more when deciding how to avoid losses than when seeking gains. The firing rate of neuronal cells in the brain’s amygdala predicts decisions to explore in both learning strategies, but neuronal ‘noise’ predicts exploration decisions only when avoiding losses. Together, these signals explain the increased exploration when risking losses.

rows.title: Latent resistance mechanisms of steel truss bridges after critical failures
rows.summary: Experimental tests and computational simulations of a scaled-down specimen of a real steel truss bridge identify and characterize the latent resistance mechanisms following critical failures, demonstrating how loads supported by failed components can be redistributed and enable structure resilience.

rows.title: DNA2 enables growth by restricting recombination-restarted replication
rows.summary: DNA2 suppresses recombination-restarted replication and checkpoint activation at stalled forks, and its loss triggers recombination-dependent synthesis, checkpoint signalling and cell-cycle exit, highlighting its essential role in proliferation and growth failure in primordial dwarfism.

rows.title: A prudent planetary limit for geologic carbon storage
rows.summary: A risk-based, spatially explicit analysis of carbon storage in sedimentary basins establishes a prudent planetary limit of around 1,460 Gt of geological carbon storage, which requires making explicit decisions on priorities for storage use.

rows.title: A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour
rows.summary: The International Brain Laboratory presents a brain-wide electrophysiological map obtained from pooling data from 12 laboratories that performed the same standardized perceptual decision-making task in mice.

rows.title: Divergent evolutionary strategies pre-empt tissue collision in gastrulation
rows.summary: Flies have evolved two distinct strategies for managing mechanical stresses during embryogenesis: out-of-plane cell division in midges and transient out-of-plane tissue folding in fruit flies.

rows.title: Analog optical computer for AI inference and combinatorial optimization
rows.summary: An analog optical computer that combines analog electronics, three-dimensional optics, and an iterative architecture accelerates artificial intelligence inference and combinatorial optimization in a single platform, paving a promising path for faster and sustainable computing.

rows.title: Single-cell transcriptomic and genomic changes in the ageing human brain
rows.summary: Sequencing analyses of human prefrontal cortex from donors ranging in age from 0.4 to 104 years show that ageing correlates with an accumulation of somatic mutations in short housekeeping genes and a reduction in the expression of these genes.

rows.title: A circuit that integrates drive state and social contact to gate mating
rows.summary: Analyses of consummatory reproductive behaviours in male mice uncover a brain mechanism whereby an internal state can attribute a social quality to a generic touch to initiate purposeful reproductive actions.

rows.title: Spatial joint profiling of DNA methylome and transcriptome in tissues
rows.summary: DNA-methylation and gene-expression profiling of tissue sections at near single-cell resolution can be used to create detailed spatial maps showing how methylation and transcription interact to shape cell identity and tissue development.

rows.title: Patterned invagination prevents mechanical instability during gastrulation
rows.summary: In Drosophila , the cephalic furrow counteracts mechanical stress as the developing head and the trunk tissues meet, providing evidence for how mechanical forces influence the evolution of morphogenetic innovations in early development.

rows.title: Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making
rows.summary: Brain-wide recordings in mice reveal that prior expectations are distributed through recurrent loops across all levels of cortical and subcortical processing.

rows.title: A nanobody specific to prefusion glycoprotein B neutralizes HSV-1 and HSV-2
rows.summary: A neutralizing nanobody specific to the prefusion conformation of herpes simplex virus glycoprotein B has cross-species activity and offers insights into virus neutralization, possible immunogens and an attractive avenue for antiviral interventions.

rows.title: Cas9 senses CRISPR RNA abundance to regulate CRISPR spacer acquisition
rows.summary: Cas9 in type II-C CRISPR–Cas systems functions independently of its RNA partners to regulate spacer acquisition, dynamically adjusting the process on the basis of crRNA abundance to maintain a sufficient CRISPR array size and immune memory.

rows.title: Training of physical neural networks
rows.summary: Methods to train physical neural networks, such as backpropagation-based and backpropagation-free approaches, are explored to allow scaling up of artificial intelligence models far beyond present small-scale laboratory demonstrations, potentially enhancing computational efficiency.

rows.title: Adaptive and context-aware volumetric printing
rows.summary: A new approach combining 3D imaging, computer vision and parametric modelling, named GRACE, is introduced, enabling adaptive and context-aware 3D printing of structures around features ranging from cellular to macroscopic scales with minimal user intervention.

rows.title: 3D-printed micro ion trap technology for quantum information applications
rows.summary: High-resolution 3D printing technology making use of two-photon polymerization instead of traditional machining is described, allowing low-cost and scalable production of large arrays of high-quality 3D Paul traps.

rows.title: Supervised learning in DNA neural networks
rows.summary: DNA molecules can be programmed to autonomously carry out supervised learning in vitro, with the system learning to perform pattern classification from molecular examples of inputs and desired responses.

rows.title: Commensal yeast promotes Salmonella Typhimurium virulence
rows.summary: Commensal Candida albicans enhances the virulence and dissemination of Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium.

rows.title: PICALM Alzheimer’s risk allele causes aberrant lipid droplets in microglia
rows.summary: A PICALM allele associated with increased risk of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease has a microglial-specific role in lipid droplet accumulation.

rows.title: Infrastructure deficits and informal settlements in sub-Saharan Africa
rows.summary: A new network approach maps every street block in sub-Saharan Africa using high-resolution building and street data, pinpointing infrastructure needs and revealing development gradients from neighbourhoods to cities and rural areas.

rows.title: Amygdala–liver signalling orchestrates glycaemic responses to stress
rows.summary: Studies in mice show that acute stress activates hyperglycaemia via activation of a medial amygdala–ventral hypothalamic circuit that controls glucose metabolic responses in the liver, independently of adrenal and pancreatic hormones.

rows.title: Multiple overlapping binding sites determine transcription factor occupancy
rows.summary: A new method enables comprehensive screening and identification of low-affinity DNA binding sites for transcription factors, and reveals that nucleotides flanking high-affinity binding sites create overlapping low-affinity binding sites that modulate transcription factor binding in vivo.

rows.title: Genetic suppression features ABHD18 as a Barth syndrome therapeutic target
rows.summary: The enzyme ABHD18 is shown to have a key role in cardiolipin metabolism in mitochondria, offering a potential route for a small-molecule treatment of the rare genetic disease Barth syndrome.

rows.title: One mother for two species via obligate cross-species cloning in ants
rows.summary: In a case of obligate cross-species cloning, female ants of Messor ibericus need to clone males of Messor structor to obtain sperm for producing the worker caste, resulting in males from the same mother having distinct genomes and morphologies.

rows.title: Dynamic fibroblast–immune interactions shape recovery after brain injury
rows.summary: Spatial transcriptomic studies and lineage tracing reveal that, after brain injury, transient profibrotic fibroblasts develop from existing brain fibroblasts, infiltrate lesions, regulate the local immune response and lead to beneficial scar tissue formation.

rows.title: Rewiring of cortical glucose metabolism fuels human brain cancer growth
rows.summary: The cortex fuels essential physiological processes with glucose-derived carbon, while gliomas fuel their aggressiveness by rerouting glucose carbon pathways and scavenging alternative carbon sources such as environmental amino acids, providing a potential therapeutic target.

rows.title: Seismic detection of a 600-km solid inner core in Mars
rows.summary: An analysis of seismic data acquired by the InSight mission demonstrates that Mars has a 600-km solid inner core.

rows.title: Ancient DNA connects large-scale migration with the spread of Slavs
rows.summary: Analyses of ancient human DNA show that cultural and political transformations in Central Europe during the second half of the first millennium ce were associated with movements of Slavic populations into Germany, Poland and Croatia.

rows.title: Liquid-crystal specs refocus with the push of a button
rows.summary: Bifocals for the touchscreen era accommodate users who mix near- and far-sightedness.

rows.title: AI-agent ethics should consider sentient non-human animals
China’s chikungunya virus outbreak is a wake up call
Experiment puts ‘spoon bending’ to the test

rows.title: Include climate impacts when protecting infrastructure
Veterinarians need to be part of West Nile disease storytelling
Is this the future of food? 'Sexless' seeds that could transform farming
rows.summary: Scientists are tinkering with plant genes to create crops that seed their own clones, with a host of benefits for farmers.

rows.title: Air taxis will soon be in our skies — if batteries can be made safer
rows.summary: Small electric aeroplanes flying at low altitude will need energy sources that can withstand crashes and deliver power reliably. Standards need to be decided now.

rows.title: AI-powered brain device allows paralysed man to control robotic arm
rows.summary: The human user and AI have shared autonomy and constantly interact to complete tasks.

rows.title: These ‘glass straw’ optical fibres could speed up the Internet
rows.summary: A cable design that sends light through air, rather than solid glass, could cut signal loss and make long-distance transmissions cheaper.

rows.title: Unifying gravity and quantum theory requires better understanding of time
rows.summary: Textbooks give strange, imprecise explanations of where things happen in quantum mechanics. Consistency with gravity needs a fresh approach.

rows.title: A mammoth toothache: bacterial community discovered in mouth of ancient mammal
rows.summary: Genetic-sequencing techniques have uncovered the oldest host-associated microbial DNA ever recorded — inside samples of teeth and bones from woolly and steppe mammoths.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Epigenetic atlas shows how ageing tweaks DNA
rows.summary: Researchers paint the most comprehensive picture to date of how ageing modifies our genes. Plus, a new type of optical fibre and why scientists are flocking to Substack.

rows.title: ‘The wolf is not the bad guy’: working with farmers to protect a reintroduced species
rows.summary: Carmen García-Chávez monitors the activities of wolves after their reintroduction to Chihuahua, northern Mexico.

rows.title: The grant lottery: award rates at UK national funding agency fall below 20%
rows.summary: Application volume is outpacing available funding, intensifying competition and worsening pressure on the peer-review system. But those who win grants are now getting more.

rows.title: How ageing changes our genes — huge epigenetic atlas gives clearest picture yet
rows.summary: A map of DNA methylation changes in human organs could help researchers to discover more targets for anti-ageing therapies.

rows.title: Do social-media bans benefit young people? These data could offer clues
rows.summary: Australia’s Online Safety Amendment Act provides the chance for researchers to analyse the complex relationship between social-media use and mental health in adolescents, but results should be interpreted with caution.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Spouses tend to share the same psychiatric disorders
rows.summary: When one partner is diagnosed with a psychiatric condition, the other is significantly more likely to be diagnosed with the same condition. Plus, the month’s best science images and former CDC directors sound the alarm about US health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

rows.title: States now have a legal duty to prevent climate harm — justice is in reach
rows.summary: A July ruling from the International Court of Justice is clear: nations can face consequences if they don’t act on the climate crisis.

rows.title: Clarity or accuracy — what makes a good scientific image?
rows.summary: Photography is not just illustrative, it is investigative. A revealing book cautions us to look closely at what pictures are really telling us.

rows.title: When will life expectancy reach 100? No time soon
rows.summary: Average expected lifespan is still increasing in high-income countries, but the rate of increase is slowing.

rows.title: Author Correction: Dual neuromodulatory dynamics underlie birdsong learning
Audio long read: How to detect consciousness in people, animals and maybe even AI
rows.summary: Scientists are searching for awareness in all its possible forms — insights from human brains could inform that quest.

rows.title: The vibrant colours of a house-hunting crab — August’s best science image
rows.summary: The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.

rows.title: Research posts on Bluesky are more original — and get better engagement
rows.summary: Bluesky posts about science garner more likes and reposts than similar ones on X.

rows.title: Daily briefing: There are two kinds of beer drinkers — these are the flavours that divide them
rows.summary: Lager drinkers fall into two distinct categories: those who prefer strong flavour chemicals and those who prefer mellow ones. Plus, a deep-sea worm that produces a pigment favoured by Rembrandt and the evidence around chemical exposure from beauty products.

rows.title: How LinkedIn helped me to carve out a career path after my PhD
rows.summary: The professional-networking platform helped Elena Hoffer to launch a company and sparked a global conversation to re-imagine academia.

rows.title: Spouses tend to share psychiatric disorders, massive study finds
rows.summary: Analysis of almost 15 million people shows the trend increases with each decade, across cultures and generations.

rows.title: Trump called for ‘gold-standard science’: how the NIH, NSF and others are answering
rows.summary: Some researchers say that US-agency policies provide opportunities for political interference.

rows.title: Why scientists are flocking to Substack
rows.summary: A new generation of researchers is using the platform to build audiences and monetize their knowledge.

rows.title: Hundreds of suspicious journals flagged by AI screening tool
rows.summary: System that searches for signs of bad practice could help to weed out questionable titles.

rows.title: This deep-sea worm creates a toxic yellow pigment found in Rembrandt and Cézanne paintings
rows.summary: Paralvinella hessleri is the first known animal to create orpiment, which was used by artists for centuries.

rows.title: Even dinosaurs weren’t safe from this giant croc-like predator
rows.summary: The creature might have been more than 3.5 metres long, with powerful jaws and serrated, flesh-cutting teeth.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Deliberate fearmongering spread like a virus through revolutionary France
rows.summary: Rumours that fuelled the Great Fear in revolutionary France were transmitted similarly to a viral disease. Plus, glow-in-the-dark succulents and a new treatment for acne.

rows.title: Beer lovers fall into two flavour camps — which one are you in?
rows.summary: Research shows that beer drinkers are split depending on which types of flavour chemicals they prefer.

rows.title: Author Correction: Endophilin marks and controls a clathrin-independent endocytic pathway
Skin: preserving the health of a multi-talented organ
rows.summary: Longer-lasting treatments and smarter care practices can protect and repair the most visible part of the body.

rows.title: Viral spread: how rumours surged in revolutionary France
rows.summary: Modern epidemiological models shed light on the causes of the ‘Great Fear’ — plus, Nature ’s big quantum interpretation quiz.

Five single-celled species that dabble in multicellularity
rows.summary: Animals’ closest cousins provide insight into how we became multicellular creatures.

rows.title: Bright city lights make birds around the world sing longer
rows.summary: Big-eyed species are especially vulnerable to the effects of light pollution, a citizen-science effort shows.

rows.title: AI versus skin cancer: the future of dermatology diagnosis
rows.summary: England’s health service is trialling an artificial-intelligence tool that can identify skin cancer as accurately as a physician.

rows.title: A psoriasis cure could be in touching distance
rows.summary: Today’s antibody therapies must be taken for life to avoid severe setbacks. Researchers are pushing for a more durable treatment.

rows.title: Five highlights from skin research
rows.summary: Demystifying itching, giving robots facial expressions, and other key studies and trials.

rows.title: Hazardous science that helps to save and improve lives needs more support
rows.summary: Research into the growing environmental problem of urban gullies highlights the challenging conditions under which many socially important studies are done.

rows.title: How humans became upright: key changes to our pelvis found
rows.summary: Genetic and anatomical data reveal how the human pelvis acquired its unique shape, enabling our ancestors to walk on two legs.

rows.title: How did life get multicellular? Five simple organisms could have the answer
rows.summary: Single-celled species that often stick together in colonies have researchers rethinking the origin of animals.

rows.title: Dermatology has a skin-colour dilemma
rows.summary: Classifications drawn from outmoded concepts of race impede research and clinical practice.

rows.title: A closer look at how cells sense dietary nutrients
rows.summary: Cells need to sense the presence or absence of nutrients so that they can adjust their metabolism and growth accordingly. A key node in cellular nutrient sensing is the protein complex GATOR2. The mechanisms of how two nutrient-sensing proteins bind to and alter the configuration of GATOR2 have been determined.

rows.title: Gene therapy marks a turning point for rare skin diseases
rows.summary: Fresh treatments shift the focus from symptom management to repair, and help children with skin conditions to live active lives.

rows.title: Daily briefing: What we know about autism and why it’s on the rise
rows.summary: What decades of research can tell us about the causes of autism. Plus, a meticulous single-atom version of an iconic physics experiment and how unicellular organisms are helping us uncover what sparked multicellular animal life.

rows.title: An abiding mystery of the French Revolution is solved — by epidemiology
rows.summary: The period of panic and unrest called the Great Fear was triggered by deliberately spread rumours, according to methods borrowed from pandemic playbooks.

rows.title: Acne vaccines could offer robust defence
rows.summary: Researchers are hoping to trick the immune system into fighting back against the bane of adolescents everywhere.

rows.title: Why Texas is the hottest place for space right now
rows.summary: Companies and students are flocking to the state, drawn by growth and employment opportunities in the aerospace sector.

rows.title: Origins of life: the molecules that could have unlocked peptide synthesis
rows.summary: For life to emerge on Earth, peptides must first have formed without the aid of enzymes — but how? Reactions of sulfur-containing molecules might have been key.

rows.title: Gully formation in cities is displacing tens of thousands of people
rows.summary: Gullies are incising into rapidly developing tropical cities. An analysis in the Democratic Republic of the Congo casts light on the extent and effect of this on city dwellers.

rows.title: Will the latest skin substitutes revolutionize the treatment of burns and other wounds?
rows.summary: Engineered multilayered tissues are showing great promise in the clinic, and could also provide more-accurate models for studying skin disease.

rows.title: A contested skin condition triggered by medicines
rows.summary: Some people who stop using topical steroids go through a withdrawal that leads to aggressive flare-ups. But not all physicians take the problem seriously.

rows.title: How the pelvis evolved to enable human bipedalism
rows.summary: Analyses of pelvis development in humans and other primates reveal how changes in bone-patterning processes helped humans to gain the ability to walk upright.

rows.title: A spiky armoured dinosaur from Africa causes a rethink of ankylosaur evolution
rows.summary: The body of Spicomellus , an armoured dinosaur (ankylosaur) from Morocco, was covered in extravagant spines, including spikes measuring nearly one metre in length that extended from a bony collar around the dinosaur’s neck. This elaborate armour might have been used for display, challenging the current theory of why ankylosaurs evolved their extensive body armour.

rows.title: How tree shrews see the world
rows.summary: In primates, visual information is processed hierarchically, moving from early brain regions that respond to low-level features to later-stage areas that recognize complex features and objects. In the tree shrew, a non-primate mammal, this hierarchy is evolutionarily conserved but is compressed, using the equivalent of an early primate brain area to recognize objects.

rows.title: Machine-learning model generates images using light
rows.summary: An optical system that induces random fluctuations in a laser beam could be faster and more efficient at generating images than conventional computers are.

rows.title: Glow-in-the-dark houseplants shine in rainbow of colours
rows.summary: Succulents become rechargeable night lights after injection with tiny phosphor particles.

rows.title: Here’s how to break into the Texas space industry
rows.summary: Four individuals from areas of academia to private industry share their tips on cracking into the state’s evolving aerospace industry.

rows.title: Deep gashes in the earth are slicing up cities, swallowing houses and displacing vast numbers of people
rows.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people are at risk of displacement from expanding ‘gullies’ in cities across Africa.

rows.title: Explaining the mental-health burden of atopic dermatitis
rows.summary: People with the inflammatory skin disease are at greater risk of neuropsychiatric conditions. Researchers are trying to find out why.

rows.title: Rewire
rows.summary: Steps towards a new life.

rows.title: Childhood eczema linked to mother’s stress during pregnancy
rows.summary: The causes of early-life eczema have been unclear, but evidence indicates that changes to fetal immune cells and sensory neurons during pregnancy play a key part.

rows.title: Ultrabroadband on-chip photonics for full-spectrum wireless communications
rows.summary: Adaptive wireless communication over an unprecedented frequency range spanning over 100 GHz can be achieved by a thin-film lithium niobate photonic wireless system, which can process a large flux of information at high speed.

rows.title: Thioester-mediated RNA aminoacylation and peptidyl-RNA synthesis in water
rows.summary: Aminoacyl-thiols reacting selectively with RNA diols over amine nucleophiles and demonstration of chemically controlled formation of peptidyl-RNA in water at neutral pH suggest an important role for thiol cofactors before the evolution of enzymes.

rows.title: Mapping urban gullies in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
rows.summary: An assessment at the scale of the Democratic Republic of the Congo shows that urban gullies are a growing problem, with 118,600 people displaced between 2004 and 2023.

rows.title: Rate and noise in human amygdala drive increased exploration in aversive learning
rows.summary: Human exploration is driven by two distinct neural mechanisms, a valence-independent rate signal and a valence-dependent global noise signal.

rows.title: Crystal structures of agonist-bound human cannabinoid receptor CB 1
rows.summary: Crystal structures of human CB 1 bound to two cannabinoid agonists reveal key features, including a twin toggle switch and binding pocket reduction, advancing understanding of receptor dynamics and guiding cannabinoid drug design.

rows.title: Maternal stress triggers early-life eczema through fetal mast cell programming
rows.summary: Prenatal stress triggers molecular dysregulations in fetal neuroimmune circuits, leading to altered mast cell and sensory neuron function, which predisposes offspring to develop eczema in response to otherwise harmless mechanical friction after birth.

rows.title: Electrically driven lasing from a dual-cavity perovskite device
rows.summary: An electrically driven perovskite laser is constructed by vertically integrating a low-threshold single-crystal perovskite microcavity sub-unit with a high-power microcavity perovskite LED sub-unit.

rows.title: Mechanical confinement governs phenotypic plasticity in melanoma
rows.summary: Mechanical confinement of cancer cells at the tumour–microenvironment interface induces phenotype switching through chromatin remodelling by HMGB2, leading to a more invasive and drug-resistant state in melanoma.

rows.title: Neural networks of the mouse visceromotor cortex
rows.summary: The dorsal peduncular area of the mouse brain functions as a network hub that integrates diverse cortical and thalamic inputs to regulate neuroendocrine and autonomic responses.

rows.title: Two-billion-year transitional oxygenation of the Earth’s surface
rows.summary: A 2.5-billion-year record of oxygen isotopes in sedimentary sulfate reveals the transitional oxygenation of the Earth’s surface and provides constraints on the dynamic, lengthy co-oxygenation of Earth’s atmosphere and oceans.

rows.title: One-shot design of functional protein binders with BindCraft
rows.summary: BindCraft, an open-source, automated pipeline for de novo protein binder design with experimental success rates of 10–100%, leverages AlphaFold2 weights to generate binders with nanomolar affinity without the need for high-throughput screening.

rows.title: Topological prethermal strong zero modes on superconducting processors
rows.summary: Stable and robust topological edge modes are observed at finite temperatures in an array of 100 programmable superconducting qubits because of emergent symmetries present in the prethermal regime of this system.

rows.title: Microbial iron oxide respiration coupled to sulfide oxidation
rows.summary: Genomic and biochemical analyses of prokaryotic sulfur metabolism identify diverse microorganisms with the capacity to oxidize sulfide using iron( iii ).

rows.title: Attosecond control and measurement of chiral photoionization dynamics
rows.summary: By introducing chiroptical spectroscopy with attosecond pulses, attosecond coherent control over photoelectron circular dichroism is demonstrated and measurements of chiral asymmetries in the forward–backward and angle-resolved photoionization delays of chiral molecules are reported.

rows.title: Global phenology maps reveal the drivers and effects of seasonal asynchrony
rows.summary: A global land surface phenology map predicts complex geographical discontinuities in flowering phenology, genetic divergence and harvest seasonality across a range of taxa.

rows.title: Haematopoietic stem cell number is not solely defined by niche availability
rows.summary: Haematopoietic stem cell numbers are restricted at both systemic and local levels.

rows.title: Dual-scale chemical ordering for cryogenic properties in CoNiV-based alloys
rows.summary: Dual-scale chemical ordering in CoNiV-based alloys improves the synergy of strength and ductility at cryogenic temperatures, providing an approach for obtaining high-performance metallic materials for cryogenic applications.

rows.title: A compressed hierarchy for visual form processing in the tree shrew
rows.summary: Tree shrews show a primate-like hierarchical organization in their visual pathway and object decoding accuracy, along with strongly face-selective cells, demonstrating how core computational principles of visual form processing found in primates are conserved yet compressed.

rows.title: Cocaine chemogenetics blunts drug-seeking by synthetic physiology
rows.summary: Cocaine chemogenetics in rats is a selective approach for countering drug reinforcement by clamping dopamine release in the presence of cocaine.

rows.title: Optical generative models
rows.summary: Optical generative models are demonstrated for the rapid and power-efficient creation of never-seen-before images of handwritten digits, fashion products, butterflies, human faces and Van Gogh-style artworks.

rows.title: The evolution of hominin bipedalism in two steps
rows.summary: The human pelvis exhibits distinct spatiotemporal ossification patterns and an ilium cartilage growth plate that is shifted perpendicularly compared with those of other mammals and non-human primates—two key adaptations that underlie bipedalism.

rows.title: Extreme armour in the world’s oldest ankylosaur
rows.summary: The ankylosaurian dinosaur Spicomellus afer possessed a tail weapon and uniquely elaborate dermal armour.

rows.title: Epidemiology models explain rumour spreading during France’s Great Fear of 1789
rows.summary: Epidemiological methods are used to show that the Great Fear of 1789, a series of peasant insurrections in rural revolutionary France, was driven by deliberate political action rather than spontaneous fear.

rows.title: Emotional AI is here — let’s shape it, not shun it
Scientific meetings debate the effect of climate change on future food production
rows.summary: The threat to global agriculture from climate change gains scientific consensus, and a musing about the reasoning ability of domestic cats in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

Arguments for blind peer review also need to be recognized

rows.summary: Lungs are complex organs to transplant, but the surgery is a step towards clinical trials.

rows.title: Author Correction: Disease-associated astrocyte epigenetic memory promotes CNS pathology
Five reasons why Nepal struggles to attract women into science
rows.summary: Biochemist Babita Paudel urges her female colleagues to dream big, work hard, take risks and embrace challenges.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Repeated heatwaves make your biological clock run fast
rows.summary: Repeated heatwaves can age you as much as smoking or drinking alcohol. Plus, a US Supreme Court ruling has derailed researchers’ efforts to reinstate cancelled research grants and six quantum myths debunked.

rows.title: Climate models need more frequent releases of input data — here’s how to do it
rows.summary: Annual updates to ‘climate forcing’ data sets would allow simulations to keep pace as global warming accelerates.

rows.title: Trial and error: research and the criminal justice system
rows.summary: Three researchers share their experiences working in and around the structures and systems of crime and punishment.

rows.title: NASA’s Earth-observing satellites are crucial — commercial missions cannot replace them
rows.summary: Private companies can track many changes on Earth from space, but both public and commercial satellite missions are needed to understand and protect the environment.

rows.title: Einstein hated entanglement — and five other quantum myths
rows.summary: There’s nothing intuitive about quantum theory — six physicists debunk some of the most common misconceptions.

rows.title: Author Correction: Complex genetic variation in nearly complete human genomes
