rows.summary: RFK Jr has vowed to find out what’s responsible, but scientists say he is ignoring answers from decades of research.

rows.title: Repeated heatwaves can age you as much as smoking or drinking
rows.summary: Long-term study suggests that the more heatwaves people are exposed to, the more it accelerates body ageing.

rows.title: Scalable total synthesis of saxitoxin and related natural products
rows.summary: Using a combination of radical retrosynthesis, biocatalysis and C–H functionalization logic, a concise and scalable approach to the synthesis of saxitoxin and derivatives thereof in fewer than ten steps is presented.

rows.title: I trawl coastlines to study the impacts of microplastics on marine life
rows.summary: Biologist Lorenzo Cozzolino examines how these tiny particles are affecting the behaviour and physiology of molluscs, crustaceans and seaweeds.

rows.title: My moonshot to preserve endangered species
rows.summary: Coral cryobiologist Mary Hagedorn wants to bank biological samples at the frozen lunar south pole.

rows.title: How a self-taught biologist transformed nature writing — and inspired Darwin
rows.summary: Gilbert White’s journals reveal his intimate relationship with his surroundings — and call attention to changes wreaked by climate change today.

rows.title: Does dark energy spawn from black holes? Could be a bright idea
rows.summary: Cosmic maps appear consistent with the proposal that black holes could cause the Universe's accelerating expansion.

rows.title: How a fraudulent scientist faked his career and other cautionary tales: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: Glitch cop
rows.summary: The wrong arm of the law.

rows.title: RFK Jr demanded a vaccine study be retracted — the journal said no
rows.summary: In a rare move for a US public official, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr called for a Danish paper finding no link between aluminium in vaccines and disease to be retracted.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Primates might have evolved in the cold climate of North America
rows.summary: The common ancestors of all modern primates might have flourished in cold winters, not the warm jungle. Plus, peer reviewers are more likely to approve articles that cite their own work and what’s really behind thirst.

rows.title: US Supreme Court allows NIH to cut $2 billion in research grants
rows.summary: The decision will hinder lawsuits against grant terminations, legal specialists say.

rows.title: Net zero needs AI — five actions to realize its promise
rows.summary: Without artificial-intelligence technologies, balancing human-caused greenhouse-gas emissions with carbon removals by 2050 is out of reach. Action in five areas is needed to keep this goal alive.

rows.title: Author Correction: Macrophages excite muscle spindles with glutamate to bolster locomotion
Human brain organoids reveal new path for Alzheimer’s drugs
rows.summary: Organ models with hallmarks of the disease show marked improvement when a protein’s levels are restored.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Plastics pollution talks end in stalemate
rows.summary: Negotiations over a global plastic pollution treaty have failed, for now. Plus, how the brain adapts after a limb is amputated and how to make electric cars more affordable.

rows.title: David Nabarro obituary: global-health leader who fought malnutrition, malaria, Ebola and COVID-19
rows.summary: Persuasive physician who brought research evidence to the heart of global policy decisions.

rows.title: Peer reviewers more likely to approve articles that cite their own work
rows.summary: Preprint examines how citations can influence the review process.

rows.title: ORCID launched more than a decade ago, but has yet to fulfil its potential
rows.summary: Many author-identifier profiles are ‘empty’, making it difficult to track who’s publishing what.

rows.title: The brain’s map of the body is surprisingly stable — even after a limb is lost
rows.summary: Study challenges the textbook idea that the brain region that processes body sensations reorganizes itself after limb amputation.

rows.title: Water in the ‘Devil’s Comet’ shares a source with Earth’s oceans
rows.summary: Chemical profiling traces the source of water in one of the brightest known comets to keep returning to the Solar System.

rows.title: The world’s largest methane emitter manages to curb one source
rows.summary: Output of the powerful greenhouse gas by China’s energy sector peaked in 2014, an inventory shows.

rows.title: Fusion energy gets a boost from cold fusion chemistry
rows.summary: Chemists used an electrochemical method to enhance the rates of fusion in a desktop reactor — plus, how microbes give chocolate its taste.

rows.title: When will dengue strike? Outbreaks sync with heat and rain
rows.summary: Analysis uncovers seasonal patterns of the mosquito-borne disease across the Americas, which could anticipate future outbreaks.

rows.title: Could these five future agricultural innovations slow down climate change?
rows.summary: From AI-powered bee monitors to genetically modified yeasts that make protein, here are some solutions that are set to revolutionize the future of food.

rows.title: Dying star reveals its inner structure
rows.summary: A star that was stripped of its outer layers shortly before it exploded as a supernova offers astronomers an unprecedented glimpse of a stellar interior.

rows.title: What counts as plagiarism? AI-generated papers pose new risks
rows.summary: Researchers argue over whether ‘novel’ AI-generated works use others’ ideas without credit.

rows.title: Before making a career move, try an experiment
rows.summary: How to use a curiosity-led strategy to find the right role.

rows.title: Securing climate justice in the courtroom
rows.summary: Advances in climate modelling are clarifying accountability for global warming.

rows.title: Rare skeletal condition caused by enzyme’s failure to rescue a catalytic cycle
rows.summary: When enzymes require rescue strategies to complete progression through their reaction, but natural safety nets fail, disease states can ensue.

rows.title: Pay gap between nationals and migrants mainly due to unequal access to high-paying jobs
rows.summary: In high-income nations, immigrants earn substantially less than do people born in those countries, mainly because of a lack of access to high-paying jobs. Addressing this economic disparity will require policy efforts that expand access to better-paying occupations and firms rather than just enforcing policies of equal pay for equal work.

rows.title: How citizen science can help to solve the global freshwater crisis
rows.summary: Encouraging people to test their local rivers and lakes with simple kits could spark a shift in how we manage water.

rows.title: ‘A double-whammy problem’: how plastic dust is altering natural processes
rows.summary: Carbon emissions from plastics production are no surprise. But when plastic turns to dust, it also affects how the planet absorbs carbon from the air, on land and in the oceans.

rows.title: Low-energy nuclear fusion boosted by electrochemistry
rows.summary: Electrochemistry can boost processes that trap atoms inside a metal. A reactor uses these trapped atoms, combined with an ion beam, as fuel for nuclear fusion.

rows.title: Feeding bees with engineered yeast combats colony decline
rows.summary: Nutritionally complete food for honeybees ( Apis mellifera ) has been generated by engineering yeast to produce rare but essential sterol molecules found in pollen. Honeybee colonies fed with the yeast-supplemented diet produced offspring for longer periods than did those fed sterol-deficient diets. This approach makes it possible to rear honeybees without pollen.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Tiny marsupial bounces back from near-extinction
rows.summary: The comeback of an Australian animal, a new moon of Uranus and how a scientist invented a life-saving frog sauna.

rows.title: Visualizing lipid transport in cells
rows.summary: Lipid molecules form the membranes that organize cellular biochemistry in all domains of life. Imaging approaches have been developed to visualize different types of lipid at subcellular scales and show that these molecules are sorted into membranes by lipid transfer proteins, rather than by vesicles.

rows.title: Anticancer compounds that exploit a compromised checkpoint in the cell cycle
rows.summary: Many cancer-driving mutations disable a key checkpoint in the cell’s cycle between growth and division, resulting in unchecked activity of the E2F family of transcription factor proteins. A set of compounds developed to directly block key regulators of the cell cycle called cyclins can suppress the growth of cancers driven by high E2F activity.

rows.title: Time’s arrow
rows.summary: Know your place.

rows.title: Structural basis for the dynamic regulation of mTORC1 by amino acids
rows.summary: Using cryo-electron microscopy, the interactions of Sestrin2 and CASTOR1 with GATOR2 were resolved, revealing how mTORC1 activation is regulated and how nutrient availability triggers signalling for cellular growth.

rows.title: mAChR4 suppresses liver disease via GAP-induced antimicrobial immunity
rows.summary: Chronic alcohol use in humans and mice downregulates small intestinal mAChR4 and reduces goblet-cell-associated antigen passage formation, disrupting antimicrobial immunity.

rows.title: Molecular mechanism of ultrafast transport by plasma membrane Ca 2+ -ATPases
rows.summary: Structural insights into ultrafast Ca 2+ transport by plasma membrane Ca 2+ -ATPases are provided, highlighting an essential role for PtdIns(4,5)P 2 dynamics.

rows.title: Proximity screening greatly enhances electronic quality of graphene
rows.summary: Screening by a graphite gate placed at 1 nm proximity to graphene produces transformative improvement in its electronic quality, reducing charge inhomogeneity by two orders of magnitude.

rows.title: TCF1 and LEF1 promote B-1a cell homeostasis and regulatory function
rows.summary: The transcription factors TCF1 and LEF1 promote self-renewal and regulatory functions in B-1a cells.

rows.title: Experimental determination of partial charges with electron diffraction
rows.summary: An experimental method is used to assign partial charges based on crystal structure determination through electron diffraction, applicable to any crystalline compound.

rows.title: Targeting G1–S-checkpoint-compromised cancers with cyclin A/B RxL inhibitors
rows.summary: Dual cyclin A/B RxL inhibitors selectively kill small cell lung cancer cells and other cancer cells with high E2F activity.

rows.title: Realization of a doped quantum antiferromagnet in a Rydberg tweezer array
rows.summary: A doped quantum antiferromagnet is obtained by using a Rydberg tweezer array comprising three levels encoding spins and holes to implement a tunable model that allows the study of previously inaccessible parameter regimes.

rows.title: Electron flow matching for generative reaction mechanism prediction
rows.summary: A new tool based on generative machine learning called FlowER uses flow matching to model reactions as the redistribution of electrons between reactants and products, enabling the enforcement of mass conservation in reaction prediction.

rows.title: A fluorescent-protein spin qubit
rows.summary: An optically addressable fluorescent-protein spin qubit is realized using enhanced yellow fluorescent protein; the qubit can be coherently controlled at liquid-nitrogen temperatures and the spin detected at room temperature in cells.

rows.title: Electrochemical loading enhances deuterium fusion rates in a metal target
rows.summary: A benchtop fusion reactor, called the Thunderbird Reactor, is described, showing that electrochemically loading a metal lattice with deuterium could enhance nuclear fusion rates when that metal is also bombarded by deuterium ions.

rows.title: Thymic epithelial cells amplify epigenetic noise to promote immune tolerance
rows.summary: The activity of the tumour-suppressor protein p53 is repressed in the thymus to augment fluctuations in background chromatin accessibility as a means of mediating ectopic gene expression and immune tolerance.

rows.title: Emerging evidence of abrupt changes in the Antarctic environment
rows.summary: Abrupt changes are developing across Antarctica’s ice, ocean and biological systems; some of these changes are intensifying faster than equivalent Arctic changes, potentially irreversibly, and their interactions are expected to worsen other impacts across the Antarctic environment and global climate system.

rows.title: Engineered yeast provides rare but essential pollen sterols for honeybees
rows.summary: Genetic engineering of a yeast strain provides rare but essential pollen sterols for honeybee colonies.

rows.title: Extremely stripped supernova reveals a silicon and sulfur formation site
rows.summary: Observations of SN 2021yfj reveal that its progenitor is a massive star stripped down to its O/Si/S core, which remarkably continued to expel vast quantities of silicon-, sulfur-, and argon-rich material before the explosion, informing us that current theories for how stars evolve are too narrow.

rows.title: Atomic dynamics of gas-dependent oxide reducibility
rows.summary: Environmental transmission electron microscopy reveals distinct atomistic pathways for the reduction of NiO to metallic nickel by CO and H 2 , with H 2 more effective in transforming the entire bulk material.

rows.title: Cancer-induced nerve injury promotes resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy
rows.summary: Perineural invasion and cancer-induced nerve injury of tumour-associated nerves are associated with poor response to anti-PD-1 therapy, which can be reversed by combining anti-PD-1 therapy with anti-inflammatory interventions.

rows.title: A novel bacterial protein family that catalyses nitrous oxide reduction
rows.summary: Cultivation of tropical soil microorganisms combined with physiological experiments and bioinformatics analyses identify a family of clade III lactonase-type nitrous oxide reductases with low sequence identity but high 3D structural similarity to known nitrous oxide reductases.

rows.title: SLC45A4 is a pain gene encoding a neuronal polyamine transporter
rows.summary: The SLC45A4 gene encodes a neuronal polyamine transporter and is linked to pain response in humans and mice.

rows.title: Silicate precursor silane detected in cold low-metallicity brown dwarf
rows.summary: Silane, which is a precursor to the sandy surfaces of rocky planets and dusty clouds on gas giants, is seen directly in another world—a low-metallicity brown dwarf in which oxidation is slow and gas mixing is fast.

rows.title: A missing enzyme-rescue metabolite as cause of a rare skeletal dysplasia
rows.summary: In mammals, the enzyme TGDS produces UDP-4-keto-6-deoxyglucose, which binds to the catalytic pocket of UDP-xylose synthase, thereby regenerating the essential NAD + cofactor of UDP-xylose synthase in conditions of low NAD + .

rows.title: Quantitative imaging of lipid transport in mammalian cells
rows.summary: Directional, non-vesicular lipid transport is responsible for fast, species-selective lipid sorting into organelle membranes.

rows.title: Discovery of a widespread chemical signalling pathway in the Bacteroidota
rows.summary: The N- acyl-cyclolysine system regulates the expression of co-localized operons encoding diverse secreted molecules in Bacteroidota.

rows.title: Flat-panel laser displays through large-scale photonic integrated circuits
rows.summary: Photonic integrated circuits allow laser displays to be flattened into a compact form factor while improving efficiency and colour performance.

rows.title: STING induces ZBP1-mediated necroptosis independently of TNFR1 and FADD
rows.summary: STING-activation-induced necroptosis (STAIN) is a central pathogenic mechanism in both caspase-8-deficient inflammation and STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy.

rows.title: Network synchrony creates neural filters promoting quiescence in Drosophila
rows.summary: In Drosophila , coherent slow-wave activity between sleep-promoting and locomotion-promoting neural networks provides a brain state structure that allows for quiescent behaviours.

rows.title: Axonal injury is a targetable driver of glioblastoma progression
rows.summary: Axonal injury, induced in the white matter by expansion of early tumour cells, is a key driver of glioblastoma progression.

rows.title: African countries must rethink health-care financing

rows.summary: John Scopes convicted for teaching human evolution, and a discussion of international collaboration in X-ray astronomy, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: A baby benefits from personalized gene editing in the clinic
rows.summary: An infant with an inherited life-threatening metabolic condition has responded to a tailored therapy that uses the gene-editing tool CRISPR to correct a specific mutation.

rows.summary: Most studies on how exercise affects the survival of people with cancer have been observational. A clinical trial provides compelling evidence of the benefits of physical activity.

rows.title: People are having fewer babies: Is it really the end of the world?
rows.summary: Steep population declines in most countries are expected to have negative impacts over the next several generations, but adaptation is possible.

rows.title: Ancient coins unveil web of trade across southeast Asia
rows.summary: Images on first-millennium coins hint at economic relationships across the region.

rows.title: Raw ingredients: turning algal protein into mock meat

rows.title: Why chocolate tastes so good: microbes that fine-tune its flavour
rows.summary: Manipulating the microbial communities involved in cocoa-bean fermentation could make chocolate even more delicious.

rows.title: Why nurturing the gut microbiota could resolve depression and anxiety

rows.title: Beyond AlphaFold: how AI is decoding the grammar of the genome

rows.title: Why amphibious, wet environments hold the key to climate adaptation
rows.summary: As the planet braces for climate-change-induced fluctuations, the wisdom of communities living at the intersection of land and water could offer valuable lessons.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Why some places on our bodies heal without scars

rows.title: Watch rappelling robots dive into a lava tube — for science
rows.summary: Test run shows how a team of three autonomous robots could search for extraterrestrial environments suitable for sheltering humans.

rows.title: These tiny flyers levitate on the Sun’s heat alone
rows.summary: Design could help to probe the ‘ignorosphere’, a layer of ultra-thin air that has largely escaped exploration by balloons, aircraft and satellites.

rows.title: Many planets might be born with orbits misaligned from the spin of their stars
rows.summary: An analysis of the geometry of young Sun-like stars with planet-forming disks, measured by ground- and space-based observatories, shows that at least one-third of disks are misaligned with the spin of their central star. This distribution of star–disk configurations seeds the later diversity of planetary system architectures.

A humidity measure that accounts for redistribution of water across the landscape
rows.summary: A humidity index has been developed that considers lateral flow along rivers and groundwater systems, as well as precipitation, potential evaporation and plant transpiration. It performs better than a conventional humidity index when describing water availability for ecosystems and societies in arid regions.

rows.title: Just how bad will climate change get? The only way to know is to fund basic research
rows.summary: Predictions of global warming are uncertain. That’s why we need to keep finding out how the climate system works.

rows.title: The perplexing body plan of arrow worms decoded
rows.summary: A genome sequence and single-cell atlas of a marine worm species point towards bursts of gene emergence, duplication and loss as the drivers of lineage-specific body traits.

rows.title: Levitating platform could ride sunlight into the ‘ignorosphere’
rows.summary: A nano-engineered structure that levitates when a laser of a similar intensity to sunlight is shone on it could help scientists to study a hard-to-reach region of the atmosphere.

Octopus motion in the ocean tracked by a deep-sea 3D camera
rows.summary: The EyeRIS camera system collects 3D visual data in near real time about the structure and biomechanics of marine life. Filming pearl octopuses ( Muusoctopus robustus ) with this system has provided a detailed look at the locomotion of free-living octopuses.

rows.title: Spatial correlation in economic analysis of climate change
Oestrogen defends against kidney damage caused by iron-dependent cell death
rows.summary: Differences in protection against ferroptosis explain why men and postmenopausal women are more susceptible than premenopausal women to acute kidney injury.

rows.title: Air pollution could be reduced by incentivizing local government officials to control crop burning
rows.summary: Crop-residue burning in South Asia decreases by up to 14.5% when smoke from fires would affect bureaucrats’ home districts instead of neighbouring ones. Bureaucratic action to punish farmers deters future fires by a further 13%. Thus, using administrator incentives to control crop burning could guide policy towards improving air quality and reducing infant and child mortality.

rows.title: Acidic oxygen reduction by single-atom Fe catalysts on curved supports
rows.summary: A new type of Fe/N–C catalyst composed of numerous nanoprotrusions dispersed on two-dimensional carbon layers with inner-embedded single Fe-atom sites has been developed that delivers a high-performance platinum group metal-free proton-exchange membrane fuel cell.

rows.title: The geologic history of marine dissolved organic carbon from iron oxides
rows.summary: A direct proxy for past dissolved organic carbon signatures using co-precipitated organic carbon in iron ooids enables reconstruction of marine dissolved organic carbon signals dating back to the Palaeoproterozoic.

rows.title: New discoveries of Australopithecus and Homo from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia
rows.summary: Hominin fossils from the Ledi-Geraru Research Project area, Ethiopia, suggest that early Homo and Australopithecus species co-existed in the region more than 2.5 million years ago.

rows.title: Expanding the cytokine receptor alphabet reprograms T cells into diverse states
rows.summary: Orthogonal chimeric receptors containing intracellular domains for IL-4R, IL-20R, IL-22R and GCSFR reprogram T cells to promote distinct natural and synthetic cell states with functional and therapeutic implications.

rows.title: NASP modulates histone turnover to drive PARP inhibitor resistance
rows.summary: PARP inhibitor treatment triggers histone release from the chromatin in cancer cells; consequently, targeting the histone chaperone NASP renders cells vulnerable to PARP inhibition.

rows.title: Clone copy number diversity is linked to survival in lung cancer
rows.summary: A study presents ALPACA, a computational method for inferring clone- and allele-specific copy numbers of individual clones from multi-sample bulk DNA-sequencing data, and demonstrates its use to study metastasis trajectories.

rows.title: Bending the curve of land degradation to achieve global environmental goals
rows.summary: The Rio Conventions’ objectives can be met by transforming food systems to bend the curve of land degradation.

rows.title: Establishment of chromatin architecture interplays with embryo hypertranscription
rows.summary: A study reveals progressive cohesin loading and a hypertranscription state responsible for the formation of genic cohesin islands at active regulatory genes in mouse embryos, highlighting an interplay between chromatin architecture and transcription as they are established for the first time.

rows.title: Multiple oestradiol functions inhibit ferroptosis and acute kidney injury
rows.summary: 17β-oestradiol establishes an anti-ferroptotic state in female kidney tubules.

rows.title: Human emissions drive recent trends in North Pacific climate variations
rows.summary: The main multidecadal variations in the PDO index during the twentieth century, including the ongoing, decades-long negative trend, were largely driven by human emissions of aerosols and greenhouse gases rather than internal processes.

rows.title: Elementary 3D organization of active and silenced E. coli genome
rows.summary: An ultra-high-resolution chromatin organization map of E. coli , using Micro-C, reveals intricate chromatin structures involved in the silencing of horizontally transferred genes and those associated with active operons.

rows.title: The genomic origin of the unique chaetognath body plan
rows.summary: Genomic, single-cell transcriptomic and epigenetic analyses show that chaetognaths, following extensive gene loss in the gnathiferan lineage, relied on newly evolved genes and lineage-specific tandem duplications, not caused by a whole-genome duplication event, to shape their distinctive body plan.

rows.title: Delocalized electrolyte design enables 600 Wh kg −1 lithium metal pouch cells
rows.summary: Lithium metal battery performance is optimized using a delocalized electrolyte design that induces a disordered solvation microenvironment, thereby combining the advantages of the solvent-dominated and anion-dominated structures of conventional electrolytes.

rows.title: n-Type thermoelectric elastomers
rows.summary: A microphase crosslinking strategy, leveraging aziridine-based crosslinkers, is used to render organic thermoelectric materials stretchable and elastic.

rows.title: Calving-driven fjord dynamics resolved by seafloor fibre sensing
rows.summary: Iceberg calving can act as a submarine melt amplifier through excitation of transient internal waves.

rows.title: Countrywide natural experiment links built environment to physical activity
rows.summary: By analysing the smartphone data of 2,112,288 participants, in particular observing and comparing the activity of the same individual in two different environments, we find that increases in the walkability of environments result in increases in daily physical activity, providing evidence of the importance of the built environment on physical health.

rows.title: Large riverbed sediment flux sustained for a decade after an earthquake

rows.title: Photophoretic flight of perforated structures in near-space conditions
rows.summary: A photophoretic aircraft that can levitate via thermal transpiration is achieved under near-space conditions, providing a potential platform for climate sensing, communications and Martian exploration.

rows.title: Can creativity in science be learnt? These researchers think so

rows.summary: Indigenous scholars set out eight steps to stop marginalization in academia and to enable a shared Indigenous agenda in science.

rows.title: The peer-review crisis: how to fix an overloaded system

rows.title: Is your AI benchmark lying to you?
rows.summary: Artificial intelligence models are too often assessed against flawed goals — a stumbling block for progress.

rows.title: Does lithium deficiency contribute to Alzheimer’s disease?
rows.summary: Lithium in the brain has been found to protect against cognitive decline. Restoring lost lithium could be a new angle from which to tackle Alzheimer’s disease.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: NINJ1 regulates plasma membrane fragility under mechanical strain
Whole-genome sequencing of 490,640 UK Biobank participants
rows.summary: A study reports whole-genome sequences for 490,640 participants from the UK Biobank and combines these data with phenotypic data to provide new insights into the relationship between human variation and sequence variation.

rows.title: Novel assembly of a head–trunk interface in the sister group of jawed vertebrates
rows.summary: Imaging of a Devonian jawless fish reveals advanced features previously thought to be exclusive to jawed vertebrates, challenging the idea that jaws were the primary driver for the evolution of derived traits in the vertebrate body plan.

rows.title: Hominins on Sulawesi during the Early Pleistocene
rows.summary: Early Pleistocene artefacts at Calio suggest that Sulawesi was populated by hominins at around the same time as Flores, if not earlier.

rows.title: RNA N-glycosylation enables immune evasion and homeostatic efferocytosis
rows.summary: N-glycans on glycoRNAs prevent innate immune sensing of endogenous small RNAs, and the natural mechanism they use demonstrates how glycoRNAs exist on the cell surface and in the endosomal network without inducing autoinflammatory responses.

rows.title: In situ light-field imaging of octopus locomotion reveals simplified control
rows.summary: Using an advanced imaging system called EyeRIS, locomotion in deep-sea octopuses could be studied, revealing simplified crawling patterns that could inspire the design of robots.

rows.title: Therapeutic genetic restoration through allogeneic brain microglia replacement
rows.summary: Brain-restricted allogeneic transplantation of myeloid progenitors enables microglia replacement without the need for genetic engineering or systemic cytotoxic preconditioning.

rows.title: Microglia regulate GABAergic neurogenesis in prenatal human brain through IGF1
rows.summary: Microglia-derived IGF1 promotes the proliferation of GABAergic progenitors and neuroblasts in the human medial ganglionic eminence, contributing to the extended production of GABAergic neurons and an expanded cognitive capacity in the human brain.

rows.title: NSD2 inhibitors rewire chromatin to treat lung and pancreatic cancers
rows.summary: A highly potent and selective small-molecule catalytic inhibitor of the protein lysine methyltransferase NSD2 shows therapeutic efficacy in preclinical models of KRAS-driven pancreatic cancer and lung cancer.

rows.title: High-accuracy laser spectroscopy of \({{\bf{H}}}_{{\bf{2}}}^{{\boldsymbol{+}}}\) and the proton–electron mass ratio
rows.summary: Doppler-free laser spectroscopy is used to measure with high precision a rovibrational transition frequency of trapped and cooled \({{\rm{H}}}_{2}^{+}\) ions.

rows.title: Structural basis of fast N-type inactivation in K v channels
rows.summary: This paper explores how voltage-gated potassium channels can plug the pore to prevent the conductance of ions during inactivation.

rows.title: Excised DNA circles from V(D)J recombination promote relapsed leukaemia
rows.summary: Excised signal circles are circular DNA by-products of V(D)J recombination that form a complex with the V(D)J recombinase, and when increased in abundance, result in increased mutagenesis, causing adverse outcomes in cancer.

rows.title: A diverse and distinct microbiome inside living trees
rows.summary: Microbiome analyses of living trees show that a single tree can host approximately one trillion bacteria, with microbial communities distinctly partitioned between heartwood and sapwood and with minimal similarity to other tissues or ecosystem components.

rows.title: Data-driven de novo design of super-adhesive hydrogels
rows.summary: A data-driven approach integrates data mining, experimentation and machine learning to design high-performance adhesive hydrogels from scratch, tailored for demanding underwater environments.

rows.title: Stronger El Niños reduce tropical forest arthropod diversity and function
rows.summary: Time-series data from tropical forests tracking weather and declines in arthropod diversity and function show that fluctuations in species were largely dependent on their El Niño sensitivity and ecological specialization.

rows.title: Optical control of resonances in temporally symmetry-broken metasurfaces
rows.summary: The ultrafast optical control of resonances in temporally symmetry-broken metasurfaces allows resonances to be created, annihilated or programmably manipulated, which is useful for applications that require active real-time tunability.

rows.title: Lithium deficiency and the onset of Alzheimer’s disease
rows.summary: Lithium has an essential role in the brain and is deficient early in Alzheimer’s disease, which can be recapitulated in mice and treated with a novel lithium salt that restores the physiological level.

rows.title: A global humidity index with lateral hydrologic flows
rows.summary: Estimating lateral subsidies by river and groundwater using a global hydrology model and incorporating them into the conventional global humidity index reduces aridity in the receiving lowlands and better explains ecosystem patterns.

rows.title: EBV induces CNS homing of B cells attracting inflammatory T cells
rows.summary: Epstein–Barr virus infection generates a neuroinvasive B cell subset, which recruits activated T cells to the central nervous system, promoting multiple sclerosis.

rows.title: The science fiction science method
rows.summary: The ‘science fiction science’ method simulates future technologies and collects quantitative data on the attitudes and behaviours of participants in various future scenarios, with the aim of predicting impacts of future technologies before they arrive.

rows.title: Microglia–neuron crosstalk through Hex–GM2–MGL2 maintains brain homeostasis
rows.summary: A mode of bidirectional microglia–neuron crosstalk through Hex–GM2–MGL2 and centred around GM2 ganglioside turnover is essential for homeostatic regulation of central nervous system membrane components.

rows.title: One-third of Sun-like stars are born with misaligned planet-forming disks
rows.summary: Assessment of the stellar obliquities of a sample of resolved protoplanetary disk systems indicates that one-third of Sun-like stars are born with misaligned planet-forming disks, suggesting that the origin of star–planet configurations, including many misaligned planetary orbits, may be primordial.

rows.title: Parent-of-origin effects on complex traits in up to 236,781 individuals
rows.summary: A novel multistep strategy reveals how parent-of-origin effects shape complex traits in large-scale biobanks.

rows.title: Kinetic turbulence drives MHD equilibrium change via 3D reconnection
rows.summary: Observations from laboratory experiments involving two flux ropes show that electron beams induce magnetic turbulence and abruptly merge into a single structure, altering the magnetic topology in the magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) regime — a process supported by three-dimensional (3D) particle-in-cell simulations.

rows.title: Breed giant prawns to withstand disease and climate change
Conserve marine migratory species to protect ecological links between land and sea
Tackle fake citations generated by AI
Mystery of billions of sea-star deaths solved at last
rows.summary: Experiments identify a bacterium as the cause of sea-star wasting disease, which has devastated populations along the western coast of North America.

rows.title: Plan-B careers can be a force for good in science
Don’t train medical AI on patients’ data without their knowledge
Tiny motor uses heat to perform molecular magic
rows.summary: A nanoscopic machine transforms a molecular chain into interlocking loops.

rows.title: Protect Palestinian archaeological sites during war
Baboons defend themselves by throwing stones
rows.summary: Fieldworkers dodge monkeys’ rocky missiles, and abandoned plans to make cork mattresses, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Overcome threats to renewable energy through skilful statecraft
Protection from biological hazards at work arrives at last
Scientists can help stop a slide to nuclear war — don’t shut them out again
rows.summary: It has taken the United Nations nearly 40 years to commission another study on the effects of nuclear conflict. Better late than never.

rows.title: Version control: how I combat the rise of generative AI in the classroom
rows.summary: I was worried that ChatGPT was composing my students’ essays. Looking at the writing process step by step can combat this and has other benefits, too.

rows.title: ‘The Sun had fallen to Earth’ — a survivor’s recollection of the Hiroshima bombing
rows.summary: Eighty years after the atomic bomb was dropped on Japan, it is crucial that witness accounts are saved. Here is what one man told me.

rows.title: Daily briefing: This marsupial is biofluorescent — the month’s best science images
rows.summary: A glowing marsupial and science-inspired Haute Couture are among the month’s sharpest science shots. Plus, ultra-processed foods could make it harder to shed weight and a scientific clash over bold ‘de-extinction’ claims.

rows.title: Why suppressing all wildfires has made today’s megafires worse
rows.summary: Satellites, drones and artificial-intelligence tools can improve fire management — but they must be informed by wildfire science, or we risk worsening the problem for decades.

rows.title: Does ResearchGate have a growing credibility problem?
rows.summary: A librarian who claims researchers are gaming the system by using fake profiles and inflated metrics explains how the platform can combat misuse.

rows.title: How I’m electrifying transportation in Tanzania
rows.summary: Technician Erasto Job assembles and fixes electric three-wheelers for TRí, a sustainable transportation company in Dar es Salaam.

rows.title: Glow-in-the-dark marsupial shows off its luminous fur — July’s best science images
rows.summary: The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’ s photo team.

rows.title: This company claimed to ‘de-extinct’ dire wolves. Then the fighting started
rows.summary: Colossal’s bold announcements have drawn criticism from many scientists, but the billion-dollar firm is not backing down.

rows.title: Eating ultra-processed foods could make it harder to lose weight
rows.summary: Trial compared effects of diets with differing levels of food processing.

rows.title: Environmental politics is doomed to fail — unless we tell better stories
rows.summary: Political thinking on global crises has become trapped. We need a new narrative.

rows.title: We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents
rows.summary: The deployment of capable AI agents raises fresh questions about safety, human–machine relationships and social coordination.

rows.title: To save lives in heatwaves, focus on how human bodies work
rows.summary: Strategies for heat-health preparedness should concentrate on cooling people, not just the air.

rows.title: What it’s like fighting racism and sexism in shark science
rows.summary: Jaida Elcock, a co-founder of Minorities in Shark Sciences, talks about how pushback drives her forward.

rows.title: Why I co-developed a research career launchpad for first generation students
rows.summary: Arezoo Khodayari and a colleague at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory provide paid internships aimed at under-represented groups in science.

rows.title: Exclusive: retraction-prone editors identified at megajournal PLoS ONE
rows.summary: Study says small editor group handled many problematic manuscripts — and a Nature investigation finds out who they are.

rows.title: Real-time in situ magnetization reprogramming for soft robotics
rows.summary: A real-time in situ magnetization reprogramming method for magnetic soft robots enables dynamic shape control, cooperative multi-tool manipulation and expanded actuation abilities.

rows.title: Direct identification of Ac and No molecules with an atom-at-a-time technique
rows.summary: Mass number measurements of the molecular species produced when ions of actinium (Ac) and nobelium (No) are exposed to trace amounts of H 2 O and N 2 demonstrate direct species identification using an atom-at-a-time technique for heavy elements.

rows.title: I could not have become an astronomer on my own
rows.summary: An astronomy conference changed the course of Brenda Namumba’s career and taught her the importance of networks.

rows.title: India to penalize universities with too many retractions
rows.summary: Having a lot of withdrawn papers will soon count against institutions but some warn the policy could create issues.

rows.title: ‘Congress has your back’: US senators tell scientists they want to protect NIH budget
rows.summary: Senate budget bill includes small increase for the health-research agency — but faces a long road before being signed into law.

rows.title: mRNA vaccines for HIV trigger strong immune response in people
rows.summary: Results from early-stage trial show that 80% of participants who received one of two HIV vaccine candidates produced antibodies against viral proteins.

rows.title: Potato, tomato: the roots of the modern tater
rows.summary: A meet-cute millions of years ago gave rise to the tubers of today’s potatoes.

rows.title: The ocean's deepest animal ecosystem
rows.summary: Six miles below the surface of the Pacific an unexpected array of life flourishes.

rows.title: Intricate origins of ice mummy’s ink revealed
rows.summary: Imaging suggests that more than one tattooist applied pigment to the hands and forearms of a woman who lived more than two millennia ago.

rows.title: How allergens make us cough and wheeze — by poking holes in airway cells
rows.summary: The immune system senses damage to cell membranes caused by pore-forming proteins and mounts a response.

rows.title: My AI chatbot thinks my idea is fundable
rows.summary: A dialogue with artificial intelligence has changed how Angela Steinauer thinks through her ideas. The trick is staying sceptical and asking better questions.

rows.title: Google AI model mines trillions of images to create maps of Earth ‘at any place and time’
rows.summary: The system will save time spent on processing satellite data, researchers say — but they hope the tech firm will share more about how it works.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Respiratory illness can ‘wake up’ dormant cancer cells
rows.summary: Illnesses such as COVID-19 and flu can rouse sleeping cancer cells. Plus, a miniature neutrino detector and methane-loving life at the bottom of the Pacific ocean.

rows.title: Retraction Note: Parkin and PINK1 mitigate STING-induced inflammation
Author Correction: Dendritic, delayed, stochastic CaMKII activation in behavioural time scale plasticity
Author Correction: Dual interfacial H-bonding-enhanced deep-blue hybrid copper–iodide LEDs
Earth’s deepest ecosystem discovered six miles below the sea
rows.summary: Submersible dives reveal a startling diversity of life in the depths of the Pacific Ocean — plus, how respiratory infections could awaken dormant cancer cells.

rows.title: Lava planets’ atmospheres give away what lies beneath
rows.summary: Modelling suggests that data collected by JWST will be able to distinguish between planets that are molten to the core and those that are not.

rows.title: ‘Sleeping’ cancer cells in the lungs can be roused by COVID and flu
rows.summary: Inflammation from the respiratory infections seems to be the culprit, study in mice finds.

rows.title: Chemicals seeping from the sea floor sustain an extreme-depth ecosystem
rows.summary: Thriving communities that derive their energy from chemical reactions have been discovered at the bottom of deep trenches in the northwest Pacific Ocean. The presence of these chemosynthetic ecosystems challenges long-standing assumptions about life’s potential at extreme depths and the intricate carbon cycle of the deep ocean.

rows.title: Miniature neutrino detector promises to test laws of physics
rows.summary: Neutrinos from a nuclear reactor are caught by a technique known as coherent scattering.

rows.title: SMART tool builds proteins on cell surfaces
rows.summary: Researchers can target effector proteins to cells on the basis of which molecules those cells express.

rows.title: Daily briefing: What does quantum mechanics mean anyway?
rows.summary: A Nature survey reveals that physicists disagree on even the basics of what quantum mechanics means in reality. Plus, sugars on a cell’s surface mapped at unprecedented resolution and the world’s wildest biology conference.

rows.title: Laser beams programmed to form various shapes by nanodisk arrays
rows.summary: ‘Metalasers’ have been developed using metasurfaces comprising nanodisks, each with an off-centre hole. By changing the rotation angle of the nanodisks’ holes, the wavefront of the metalaser’s emission can be modified to generate arbitrarily shaped beam profiles, including focal spots, vortices and holograms, with notably low levels of ‘speckle’ noise.

rows.title: Changes in Mars’s habitability could have been driven by carbonate formation and transient oases
rows.summary: Mars has had periods of potential habitability, seen in its geological record of surface water and shallow groundwater. Models that incorporate feedback between carbon sequestration, atmospheric pressure and temperature — backed by discoveries of carbonates by NASA’s Curiosity rover — suggest that this intermittent habitability could have arisen through self-regulating feedback loops on the planet’s surface.

rows.title: The tiny mouse lemur could make for a mighty model organism
rows.summary: A cellular atlas for a small, fast-reproducing primate could set the stage for scientists to use it as a model organism that has more human relevance than rodents.

rows.title: Allergy-triggering proteins share a common characteristic
rows.summary: Why do only certain molecules drive allergies? A feature now identified among some allergy-causing proteins is their ability to form pores in cells.

rows.title: Scientific bedlam at the world’s weirdest and wildest research conference
rows.summary: Woodstock Bio 2 + Night Science aimed to encourage collaborations through creativity. The walk-on music for presentations was fun, too.

rows.title: Powerful satellite will map changes on Earth in stunning detail — down to a centimetre
rows.summary: But will the US–India mission be the last for NASA for a long time to come?

rows.title: Cloud-motion data identify changes in atmospheric circulation
rows.summary: Large-scale shifts in atmospheric circulations can reshape global weather patterns and extremes, and they imprint their signatures in cloud motion. Decades of satellite-observed cloud motion reveal that cloud speeds in the jet streams have increased, the polar fronts have shifted polewards and a tropical circulation pattern called the Hadley cell has widened northwards.

rows.title: Observation of elusive interaction between neutrinos and atomic nuclei
rows.summary: Neutrinos are particles that are notoriously hard to detect, but observations of a process called coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering could enable physicists to develop better ways of studying them.

rows.title: Physicists should revel in the diversity of ways to understand quantum mechanics
rows.summary: Nature survey shows that disagreement about the meaning of quantum physics remains strong, even 100 years in. And that’s OK.

rows.title: From bench to big boss: mitigating the widening gap between PI and lab
rows.summary: Laboratory dynamics can change as the age and experience of the principal investigator increase. But there are ways to combat this.

rows.title: Inflammation during viral infection can rouse dormant cancer cells
rows.summary: Sometimes, cancer cells that have spread become ‘dormant’ but can start proliferating again later. A cue that can reactivate them has been discovered.

rows.title: ‘Smart’ tool pieces together proteins in response to combinations of cell-surface cues
rows.summary: Human cells display diverse surface proteins that vary by cell type and state. A modular system has been developed that triggers the joining of two parts of a full output protein only when specific cell-surface cues are met, enabling precise control of where functional proteins are generated and how they act.

rows.title: Physicists disagree wildly on what quantum mechanics says about reality, Nature survey shows
rows.summary: First major attempt to chart researchers’ views finds interpretations in conflict.

rows.title: AI expands the repertoire of CRISPR-associated proteins for genome editing
rows.summary: A generative artificial-intelligence tool has designed a synthetic CRISPR system that successfully edits human DNA and sharply reduces off-target effects.

rows.title: Sleuths and scientific institutions are not rivals
rows.summary: Science detectives are helping the research community to hold itself to account. All involved must find better ways to work together.

rows.title: Things I miss about civilization
rows.summary: The joys of space exploration.

rows.title: Flourishing chemosynthetic life at the greatest depths of hadal trenches
rows.summary: The discovery of chemosynthesis-based benthic communities at depths of 5,800 m to 9,533 m in the Kuril–Kamchatka and western Aleutian trenches challenges traditional perspectives on the energy sources sustaining hadal fauna.

rows.title: Repurposing haemoproteins for asymmetric metal-catalysed H atom transfer
rows.summary: Cytochrome P450 enzymes can be repurposed to catalyse asymmetric metal–hydride hydrogen atom transfer, a new-to-nature reaction.

rows.title: Remodelling of corticostriatal axonal boutons during motor learning
rows.summary: Individual boutons on mouse corticostriatal axons exhibit differential selectivity for rewarded and unrewarded movements during motor learning, and the proportion of reward-responsive boutons increases.

rows.title: Synthesis of bulk hexagonal diamond
rows.summary: The synthesis, recovery and detailed characterization of bulk hexagonal diamond under high pressure and temperature conditions using precursor graphite carbon is described, demonstrating the first successful synthesis in the 100 µm to millimetre size range.

rows.title: A hypothalamic circuit that modulates feeding and parenting behaviours
rows.summary: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of mouse hypothalamus and behavioural experiments show that specific hypothalamic networks regulate conflicting feeding versus parenting behaviours of female mice.

rows.title: Programmable protein ligation on cell surfaces
rows.summary: A synthetic biology system called SMART has been developed that uses conditional protein splicing for the programmable ligation of functional proteins from previously defined molecular combinations on cell surfaces.

rows.title: Direct observation of coherent elastic antineutrino–nucleus scattering
rows.summary: Direct observation of coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering is reported using the data from the CONUS+ experiment in which the antineutrinos with energy less than 10 MeV are produced in a nuclear reactor.

rows.title: Invariance of dynamo action in an early-Earth model
rows.summary: Early-Earth geometry models are presented, producing magnetic field intensity and morphologies agreeing with palaeomagnetic data in the deep past and demonstrating the negligible role of fluid viscosity in the Earth’s early geodynamo.

rows.title: ACLY inhibition promotes tumour immunity and suppresses liver cancer
rows.summary: Using metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis-driven hepatocellular carcinoma mouse models, an ATP citrate lyase inhibitor reduces tumour burden and enhances efficacy of current standards of care.

rows.title: Respiratory viral infections awaken metastatic breast cancer cells in lungs
rows.summary: Mouse models show that respiratory infections from viruses such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2 can trigger metastasis of dormant breast cancer cells in the lungs, a finding supported by epidemiological data from two large human cohorts.

rows.title: Transient APC/C inactivation by mTOR boosts glycolysis during cell cycle entry
rows.summary: APC/C activity is transiently inhibited to generate a pulse of glycolysis that is required for mammalian cell cycle entry.

rows.title: A molecular cell atlas of mouse lemur, an emerging model primate
rows.summary: Together with a companion paper, the generation of a transcriptomic atlas for the mouse lemur and analyses of example cell types establish this animal as a molecularly tractable primate model organism.

rows.title: Determinants of successful AAV-vectored delivery of HIV-1 bNAbs in early life
rows.summary: A single dose of an adeno-associated virus vector encoding an HIV-1 broadly neutralizing antibody given shortly after birth results in persistent antibody expression and protection from infection in rhesus macaque models of human HIV-1 transmission through breastfeeding and sexual intercourse.

rows.title: Securing the forest carbon sink for the European Union’s climate ambition
rows.summary: Actionable research recommendations are outlined to improve the monitoring and modelling of forest resources and their carbon sink, and to better inform forest management decisions and the European Green Deal.

rows.title: Towards more effective nature-based climate solutions in global forests
rows.summary: A strategy to improve the implementation of nature-based climate solutions in global forests for climate mitigation is described, comprising four key components to highlight notable science and policy considerations and providing solutions to improve rigour.

rows.title: Diffusing protein binders to intrinsically disordered proteins
rows.summary: Using RFdiffusion, a general method for targeting intrinsically disordered proteins and regions for protein design has been developed.

rows.title: Tropical response to ocean circulation slowdown raises future drought risk
rows.summary: An Atlantic meridional overturning circulation slowdown drives widespread shifts in tropical rainfall through the propagation of high-latitude cooling into the tropical North Atlantic.

rows.title: SuFEx-based antitubercular compound irreversibly inhibits Pks13
rows.summary: A preclinical covalent compound, CMX410, contains a aryl fluorosulfate warhead that targets the acyltransferase domain of Mtb Pks13, an essential enzyme in cell-wall biosynthesis, making it a promising candidate for tuberculosis treatment regimens.

rows.title: Design of highly functional genome editors by modelling CRISPR–Cas sequences
rows.summary: Gene editors designed using artificial intelligence can undertake precision editing of the human genome.

rows.title: Mouse lemur cell atlas informs primate genes, physiology and disease
rows.summary: Together with an accompanying paper presenting a transcriptomic atlas of the mouse lemur, interrogation of the atlas provides a rich body of data to support the use of the organism as a model for primate biology and health.

rows.title: Epithelial cell membrane perforation induces allergic airway inflammation
rows.summary: The ability to form pores in the plasma membrane of host airway epithelial cells is a common feature of many structurally diverse allergens that induce type 2 immune responses by stimulating IL-33 release and causing Ca 2+ influx.

rows.title: Can science address painters’ problems?
rows.summary: Wall decorators and artists seek solutions, and insects plunge to their pitcher-plant fate, in this week’s pick from Nature’ s archive.

rows.title: The brain fires up immune cells when sick people are nearby
rows.summary: When people viewed virtual avatars with coughs or rashes, their brains triggered an immune response.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The brain deploys immune cells at the mere sight of sickness
rows.summary: When we see a sick person, our brains kickstart an immune response mimicking the body’s response to an actual infection. Plus, evolution has a predilection for anteaters and how researchers are testing people, animals and artificial intelligence for consciousness.

rows.title: Cell’s sugar coating mapped at below-nanometre resolution
rows.summary: Super-resolution technique works with off-the-shelf optical microscopes.

rows.title: How China’s bold talent recruitment has shaped science
rows.summary: Many Chinese researchers have received enviable benefits and positions after returning from training abroad.

rows.title: Africa needs to invest in science communication — here’s how
rows.summary: Science journalism is almost non-existent in Africa, even in the countries that are becoming crucial hubs for research. This gap must be addressed to help protect Africans from misinformation.

rows.title: Scientists mourn Tom Lehrer — nerdiest of singer-songwriters
rows.summary: The mathematician’s memorable satires are beloved by generations of researchers.

rows.title: Could machine learning help to build a unified theory of cognition?
rows.summary: Two distinct computational approaches provide opportunities for bringing together different theories of cognition.

rows.title: AI models are neglecting African languages — scientists want to change that
rows.summary: Scientists record 9,000 hours of languages spoken in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa as free-access training data for AI models.

rows.title: How to detect consciousness in people, animals and maybe even AI
rows.summary: Insights from human brains could inform how scientists search for awareness in all its possible forms.

rows.title: Columbia researchers eager to restart science after university’s deal with Trump
rows.summary: The institution agreed to increased federal oversight in exchange for restored grants and an end to government investigations.

rows.title: Could bridging science and the arts be the key to better policies?
rows.summary: To be successful, policymakers need to consider diverse perspectives. Here’s how we’re reimagining policy process.

rows.title: The Virtual Lab of AI agents designs new SARS-CoV-2 nanobodies
rows.summary: Human collaboration with a team of artificial intelligence (AI) agents powered by large language models was used to efficiently design a complex interdisciplinary research project leading to the design of novel nanobodies against SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.

rows.title: How I’m helping to develop more-resilient food systems
rows.summary: Geographer Bhogtoram Mawroh works with Indigenous People in Meghalaya, India, to adapt agriculture to climate change.

rows.title: ‘Wind droughts’ driven by climate change put green power at risk
rows.summary: Warming in the Arctic shifts storm patterns, leading to reductions in wind speeds in places that rely on turbines for clean electricity.

rows.title: Hard paths: how courage differs from bravery in science
rows.summary: ‘If it’s easy, someone else will do it.’ Leah Ellis, chief executive of Sublime Systems, explains the challenge and appeal of slashing carbon emissions from cement production.

rows.title: Artificial diamonds are forever: 70 years of synthesizing these iconic gems
rows.summary: In 1955, a reproducible method for synthesizing diamonds launched a global industry — and pointed the way to applications ranging from X-ray lenses to nuclear fusion.

rows.title: Physicists unleashed the power of the atom — but to what end?
rows.summary: From laboratory quirks to Earth-shattering weapons, a chain of discoveries reached a devastating conclusion.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Ageing accelerates after 50 — but not all organs age at the same rate
rows.summary: The aorta and other blood vessels seem to age more quickly than other organs. Plus, an unexpected ingredient in a Neanderthal’s diet and how developing food systems for space missions could benefit people on Earth.

rows.title: China reins in the spiralling construction costs of nuclear power — what can other countries learn?
rows.summary: Strengthening regulations and domestic supply chains could be key to making nuclear power more economically viable.

rows.title: Why space foods aren’t just for space
rows.summary: Space agencies looking to set up long-term bases on the Moon need sustainable ways to feed astronauts. The approaches they are testing could also help to tackle challenges on Earth.

rows.title: Postdocs get more equipment time when applications are anonymized
rows.summary: Early-career researchers’ access to neutron-beam instruments jumped from 61% to 78% at one Australian facility.

rows.title: ‘For AI to change how economies work, it has to represent all of us’
rows.summary: Computer scientist Vukosi Marivate works to ensure Africa is not left behind in the drive to deliver artificial intelligence’s societal benefits.

rows.title: Ageing accelerates at around age 50 ― some organs faster than others
rows.summary: An analysis of how various tissues age is the latest to suggest that ageing does not march to a steady beat.

rows.title: Mystery food in Neanderthal diet might be maggots
rows.summary: Study of rotting human cadavers hints that a puzzling chemical marker in Neanderthal remains could be from eating the larvae.

rows.title: Author Correction: Immune evasion through mitochondrial transfer in the tumour microenvironment
How to tackle research misconduct: survey finds stark disagreement
rows.summary: Data sleuths and research-integrity officers have different views on how to handle allegations of wrongdoing in science.

rows.title: Meet the early-career scientists planning to leave the United States
rows.summary: Decreased funding, reduced opportunities and growing uncertainty has made life tough for international postdocs living in the US.

rows.title: Daily briefing: ‘Arsenic life’ paper retracted after 15 years — against its authors’ will
rows.summary: Some scientists are celebrating the retraction of the ‘arsenic life’ paper, but the authors say that it’s unwarranted. Plus, a jeopardized telescope could find a home in Europe and some penguins take advantage of energy-efficient routes across the ocean.

rows.title: Author Correction: Human HDAC6 senses valine abundancy to regulate DNA damage
This fish-inspired suction cup can stick to your organs
rows.summary: The device could be swallowed for drug delivery or medical monitoring.

rows.title: Unexpected danger lurks in this giant fault in the Yukon
rows.summary: The Tintina fault has triggered many more earthquakes than was thought — and a build-up of strain poses a hazard.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Damaging the climate could violate international law, court rules
rows.summary: A landmark court ruling could open the door for nations most affected by climate change to sue the most polluting countries. Plus, an artificial intelligence model that can predict lost Latin text and a fish-inspired medical device that sticks to slippery surfaces.

rows.title: DeepMind and OpenAI models solve maths problems at level of top students
rows.summary: For the first time, large language models performed on a par with gold medallists in the International Mathematical Olympiad.

rows.title: Spain bids €400 million to host mega telescope at risk in US budget cuts
rows.summary: New Canary Islands home could save controversial Thirty Meter Telescope first proposed for Hawaii.

rows.title: I won three competitive grants in a row. Here’s how I learnt what to do
rows.summary: It took time and rejections to understand what granting agencies look for. This is how I picked up application-writing skills.

rows.title: Controversial ‘arsenic life’ paper retracted after 15 years — but authors fight back
rows.summary: The journal Science retracts a headline-grabbing study, but the authors vigorously defend their data and say the retraction is unwarranted.

rows.title: Rumble in the Miocene: terror bird versus caiman
rows.summary: Toothmarks on a fossilized bone tell a story of two mega-predators.

rows.title: Giant laser heats solid gold to 14 times its melting point
rows.summary: A 50 nm thick sheet of solid gold was heated well beyond a theoretical limit, suggests new study — plus, what researchers think about the threat of nuclear war.

rows.title: Ageing stem cells in the knees drive arthritis damage
rows.summary: Mice with a version of osteoarthritis experienced symptom relief after expression of a protein targeting a stem-cell receptor was blocked.

rows.title: The last parliament
rows.summary: A debatable prospect.

rows.title: Molecule eases neurological symptoms of mitochondrial deficiency in coenzyme Q 10
rows.summary: The symptoms of primary deficiencies of the mitochondrial antioxidant coenzyme Q 10 (CoQ 10 ) caused by loss of CoQ 10 synthesis do not respond readily to CoQ 10 treatment. Molecular precursors of the CoQ 10 headgroup increase the survival of mice that cannot make the headgroup and improve neurological symptoms in an individual with primary CoQ 10 deficiency.

rows.title: Protect the integrity of the US National Institutes of Health
Researchers in dismay as US exits world science body UNESCO … again
rows.summary: The Trump administration plans the departure for the end of 2026 and criticizes the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

rows.title: Unusual fossil skin appendage is not a feather
rows.summary: Although large, elongated protrusions on a 247-million-year-old reptile fossil have some similarities to feathers, they are not feathers.

rows.title: Missing steps uncovered in a pathway plants use to produce the defence molecule salicylic acid
rows.summary: A long-standing mystery about a pathway that makes a key defence molecule in various valuable crop plants is finally solved.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Scans reveal that optimists share similar brain-activity patterns
rows.summary: All optimists’ brain patterns are alike, but each pessimist’s brain is unhappy in its own way. Plus, the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated brain ageing and how tenure affects publication output.

rows.title: There’s a new acid in our rain — should we be worried?
rows.summary: Scientists and regulators are divided over the threat posed by rising levels of a chemical called TFA.

rows.title: Superheated gold stays solid well past its predicted melting point
rows.summary: Heating that lasted only trillionths of a second raised a gold sample’s temperature to 19,000 K without melting it, a study suggests.

rows.title: Reply to: Experiments implementing small commuting models lack gravitational features
Experiments implementing small commuting models lack gravitational features
AI for Latin inscriptions supplies missing text and predicts date and location
rows.summary: An artificial-intelligence tool helps historians to interpret Latin inscriptions by assigning a date and location and suggesting text for missing parts.

rows.title: Meet Aeneas: the AI that can fill in the gaps of damaged Latin texts
rows.summary: The best results come when a human and the model work together.

rows.title: Solid gold superheated to 14 times its melting temperature
rows.summary: Lasers have been used to heat solid gold well beyond its melting temperature without losing the metal’s crystalline structure — exceeding a theoretical superheating limit.

rows.title: The deep sea is a globally connected habitat
rows.summary: The deep sea is a distinctive environment, distinguished from surface waters by darkness, cold and immense pressures. Global data reveal how much more connected deep-sea life is than life in the shallows; a deep-sea animal has spread from Iceland to Tasmania, Australia, over a relatively short evolutionary time period.

rows.title: Nanobody therapy rescues behavioural deficits of NMDA receptor hypofunction
rows.summary: A bivalent biparatopic nanobody penetrates the brain, binds to and potentiates the activity of homodimeric metabotropic glutamate receptor 2, correcting cognitive deficits in two preclinical mouse models with endophenotypes resulting from NMDA receptor hypofunction.

rows.title: Three-step biosynthesis of salicylic acid from benzoyl-CoA in plants
rows.summary: The salicylic acid (SA) biosynthesis pathway—involving ligation of benzoyl coenzyme A and benzyl alcohol to give benzyl benzoate; hydroxylation of benzyl benzoate to give benzyl salicylate; and cleavage of benzyl salicylate to give SA—is highly conserved in plants.

rows.title: Complex genetic variation in nearly complete human genomes
rows.summary: Using sequencing and haplotype-resolved assembly of 65 diverse human genomes, complex regions including the major histocompatibility complex and centromeres are analysed.

rows.title: NNMT inhibition in cancer-associated fibroblasts restores antitumour immunity
rows.summary: An NNMT inhibitor reduces tumour burden and metastasis in multiple mouse cancer models and restores immune checkpoint blockade efficacy by decreasing cancer-associated-fibroblast-mediated recruitment of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and reinvigorating CD8 + T cell activation.

rows.title: Humoral determinants of checkpoint immunotherapy
rows.summary: Rapid extracellular antibody profiling reveals a contribution of autoantibodies to the effectiveness of checkpoint immunotherapy for cancer.

rows.title: Pre-rRNA spatial distribution and functional organization of the nucleolus
rows.summary: The evolutionary emergence of a nested fibrillar centre–dense fibrillar component may have optimized pre-rRNA processing.

rows.title: Precisely defining disease variant effects in CRISPR-edited single cells
rows.summary: A plate-based assay called CRAFTseq has been developed that uses ‘multi-omic’ single-cell RNA sequencing and direct genotyping of CRISPR edits to test the functional effects of genetic variants on cell state and function.

rows.title: Triassic diapsid shows early diversification of skin appendages in reptiles
rows.summary: A Middle Triassic diapsid is presented that has a distinctive crest consisting of integumentary appendages that are structurally distinct from avemetatarsalian feathers.

rows.title: Magnon spectroscopy in the electron microscope
rows.summary: A method combining scanning transmission electron microscopy with high-resolution electron energy-loss spectroscopy enables the observation of magnons and their dispersion, and provides a way to examine magnetic inhomogeneities with nanometre spatial resolution.

rows.title: A gut sense for a microbial pattern regulates feeding
rows.summary: A study reveals a gut–brain sensory pathway through which the microbial component flagellin activates neuropod cells in the colon to signal the brain and reduce feeding in mice.

rows.title: Integrated biotechnological and AI innovations for crop improvement
rows.summary: The integration of omics technologies, genome editing and protein design with artificial intelligence (AI) promises rapid advances in the field of crop improvement that will improve global food security.

rows.title: Contextualizing ancient texts with generative neural networks
rows.summary: Aeneas, a generative neural network trained on ancient texts, helps historians contextualize inscriptions and perform epigraphic tasks, offering an improved starting point for historical research.

rows.title: Hippocampal representations drift in stable multisensory environments
rows.summary: Tracking of individual place cells in mouse CA1 shows that representational drift is not influenced by changes in environment or behaviour, and is lower for more excitable place cells.

rows.title: Deciphering phenylalanine-derived salicylic acid biosynthesis in plants
rows.summary: Diverse plant species synthesize salicylic acid from phenylalanine through a pathway that includes a conserved triple-enzyme module that converts benzoyl-CoA to salicylic acid.

rows.title: Mechanical underwater adhesive devices for soft substrates
rows.summary: A remora-inspired mechanical underwater adhesive device adheres securely to a range of soft substrates and maintains performance under extreme pH and moisture conditions, with potential applications in biosensing and drug delivery.

rows.title: Coherent spectroscopy with a single antiproton spin
rows.summary: Coherent quantum transition spectroscopy of the spin of a single antiproton is reported, demonstrating Rabi oscillations of the spin and enabling improved measurement of matter/antimatter symmetry using proton and antiproton magnetic moments.

rows.title: Eye structure shapes neuron function in Drosophila motion vision
rows.summary: In Drosophila , the physical structure of the eye has a key role in the directional tuning of motion-sensitive neurons, showing how navigational behaviour is tightly associated with anatomy.

rows.title: Driving a protective allele of the mosquito FREP1 gene to combat malaria
rows.summary: Coupling of a FREP1 variant to a gene-drive system allows the spread of a host malaria resistance allele through the mosquito population.

rows.title: Spatiotemporal faunal connectivity across global sea floors
rows.summary: We analyse a global dataset of genomic DNA sequences for Ophiuroidea to gain an understanding of phylogenetic divergence and biotic movement across oceans, finding phylogentically divergent faunas at shelf depths but greater connectivity of species at deep-sea depths.

rows.title: A generic non-invasive neuromotor interface for human-computer interaction
rows.summary: A high-bandwidth neuromotor interface offers performant out-of-the-box generalization across people.

rows.title: Structural variation in 1,019 diverse humans based on long-read sequencing
rows.summary: Intermediate-coverage long-read sequencing in 1,019 diverse humans from the 1000 Genomes Project, representing 26 populations, enables the generation of comprehensive population-scale structural variant catalogues comprising common and rare alleles.

rows.title: The neural basis of species-specific defensive behaviour in Peromyscus mice
rows.summary: Visual threat triggers contrasting freeze and escape defensive responses in two species of deer mice as a result of different activation thresholds downstream of the superior colliculus in the dorsal periaqueductal grey.

rows.title: Complete biosynthesis of salicylic acid from phenylalanine in plants
rows.summary: Characterization of four SALICYLIC ACID-DEFICIENT GENEs in rice identifies an ancestral pathway for biosynthesis of salicylic acid from phenylalanine and provides genetic targets for engineering disease resistance in crop plants.

rows.title: Superheating gold beyond the predicted entropy catastrophe threshold
rows.summary: Gold samples can be heated to more than 14 times their melting point while retaining their crystalline structure, far surpassing the predicted entropy catastrophe threshold and suggesting a substantially higher or potentially no limit for superheating.

rows.title: Global hotspots of mycorrhizal fungal richness are poorly protected
rows.summary: Machine-learning algorithms trained on 25,000 geolocated soil samples are used to create high-resolution global maps of mycorrhizal fungi, revealing that less than 10% of their biodiversity hotspots are in protected areas.

rows.title: A natural nuclear reactor
rows.summary: Questions raised by a fission chain reaction that occurred billions of years ago, and making silver compounds lighter with light, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Why publishing referee reports could backfire on public trust
Encouraging a ‘data sufficiency’ mindset is key for responsible research
Brazil must not weaken environmental planning rules
The optimistic brain: scans reveal thought patterns shared by positive thinkers
rows.summary: Insights from brain imaging could have implications for mental-health research.

rows.title: Breaking point: mechanical stress helps NINJ1 protein to rupture membranes
rows.summary: The protein NINJ1 enables cells to break open during certain types of cell death. Modulation of physical forces on the membrane reveals how NINJ1 acts.

rows.title: The COVID-19 pandemic transformed this scientist into a research-integrity sleuth
rows.summary: Lonni Besançon has faced online abuse, threats and legal challenges. But he remains proud of his service to science and society.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The restaurant at the centre of the mathematical universe
rows.summary: A free-wheeling 1930s cafe that nurtured mathematical ideas holds lessons for how to spur creative thought today. Plus, a dental-floss vaccine and the benefits of a four-day work week.

rows.title: Fund scholars who tackle urgent issues — from misinformation to error spotting
rows.summary: Scientists who are not tied down by fixed research agendas can pivot nimbly to work where they are most needed. It’s time to build career paths with these researchers in mind.

rows.title: Researchers value null results, but struggle to publish them
rows.summary: Survey finds that fear of reputational harm and a lack of support and publication platforms are among respondents’ key concerns.

rows.title: China’s fossil-fuel challenge — how to build a bridge to renewables
rows.summary: The world’s largest emitter of carbon dioxide relies on coal, oil and gas for its economic growth. But all is not lost if China can lead on cleaning up through carbon capture, utilization and storage.

rows.title: China is boosting its Antarctic research. What does that mean for the world?
rows.summary: With US investment in polar science under threat, scientists hope that China’s interest in the region will benefit research.

rows.title: Help save 2 million lives: close the vaccine funding gap
rows.summary: Gavi, the vaccine provider for the world’s poorest people, needs an extra US$3 billion to protect infants and other vulnerable groups. More donors must step up.

rows.title: How I’m advocating in Congress for the next generation of US scientists
rows.summary: Adriana Bankston’s year-long policy fellowship allows her to fight for science and scientists at a crucial time.

rows.title: People’s brains aged faster during the COVID pandemic — even the uninfected
rows.summary: Study of nearly 1,000 people showed that brain ageing was not linked to infection status, but cognitive decline was.

rows.title: Made-to-order DNA goes big: new tech doubles size of custom genetic sequences
rows.summary: Enzyme-based techniques and refinements in organic chemistry ease the generation of extended DNA sequences.

rows.title: How getting tenure changes researchers’ publication habits — and citations
rows.summary: Paper output varies between disciplines, as does the trend after tenure is achieved.

rows.title: Author Correction: Early versus deferred use of CDK4/6 inhibitors in advanced breast cancer
Author Correction: Stress dynamically modulates neuronal autophagy to gate depression onset
Budget brainwaves: low-cost system collects brain data outside the lab
rows.summary: Neuroscience initiative in India and Tanzania amasses a trove of high-quality EEG recordings from diverse populations.

rows.title: ‘Immortal’ stars have an elixir of youth: dark matter
rows.summary: Modelling suggests that annihilation of this strange, invisible matter helps stars to retain that youthful glow.

rows.title: AI, bounties and culture change, how scientists are taking on errors
rows.summary: Researchers are trialling myriad approaches to prevent errors in science. In this podcast, we explore their different approaches and ask how can science be improved.

rows.title: ‘We have less than ten minutes’: how I communicate with spacecraft from the ground
rows.summary: Loren Chang designs satellites and other spacefaring machinery destined for low Earth orbit.

rows.title: How AI can deepen inequities for non-native English speakers in science
rows.summary: Journals and conference organizers could do more to help researchers overcome language barriers, but artificial intelligence might widen inequalities, warns Tatsuya Amano.

rows.title: ‘We dissent’: NASA staff declare opposition to Trump cuts
