rows.summary: Space-agency declaration of dissent and NSF petition join similar documents from staff at the EPA and the NIH.

rows.title: Scientific jargon can be ‘satisfying’ — but misleading
rows.summary: Research shows that jargon can make weak explanations feel complete by masking their gaps. What can experts do to communicate science effectively to laypeople?

rows.title: Solving aviation’s climate-action conundrum
rows.summary: A decision-making tool for the aviation sector helps to assess the likelihood of a net positive outcome from climate actions that can have competing effects on warming.

rows.title: Should we treat rivers as living things?
rows.summary: Rivers are born, evolve and die, and can bring life — and death. We might respect them more if we saw them as animated by spirits of their own.

rows.title: Daily briefing: NASA staff speak out against Trump cuts
rows.summary: More than 280 NASA employees have signed a declaration to oppose unprecedented budget cuts proposed by the administration of US President Donald Trump. Plus, how Canada became the hotbed of measles in North America and the biotech-company founders driven by their child’s rare disease.

rows.title: Why evaluating the impact of AI needs to start now
rows.summary: Artificial-intelligence technologies are being deployed rapidly across industries, yet most organizations lack even basic guidelines to assess the tools’ effects.

rows.title: Biggest trial of four-day work week finds workers are happier and feel just as productive
rows.summary: Compressing five days of work into four can create stress, but the benefits outweigh the downsides, sprawling study shows.

rows.title: Meet the biotech-company founders driven by their child’s rare disease
rows.summary: For some parents, finding a cure for their child’s illness is the ultimate motivation to start a company.

rows.title: How your research can survive a US federal grant termination
rows.summary: Researchers in the United States are filing appeals, seeking court remedies, turning to philanthropy and starting GoFundMe campaigns.

rows.title: To the Moon and quack: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: Asia’s haze affects ice and weather on the Frozen Continent
rows.summary: Pollution emitted by fossil-fuel usage in Asia influences sea-ice coverage in Antarctica.

rows.title: This ancient mega-predator was built for stealth
rows.summary: Fossil evidence suggests that Temnodontosaurus 's fore-fin had adaptations to reduce low frequency noise.

rows.title: Sex at birth is not always random — mum’s age and genetics can play a part
rows.summary: Families with three or more boys, for example, are more likely to have another boy than a girl as the next child.

rows.title: Class of 2025: five PhD students reveal realigned priorities in wake of COVID and cuts
rows.summary: Scientists who began their doctoral studies in 2020 found their feet during a global pandemic and are graduating into an uncertain and chaotic future.

rows.title: Should I tell anyone that I suspect misconduct in a paper I’m reviewing?
rows.summary: A cancer researcher is suspicious about a paper they’ve been asked to review. What steps should they take?

rows.title: Daily briefing: How the brain boots up from sleep to wakefulness
rows.summary: A wave of wakefulness spreads from the front of the brain to the back as we rouse from slumber. Plus, the underappreciated risk of a nuclear war and the best way to update a long-lived data set.

rows.title: Pathology-oriented multiplexing enables integrative disease mapping
rows.summary: Pathology-oriented multiplexing (PathoPlex) represents a framework for widespread access to multiplexed imaging and computational image analysis of clinical specimens at a relatively high throughput and subcellular resolution.

rows.title: How the world’s biggest bats got their enormous wingspans
rows.summary: Genetic analysis helps to reveal why flying foxes can measure almost 2 metres from wingtip to wingtip.

rows.title: How sugar overload in early life affects the brain later
rows.summary: A study in mice finds that a high-sucrose diet during youth has long-term implications for learning and brain connectivity.

rows.title: How the brain wakes up from sleep — and produces that morning feeling
rows.summary: Certain patterns of brain activity during awakening correlate with a lower likelihood of the bleary-eyed state called ‘sleep inertia’.

rows.title: How to avoid nuclear war in an era of AI and misinformation
rows.summary: Nuclear deterrence is no longer a two-player game, and emerging technologies further threaten the status quo. The result is a risky new nuclear age.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The birth of a solar system caught ‘on camera’ for the first time
rows.summary: Researchers have spotted a baby star at the beginning of its planet forming era. Plus, eight babies conceived via ‘three-person in vitro fertilization’ are living healthy lives and the best popular science and scholarly books to read now.

rows.title: Google tapped billions of mobile phones to detect quakes worldwide — and send alerts
rows.summary: Study reveals how the tech behemoth is using the motions sensors on phones to expand quake warnings to more countries.

rows.title: Robots demonstrate principles of collective intelligence
rows.summary: Lessons from developmental biology can be used to guide the behaviour of robot swarms.

rows.title: Heart from organ donor restarted outside the body — technique offers new source of organs
rows.summary: Current procedures for reviving a heart for transplant are ethically fraught or expensive.

rows.title: AI and misinformation are supercharging the risk of nuclear war
rows.summary: Emerging dangers are reshaping the landscape of nuclear deterrence and increasing the threat of mutual annihilation. Scientists must speak truth to power.

rows.title: ‘Controlled chaos’: how to create an environment that fosters genius
rows.summary: One free-wheeling 1930s cafe nurtured mathematical ideas including the theory of the nuclear bomb. That holds lessons for how to spur creative thought today.

rows.title: ‘Stealth flippers’ helped this extinct mega-predator stalk its prey
rows.summary: 180-million-year-old fossil suggests Temnodontosaurus had several adaptations for quiet swimming — plus, why damage to mitochondria during waking hours might explain the need for sleep.

rows.title: Redox-powered autonomous directional C–C bond rotation under enzyme control
rows.summary: A redox reaction network, comprising concurrent oxidation and reduction pathways, is described that can drive autonomous unidirectional motion about a C–C bond in a structurally simple synthetic molecular motor based on an achiral biphenyl.

rows.title: Star flares when an orbiting planet gets too close
rows.summary: A planet that orbits closely to its young host star has been observed to induce large magnetic eruptions on the star. These flares might rapidly blow away the planet’s atmosphere, leaving behind a dense core within a few hundred million years.

rows.title: Author Correction: BNT162b2 vaccine induces neutralizing antibodies and poly-specific T cells in humans
The breakthrough proof bringing mathematics closer to a grand unified theory
rows.summary: The Langlands programme has inspired and befuddled mathematicians for more than 50 years. A major advance has now opened up new worlds for them to explore.

rows.title: Human activity redistributes nitrogen fixation across the terrestrial biosphere
rows.summary: Detailed spatial estimates from a global analysis of biological nitrogen fixation on land reveal that natural environments sustain much less nitrogen fixation than was thought. But agricultural cultivation of nitrogen-fixing crops and forage drastically increases local nitrogen inputs, so that total agricultural nitrogen fixation nearly equals that of all natural lands combined.

rows.title: The origin of the oldest solid objects in the Solar System
rows.summary: Observations of a young star offer a glimpse of the high-temperature conditions that shaped rock formation in the early Solar System.

rows.title: Gut bacteria make a molecule that promotes plaque build-up in arteries
rows.summary: A bacterially produced molecule circulates in the bloodstream and increases the risk of cardiovascular disease by hijacking immune-cell signalling.

rows.title: ‘Another DeepSeek moment’: Chinese AI model Kimi K2 stirs excitement
rows.summary: The latest version of the chatbot, developed by start-up Moonshot AI, is open for researchers to build on.

rows.title: How a bipolar diagnosis benefits my research
rows.summary: Mental illness cost this researcher almost a decade of their academic life. Now it motivates them to help find effective treatments.

rows.title: Genome doubling fuels ovarian cancer evolution and immune dysregulation
rows.summary: Single-cell analysis reveals the extent of genome doubling in ovarian cancer, its variability and its role in enabling tumours to evade the immune system.

rows.title: Birth of a solar system caught ‘on camera’ for first time
rows.summary: Astronomers get rare glimpse of earliest stages of planet formation around a baby star.

rows.title: Super-resolution spectroscopy with ‘spiky’ X-ray lasers
rows.summary: Random fluctuations in the intensity and energy of X-ray lasers, which generally limit performance, have been harnessed for high-resolution spectroscopy.

rows.title: ‘Landmark’ study: three-person IVF leads to eight healthy children
rows.summary: Long-awaited results suggest that mitochondrial donation can prevent babies from inheriting diseases caused by mutant mitochondria.

rows.title: Plant immune receptor engineered to protect against more than 100 viruses
rows.summary: Plant diseases constitute a constant threat to global food security. A protein-engineering strategy, in which a constitutively active form of an immune receptor is kept inactive by a peptide until it is cleaved by pathogen protease enzymes, confers durable and complete resistance against many viruses that affect crop plants.

rows.title: Giant study finds a research field that’s mostly reproducible
rows.summary: Researchers assessed more than 1,000 results from fruit-fly immunity research published between 1959 and 2011. The majority of findings look verifiable.

rows.title: Birds use a tiny RNA fragment to balance sex chromosomes
rows.summary: Birds use a unique mechanism to balance gene expression from their sex chromosomes. MiR-2954 is a microRNA that suppresses specific target genes, preventing them from being overexpressed in male birds and ensuring the males’ survival. It is not required in females.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The breakthrough proof bringing mathematics closer to a grand unified theory
rows.summary: Researchers have unveiled a proof that’s forging bridges between different mathematical lands. Plus, open-access health databases are being exploited to churn out low-quality papers and how one gene raises the risk of a host of neurodegenerative conditions.

rows.title: How to de-Americanize global science
rows.summary: The US science crisis presents an opportunity to reinvent funding and management of the global research enterprise.

rows.title: Punchlines for peace
rows.summary: Have you heard the one about …?

rows.title: Imidazole propionate is a driver and therapeutic target in atherosclerosis
rows.summary: Imidazole propionate produced by gut microbiota is associated with atherosclerosis in mouse models and in humans, and causes the development of atherosclerosis through activation of the imidazoline-1 receptor in myeloid cells.

rows.title: A male-essential miRNA is key for avian sex chromosome dosage compensation
rows.summary: Birds have evolved a unique sex chromosome dosage compensation mechanism involving the male-biased microRNA (miR-2954), which is essential for male survival by regulating the expression of dosage-sensitive Z-linked genes.

rows.title: Immigrant–native pay gap driven by lack of access to high-paying jobs
rows.summary: Data from nine European and North American countries reveal that the disparity in earnings between immigrants and natives is largely a result of segregation of immigrant workers into lower-paying jobs.

rows.title: Neutrophils drive vascular occlusion, tumour necrosis and metastasis
rows.summary: Neutrophils actively induce tumour necrosis, driving vascular occlusion, pleomorphic necrosis and metastasis.

rows.title: Super-resolution stimulated X-ray Raman spectroscopy
rows.summary: A high-resolution spectroscopic tool is demonstrated using the stochastically fluctuating intensity spikes in time and energy domains of a self-amplified spontaneous emission X-ray free-electron laser.

rows.title: Mitochondrial origins of the pressure to sleep
rows.summary: Research on Drosophila neurons shows links between the need to sleep and aerobic metabolism, indicating that the pressure to sleep may have a mitochondrial origin.

rows.title: Dynamic kinetic resolution of phosphines with chiral supporting electrolytes
rows.summary: Using a dynamic-kinetic-resolution strategy and chiral phosphate salts as supporting electrolytes, racemic trivalent phosphines can be oxidized to afford enantioenriched phosphine oxides.

rows.title: Ongoing genome doubling shapes evolvability and immunity in ovarian cancer
rows.summary: A single-cell sequencing study using more than 30,000 tumour genomes from human ovarian cancers shows that whole-genome doubling is an ongoing mutational process that drives tumour evolution and disrupts immunity.

rows.title: Identification of medication–microbiome interactions that affect gut infection
rows.summary: An analysis of prescription medications shows that several non-antibiotic drugs, such as the heart medication digoxin, can reduce the immune response to pathogens and increase the risk of gastrointestinal infections by altering the composition of the microbiome.

rows.title: Non-antibiotics disrupt colonization resistance against enteropathogens
rows.summary: Non-antibiotic drugs from a wide range of therapeutic classes can alter the ability of gut commensals to resist invasion by enteropathogens, a previously underappreciated side effect of such drugs.

rows.title: Long-range hyperbolic polaritons on a non-hyperbolic crystal surface
rows.summary: Real-space nanoimaging and theoretical analyses show the emergence of hyperbolic phonon polaritons on the surface of a non-hyperbolic material and that the polariton dispersions can be manipulated by varying the temperature.

rows.title: Remodelling autoactive NLRs for broad-spectrum immunity in plants
rows.summary: Cleavage by pathogen-derived proteases of an engineered chimeric protein activates its plant immune receptor component, enabling broad-spectrum resistance to pathogens in plants.

rows.title: Adaptations for stealth in the wing-like flippers of a large ichthyosaur
rows.summary: Analysis of a fossilized front flipper of the Jurassic ichthyosaur Temnodontosaurus that preserves details of soft tissue indicates the presence of a serrated trailing edge that would have reduced noise generated while swimming, enabling stealth hunting and hiding from predators.

rows.title: Dual interfacial H-bonding-enhanced deep-blue hybrid copper–iodide LEDs
rows.summary: A dual interfacial hydrogen-bond passivation strategy and a hybrid copper–iodide are used to fabricate deep-blue light-emitting diodes with excellent external quantum efficiency and lifetime.

rows.title: Longer scans boost prediction and cut costs in brain-wide association studies
rows.summary: Although the number of participants is important for phenotypic prediction accuracy in brain-wide association studies using functional MRI, scanning for at least 30 min offers the greatest cost effectiveness.

rows.title: Functional regimes define soil microbiome response to environmental change
rows.summary: Experimental perturbation of soil pH leads to a generalizable model of the soil microcosm comprising three functional regimes with distinct mechanisms linking environmental change to metabolite dynamics.

rows.title: Detecting structural heart disease from electrocardiograms using AI
rows.summary: EchoNext, a deep learning model for electrocardiograms trained and validated in diverse health systems, successfully detects many forms of structural heart disease, supporting the potential of artificial intelligence to expand access to heart disease screening at scale.

rows.title: Biphasic liquids with shape-shifting and bistable microdomains
rows.summary: A liquid-crystal-in-oil emulsion system exhibits bistable opacity or transparency, with rapid switching between the two, faster than, for example, electrochromics that can be found in smart windows.

rows.title: Refractory solid condensation detected in an embedded protoplanetary disk
rows.summary: Observations at infrared and millimetre wavelengths of the young protostar HOPS-315 show a gaseous disk captured at the point at which solids are first starting to condense, the t = 0 for planet formation.

rows.title: Liquid–liquid interfacial tension stabilized Li-metal batteries
rows.summary: Using an electrolyte micro-emulsion strategy, a lithium anode and high-voltage cathode can be simultaneously stabilized by liquid–liquid interfacial tension to achieve high-energy-density lithium-metal batteries.

rows.title: Observation of charge–parity symmetry breaking in baryon decays
rows.summary: The LHCb experiment at CERN has observed significant asymmetries between the decay rates of the beauty baryon and its CP-conjugated antibaryon, thus demonstrating CP violation in baryon decays.

rows.title: Global terrestrial nitrogen fixation and its modification by agriculture
rows.summary: Biological nitrogen fixation may impose stronger constraints on the carbon sink in natural terrestrial biomes and represent a larger source of agricultural nitrogen than is generally considered in analyses of the global nitrogen cycle.

rows.title: Temperature-related hospitalization burden under climate change
rows.summary: Temperature-related risks among the climate-sensitive diseases in northwestern and southwestern China have been historically high, with associated hospitalization burdens projected to rise consistently.

rows.title: Prophages block cell surface receptors to preserve their viral progeny
rows.summary: Zip promotes the accumulation of free phages in bacterial lysogen communities, safeguarding phage progeny.

rows.title: A canine friend to a feline family
rows.summary: Pondering the difficulties faced by metaphysicians, and a dog strikes up an unlikely friendship with a cat and her kittens, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Map endemic species before they vanish unrecorded
Invest in data resources to make FAIR a reality
China’s journal ranking system stands up to scrutiny
Critical commentaries such as ‘Matters arising’ have flawed formats
The mysterious missing ingredient in the highest-energy cosmic rays
rows.summary: Data from a South Pole observatory show that the fraction of protons in ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays is lower than expected.

rows.title: Low-quality papers based on public health data are flooding the scientific literature
rows.summary: The appearance of thousands of formulaic biomedical studies has been linked to the rise of text-generating AI tools.

rows.title: One potent gene raises risk of Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and other brain diseases
rows.summary: Massive proteomics database links gene variant APOE 4 to chronic inflammation.

rows.title: Without science, there can be no development
rows.summary: A United Nations conference on financing sustainable development was a missed opportunity to fund the science needed to create a better world.

rows.title: Bring science into business schools to train the leaders of tomorrow
rows.summary: The next generation of managers must be fit for a net-zero, nature-positive economy.

rows.title: Why the global economy is more uncertain than ever, and what to do about it
rows.summary: Unexpected events, such as pandemics and wars, are on the rise. Financial markets need tools to help them cope with unforeseen losses.

rows.title: Monster black hole merger is biggest ever seen
rows.summary: Gravitational-wave detector LIGO spots fast-spinning ‘forbidden’ black holes that challenge physics models.

rows.title: Smart brain-zapping implants could revolutionize Parkinson’s treatment
rows.summary: The next generation of deep-brain stimulation automatically corrects the precise brain waves that create symptoms of Parkinson’s disease. Can this approach target other conditions?

rows.title: Scientists everywhere must be protected
A motorcycle ride through the forest: how I protect Nigeria’s wildlife
rows.summary: Emmanuel Barde Elisha is a research coordinator for a non-profit organization dedicated to managing protected areas for conservation and local development.

rows.title: Embattled US scientific society names palaeontologist for top job
rows.summary: Neil Shubin, a University of Chicago researcher known for co-discovering a ′missing link’ fossil fish, will lead the National Academy of Sciences if the decision is ratified by members.

rows.title: Need to update your data? Follow these five tips
rows.summary: Researchers engaged in long-term projects often need to update their data sets over time. Here’s how to do it while maintaining reproducibility.

rows.title: Giant radio telescope was ‘a natural magnet’ for African talent
rows.summary: Roger Deane has seen the investment in astronomy on the continent pay off both in his own career and with more young scientists joining the field.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Targeting GRPR for sex hormone-dependent cancer after loss of E-cadherin
AI hype, crackling northern lights and more: take it all in with these holiday reads
rows.summary: Ten of Nature ’s recent contributors share their current book obsessions.

rows.title: Why I study trauma's genetic legacy
rows.summary: Rana Dajani's research includes identifying risk factors for type 2 diabetes, and genetic links to trauma.

rows.title: Why do ageing rates vary by country? Massive study says politics play a part
rows.summary: Social inequality and the decay of democratic institutions are linked to accelerated ageing — but education seems to slow the process.

rows.title: Exclusive: NIH to dismiss dozens of grant reviewers to align with Trump priorities
rows.summary: The move would undo years of work, leaving advisory councils understaffed, and without the full expertise needed for reviews.

rows.title: Daily briefing: A new blood group has been discovered — and only one person has it
rows.summary: A woman in Guadeloupe has blood belonging to the newly-characterized group ‘Gwada-negative’. Plus, signs of a ‘forbidden’ black-hole collision and how researchers are trying to hoodwink peer-reviewers’ AI tools.

rows.title: Found: a human gut microbe that makes cancer therapy more effective in mice
rows.summary: Cancer therapies called checkpoint inhibitor drugs, which ratchet up the immune system, work better when this bacterium is around.

rows.title: China’s shift towards ‘organized research’: how can coordination and innovation co-exist?
rows.summary: Beijing’s reorganization of science is a broad, systemic effort to reshape how research is conducted, applied and evaluated nationwide.

rows.title: Microbiota-driven antitumour immunity mediated by dendritic cell migration
rows.summary: A newly identified bacterial strain (YB328) isolated from the faeces of patients who responded to immune checkpoint blockade therapies can promote antitumour immunity through the activation of tumour-specific CD8 + T cells.

rows.title: Experimental demonstration of logical magic state distillation
rows.summary: Magic state distillation is achieved with logical qubits on a neutral-atom quantum computer using a dynamically reconfigurable architecture for parallel quantum operations.

rows.title: Three weeks in a hide to spot one elusive bear: the life of a wildlife film-maker
rows.summary: Vianet Djenguet joins us to talk about working with conservation researchers in the documentary series The Wild Ones .

rows.title: Lonely spacecraft can navigate the stars
rows.summary: NASA’s New Horizons probe, which hurtled past Pluto in 2015, demonstrates that it can sail through interstellar space using its onboard camera.

rows.title: Author Correction: Adhesive anti-fibrotic interfaces on diverse organs
Daily briefing: The true nature of Greenland’s unique sled dogs revealed by centuries-old DNA
rows.summary: The sled dogs kept by Inuit in Greenland for nearly 1,000 years don’t share much DNA with wolves. Plus, stunning images of nerves across a mouse’s body and what needs to be done to stop the tsunami of plastic pollution.

rows.title: Mini hearts, lungs and livers made in lab now grow their own blood vessels
rows.summary: These sophisticated models will be used for human-development studies and drug testing.

rows.title: Scientists hide messages in papers to game AI peer review
rows.summary: Some studies containing instructions in white text or small font — visible only to machines — will be withdrawn from preprint servers.

rows.title: Author Correction: Genome-wide CRISPR screen in human T cells reveals regulators of FOXP3
Promising vaccine against deadly Nipah virus can also treat infection
rows.summary: In animals, the drug reduced the effects of the virus, which currently has no treatment.

rows.title: Survey of US postdocs finds threefold increase in job losses
rows.summary: Country-wide cuts are difficult to determine, but a survey by the National Postdoctoral Association reveals mounting pressures.

rows.title: US senators poised to reject Trump’s proposed massive science cuts
rows.summary: Committee gives first hint that policymakers might preserve, rather than slash, funding for US National Science Foundation and other agencies.

rows.title: Author Correction: Spatial immune scoring system predicts hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence
OpenAI’s o3 tops new AI league table for answering scientific questions
rows.summary: SciArena uses votes by researchers to evaluate large language models’ responses on technical topics.

rows.title: Centuries-old DNA reveals origins of Greenland’s unique dogs
rows.summary: Genomic data shed light on how populations of sled dogs — and their human handlers — have shifted over past 800 years.

rows.title: Giant map details nerves across a mouse’s body: see stunning pics
rows.summary: High-resolution imaging method could lead to wiring diagram for the whole body.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Research sleuthing is being ‘twisted’ to cast doubt on science
rows.summary: Research-integrity sleuths worry that their work is being used out of context to discredit long-held scientific knowledge. Plus, ancient proteins rewrite the evolutionary history of rhinos and a ‘super sponge’ material for sucking up carbon dioxide.

rows.title: Extreme river flood exposes latent erosion risk
rows.summary: Analysis of the 2021 Meuse River flood reveals potential erosion risks due to uneven river widening and subsoil variability, highlighting challenges for river engineering and flood mitigation in a changing climate.

rows.title: Why quantum physicists are still arguing after 100 years
rows.summary: Six experts explain why quantum mechanics is a topic no-one can agree on.

rows.title: Ancient DNA reveals farming led to more human diseases
rows.summary: The transition to agriculture introduced many new diseases to humans from animals — plus, how whale poo is helping researchers study harmful algal blooms.

rows.title: Sweet or sour? AI-powered device achieves human-like sense of taste
rows.summary: Graphene-based sensor is a step towards restoring taste for people with neurological conditions.

rows.title: Workouts can help gut microbes to quell cancer
rows.summary: Mice that exercised produced higher levels of an immune-cell-stimulating molecule than sedentary rodents did.

rows.title: World’s most porous sponges: intricate carbon-trapping powders hit the market
rows.summary: Metal-organic frameworks were the next big thing in chemistry when they were invented more than three decades ago. Now, these intriguing materials are becoming commercial tools for capturing carbon dioxide and harvesting water from the air.

rows.title: First returned rock samples shine a light on the Moon’s ‘dark side’
rows.summary: Soil samples from the far side of the Moon provide clues about the origin of lunar asymmetry and the effects of ‘mega-basin’ impacts on the evolution of rocky planets

rows.title: Lack of evidence for the transitional cerebellar progenitor
Symbolic ‘science fair’ showcases research cut by Trump team
rows.summary: Democrats hosted a protest event featuring ‘things we’ll never know’ because of the US government’s cuts to science.

rows.title: Weight loss alters adipose tissue beyond just reducing fat
rows.summary: Cellular changes to adipose tissue after weight-loss surgery could point to pathways responsible for the metabolic benefits of this procedure.

rows.title: Millions of tonnes of nanoplastics are polluting the ocean
rows.summary: These plastic particles smaller than a human hair can pass through cell walls and enter the food web

rows.title: Research is powered by technical talent — and recognition is finally on the rise
rows.summary: Take time to understand who your technician colleagues are, and what they bring to your research, says Kelly Vere.

rows.title: Cold coffee effect
rows.summary: Time for a break.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The first malaria treatment for babies wins approval
rows.summary: A dissolvable malaria drug formulated specifically for infants will soon be available in parts of Africa. Plus, biologically inspired high fashion hits the runway in Paris and whether anyone truly understands quantum physics.

rows.title: Integrated cryogenic chip controls spin qubits
rows.summary: Building a quantum computer out of silicon allows the computer’s qubits to be integrated seamlessly with their control electronics, but the control circuits can degrade qubit performance. A cryogenic control chip counters this risk and holds promise for scaling up the number of qubits.

rows.title: Animal diseases leapt to humans when we started keeping livestock
rows.summary: When hunter-gatherers began living close to animals, the pathogens that cause the plague and leprosy got closer too.

rows.title: Highly efficient air filter inspired by mucus-covered nasal hair
rows.summary: Airborne particles adhere to filters only weakly. A filtration strategy that mimics the effects of the mucus layer coating nasal hairs captures particulate matter effectively, owing to a mechanism called capillary adhesion. Filters using this technology perform better than conventional air filters and have a longer lifespan.

rows.title: Plastics pollution is surging — the planned UN treaty to curb it must be ambitious
rows.summary: New research on nanoplastics pollution and ‘chemicals of concern’ underscores the need for a strong agreement when negotiations restart in Switzerland next month.

rows.title: Retraction Note: Human fetal cerebellar cell atlas informs medulloblastoma origin and oncogenesis
Nanoplastics make up most of the plastic pollutants in the North Atlantic Ocean
rows.summary: A landmark field study reveals widespread pollution of the Atlantic Ocean by nanoscale plastic debris — raising questions about the risk to marine ecosystems.

rows.title: Ancient proteins rewrite the rhino family tree — are dinosaurs next?
rows.summary: Molecules from 20-million-year-old teeth are among the oldest ever sequenced.

rows.title: Will algorithms choose your next lab colleague?
rows.summary: AI tools have been slow to enter academic recruitment — but recent developments could change that.

rows.title: Lab drowning in paperwork? Hire an in-house writer
rows.summary: Hiring a postdoc to take over writing tasks makes good sense, argues Béla Z. Schmidt.

rows.title: Enormous inventory of plastic chemicals could shape safer future use
rows.summary: If plastics are to be made more sustainable, they must first be made safer in terms of the chemicals they contain and release. A comprehensive inventory of more than 16,000 known plastic chemicals, including particularly problematic ones, supports scientists and stakeholders in understanding and improving the safety of plastics.

rows.title: Research-integrity sleuths say their work is being ‘twisted’ to undermine science
rows.summary: Some sleuths fear that the business of cleaning up flawed studies is being weaponized against science itself.

rows.title: The curious case of how bird wrists evolved
rows.summary: Wrist evolution helped birds to conquer the air. Fossil data and analysis of a modern bird’s development reveal that this evolution preceded bird origins

rows.title: A single-cell multi-omics atlas of rice
rows.summary: A single-cell multi-omics atlas of rice is revealed, providing insight into cell-type functions and molecular programs.

rows.title: The spatiotemporal distribution of human pathogens in ancient Eurasia
rows.summary: Screening shotgun-sequencing data from ancient humans covering 37,000 years of Eurasian history uncovers the widespread presence of ancient bacterial, viral and parasite DNA and zoonotic pathogens coincide with the widespread domestication of livestock.

rows.title: How short peptides disassemble tau fibrils in Alzheimer’s disease
rows.summary: Cryo-electron and atomic force microscopy shed light on how fibrils of the protein tau, which accumulate in the brain of people with Alzheimer’s disease, can be disassembled by short peptides, providing a possible route towards developing treatments.

rows.title: Decadal changes in atmospheric circulation detected in cloud motion vectors
rows.summary: Analysis of cloud motion vectors from the Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer over the past two decades indicates an acceleration and poleward shift of atmospheric circulation, and comparison with ERA5 reanalysis winds suggests probable ERA5 biases in the upper troposphere.

rows.title: A haplotype-resolved pangenome of the barley wild relative Hordeum bulbosum
rows.summary: A study describes the assembly and analysis of a haplotype-resolved pangenome of bulbous barley with the potential to improve domesticated barley and illustrates its use in evolutionary research and trait mapping.

rows.title: Metalasers with arbitrarily shaped wavefront
rows.summary: A metalaser is described, in which light can have an arbitrarily shaped wavefront, enabling the metalaser emission to have any desired profile, such as focal spots, focal lines, vector beams, vortex beams and even holograms.

rows.title: Nutrients activate distinct patterns of small-intestinal enteric neurons
rows.summary: Calcium imaging of the mouse jejunum shows that specific nutrients in the intestinal lumen are detected by epithelial cells, which activate specific sets of enteric neurons through a serotonin-mediated signalling process.

rows.title: Bowhead whale faeces link increasing algal toxins in the Arctic to ocean warming
rows.summary: An analysis of bowel samples from bowhead whales collected yearly from 2004–2022 indicates increasing algal toxin concentrations in Arctic food webs due to warming ocean conditions.

rows.title: Ultra-depleted mantle source of basalts from the South Pole–Aitken basin
rows.summary: Extreme Sr–Nd depletion in 2.8-billion-year-old basalt fragments from the lunar farside South Pole–Aitken basin suggests an ultra-depleted mantle source resulting from lunar magma ocean crystallization and/or later impact-related melt extraction.

rows.title: Loss of FCoV-23 spike domain 0 enhances fusogenicity and entry kinetics
rows.summary: The molecular mechanisms of cell entry for the recently identified highly pathogenic feline coronavirus FCoV-23 are characterized in detail.

rows.title: Replay and representation dynamics in the hippocampus of freely flying bats
rows.summary: Wireless large-scale recordings of neural activity in freely flying fruit bats reveal that hippocampal ensemble properties are associated with sensorimotor rhythms, and that previous models of replay and sequential dynamics, based on experiments in rodents, might not be applicable to other species.

rows.title: Selective remodelling of the adipose niche in obesity and weight loss
rows.summary: An atlas study of adipose tissue in people with obesity undergoing weight loss and their lean counterparts reveals that weight loss reduces cell senescence but cannot reverse all the metabolic problems caused by obesity.

rows.title: Control of toxicity of fine particulate matter emissions in China
rows.summary: A relative potency-adjusted inventory of fine-particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) established in China reveals sectoral and regional disparities in PM 2.5 emissions, exposures and associated toxic potencies.

rows.title: The role of metabolism in shaping enzyme structures over 400 million years
rows.summary: By combining structural biology and evolutionary genomics analyses, the evolution of enzymes over 400 million years is shown to be governed by catalytic function, metabolic network architecture, cost and molecular interactions.

rows.title: Cryptic variation fuels plant phenotypic change through hierarchical epistasis
rows.summary: Gene regulatory network architecture and complex dosage effects from paralogue diversification converge to shape phenotypic space, producing the potential for both strongly buffered phenotypes and sudden bursts of phenotypic change.

rows.title: Phylogenetically informative proteins from an Early Miocene rhinocerotid
rows.summary: Protein sequences from fossil tooth enamel of a rhinocerotid from Canada’s High Arctic are used to develop phylogenetic frameworks from a specimen too old to preserve ancient DNA.

rows.title: Mapping the chemical complexity of plastics
rows.summary: An inventory of 16,325 known plastic chemicals, including >4,200 hazardous compounds, supports the development of safer plastics.

rows.title: Eighteen million years of diverse enamel proteomes from the East African Rift
rows.summary: The isolation of dental proteins from fossils deposited 1.5 million to 18 million years ago in the Turkana Basin in Kenya, a tropical region, demonstrate the promise of dental enamel for palaeoproteomic and evolutionary studies.

rows.title: Quantum correlations of spontaneous two-photon emission from a quantum dot
rows.summary: Quantum correlations of spontaneous two-photon emission emitted from a bright quantum dot device are revealed, facilitating the creation of entangled photons with near-unity fidelity.

rows.title: Moiré materials based on M-point twisting
rows.summary: A new class of moiré materials based on monolayers with triangular lattices and low-energy states at the M points of the Brillouin zone is introduced, demonstrating emergent momentum-space non-symmorphic symmetries, a kagome plane-wave lattice structure, and potential quasi-one-dimensionality.

rows.title: Feline infectious peritonitis epizootic caused by a recombinant coronavirus
rows.summary: The emergence of a highly pathogenic FCoV–CCoV recombinant is responsible for a rapidly spreading outbreak of feline infectious peritonitis originating in Cyprus.

rows.title: Synthesis of deuterated acids and bases using bipolar membranes
rows.summary: A method making use of heavy water dissociation in bipolar membranes to synthesize deuterated acids and bases is described, which requires particularly mild conditions and inexpensive D 2 O and K 2 SO 4 and is also environmentally friendly.

rows.title: Nanoplastic concentrations across the North Atlantic
rows.summary: Observations from 12 hydrocast stations along a transect crossing the North Atlantic from the subtropical gyre to the northern European shelf provide evidence of large amounts of nanoplastics throughout the entire water column.

rows.title: Coenzyme Q headgroup intermediates can ameliorate a mitochondrial encephalopathy
rows.summary: Decreased brain coenzyme Q 10 levels cause encephalopathy and are associated with neurodegeneration; supplementation with 4-HMA or 4-HB restores coenzyme Q 10 synthesis in mice and humans with HPDL variants, improving survival and neurological symptoms in HPDL -driven mitochondrial encephalopathy.

rows.title: Single nuclear spin detection and control in a van der Waals material
rows.summary: The detection and coherent control of single 13 C nuclear spins in hexagonal boron nitride at room temperature enables the use of van der Waals materials in upcoming quantum technologies.

rows.title: Reorganization of the theropod wrist preceded the origin of avian flight
rows.summary: The forelimbs of two Late Cretaceous theropod dinosaurs show the presence of the pisiform bone, previously thought to have been lost early in theropod evolution and regained in birds during the evolution of flight, indicating that a birdlike pisiform appeared prior to the evolution of flight.

rows.title: Memory gets a boost from positive emotion
rows.summary: Study participants’ memory faltered when they learnt while experiencing negative or neutral emotions.

rows.title: Support Sudan’s displaced young scientists
Address Colombia’s brain-health crisis
Old CO₂ released from rivers complicates evaluations of fossil-fuel emissions
Inventions that made the United States a powerhouse of innovation
rows.summary: Lessons learnt from early lunar research, and the birthplace of ‘pictures that live and move’, in our weekly peek at Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Hot air: the most extreme heatwaves are accelerating the fastest
rows.summary: Tropical regions where heatwaves are already common will be hardest hit by this trend.

rows.title: Expand biobank sampling to three or more generations
Daily briefing: Stress can make you sick, and scientists are learning why
rows.summary: Scientists are grappling with the connections between stress and health. Plus, the science that underlies escalating heatwaves and a rabies vaccine that can be spread through licks.

rows.title: Metascience can improve science — but it must be useful to society, too
rows.summary: Researchers studying research must avoid the temptation to get too stuck in the academic weeds.

rows.title: Genetic mutation predicts survival after immunotherapy for ovarian cancer
rows.summary: Women with a rare type of ovarian cancer have prolonged survival after receiving immune-checkpoint blockade if their tumour cells carry a mutation in the gene PPP2R1A .

rows.title: Deaf scientists hit by drastic NIH cuts — the research community must support them
rows.summary: Severe blows to the ‘deaf-scientist pipeline’ must not mean abandoning its best practices. Here is how to support current and future students.

rows.title: Science on the catwalk: Iris van Herpen gives gowns a glow up
rows.summary: Microorganisms, materials and movement inspire high-fashion dress designs.

rows.title: How to chart a moral future for space exploration
rows.summary: Expanding human influence in outer space will require an ethical compass that is more expansive than the one conventionally used.

rows.title: Highly efficient enzymes designed from scratch
rows.summary: A computational workflow designs proteins with catalytic efficiencies comparable to those of some natural enzymes — a landmark result for the field.

rows.title: Stress is wrecking your health: how can science help?
rows.summary: Better stress assessment and tailored interventions could give clinicians the tools they need to fend off lasting damage.

rows.title: How monitoring a remote Finnish peatland helps climate science
rows.summary: Risto Taipale works on the maintenance of a research station that provides publicly accessible data on climate change.

rows.title: Author Correction: Adipose tissue retains an epigenetic memory of obesity after weight loss
Turbocharged ‘killer’ cells show promise for autoimmune disease
rows.summary: Experimental treatment could offer a safer, cheaper alternative to CAR-T-cell therapies for disorders such as lupus.

rows.title: Rubbish years: how to boost lab group morale when world events crash in
rows.summary: Award-winning mentors share best practice to keep your team going amid political upheavals, economic downturns and other events.

rows.title: Will AI speed up literature reviews or derail them entirely?
rows.summary: The publication of ever-larger numbers of problematic papers, including fake ones generated by artificial intelligence, represents an existential crisis for the established way of doing evidence synthesis. But with a new approach, AI might also save the day.

rows.title: The Māori values that make good sense in science
rows.summary: The Indigenous beliefs underpinning soil chemist Amanda Black's approach could deliver a more inclusive research culture, she says.

rows.title: Daily briefing: A worst-case weather scenario drove deadly flooding in Texas
rows.summary: A maximum in rainfall coinciding with the headwaters of a particularly flash-flood-prone river resulted in deadly flash flooding in Texas on 4 July. Plus, turbocharged ‘killer’ cells that could help treat autoimmune diseases and whether at-home medical tests are worth it.

rows.title: Efficient perovskite/silicon tandem with asymmetric self-assembly molecule
rows.summary: An asymmetric self-assembled monolayer improves the efficiency of perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells compared with symmetric self-assembled monolayers, resulting in a certified power conversion efficiency of up to 34.58%.

rows.title: Rise of the planet of the zombie bugs: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: How breaking the ‘reciprocity law’ could improve green energy
rows.summary: A material that emits less energy than it absorbs has the potential to save some of the sunlight wasted by solar collectors.

rows.title: Audio long read: How to speak to a vaccine sceptic — research reveals what works
rows.summary: In the face of growing vaccine hesitancy levels, studies show there are ways to address people’s questions.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Neanderthals boiled bones in ‘fat factories’
rows.summary: New evidence suggests that Neanderthals rendered fat from bones to stave off protein poisoning. Plus an interstellar object is about to pass through our Solar System and why some animal mimics aren’t great replicas.

rows.title: Japan requires name change after marriage — with big effects on female scientists
rows.summary: Survey finds law requiring married couples to share the same family name causes havoc for researchers.

rows.title: Celebrating researchers who make the scientific workplace more inclusive
rows.summary: Eight scientists who appeared in Nature's Changemaker series are to feature in a forthcoming podcast series. Kendall Powell and Deborah Daley introduce them.

rows.title: China pours money into brain chips that give paralysed people more control
rows.summary: Brain–computer interfaces being trialled in China offer some advantages over Neuralink and other leading US devices.

rows.title: I help to build support systems for Latina researchers
rows.summary: After leaving academia, chemist Daisy Rosas Vargas starting leading outreach to encourage Latina people in pursuit of science careers.

rows.title: Poo of farm animals teems with drug-resistance genes
rows.summary: A global map reveals the prevalence of thousands of genes that arm pathogens against antibiotics.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The first full ancient Egyptian human genome sequence
rows.summary: Teeth from 4,800-year-old remains have yielded the first full human genome sequence from ancient Egypt. Plus, the orbit of a ‘clingy’ planet could cause its own demise and how climate change is ravaging the iconic moai statues on Rapa Nui.

rows.title: How we’re rebuilding the Weizmann Institute — and our hopes for a better future
rows.summary: Scientific research is at the heart of Israel’s success and has worldwide benefits. Our work will continue despite adversity.

rows.title: ‘Tour de force’ experiment probes quantum tunnelling in action
rows.summary: Probing photons inside a barrier also challenges a long-standing interpretation of quantum physics.

rows.title: Rare find: interstellar visitor seen blazing through our Solar System
rows.summary: The comet-like body — called 3I/ATLAS or C/2025 N1 — is zipping past Jupiter.

rows.title: Academic language has become a proxy for European culture wars
rows.summary: Some European governments are rethinking the use of English in universities, exposing tensions between internationalization and national priorities.

rows.title: Home medical tests miss the mark
rows.summary: Kits sold directly to consumers to check a variety of health metrics provide little value when it comes to guiding health decisions.

rows.title: Neanderthals boiled bones in ‘fat factories’ to enrich their lean diet
rows.summary: Germany digs reveal a large-scale operation 100,000 years earlier than oldest known fat rendering by modern humans.

rows.title: Ancient DNA helps trace stinky Roman fish sauce to its source
rows.summary: Mangled bones found at a one-time manufacturing facility pinpoint species used to make a quintessential condiment.

rows.title: Three tips for talking to a vaccine sceptic
rows.summary: Research gives specific advice for conversations about vaccine hesitancy.

rows.title: 3D-printed fake wasps help explain bad animal mimicry
rows.summary: Experiments show some predators are easier to fool than others — plus, the researchers who built a Stone Age canoe and took it out to sea.

rows.title: Massive submarine eruption darkened clouds half a world away
rows.summary: Sound-wave created by eruption in Tonga caused the atmosphere to warm over Mexico and the Caribbean.

rows.title: This AI ‘thinks’ like a human — after training on 160 psychology studies
rows.summary: The Centaur model goes beyond single tasks and predicts a wide array of human behaviour.

rows.title: Daily briefing: A unique methane-detecting satellite has been lost
rows.summary: MethaneSAT, a satellite designed to detect sources of the most powerful greenhouse gas, has been lost 15 months into its 5-year mission. Plus, how brain scans can reveal the pace of biological ageing and what it’s like to do science with an AI team.

rows.title: Viral genomes track the transmission of mpox in humans before 2017 outbreak
rows.summary: An analysis of mpox virus genomes from individuals infected between 2018 and 2023 has provided insights into how the virus emerged in the human population. The study revealed key drivers associated with animal-to-human transmission of the virus in the biodiverse border regions of Cameroon and Nigeria, and human-to-human transmission in Nigeria.

rows.title: First human genome from ancient Egypt sequenced from 4,800-year-old teeth
rows.summary: Forty years after the first effort to extract mummy DNA, researchers have finally generated a full genome sequence from an ancient Egyptian.

rows.title: Tunnelling photons challenge interpretation of quantum mechanics
rows.summary: Measurements with confined photons challenge a prediction that particles that ‘quantum tunnel’ into infinitely long barriers will get stuck.

rows.title: Injured plants use gaseous cues to initiate repair of their outer layers
rows.summary: The periderm layers of plants form an outer protective barrier. If the periderm is broken, movement of the gases ethylene and oxygen triggers a healing process.

rows.title: What we stand to lose when foreign students are seen as a threat
rows.summary: International students enrich university communities and strengthen civic life. We must defend their place in global education.

rows.title: AI ‘scientists’ joined these research teams: here’s what happened
rows.summary: Emerging ‘co-scientist’ systems use chatbots to mimic the deliberations of a research group. Nature asked researchers to test them out.

rows.title: Leadership change at African journal sparks calls for bold reform
rows.summary: The Journal of Public Health in Africa faces a pivotal moment, and researchers say it must evolve to better serve the scientific community.

rows.title: 3D printing offers a way to study mimicry by insects
rows.summary: Predation experiments using models of edible flies and stinging wasps provide some answers to a long-standing evolutionary puzzle in mimicry research.

rows.title: Brain implant decodes neural activity to produce expressive speech
rows.summary: A brain–computer interface has enabled a man with paralysis to speak through a computer. The system records the activity of hundreds of neurons and translates them into voice in real time, effectively creating a digital voice box. The system enables the man to have conversations with his family, vary his intonation and even sing.

rows.title: Wherever we go in this system, there we are
rows.summary: A voyage of discovery.

rows.title: Signs of AI-generated text found in 14% of biomedical abstracts last year
rows.summary: Abstracts included telltale words, such as ‘unparalleled’ and ‘invaluable’, that are common in text generated by large language models.

rows.title: A genome from ancient Egypt
rows.summary: The genome of a man buried at Nuwayrat in Middle Egypt about 4,500–4,800 years ago has been sequenced. Compared with published genomes of ancient individuals, most of the man’s ancestry best matches those of older individuals from North Africa, although around one-fifth best matches those of earlier ones from Mesopotamia. The study marks 40 years of progress in ancient-DNA research.

rows.title: Molecular gas in a low-dust galaxy hints at how stars formed in the early Universe
rows.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has detected molecular hydrogen in a nearby galaxy that has a very low proportion of metals. This implies that considerable quantities of molecular gas can form at low metallicities, and provides insight into similarly metal-poor galaxies in the early Universe.

rows.title: Boron-mediated modular assembly of tetrasubstituted alkenes
rows.summary: A method based on boron-mediated assembly is described for the synthesis of tetrasubstituted alkenes, molecules with four substituents around the central C=C bond, with complete control over the double-bond geometry.

rows.title: Stereodivergent transformation of a natural polyester to enantiopure PHAs
rows.summary: Stereoselective synthetic routes use P3HB (a polyester produced by bacteria) as a chiral feedstock for related polymers that have properties more amenable to processing and use.

rows.title: Mapping the adaptive landscape of Batesian mimicry using 3D-printed stimuli
rows.summary: Birds have an excellent ability to learn to discriminate harmless insects from those that they mimic on the basis of subtle differences in appearance.

rows.title: Functional amyloid proteins confer defence against predatory bacteria
rows.summary: Escherichia coli uses curli fibres, oligomers of the functional amyloid CsgA, as a barrier to protect against the predatory bacteria Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus and Myxococcus xanthus in a mechanism that is independent of genes required for biofilm formation.

rows.title: Plants monitor the integrity of their barrier by sensing gas diffusion
rows.summary: A study using Arabidopsis shows that plants can monitor the integrity of their outer barriers by sensing gas diffusion, enabling them to initiate wound repair to prevent water loss and pathogen entry.

rows.title: A mouse brain stereotaxic topographic atlas with isotropic 1-μm resolution
rows.summary: A stereotaxic atlas of the whole mouse brain, based on a Nissl-stained cytoarchitecture dataset with isotropic 1-μm resolution, achieved through continuous micro-optical sectioning tomography, promises to be a versatile brainsmatics tool for studying the whole brain at single-cell level.

rows.title: Whole-genome ancestry of an Old Kingdom Egyptian
rows.summary: Whole-genome sequencing of an ancient male Egyptian revealed a mixture of North African Neolithic and eastern Fertile Crescent ancestry, suggesting human migration between Egypt and Mesopotamia by the Old Kingdom period.

rows.title: The mutagenic forces shaping the genomes of lung cancer in never smokers
rows.summary: An analysis of data from the Sherlock- Lung study provides insight into the mutational processes that contribute to lung cancer in never smokers, and looks at the possible role of factors such as air pollution and passive smoking.

rows.title: The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues Network
rows.summary: The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues Network aims to create a reference catalogue of somatic mosaicism across different tissues and cells within individuals.

rows.title: Mapping and engineering RNA-driven architecture of the multiphase nucleolus
rows.summary: Spatially segregated rRNA processing dictates nucleolar morphology and drives outward progression of pre-ribosomal RNA through nucleolar phases.

rows.title: Trade-offs in aviation impacts on climate favour non-CO 2 mitigation
rows.summary: A climate-trade-off risk curve derived from uncertainties in the radiative-forcing components indicates that focusing on reducing contrails or nitrogen oxide emissions is more effective than reducing CO 2 emissions.

rows.title: Energy–speed relationship of quantum particles challenges Bohmian mechanics
rows.summary: The study of the relationship between particle speed and negative kinetic energy, arising in regions in which, according to classical mechanics, particles are not allowed to enter, reveals behaviour that appears to contradict the predictions of Bohmian mechanics.

rows.title: Range extender mediates long-distance enhancer activity
rows.summary: The REX element is associated with long-range enhancer–promoter interactions.

rows.title: Ancient DNA reveals the prehistory of the Uralic and Yeniseian peoples
rows.summary: Genome-wide sequencing of 180 ancient individuals shows a continuous gradient of ancestry in Early-to-Mid-Holocene hunter-gatherers from the Baltic to the Transbaikal region and distinct contemporaneous groups in Northeast Siberia, and provides insights into the origins of modern Uralic and Yeniseian speakers.

rows.title: Hybrid quantum network for sensing in the acoustic frequency range
rows.summary: A hybrid quantum network combining entangled light with an atomic spin ensemble engineered to act as a negative-mass oscillator enables frequency-dependent quantum noise reduction for measurements in the acoustic noise frequency range relevant for gravitational-wave detection.

rows.title: Electron flow in hydrogenotrophic methanogens under nickel limitation
rows.summary: Two distantly related methanogens shift the methanogenic pathway under nickel limitation, suggesting that methanogens adapt to changing bioavailability of nickel by rerouting electron flow between two different pathways.

rows.title: Rewiring endogenous genes in CAR T cells for tumour-restricted payload delivery
rows.summary: A CRISPR knock-in strategy that uses endogenous gene regulatory mechanisms can engineer ‘armoured’ CAR T cells that secrete proinflammatory cytokines directly within a tumour without causing toxicity, leading to prolonged survival in mice.

rows.title: Inter-brain neural dynamics in biological and artificial intelligence systems
rows.summary: Shared inter-brain neural dynamics, reflecting aspects of social interaction including self and other’s behaviours, arise in GABAergic neurons of the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex of socially interacting mice, as well as in the neurons of socially interacting artificial intelligence agents.

rows.title: Close-in planet induces flares on its host star
rows.summary: Planet-induced flares on HIP 67522, a 17 million-year-old G dwarf star with two known close-in planets, were detected.

rows.title: A foundation model to predict and capture human cognition
rows.summary: A computational model called Centaur, developed by fine-tuning a language model on a huge dataset called Psych-101, can predict and simulate human nature in experiments expressible in natural language, even in previously unseen situations.

rows.title: WSTF nuclear autophagy regulates chronic but not acute inflammation
rows.summary: During chronic but not acute inflammation, chromatin remodelling is influenced by nuclear autophagy through WSTF interaction with ATG8 in the nucleus, leading to WSTF nuclear export and its subsequent degradation.

rows.title: PPP2R1A mutations portend improved survival after cancer immunotherapy
rows.summary: Inactivating PPP2R1A mutations correlate with better survival after immune checkpoint blockade in patients with ovarian clear cell carcinoma, suggesting that targeting the phosphatase 2A (PP2A) pathway may represent an effective startegy for improving responses to immunotherapy.

rows.title: Discovering cognitive strategies with tiny recurrent neural networks
rows.summary: Modelling biological decision-making with tiny recurrent neural networks enables more accurate predictions of animal choices than classical cognitive models and offers insights into the underlying cognitive strategies and neural mechanisms.

rows.title: Carbonate formation and fluctuating habitability on Mars
rows.summary: A modelling study suggests that Mars had a desert-like climate with intermittent liquid-water oases regulated by a negative feedback among solar luminosity, liquid water and carbonate formation.

rows.title: Ultrabroadband and band-selective thermal meta-emitters by machine learning
rows.summary: An unconventional machine learning-based inverse design framework enables the generation of ultrabroadband and band-selective thermal meta-emitters with complex 3D architectures and diverse material compositions.

rows.title: It should be free to apply to graduate school
Publisher Correction: Metabolic adaptations direct cell fate during tissue regeneration
Human space travel risks contaminating Mars
How much energy is wasted from making a cup of tea?
rows.summary: Lukewarm efforts to get Britain to save on the energy bill, and a mysterious string of house-fly deaths, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Author Correction: Targeting the SHOC2–RAS interaction in RAS-mutant cancers

Turmoil at US science academy as Trump cuts force layoffs
rows.summary: Efforts by leaders of the US national academies to adjust to the new political reality have spurred member concerns about capitulation and censorship.

rows.title: How to speed up peer review: make applicants mark one another
rows.summary: ‘Distributed peer review’ of grants makes process more than twice as fast — and includes some cheat-prevention measures.

rows.title: How fast are you ageing? Ordinary brain scans reveal the pace
rows.summary: Images hold clues to risk of dementia and various age-related diseases.

rows.title: Extend your reach by turning your lessons into podcasts
rows.summary: By taking a few technical steps, I’ve made my teaching more accessible to my students — and to biologists around the world.

rows.title: ‘Place’ neurons recognize the same spot from close by and far away
rows.summary: Place cells are neurons that encode spatial locations. Experiments in chickadees reveal that the cells activate even when those locations are viewed from a distance.

rows.title: Transparent research: can big tech learn from big pharma?
rows.summary: The results of technology research and development must find their way into the published literature. New models of regulation could help.

rows.title: Human embryo research: how to move towards a 28-day limit
rows.summary: The decades-old limit on how long human embryos can be grown in culture is under debate. A new road map outlines how to extend the length of culture responsibly.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Industrialization might cause ‘inflammaging’
rows.summary: Ageing isn’t linked to increased inflammation in people living in Indigenous communities. Plus, the month’s best science images and the first independent survey of the number of deaths in Gaza since October 2023.

rows.title: Postdocs file for union recognition at University of Michigan
rows.summary: International scholars targeted by Trump administration are among those seeking greater protection.

rows.title: Why we need mandatory safeguards for emotionally responsive AI
rows.summary: Virtual chatbots that simulate conversations with famous actors or sci-fi characters can have real-world consequences.

rows.title: Architecture, dynamics and biogenesis of GluA3 AMPA glutamate receptors
rows.summary: The GluA3 homomer substantially diverges from other AMPA-type glutamate receptors.

rows.title: Natural nappers: monitoring the sleeping patterns of wild orangutans
rows.summary: How being near to other orangutans affects the duration of sleep.

rows.title: I pioneered my country’s newborn health-screening programme

rows.title: Daily briefing: NIH still uses directives deemed illegal to screen grants
rows.summary: The US National Institutes of Health is still screening grants in process a judge ruled illegal last week. Plus, one researcher’s 40-year project to communicate with dolphins and a wake-up call about computer-vision research.

rows.title: If you’re a US researcher, now is the time to establish a plan B
rows.summary: The scale of funding cuts in the United States means that countless scientists will lose their jobs. It would be naive not to start thinking about alternative career paths.

rows.title: ‘We couldn’t live without it’: the UCSC Genome Browser turns 25
rows.summary: After a quarter of a century, the website remains an essential tool for navigating the genome and understanding its structure, function and clinical impact.

rows.title: Obesity drugs made in China could power next wave of treatments
rows.summary: Drugs currently being tested target complications associated with obesity such as heart disease, fatty liver disease and type 2 diabetes.

rows.title: Stare into a whale’s colossal eye — June’s best science images
rows.summary: The month’s sharpest science shots — selected by Nature ’s photo team.

rows.title: Trump team says it’s axing some contracts with publishing giant Springer Nature
rows.summary: The action comes as high-ranking US officials criticize leading journals as ‘woke’ and ‘corrupt’.

rows.title: Ageing is linked to inflammation — but only in the industrialized world
rows.summary: Inflammation, thought to be a driver of age-related disease, does not worsen with age in some Indigenous communities.

rows.title: What do dolphins talk about? One biologist is trying to listen in
rows.summary: A marine ecologist’s 40-year struggle to understand how animals signal to one another.

rows.title: Deciphering how dog roses with an odd chromosome copy number sexually reproduce
rows.summary: Most sexually reproducing species have an even chromosome copy number, but the dog rose does not. What explains its unusual pattern of chromosome inheritance?

rows.summary: Directives by the Trump administration are still being applied to grant materials despite court order.

rows.title: Can AI build a virtual cell? Scientists race to model life’s smallest unit
rows.summary: Several groups hope to develop artificial-intelligence models that can predict how cells behave.

rows.title: First independent survey of deaths in Gaza reports more than 80,000 fatalities
rows.summary: Results align with other efforts to count the number of people killed amid the ongoing conflict.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The oldest rocks on Earth
rows.summary: Rocks on Hudson Bay, Canada are the only piece of Earth’s crust known to have survived from the planet’s earliest eon. Plus, sea slugs steal photosynthetic equipment from algae to use as an energy source and how artificial-intelligence research is used to bolster surveillance.

rows.title: Niède Guidon obituary: Brazilian archaeologist who upended ideas on early human migration
rows.summary: Researcher used carbon dating to provide evidence that humans had arrived in Brazil much earlier than previously thought.

rows.title: Everyday painkiller made from plastic — by E. coli
rows.summary: Study highlights potential for sustainable synthesis of paracetamol.

rows.title: Killer whales exfoliate each other with home-made scrubbers
rows.summary: Kelp ‘loofahs’ might be first example of toolmaking by marine mammals.

rows.title: Are these the world’s oldest rocks? Fresh data confirm contested claim
rows.summary: Scientists debate age of ancient Canadian crust as Inuit leaders work to preserve the location.

rows.title: Addendum: Unravelling cysteine-deficiency-associated rapid weight loss
Daily briefing: Researchers re-enact an epic ancient canoe trip
rows.summary: Researchers have shown how Stone Age people might have canoed from Taiwan to Japan more than 30,000 years ago by doing it themselves. Plus, cancer cells can steal energy-making machinery from nerve cells and what the battle between the Trump administration and Harvard University means for science.

rows.title: NIH-funded science must now be free to read instantly: what you should know
rows.summary: US biomedical agency’s public-access policy kicks in on 1 July. Nature talks to specialists about how to comply.

rows.title: ‘I didn’t know someone could pursue astronomy as a career’
rows.summary: Astronomer Willice Obonyo describes how scholarship programmes seeded a fresh crop of radioastronomers in Africa.

rows.title: RFK Jr’s vaccine advisers vote down flu-shot ingredient — but back some jabs
