rows.summary: Here’s where academic researchers are flocking to — and the topics they’re pursuing.

rows.title: Plagues of locusts could be avoided by using compounds that suppress swarming
rows.summary: The discovery of compounds that inhibit biosynthesis of the pheromone that triggers locust swarming suggests a fresh approach for controlling these pests.

rows.title: Cancer cells get power boost by stealing mitochondria from nerves
rows.summary: The theft probably helps the cells to spread around the body, and preventing it could provide a path to treatment, researchers say.

rows.title: Mixed plastics turned into valuable chemicals
rows.summary: The diverse chemical and physical properties of plastics make it hard to recycle mixtures. An innovative recycling method now tackles this issue.

rows.title: Don’t sleepwalk from computer-vision research into surveillance
rows.summary: The output of computer-vision research is overwhelmingly aimed towards monitoring humans. The potential ethical implications need more scrutiny.

rows.title: These scientists re-enacted Stone Age voyage to Japan’s remote islands
rows.summary: Experiment shows how people in dugout canoes could have crossed the treacherous straits between Taiwan and the Ryukyu Islands.

rows.title: Coherent bunching of anyons and dissociation in an interference experiment
rows.summary: The coherent bunching of anyons and their dissociation was observed in an interference experiment.

rows.title: Neuronal transfer of mitochondria to tumour cells promotes cancer spread
rows.summary: Neurons often receive organelles called mitochondria from other cells. It emerges that neurons donate mitochondria that support cancer-cell spread.

rows.title: Three science-led start-ups making their mark
rows.summary: Sometimes research needs to leave academia in order to thrive. Three spin-off founders reveal key drivers of their success.

rows.title: Can a pill replace exercise? Swigging this molecule gives mice benefits of working out
rows.summary: Betaine, a compound that becomes more abundant in men who take up jogging, could confer some of the anti-ageing advantages of physical activity.

rows.title: Droplets of three electrons behave like a liquid
rows.summary: Experiments in which systems of interacting electrons are split apart reveal the signatures of a liquid-like state — even for as few as three electrons.

rows.title: A guide to the Nature Index
rows.summary: A description of the terminology and methodology used in this supplement, and a guide to the functionality that is available free online at natureindex.com.

rows.title: Eureka! The brain science behind lightbulb moments
rows.summary: Experiences of insight come with a burst of brain activity — and a memory boost.

rows.title: Computer-vision research is hiding its role in creating ‘Big Brother’ technologies
rows.summary: Technologies that can interpret imagery have many potential applications. An innovative study of papers and patents in the field suggests one use case that overrides the others: human surveillance.

rows.title: ‘Wildest thing’: solar-powered slug steals chloroplasts and stores them for emergencies
rows.summary: Marine creatures house contraband structures in special organelles, which the animal raids for food in times of need.

rows.title: AI, peer review and the human activity of science
rows.summary: When researchers cede their scientific judgement to machines, we lose something important.

rows.title: What incentives do companies need to publish research?
rows.summary: There are good commercial reasons for firms to share their research in science journals, but the practice seems to be falling out of favour.

rows.title: Wake up call for AI: computer-vision research increasingly used for surveillance
rows.summary: One analysis suggests that 90% of studies in the field involve data relating to humans.

rows.title: Nanoscale heat transport tracked at interface between semiconductor materials
rows.summary: Phonons are quasiparticles that carry heat, and in electronic chips they can get blocked at interfaces between materials, leading to overheating. An electron-microscopy technique that relies on a phenomenon called inelastic electron scattering has been used to map phonons and temperatures with (sub-)nanometre resolution to characterize heat-transport dynamics across such interfaces.

rows.title: Change of venue: fission-yeast cell-division cues actually initiate in the nucleus
rows.summary: In yeast, the CDK and cyclin proteins that drive cell division activate first in the nucleus — a different location in the cell from where was previously thought.

rows.title: Missile defence won’t prevent the health crises that rock global security
rows.summary: As was realized after the Second World War, peace and prosperity stem from partnership and sustained investment in human development.

rows.title: Does using ChatGPT change your brain activity? Study sparks debate
rows.summary: Scientists warn against reading too much into a small experiment generating a lot of buzz.

rows.title: Family recipe
rows.summary: Food for thought.

rows.title: Here’s why China’s science and innovation model is thriving
rows.summary: A combination of government planning, academic ambition and bold entrepreneurship are hallmarks of the country’s success.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The neuroscience behind eureka moments
rows.summary: Scientists are digging into the regions of the brain involved in lightbulb moments. Plus, the man o’ war is at least four species and whether mega-funders can rescue a highly cited health database hit by US cuts.

rows.title: The economic effects of federal cuts to US science — in 24 graphs
rows.summary: Is US science facing a recession? Growing evidence points to a looming downturn.

rows.title: DeepMind’s new AlphaGenome AI tackles the ‘dark matter’ in our DNA
rows.summary: Tool aims to solve the mystery of non-coding sequences — but is still in its infancy.

rows.title: Spin-qubit control with a milli-kelvin CMOS chip
rows.summary: CMOS-based circuits can be integrated with silicon-based spin qubits and can be controlled at milli-kelvin temperatures, which can potentially help scale up these systems.

rows.title: Nerve-to-cancer transfer of mitochondria during cancer metastasis
rows.summary: A study reports the development of a method to trace intercellular transfer of mitochondria, and demonstrates that cancer cells that receive mitochondria from neurons have enhanced metastatic capabilities.

rows.title: Evidence for a sub-Jovian planet in the young TWA 7 disk
rows.summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope's Mid-Infrared Instrument, a study reports evidence for a direct detection of a cold, sub-Jupiter-mass planet in the disk of the star TWA 7.

rows.title: Decoding 4-vinylanisole biosynthesis and pivotal enzymes in locusts
rows.summary: In locusts, the aggregation pheromone 4-vinylanisole is derived from dietary phenylalanine, and its production is dependent on two 4-vinylphenol methyltransferases that are potential targets for locust pest control.

rows.title: A cost-effective all-in-one halide material for all-solid-state batteries
rows.summary: A cost-effective all-in-one halide cathode material with high energy density and exceptional cycling stability can be used to achieve energy-dense, durable cathodes for the next generation of all-solid-state batteries.

rows.title: Efficient near-infrared harvesting in perovskite–organic tandem solar cells
rows.summary: A new asymmetric non-fullerene acceptor, P2EH-1V, is designed and synthesized for constructing devices demonstrating record-high efficiencies of 26.7% (certified at 26.4%) over an aperture area greater than 1 cm 2 in perovskite–organic tandem solar cells.

rows.title: Rescuing dendritic cell interstitial motility sustains antitumour immunity
rows.summary: Disruption of dendritic cell (DC) interstitial motility in the tumour microenvironment promotes immune evasion, and enhancement of DC interstitial motility offers a route for DC-centric immunotherapy.

rows.title: Evidence of Coulomb liquid phase in few-electron droplets
rows.summary: The emergence of universal collective behaviour is demonstrated through collisions of electron droplets containing up to five particles, which exhibit strong all-body correlations characteristic of a Coulomb liquid.

rows.title: An aspirational approach to planetary futures
rows.summary: The Nature Relationship Index offers a new way to measure and engage human aspirations to shape a better future for people and all life on Earth.

rows.title: RNA codon expansion via programmable pseudouridine editing and decoding
rows.summary: An RNA codon-expansion strategy enables incorporation of non-canonical amino acids into proteins of interest orthogonally to existing methods by inserting pseudouridine codons into specific mRNA transcripts and using an engineered decoder tRNA.

rows.title: Interactions between TTYH2 and APOE facilitate endosomal lipid transfer
rows.summary: The Tweety homologue TTYH2 is identified as the lipid transfer mediator for APOE-containing lipoproteins.

rows.title: Spatiotemporal orchestration of mitosis by cyclin-dependent kinase
rows.summary: Experiments in fission yeast show that cyclin-dependent kinase is first activated in the nucleus, from which the mitotic signal is propagated from CDK at the centrosome to the cytoplasm.

rows.title: Controlling diverse robots by inferring Jacobian fields with deep networks
rows.summary: An approach that learns models of robots from video capture can predict the 3D motion outcomes of motor commands, enabling accurate control of a range of soft, biologically inspired robots from a single video camera.

rows.title: Engrafted nitrergic neurons derived from hPSCs improve gut dysmotility in mice
rows.summary: A study presents a strategy based on human pluripotent stem cells for treating neurodegenerative disorders of the gastrointestinal tract.

rows.title: The expanding repertoire of ESCRT functions in cell biology and disease
rows.summary: This Review examines recently gained insights into the roles of ESCRT complexes in viral infection, immunity, cancer and neurological disease.

rows.title: Barcoded viral tracing identifies immunosuppressive astrocyte–glioma interactions
rows.summary: Using viral barcode tracing to detect interactions between glioblastoma cells and non-malignant astrocytes in patient samples, investigators discovered a pathway that reduces tumour-specific immunity and identified potential therapeutic targets.

rows.title: The dynamics and geometry of choice in the premotor cortex
rows.summary: A population code for the dynamics of choice formation in the primate premotor cortex is revealed, with diverse single-neuron tuning to a shared decision variable.

rows.title: In-line NMR guided orthogonal transformation of real-life plastics
rows.summary: A product-oriented strategy that leverages the reactivities of different functional groups in real-life plastic mixtures can be used to obtain valuable products, opening a path for managing end-of-life plastic mixtures.

rows.title: Mechanism of cytarabine-induced neurotoxicity
rows.summary: Certain antimetabolites used to treat cancer are more neurotoxic than others, and it is now shown that this is due to their greater tendency to generate DNA double-stranded breaks, whereas less neurotoxic agents induce single-stranded breaks.

rows.title: A cation-exchange approach to tunable magnetic intercalation superlattices
rows.summary: A general two-step intercalation and cation-exchange strategy is used to produce a library of highly ordered magnetic intercalation superlattices with tunable chemical modulations and magnetic ordering.

rows.title: Soft magnetic hysteresis in a dysprosium amide–alkene complex up to 100 kelvin
rows.summary: A dysprosium amide–alkene complex shows soft magnetic hysteresis loops up to 100 kelvin, arising from the high charge density of the amide ligands and the structural role of the pendant alkene.

rows.title: Computer-vision research powers surveillance technology
rows.summary: An analysis of research papers and citing patents indicates the extensive ties between computer-vision research and surveillance.

rows.title: Broadband transient full-Stokes luminescence spectroscopy
rows.summary: A high-sensitivity, broadband, transient, full-Stokes spectroscopy setup is demonstrated, which can detect quickly varying small signals from chiral emitters.

rows.title: We need to predict the people disasters will hit, not just the places
rows.summary: Local authorities can deal with natural hazards more effectively if they know ahead of time who will be affected.

rows.title: In the face of anti-science politics, silence is not without cost
rows.summary: More scientific leaders need to speak out about anti-science agendas and threats to academic freedom across the world.

rows.title: How to make America healthy: the real problems — and best fixes
rows.summary: The United States has lower life expectancy than most similarly wealthy nations. Chronic disease is part of the cause, but so are guns, drugs and cars.

rows.title: Boys surpass girls in maths in the first year of school
rows.summary: A gender gap in mathematical ability arises shortly after children begin school — irrespective of the type of school they attend and their socio-economic background.

rows.title: Structural and functional characterization of human sweet taste receptor
rows.summary: Cryo-electron microscopy structures of the human sweet taste receptor in the apo and sucralose-bound states reveal its heterodimeric architecture and mechanisms of ligand binding and signal activation.

rows.title: Ice society: looking for life at unlikely altitudes
rows.summary: James Bradley studies the microbes thriving in extremely cold environments.

rows.title: The shattered statues of Queen Hatshepsut: the reasons for the wreckage
rows.summary: Ritual ‘retirement’ rather than family feud might explain why so many figures of the female pharaoh are broken and cracked.

rows.title: First images from world’s largest digital camera leave astronomers in awe
rows.summary: The Rubin Observatory in Chile will map the entire southern sky every three to four nights.

rows.title: Modular arene functionalization by differential 1,2-diborylation
rows.summary: A nickel-catalysed vicinal diborylation method is described, which can install two different boron functional groups on aromatic rings in a regioselective and site-selective manner, enabling the rapid synthesis of complex molecular building blocks.

rows.title: Medical AI can transform medicine — but only if we carefully track the data it touches
rows.summary: The uncontrolled deployment of machine learning in medicine can distort patient information and sacrifice long-term data reliability for short-term benefits.

rows.title: ‘Natural history museums can save the world’: anti-colonialism, conservation and climate change
rows.summary: Zoologist Jack Ashby explains why it’s vital to invest in protecting specimens stored in scientific collections.

rows.title: Did the US wipe out Iran’s nuclear programme? What researchers know

rows.title: Trump team vows to improve kids’ health: scientists are sceptical

rows.title: Daily briefing: Space shots from the largest digital camera in the world

rows.title: Obesity drugs show promise for treating a new ailment: migraine

rows.title: Will Gates and other funders save massive public health database at risk from Trump cuts?
rows.summary: UN in talks with governments and funding bodies to save highly cited, 40-year health data set used by researchers in more than 90 countries.

rows.title: Tardigrade-obsessed: meet the researchers trying to turn water bears into neuroscience models
rows.summary: For water-bear enthusiasts, it’s the creature’s legs that make it stand out.

rows.title: Gating and noelin clustering of native Ca 2+ -permeable AMPA receptors
rows.summary: Cryo-electron microscopy analyses of calcium-permeable AMPA receptors from rat brain show that they are composed primarily of GluA1 and GluA4 subunits, and biochemical studies show that noelin promotes inter-receptor interactions without modulating receptor function.

rows.title: How many PhDs does the world need? Doctoral graduates vastly outnumber jobs in academia
rows.summary: PhD programmes need to better prepare students for careers outside universities, researchers warn.

rows.title: This tiny robot moves mini-droplets with ease

rows.title: Sensors pinpoint the exact time of a Yellowstone explosion

rows.title: Where is the best place to hold a scientific conference right now?

rows.title: Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’
rows.summary: Astronomer Bernie Fanaroff helped to design South Africa’s plan to become a radioastronomy powerhouse — and it started with training the next generation.

rows.title: Early grant success attracts more funding: study of 100,000 applicants hints at why
rows.summary: Largest study of its kind explores the ‘Matthew effect’ in research.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Which is the perfect conference country?
rows.summary: Which countries offer the ideal combination of easy visas and human rights to host a scientific conference? Plus, how Jaws transformed our view of sharks and experiments to accelerate gold-standard medical reviews using AI.

rows.title: Africa’s chief diplomat for vaccine manufacturing
rows.summary: Virologist Amadou Sall is the driving force behind a world-class manufacturing hub in Senegal.

rows.title: Revealed: how the brain turns stress into a bad night’s sleep

rows.title: Homo sapiens adapted to diverse habitats before successfully populating Eurasia

rows.title: Carbon-fibre composites can be broken down into reusable components
rows.summary: Carbon fibre-reinforced polymers are high-performance materials used in various items, including aircraft, wind-turbine blades and mountain bicycles. A process has been developed that uses acetic acid to break down carbon fibre-reinforced polymers into their major components, which can then be recovered and reused, potentially enabling the recycling of these materials at scale.

rows.title: Why air-traffic controller shortages are not to blame for US airport chaos

rows.title: Migratory moths navigate using the stars
rows.summary: Australian migratory moths use the night sky to maintain their course when they travel long distances to shelter in cool caves during the arid summer.

rows.title: Author Correction: Collagenolysis-dependent DDR1 signalling dictates pancreatic cancer outcome
How dopamine neurons devalue delayed rewards
rows.summary: The activity of neuronal cells that release the neurotransmitter dopamine is thought to encode differences between predicted and actual rewards. This ‘prediction error’ is key to reinforcement learning. It emerges that dopamine neurons differ in their timescales for temporal discounting, enabling the brain to implement sophisticated reinforcement-learning algorithms along multiple timescales.

rows.title: Reply to: On the effects of fault alignment on slip stability
Investigating the molecular ‘scars’ of PTSD in the human brain
rows.summary: Trauma leaves traces in the brain. A study of alterations in gene regulation in the brains of people with post-traumatic stress disorder offers insights into its biology.

rows.title: For the future
rows.summary: Messages from history.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The most-energetic molecule ever made
rows.summary: Scientists have identified only the second known stable nitrogen molecule: hexanitrogen. Plus, much of the hunting driving pangolins to extinction in Nigeria is for food, not scales and an emergency check-up for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.

rows.title: Light detectors made from perovskite crystals see in full colour
rows.summary: Most pixels in cameras detect only red, green or blue light. A sensor made from perovskite materials absorbs all three, improving image brightness and resolution.

rows.title: Neolithic matrilineal society in ancient China
rows.summary: Studies of ancient DNA have generally found that societies in Neolithic and Bronze Age Eurasia were organized around the male line. However, investigation of the Fujia archaeological site in eastern China reveals a Neolithic community organized around two maternal clans — suggesting that this prehistoric society traced its ancestry through the maternal line.

rows.title: A ‘killswitch’ peptide solidifies protein droplets in living cells
rows.summary: Human cells contain dozens of different types of proteinaceous droplets called biomolecular condensates. A newly developed tool provides insights into the behaviour of biomolecules in condensates and into the functions of condensates in living cells.

rows.title: First ever skull from ‘Denisovan’ reveals what ancient people looked like
rows.summary: Ancient proteins and calcified dental plaque identify heavy-browed fossil from China as a Denisovan.

rows.title: Unsupervised pretraining in biological neural networks
rows.summary: During visual learning, neural plasticity is driven by unsupervised learning in mice.

rows.title: Complete computational design of high-efficiency Kemp elimination enzymes
rows.summary: We present a computational approach to the design of high-efficiency enzymes with catalytic parameters comparable to natural enzymes, enabling programming of stable, high-efficiency, new-to-nature Kemp elimination enzymes through minimal experimental effort.

rows.title: Optical nonlinearities in excess of 500 through sublattice reconstruction
rows.summary: A strategy for engineering photon-avalanche nanoparticles is proposed such that they exhibit an unprecedentedly strong nonlinear optical response and their emissions scale by more than 500th power of the pump intensity.

rows.title: Bimodal centromeres in pentaploid dogroses shed light on their unique meiosis
rows.summary: Insights into the dogrose genome and centromeres explain their ability to achieve stable sexual reproduction.

rows.title: Kupffer cell programming by maternal obesity triggers fatty liver disease
rows.summary: In a mouse model, maternal obesity during pregnancy can lead to fatty liver disease in the offspring, driven by aberrant developmental programming of Kuppfer cells.

rows.title: Strategies for climate-resilient global wind and solar power systems
rows.summary: Climate-intensified supply–demand imbalances may raise hourly costs of wind and solar power systems, but well-designed climate-resilient strategies can provide help.

rows.title: Allosteric modulation and biased signalling at free fatty acid receptor 2
rows.summary: Structural, pharmacological and computational studies reveal how different classes of positive allosteric modulators bind to distinct allosteric sites and use noncanonical mechanisms to activate the free-fatty acid receptor FFA2.

rows.title: Machine-learning design of ductile FeNiCoAlTa alloys with high strength
rows.summary: A new group of multi-principal-element alloys, designed through machine learning and extreme microstructural heterogeneities, achieve high strength (1.8-GPa yield strength) and ductility (25% uniform elongation) at room temperature.

rows.title: Impacts of climate change on global agriculture accounting for adaptation
rows.summary: Analysis of data on six stable crops, capturing two-thirds of global crop calories, allows estimation of agricultural impacts and the potential of global producer adaptations to reduce output losses owing to climate change.

rows.title: Gut inflammation promotes microbiota-specific CD4 T cell-mediated neuroinflammation
rows.summary: Dysregulated CD4 T cells that recognize gut commensal antigens are able to infiltrate the central nervous systems and are re-stimulated by host proteins, resulting in neuroinflammation.

rows.title: Targeting de novo purine biosynthesis for tuberculosis treatment
rows.summary: The validation of inhibitors targeting PurF, a novel drug target for tuberculosis drug discovery, is described.

rows.title: Morphodynamics of human early brain organoid development
rows.summary: Human brain morphodynamics are explored using organoids.

rows.title: Bioinspired capillary force-driven super-adhesive filter
rows.summary: Stable coating of filters with a thin liquid layer enhances adhesion of airborne particulates while maintaining high air permeability, resulting in longer lifetimes and higher efficiency of these filters.

rows.title: Bogong moths use a stellar compass for long-distance navigation at night
rows.summary: Every spring, Bogong moths use the starry night sky as a compass to navigate up to 1,000 km towards their alpine migratory goal.

rows.title: Major expansion in the human niche preceded out of Africa dispersal
rows.summary: Analysis of species distribution models in a pan-African database comprising chronometrically dated archaeological sites over the past 120,000 years shows major expansion in the human niche from 70 ka, driven by adaptation to diverse habitats.

rows.title: In vivo mapping of mutagenesis sensitivity of human enhancers
rows.summary: Human enhancers contain a high density of sequence features that are required for their normal in vivo function.

rows.title: Single-cell transcriptomic and chromatin dynamics of the human brain in PTSD
rows.summary: A comprehensive analysis of the cell-specific molecular regulatory mechanisms underlying post-traumatic stress disorder in the human prefrontal cortex.

rows.title: Vertically stacked monolithic perovskite colour photodetectors
rows.summary: A colour sensor array based on multilayer monolithically stacked lead halide perovskite thin-film photodetectors achieves higher quantum efficiency and superior colour accuracy compared to conventional filter-based image sensors.

rows.title: R9AP is a common receptor for EBV infection in epithelial cells and B cells
rows.summary: R9AP is a key receptor for entry of Epstein–Barr virus into human epithelial and B cells, and interacts directly with the viral glycoprotein gH/gL complex to mediate virus–host membrane fusion.

rows.title: Concerned about freedom of science and truth
Author Correction: RUNX2 promotes fibrosis via an alveolar-to-pathological fibroblast transition
US–China trade conflict threatens biomedical collaboration
Why the Royal Greenwich Observatory was chosen to mark zero degrees longitude
rows.summary: International standards set for measuring location and time, and an unusual type of lake-water movement in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

rows.title: Is there a link between gut microbes and ageing?
We need to show AI what didn’t work as well as what did
One dose of gene therapy gives years of relief from blood disorder
rows.summary: The average number of bleeding episodes for men with haemophilia B dropped almost tenfold after treatment.

rows.title: Tighter regulation is needed for AI companions
‘Killswitch’ protein lets scientists study immobilized cellular droplets
rows.summary: Synthetic peptide fixes biomolecular condensates, revealing how these enigmatic cell structures actually work.

rows.title: How China can become a biotechnology superpower
rows.summary: After decades of pioneering institutional change in Chinese research, neuroscientist Rao Yi explains why US hesitation might offer China an opportunity to catch up internationally.

rows.title: Fetal and parental genomes offer mechanistic insights into pregnancy loss
rows.summary: Genomic analyses of mother–father–fetus trios after early pregnancy loss uncover contributions from chromosomal abnormalities and subtle genetic variants.

rows.title: How I carved out a career as a ‘pracademic’
rows.summary: Julian Kirchherr craved a role with real-world impact. A career that straddles academia and management consultancy helped him to achieve his goal.

rows.title: How your brain controls ageing — and why zombie cells could be key
rows.summary: Research is revealing the cellular mechanisms that link mental well-being and longevity.

rows.title: In science’s new era, open and transparent cooperation remains key
rows.summary: As China continues its scientific ascent, the rest of the world should keep engaging.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Judge orders the restoration of hundreds of NIH grants
rows.summary: A US judge has ruled that cancelled funding for projects on diversity, equity and inclusion and COVID-19 must be restored by the National Institutes of Health. Plus, industrial slag can turn to rock within decades and the first ever artificial solar eclipse.

rows.title: PhD students face high risk of sexual harassment — can universities stop perpetrators?
rows.summary: A toolkit outlines how academia can prevent various forms of misconduct.

rows.title: Escalating Israel–Iran conflict damages science labs
rows.summary: Researchers in both countries are feeling the effects of a string of missile attacks exchanged between them.

rows.title: Sex differences in skin-cancer risk are linked to oestrogen levels
rows.summary: Premenopausal women are more likely than men to develop certain cancers. Pathways activated by the sex hormone responsible could be targeted in cancer therapies.

rows.title: I can’t show my face because of pangolin poachers
rows.summary: This interviewee rehabilitates illegally traded pangolins that fetch a high price on the black market.

rows.title: Transparent peer review to be extended to all of Nature ’s research papers
rows.summary: From today, all new submissions to Nature that are published will be accompanied by referees’ reports and author responses — to illuminate the process of producing rigorous science.

rows.title: People were wrecking the climate 140 years ago — we just lacked the tech to spot it
rows.summary: Models suggest that human-caused global warming would have been detectable in the nineteenth century with today’s know-how.

rows.title: Judge rules against NIH grant cuts — and calls them discriminatory
rows.summary: The decision means that the US biomedical agency has to restore funding to hundreds of research projects, but the government is likely to appeal.

rows.title: Daily briefing: ‘Glimmer of hope’ at UN Ocean Conference as 50 countries ratify the High Seas Treaty
rows.summary: Fifty countries have now ratified the UN High Seas Treaty, an agreement to put 30% of the ocean into protected areas. Plus, researchers have grown hearts containing human cells in pig embryos for the first time and the mysterious link between Earth’s magnetism and oxygen.

rows.title: Mice with human cells developed using ‘game-changing’ technique
rows.summary: Human cells injected into amniotic fluid find their way into fetal mouse organs.

rows.title: Freeze frame: cracking molecular motion
rows.summary: Time-resolved cryo-electron microscopy can resolve protein motion on millisecond or even microsecond timescales, but the need for highly specialized tools and skills limits the method’s reach.

rows.title: ‘One of the true final frontiers’ — Sally Ride biopic highlights the struggle of gay astronauts
rows.summary: The first US woman to fly in space said little about her personal life in public. A candid film discloses the pressures she endured.

rows.title: Could a novelty indicator improve science?
rows.summary: A competition to develop computational approaches to detect ‘novelty’ in published papers will help metascientists to study how out-of-the-box research changes the scientific landscape.

rows.title: Cryo-EM structure of a natural RNA nanocage
rows.summary: Three-dimensional structures of two natural RNA nanocages reveal unique quaternary structures without the contribution of proteins.

rows.title: Tiny human hearts grown in pig embryos for the first time
rows.summary: The hearts started to beat in the pig–human hybrids, which survived for 21 days.

rows.title: Hungry caterpillars can brew exotic molecules in their guts
rows.summary: Researchers fed moth larvae the chemical building blocks, and the insects’ enzymes did the rest.

rows.title: Why pangolins are poached: they’re the tastiest animal around
rows.summary: Trafficking of scales for traditional medicine plays a relatively small part in the hunting of pangolins in Nigeria.

rows.title: Minuscule worms form living towers to hunt for food
rows.summary: Scientists observe the nematode’s behaviour in the wild for the first time.

rows.title: Hundreds of physicists on a remote island: we visit the ultimate quantum party
rows.summary: Researchers have gathered on the island of Heligoland to celebrate the centenary of Werner Heisenberg's quantum breakthrough.

rows.title: A long-predicted cosmic collision might not happen after all
rows.summary: The pull of a third galaxy could yank the Milky Way out of the path of Andromeda.

rows.title: Recording my research led to a photojournalism career
rows.summary: Although he has pivoted to conservation photography, Sirachai (Shin) Arunrugstichai still considers the ocean as his office.

rows.title: Some US researchers want to leave the country. Can Europe take them?
rows.summary: As the Trump administration steps up attacks on US universities and scientific institutions, the European Union is campaigning hard to attract scientists from the United States. But how many can the bloc take?

rows.title: Mysterious link between Earth’s magnetism and oxygen levels baffles scientists
rows.summary: As Earth’s magnetic field has risen, so have the conditions that helped complex life to thrive — a discovery that could aid the search for life on distant planets.

rows.title: Why science recruiters struggle to find high-calibre candidates
rows.summary: Are hiring managers asking too much of job-seeking researchers? A comparison between two job ads, posted 30 years apart, offers some clues.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Breathing patterns might be as unique as a fingerprint
rows.summary: Each person’s breathing pattern could be used to identify them, or reveal their physical or mental characteristics. Plus, rings of bubbles might be a humpback whale’s attempt to communicate with us and who RFK Jr has appointed to his new vaccine panel.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Physical masks created using AI can restore damaged paintings
rows.summary: An MIT engineer has designed a way to restore damaged paintings using printed, AI-generated masks. Plus, a ‘trustworthy’ random number generator and how to keep weight off after coming off weight-loss drugs.

rows.title: Who is on RFK Jr’s new vaccine panel — and what will they do?
rows.summary: Critics fear that the anti-vaccine health-department leader’s picks for a crucial US committee will be a ‘disaster for public health’.

rows.title: How to address gender equity in science in Africa
rows.summary: Salah Obayya works to advance women’s research careers in photonics in Egypt.

rows.title: Happy birthday quantum mechanics! I got a ticket to the ultimate physics party
rows.summary: Nature reporter joins hundreds of physicists on a remote island to celebrate Heisenberg’s enlightening trip there 100 years ago.

rows.title: How you breathe is like a fingerprint that can identify you
rows.summary: Your inhalation and exhalation pattern is not only unique to you, it can be a marker of your physical and mental state, study suggests.

rows.title: An instantaneous voice-synthesis neuroprosthesis
rows.summary: A brain-to-voice neuroprosthesis enables a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to synthesize his voice in real time by decoding neural activity, demonstrating the potential of brain–computer interfaces to enable people with paralysis to speak intelligibly and expressively.

rows.title: This stretchy neural implant grows with an axolotl’s brain
rows.summary: The flexible implant measures brain activity during embryonic development in amphibians — plus, a new way to restore damaged paintings with the help of AI.

rows.title: Meet the MIT engineer who invented an AI-powered way to restore art
rows.summary: The new method could be 70 times faster than repairing painting by hand.

rows.title: A cancer-causing mutation meets its match
rows.summary: In mice, engineered immune cells shrink pancreatic and other tumours bearing a mutant version of the KRAS protein.

rows.title: Quantum physicists unveil most ‘trustworthy’ random-number generator yet
rows.summary: Upgraded system produces strings of random bits in a process that is fully traceable.

rows.title: Gene therapy could correct blood stem cells inside, rather than outside, the body
rows.summary: Experiments in mice reveal an early postnatal window of opportunity for the effective transfer of genes to blood-cell-producing haematopoietic stem cells by injecting mice with gene-carrying lentiviral vectors. This approach showed therapeutic benefit in three mouse models of severe diseases, and could expand the applicability of haematopoietic stem-cell gene therapy in the clinic.

rows.title: Major telescope hosts world’s largest digital camera: how it will transform astronomy
rows.summary: Massive telescope will map the Universe and provide an evolving record of the Solar System and distant stars.

rows.title: Cheat-proof random numbers generated from quantum entanglement
rows.summary: A quantum random-number generator has been developed that uses classical cryptography to certify that its output was produced by a quantum process.

rows.title: When do girls fall behind in maths? Gigantic study pinpoints the moment
rows.summary: Analysis of almost three million children captures when ‘mathematical gender gap’ first emerges and could help focus efforts to stop girls from falling behind.

rows.title: How to keep weight off after obesity drugs
rows.summary: Options are emerging for the tens of millions of people who stop taking GLP-1 drugs because of side effects, cost or availability.

rows.title: An open AI model could help medical experts to interpret chest X-rays
rows.summary: An accessible and adaptable artificial-intelligence model trained on a diverse set of X-ray images is better than existing models at spotting rare chest diseases.

rows.title: NIH chief stands by funding cuts to ‘politicized science’ at tense hearing
rows.summary: Jayanta Bhattacharya says the US biomedical agency can’t continue ‘business as usual’ if it wants to restore its reputation.

rows.title: Close the mathematics gender gap: huge study prompts urgent call to action
rows.summary: Researchers reveal when boys pull ahead of girls in mathematics, sounding an alarm and providing both an opportunity for schools, parents and researchers.

rows.title: Liquid carbon formed using a high-energy laser
rows.summary: Using pulses of an ultrabright X-ray free-electron laser, the structure of liquid carbon was determined at pressures exceeding one million atmospheres and temperatures of around 7,000 kelvin. This approach revealed a complex fluid with a water-like structure and an average of four neighbouring atoms around each central carbon atom.

rows.title: Trace elements in the ocean attributed to a surprising source
rows.summary: The finding that the sea floor is a source of low-abundance elements in the ocean up-ends conventional views of marine biogeochemistry.

rows.title: Digitally constructed mask brings a damaged painting back to life
rows.summary: A damaged painting has been visually restored by digitally reconstructing missing areas of paint and printing them onto a removable mask.

rows.title: World first: brain implant lets man speak with expression — and sing
rows.summary: Device translates thought to speech in real time.

rows.title: Digging foxholes in the dark
rows.summary: A safe place.

rows.title: How the brain separates real images from those it imagines
rows.summary: Neuroscientists have found the regions that keep them apart.

rows.title: Various cell types in tissues cooperate in networks that are disrupted in disease
rows.summary: Gene expression reveals that different types of human cell can work as a unit. These cellular modules, found in several tissues, change during disease.

rows.title: Seasonality dominates changes in lake-surface extent and aligns with human residence
rows.summary: The mapping of lake surfaces globally has been constrained by the limitations of single-source satellite data. A spatio-temporal fusion approach now enables high-resolution mapping of more than 1.4 million lakes, revealing seasonality as the main factor driving changes in the spread of lake surfaces, with links between seasonality and human residence.

rows.title: Computer processors built from 2D materials
rows.summary: These prototype processors made from atomically thin materials offer a glimpse into a post-silicon-transistor future, but scaling challenges remain.

rows.title: To progress, science must be truly global
rows.summary: Building scientific capacity in the global south is key to solving today’s most pressing planetary challenges.

rows.title: Biochemical breakthrough paves way to reliable supply of anticancer drug
rows.summary: ‘Missing’ genes needed for the biosynthesis of a natural anticancer drug have been discovered by perturbing and analysing individual cells of yew trees.

rows.title: Tiny rotating device puts a new spin on blood-clot removal
rows.summary: The milli-spinner thrombectomy device uses spinning-induced forces to mechanically modify blood-clot microstructure, shrinking clot volume by up to 95% for rapid, safe removal. By densifying the clot’s fibrin network and releasing red blood cells, it offers a new strategy to improve success rates in treatments of blood-clot blockages, such as stroke.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The moment that mathematics education starts to fail girls
rows.summary: A gigantic study of schoolchildren in France pinpoints the moment a ‘mathematical gender gap’ appears during school. Plus, a mysterious epidemic of kidney disease affecting young men and a deep-sea squid species caught on camera for the first time.

rows.title: Meet the engineer using deep learning to restore Renaissance art
rows.summary: As a student, Alex Kachkine can only afford damaged art in need of repair. Here’s how they turned their conservation work into a science.

rows.title: Mitochondrial molecule has unexpected role in tissue healing
rows.summary: A key component of the TCA cycle, a series of reactions that occurs in energy-generating organelles called mitochondria, can dictate the fate of intestinal stem cells.

rows.title: SP140–RESIST pathway regulates interferon mRNA stability and antiviral immunity
rows.summary: The antiviral protein SP140 negatively regulates Ifnb1 mRNA stability by directly repressing the expression of the immune regulator RESIST.

rows.title: A neutral-atom Hubbard quantum simulator in the cryogenic regime
rows.summary: A several-fold reduction in temperature is accomplished using a neutral-atom Hubbard quantum simulator by transforming a low-entropy product state into strongly correlated states of interest via dynamic control of the model parameters.

rows.title: A complementary two-dimensional material-based one instruction set computer
rows.summary: A two-dimensional one instruction set computer has been fabricated based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor technology by leveraging the heterogeneous integration of large-area n-type MoS 2 and p-type WSe 2 field-effect transistors.

rows.title: Attosecond inner-shell lasing at ångström wavelengths
rows.summary: Strong lasing effects similar to those in the optical regime can occur at 1.5–2.1 Å wavelengths during high-intensity XFEL-driven Kα 1 lasing of copper and manganese.

rows.title: Glycosaminoglycan-driven lipoprotein uptake protects tumours from ferroptosis
rows.summary: Lipoprotein uptake dependent on sulfated glycosaminoglycans linked to cell-surface proteoglycans is a key determinant of ferroptosis sensitivity in cancer.

rows.title: RIFINs displayed on malaria-infected erythrocytes bind KIR2DL1 and KIR2DS1
rows.summary: Certain RIFINs from Plasmodium falciparum can bind to both inhibitory (KIR2DL1) and activating (KIR2DS1) immune receptors on natural killer cells, demonstrating the potential role of activating killer immunoglobulin-like receptors in targeting pathogens and controlling malaria infection.

rows.title: Developmental trajectory and evolutionary origin of thymic mimetic cells
rows.summary: In mice, tissue-mimetic cells appear in thymus in two distinct waves, creating two distinct pools of mimetic cells, each expressing antigens characteristic of different cell types.

rows.title: Preparation of a neutral nitrogen allotrope hexanitrogen C 2h -N 6
rows.summary: The facile synthesis and spectroscopic identification of previously unreported hexanitrogen C 2h -N 6 is described, representing experimentally realized neutral molecular nitrogen allotropes beyond N 2 that exhibit unexpected stability.

rows.title: Probing phonon transport dynamics across an interface by electron microscopy
rows.summary: In situ vibrational electron energy-loss spectroscopy is used to examine phonon transport dynamics across the AlN–SiC interface during thermal transport at sub-nanometre resolution, demonstrating a sharp temperature drop within about 2 nm across the interface.

rows.title: Molecular hydrogen in the extremely metal- and dust-poor galaxy Leo P
rows.summary: Observations from the JWST MIRI-MRS instrument reveal the detection of rotational emission from molecular hydrogen near the only O-type star in the 3% solar metallicity galaxy Leo P, providing confirmation that significant quantities of molecular gas can form in such metal- and dust-poor environments.

rows.title: Traceable random numbers from a non-local quantum advantage
rows.summary: A study demonstrates a public generator of random numbers based on device-independent techniques, with the randomness being fully auditable and traceable.

rows.title: Weakly space-confined all-inorganic perovskites for light-emitting diodes
rows.summary: Weakly space-confined, large-grained crystals of all-inorganic perovskite were used to fabricate light-emitting diodes with a high external quantum efficiency and operational stability.

rows.title: Abyssal seafloor as a key driver of ocean trace-metal biogeochemical cycles
rows.summary: Rare earth element and neodymium isotope data combined with models of particle cycling and sediment diagenesis suggest that the abyssal seafloor is a key driver of trace-metal biogeochemical cycles.

rows.title: A new Mongolian tyrannosauroid and the evolution of Eutyrannosauria
rows.summary: A new tyrannosauroid, Khankhuuluu mongoliensis gen. et sp. nov., from lower Upper Cretaceous deposits of Mongolia provides a new perspective on eutyrannosaurian origins and evolution.

rows.title: Remote activation of place codes by gaze in a highly visual animal
rows.summary: Place cells in the chickadee hippocampus coherently represent locations in space, whether physically visited or viewed, enabling spatial reasoning at a distance through a unified process coordinated by head saccades.

rows.title: Brain implantation of soft bioelectronics via embryonic development
rows.summary: A soft mesh microelectrode array can seamlessly integrate in developing brains, enabling long-term, stable mapping of how single-neuron activity and population dynamics emerge and evolve during brain development.

rows.title: Physical restoration of a painting with a digitally constructed mask
rows.summary: A digital restoration technique for damaged paintings was developed, in which a colour-accurate bilayer mask of printed pigments on polymeric films was used, reducing treatment time and cost while adhering to ethical conservation principles.

rows.title: Dynamic assemblies and coordinated reactions of non-homologous end joining
rows.summary: Structures associated with the final steps of non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and gap filling present new targets for NHEJ inhibition to enhance efficacy of radiotherapy and accuracy of gene editing.

rows.title: Metabolic adaptations direct cell fate during tissue regeneration
rows.summary: Metabolic enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid cycle, such as 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, are differentially expressed in absorptive and secretory lineages, guiding cell fate establishment and offering insights for targeted regenerative therapies.

rows.title: Targeting GRPR for sex hormone-dependent cancer after loss of E-cadherin
rows.summary: A study finding an oestrogen-sensing signalling pathway that promotes melanoma metastasis only in female mice emphasizes the importance of recognizing sex-specific factors in cancer management.

rows.title: Discovery of FoTO1 and Taxol genes enables biosynthesis of baccatin III
rows.summary: An approach that combines single-nucleus RNA sequencing and multiplexed perturbation identifies genes that enable the biosynthesis of direct precursors of the anti-cancer drug Taxol, whose current production involves a laborious extraction process from yew trees.

rows.title: Rapid emergence of a maths gender gap in first grade
rows.summary: Boys and girls exhibit very similar maths scores upon school entry, but a gender gap in favour of boys becomes highly significant after 4 months of schooling, which increases with years of schooling, independently of age.

rows.title: A fully open AI foundation model applied to chest radiography
rows.summary: Ark + , a fully open artificial intelligence foundation model, demonstrates exceptional capabilities in diagnosing common, rare and novel thoracic diseases.

rows.title: Early life high fructose impairs microglial phagocytosis and neurodevelopment
rows.summary: Exposure of mice to high fructose during gestation or early postnatal life causes decreased microglial phagocytosis during brain development and leads to anxiety-like behaviour in adolescence.

rows.title: Making concrete sustainable globally requires technology transfer
This tiny device spins blood clots away
rows.summary: An unexpected discovery could lead to safer surgical interventions for strokes

rows.title: Not all clinical data in the United States are fragmented
Reduced investment in universities has multifaceted effects
Mathematics in ancient Egypt
rows.summary: Calculation principles found in a papyrus scroll, and an author shares his love of lichens in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

rows.title: Greening nickel extraction requires institutional and financial support
How to spot suspicious papers: a sleuthing guide for scientists
rows.summary: An open collection of tips and tools could help researchers and publishers to pick up on problematic research.

rows.title: Stressed out by PhD life? Five strategies to take back the joy
rows.summary: Doing a PhD is really hard. Here’s how I’ve learnt to enjoy the process.

rows.title: Dementia is deadly — the UN needs to take it more seriously
rows.summary: Improved recognition of dementia as a major non-communicable disease by multilateral organizations is crucial, to build awareness and increase funding to tackle this insidious illness.

rows.title: Peter Lax obituary: mathematician who pioneered computer-based solutions to real-world problems
rows.summary: The Abel prizewinner’s pragmatic approach to solving differential equations was influential across fields ranging from weather forecasting to starting nuclear chain reactions.

rows.title: How to speak to a vaccine sceptic: research reveals what works
rows.summary: Hesitancy about vaccinations is on the rise, but studies show there are specific ways to address people's questions.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Evidence-backed strategies for talking about vaccine hesitancy
rows.summary: Experts share tips for talking about vaccines with your inner circle. Plus, a tiny device that ‘spins’ blood clots away and why so many attempts to reduce fossil-fuel subsidies fail — and what to do about it.

rows.title: Silicate clouds and a circumplanetary disk in the YSES-1 exoplanet system
rows.summary: Direct observations of silicate clouds in the atmosphere of the exoplanet YSES-1 c and the first circumplanetary disk silicate emission around its sibling planet YSES-1 b are reported.

rows.title: Making slabs and sleepers from old appliances
rows.summary: Sebastián Gregui’s company uses research-backed methods to turn recovered plastic into building materials.

rows.title: Authorship for sale: Nature investigates how paper mills work
rows.summary: Companies selling authorship slots thrive in a culture that equates success with a strong publication record. Customers, sleuths and the shadowy owner of a paper mill explain why.

rows.title: How DEI is misunderstood — and the real route to gender equality
rows.summary: A provocative book explores the barriers that hold women back, why previous diversity, equity and inclusion approaches have failed and how to move forward.

rows.title: Want to enhance lab safety? Try a little role playing first
rows.summary: Simulated lab accidents train students how to respond to real emergencies.

rows.title: Dolce vita: a four-step guide to stress-free holidays from academia
rows.summary: Three-month summer holidays as a child in northwest Italy helped Stefano Sandrone to hone his relaxation and holiday-planning skills. Here’s his advice for scientists.

rows.title: Do our observations make reality happen?
rows.summary: Finally answering the most-vexed question in quantum theory might mean redefining what is real.

rows.title: Daily briefing: ‘A necessary evil’ — Cutting off rhinos’ horns to deter poachers really works
rows.summary: Removing the horns of rhinos reduces poaching by 78% on reserves where it’s done. Plus, what to expect from the new African Space Agency and the pros and cons of using newly opened shipping routes through the Arctic.

rows.title: How our student journal club built on sand developed strong foundations
rows.summary: SandClub launched as an informal discussion forum to draw students out of their post-pandemic shells. Now, it’s so much more.

rows.title: Medicine’s rapid adoption of AI has researchers concerned
rows.summary: Hospitals and universities must step up to fill gaps in regulation, experts say.

rows.title: How China is vying to attract the world’s top scientific talent
rows.summary: Hundreds of policies across the country have been designed to lure researchers and new graduates to settle there.

rows.title: NINJ1 regulates plasma membrane fragility under mechanical strain
rows.summary: The NINJ1 protein regulates plasma membrane rupture by altering membrane biomechanical properties, independent of cell death programs.

rows.title: What puzzles people, past and present: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: Trump wants to put humans on Mars: what scientists think of the plan
rows.summary: We discuss the massive costs and challenges associated with the goal, and what proposed budget cuts to NASA could mean for other space missions.

rows.title: ‘Integrity index’ flags universities with high retraction rates
rows.summary: A score based on indicators related to research quality could help to prevent institutions gaming the metrics that feed into conventional rankings.

rows.title: Skyrocketing mpox outbreak in Sierra Leone raises fears of wider spread
rows.summary: Boom in infections in the West African nation is driven by the same viral strain that caused a global outbreak in 2022.

rows.title: Author Correction: GluD1 is a signal transduction device disguised as an ionotropic receptor
Japanese spacecraft has probably crash-landed on Moon — again
rows.summary: Early investigations by the Japanese company ispace identified issues with speed and a sensor measuring the craft’s altitude.

rows.title: Africa has a new space agency — here’s what it will do
rows.summary: Pioneering organization aims to boost collaboration, track climate effects and improve disaster relief.

rows.title: How Trump’s budget cuts could derail global science collaborations
rows.summary: Europe’s ExoMars mission is among the highest-profile casualties of the US president’s plan to slash research funding.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The energy-drink ingredient taurine doesn’t seem to boost lifespan after all
rows.summary: An amino acid used as a supplement and in energy drinks might not be as closely linked to ageing as previous research has suggested. Plus, a Japanese Moon lander has crashed and Briefing readers say they’re anxious about visiting the United States.

rows.title: Thousands of endangered trees preserved for centuries inside Chinese temples
rows.summary: Survey uncovers the rich biodiversity protected at sacred sites.

rows.title: Solved: the mystery of the evaporating planet
rows.summary: An intimate look at a puffy exoplanet and its nearest star has revealed its tragic destiny.

rows.title: A message from island leaders: protect the Pacific Ocean from deep-sea mining
rows.summary: As heads of Pacific island nations, we urge governments worldwide to avoid irreversible environmental damage to the region as well as the needless economic and geopolitical risks.

rows.title: Exclusive: Start-up FutureHouse debuts powerful AI ‘reasoning model’ for science
rows.summary: The model, called ether0, outperforms other advanced AIs at chemistry tasks and is a stepping stone towards automating the entire research pipeline.

rows.title: ‘We were ready for this’: meet the scientists suing the Trump administration to reinstate terminated grants
rows.summary: Judge sets court date to hear the US government detail how termination directives were made.

rows.title: Trump moves to slash NSF: why are the proposed budget cuts so big?
rows.summary: Major US science funder could lose more than half its budget — and researchers are reeling.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Travel bans, revoked visas and yet more funding cuts — the latest in Trump’s attack on science
rows.summary: The Trump administration’s latest policies hit science hard. Plus, Chinese temples provide refuge for endangered trees and mice embryos with XY chromosomes can grow ovaries if their mother is iron-deficient.

rows.title: ‘Another blow’: how Trump’s latest travel ban could harm research
rows.summary: Restrictions on immigration from 19 countries could disrupt infectious-disease research and international collaborations.

rows.title: Anti-ageing effects of popular supplement taurine challenged
rows.summary: Massive study finds limited connection between ageing and taurine levels in people, monkeys and mice.

rows.title: How I got through the loss of my supervisors
rows.summary: When I was a postgraduate, two of my close mentors died. Here’s how I coped.

rows.title: Should I use AI to help draft my science job application?
rows.summary: Your cover letter, CV and resume need to stand out from the crowd, but using artificial intelligence to help comes with a warning.

rows.title: Quantum computers tackle unexplored particle physics
rows.summary: Two quantum-simulation experiments make a step towards understanding the forces between elementary particles.

rows.title: How researchers are shining a light on the ‘invisible’ contributions of small-scale fishers
rows.summary: A huge research project is highlighting the role that small-scale fishers play in sustainability.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Metal–support frontier orbital interactions in single-atom catalysis
Male mice can grow female organs — if their mothers lack iron
rows.summary: Iron deficiency disrupts a sex-determining pathway in mice — plus, research highlighting the role that small-scale fishers play in sustainability.

rows.title: Clustering pattern of dwarf galaxies not predicted by models of cosmic structure formation
rows.summary: A surprising pattern of spatial distribution was discovered in dwarf galaxies, whereby diffuse ones cluster more strongly than do compact ones — opposite to the trend seen in massive galaxies. This finding challenges standard models of the formation of galactic structures, calling for theories about the assembly of visible- and dark-matter structures to be revised.

rows.title: Iron deficiency in pregnant mice causes XY embryos to develop with female characteristics
rows.summary: In mice, a lack of maternal iron impairs an iron-dependent enzyme that activates the male sex-determining gene, causing some XY embryos to develop ovaries.

rows.title: Science-integrity project will root out bad medical papers ‘and tell everyone’
rows.summary: Group behind Retraction Watch aims to pinpoint the most influential flawed health data.

rows.title: Simulation of matter–antimatter creation on quantum platforms
rows.summary: Two-dimensional quantum platforms have simulated a process in particle physics called string breaking that generates matter–antimatter pairs.

rows.title: Human factors
rows.summary: A brief encounter.

rows.title: Trump wants to put humans on Mars — here’s what scientists think
rows.summary: Nature explores the massive costs and challenges of sending astronauts to the red planet.

rows.title: Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat obituary: mathematician who established that Einstein’s equations mirror the real world
rows.summary: Pioneer of general relativity and gravitational-wave theories saw her work confirmed by observations 65 years later.

rows.title: Ancient carbon released through modern rivers
rows.summary: A global analysis reveals that most carbon dioxide emitted by rivers derives not from modern plant material, as was thought, but from ancient, buried carbon.

rows.title: Sticky membranes of dead red blood cells obstruct small vessels
rows.summary: Damage to the vascular lining leads to interactions with red blood cells that hint at how to treat dangerous complications of heart attack, stroke and COVID-19.

rows.title: False positives in study of memory-related gene expression
Genomics pioneer fired from firm he founded: ‘It was not easy to domesticate me’
rows.summary: Kári Stefánsson, who last month left the Icelandic genetics company deCODE, spoke to Nature about his legacy.

rows.title: How I’m bringing the voices of local fishers into ocean policies
rows.summary: Fishing communities know what sustainability means. They must be at the decision table.

rows.title: Stop ignoring small-scale fisheries in economic models
rows.summary: Economic policies are lacking in data on small-scale fisheries. A team of researchers is determined to change that.

rows.title: Why we should protect the high seas from all extraction, forever
rows.summary: Exploitation of the high seas risks doing irreversible damage to biodiversity, climate stability and ocean equity. A consensus must be built now to save them.

rows.title: Y-chromosome loss in cancer and immune cells might worsen treatment outcomes
rows.summary: Prognosis is poor for tumours with Y-chromosome loss. Examining the interplay between cancer and immune cells sheds light on potential mechanisms.

rows.title: Male mice can grow ovaries if their pregnant mums are iron deficient
rows.summary: The study is the first to show that low iron levels can affect fetal sexual development.

rows.title: Cancer more deadly when tumours lack Y chromosomes — and the loss could be contagious
rows.summary: Losing the Y chromosome seems to make cancer cells more aggressive in men and the phenomenon might even spread between cells.

rows.title: How a mysterious epidemic of kidney disease is killing thousands of young men
rows.summary: Repeated damage from extreme heat over time seems to be a leading factor causing kidneys to fail.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Inside the wild-animal markets that could start the next pandemic
rows.summary: How researchers are studying the trade that could give rise to deadly pandemics. Plus, a spiral structure hidden in the Oort cloud and how to write a great engineering paper.

rows.title: Reply to: False positives in study of memory-related gene expression
Making robust integrated photonic qubits
rows.summary: High-performance photonic integrated chips have been demonstrated that generate robust optical quantum bits called Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill qubits. One such chip has been used to realize qubit states, reconstruct the quantum features of these states and verify the quality of the qubits.

rows.title: Dynamic range and precision of hybrid vision sensors
Milli-spinner thrombectomy
rows.summary: The milli-spinner thrombectomy facilitates fast, complete clot removal by using spinning-induced compression and shear forces to mechanically modify the clot microstructure through densifying the fibrin network and releasing red blood cells, thus reducing clot volume.

rows.title: Molecular gradients shape synaptic specificity of a visuomotor transformation
rows.summary: Gradients of cell recognition molecules wire a sensorimotor interface in Drosophila.

rows.title: A multidimensional distributional map of future reward in dopamine neurons
rows.summary: An algorithm called time–magnitude reinforcement learning (TMRL) extends distributional reinforcement learning to take account of reward time and magnitude, and behavioural and neurophysiological experiments in mice suggest that midbrain dopamine neurons use TMRL-like computations.

rows.title: Integrated photonic source of Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill qubits
rows.summary: An ultra-low-loss integrated photonic chip fabricated on a customized multilayer silicon nitride 300-mm wafer platform, coupled over fibre with high-efficiency photon number resolving detectors, is used to generate Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill qubit states.

rows.title: Maternal iron deficiency causes male-to-female sex reversal in mouse embryos
rows.summary: Iron-deficient conditions in pregnant mice can cause XY mouse embryos to develop female rather than male genitalia, revealing that iron metabolism has a role in determining male sex in mice.

rows.title: Coordination environments of Pt single-atom catalysts from NMR signatures
rows.summary: This study presents a nuclear magnetic resonance-based method to determine local structure and bonding of Pt single-atom catalysts.

rows.title: Observation of string breaking on a (2 + 1)D Rydberg quantum simulator
rows.summary: A quantum simulation of a (2 + 1)-dimensional lattice gauge theory is carried out on a quantum computer working with neutral atoms trapped by optical tweezers in a Kagome geometry.

rows.title: Ancient DNA reveals a two-clanned matrilineal community in Neolithic China
rows.summary: Analysis of ancient DNA, stable isotope data and archaeological evidence from the Fujia archaeological site in eastern China suggests it was populated by a matrilineal Neolithic community between 2750 and 2500 bc .

rows.title: Visualizing dynamics of charges and strings in (2 + 1)D lattice gauge theories
rows.summary: In a quantum simulation of a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory using a superconducting quantum processor, the dynamics of strings reveal the transition from deconfined to confined excitations as the effective electric field is increased.

rows.title: Old carbon routed from land to the atmosphere by global river systems
rows.summary: Using a global database of the radiocarbon content of rivers combining new and published measurements, isotopic mass balance suggests that about 60% of river CO 2 emissions are derived from millennial or older carbon sources.

rows.title:
RETRACTED ARTICLE: Warming accelerates global drought
            severity
rows.summary:
Increased atmospheric evaporative demand in recent years has increased
                drought severity by an average of 40% globally across both dry and wet regions, and
                the trend is likely to continue under future warming scenarios.

rows.title: CREM is a regulatory checkpoint of CAR and IL-15 signalling in NK cells
rows.summary: The transcription factor CREM is a pivotal regulator of NK cell function, making CREM a valuable target to increase the efficacy of anticancer immunotherapies based on this cell population and chimeric antigen receptors.

rows.title: Probing condensate microenvironments with a micropeptide killswitch
rows.summary: Targeting a non-natural micropeptide ‘killswitch’ to several biomolecular condensates altered condensate compositions and revealed condensate functions in human cells

rows.title: Loss of colonic fidelity enables multilineage plasticity and metastasis
rows.summary: The chromatin-remodelling enzyme ATRX and the transcription factor HNF4A are identified as pivotal regulators of colonic epithelial identity, with roles in metastasis in colorectal cancer.

rows.title: A soft-clamped topological waveguide for phonons
rows.summary: A substantial reduction of losses in a phononic waveguide can be achieved by soft clamping, through which phonons can be guided through very sharp turns with losses accounting for less than one phonon in a million.

rows.title: Multi-timescale reinforcement learning in the brain
rows.summary: Individual dopaminergic neurons encode future rewards over distinct temporal horizons.

rows.title: Increased CSF drainage by non-invasive manipulation of cervical lymphatics
rows.summary: The outflow pathway of cerebrospinal fluid into lymph nodes in the neck and how non-invasive mechanical stimulation can enhance drainage and restore impaired outflow in aged mice are explored.

rows.title: Drivers of the extreme North Atlantic marine heatwave during 2023
rows.summary: Atmospheric reanalyses combined with ocean observations and model simulations show that the extreme 2023 North Atlantic heatwave was primarily driven by anomalously weak winds leading to strongly shoaling mixed layers, with a smaller contribution from clearer skies.

rows.title: Concurrent loss of the Y chromosome in cancer and T cells impacts outcome
rows.summary: Comprehensive pan-cancer analysis of loss of the Y chromosome (LOY) in benign and malignant cells establishes a new model linking LOY in circulating and tumour-infiltrating immune cells to LOY in malignant cells.

rows.title: Ischaemic endothelial necroptosis induces haemolysis and COVID-19 angiopathy
rows.summary: A red blood cell haemostatic mechanism induced by dying ECs functions independently of platelets and fibrin.

rows.title: Acetolysis for epoxy-amine carbon fibre-reinforced polymer recycling
rows.summary: Acetic acid efficiently depolymerizes aliphatic and aromatic epoxy-amine thermosets used in carbon fibre-reinforced polymers (CFRPs) to yield recoverable monomers and pristine carbon fibres, which, based on process modelling, techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment, could enable industrial recycling of CFRPs.

rows.title: Structural insights into human Pol III transcription initiation in action
rows.summary: Reconstitution of seven human RNA polymerase III (Pol III) transcribing complexes (TC4/5/6/8/10/12/13) halted on U6 promoters with nascent RNAs of 4–13 nucleotides offers molecular insights into Pol III dynamics.

rows.title: Subnucleosome preference of human chromatin remodeller SMARCAD1
rows.summary: Human chromatin remodeller SMARCAD1 exhibits a substrate preference for subnucleosomal particles over the canonical nucleosome.

rows.title: Author Correction: DNA-guided transcription factor interactions extend human gene regulatory code
Clever cockatoos learn an easy way to quench their thirst
rows.summary: Some birds master the fine art of manoeuvring beak, feet and body weight to turn on a tap.

rows.title: Should there be a national holiday in honour of chemists?
rows.summary: A proposal to bring science to the public’s attention, and Arctic explorers set sail in style in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

rows.title: Author Correction: Methane oxidation to ethanol by a molecular junction photocatalyst
Address the psychological toll of kidney disease
Trade wars could affect food security in low-income nations
European Union’s strict conservation targets should guide global marine policy
‘You’re just not welcome’: researchers grapple with US plan to revoke Chinese student visas
rows.summary: Scientists are eyeing their legal options in anticipation of new immigration actions.

rows.title: Disaster relief needs community trust — authorities must earn it
rows.summary: Governments and institutions must shift from top-down approaches to collaborations with local communities.

rows.title: Illustrators call out journals and news sites for using AI art
rows.summary: Bot-made art undermines research and public trust in science, say illustrators frustrated by inaccurate and outlandish depictions.

rows.title: Exclusive: Inside the thriving wild-animal markets that could start the next pandemic
rows.summary: Live-animal markets are a natural laboratory for viruses to evolve and spark deadly outbreaks, yet scientists lack support to study the risks they pose.

rows.title: Brain-reading devices raise ethical dilemmas — researchers propose protections
rows.summary: Delegates to a United Nations meeting on neurotechnology ethics have devised the first set of global guidelines on maintaining users’ privacy.

rows.title: Daily briefing: NIH foreign-grant cuts could leave thousands without care worldwide
rows.summary: Cuts to US ‘foreign subawards’ will abruptly end hundreds of clinical trials abroad. Plus, an mpox outbreak is overwhelming Sierra Leone’s health system and a rock with a painted dot that just might represent a nose.

rows.title: Speeding up ginseng growth to aid drug discovery
rows.summary: Plant scientist Johan Sukweenadhi uses ‘hairy-root culture’ to improve ginseng yields at the University of Surabaya in Indonesia.

rows.title: Cancer-fighting CAR T cells show promising results for hard-to-treat tumours
rows.summary: Trial in China is one of the first times the immune therapy has worked against solid tumours.

rows.title: Web-scraping AI bots cause disruption for scientific databases and journals
rows.summary: Automated programs gathering training data for artificial-intelligence tools are overwhelming academic websites.

rows.title: The polar regions hold crucial scientific secrets — and the time to study them is running out
rows.summary: The poles hold 70% of Earth’s fresh water and are crucial to science; what’s unfolding there as the planet warms deserves greater attention.

rows.title: Daily briefing: CAR-T proves its worth in hard-to-treat solid tumours
rows.summary: A clinical trial of CAR T cells is among the first to show that the treatment can work for solid tumours. Plus, humpbacks’ big eyes are nearsighted and how researchers are turbocharging ginseng.

rows.title: Your time is valuable. Don’t give it away just for ‘exposure’
rows.summary: Academia relies on unpaid labour — but researchers should think carefully about what kind of work they’re willing to give to for-profit organizations for free, says Dritjon Gruda.

rows.title: How do I choose a principal investigator for my next postdoc?
rows.summary: A computer scientist is struggling to trust their postdoctoral research adviser after negative experiences with the previous two. How do you find one that’s right for you?

rows.title: How to keep astronauts healthy in deep space
rows.summary: The Artemis programme and others aim to send humans to the Moon and, eventually, to Mars. Innovations in health care that support the mission crew could also benefit people at home.

rows.title: Underwater kelp forests are losing a turf war
rows.summary: In warming coastal seas, a crucial ecosystem is being replaced by ‘turfs’ of red algae, which release chemicals that suppress kelp survival.

rows.title: US–China tariff war threatens global public health
Audio long read: Three ways to cool Earth by pulling carbon from the sky
rows.summary: Governments and companies are investing billions of dollars in efforts to remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere, but will it pay off?

rows.title: CRISPR helps to show why a boy felt no pain
rows.summary: Mutation in an enzyme leads to resistance to chronic and acute pain, according to research in mice.

rows.title: ‘Missing’ air pollution is tracked to its ephemeral source
rows.summary: Discrepancy between models and measurements is resolved by peering into plumes emitted from power plants and other industrial facilities.

rows.title: Gender equality in research publishing is a responsibility for everyone
rows.summary: A concerted effort is needed to support women in their choice of journal when submitting their manuscript.

rows.title: See the Milky Way dazzle during a lunar eclipse — May’s best science images
rows.summary: The month’s sharpest science shots — selected by Nature ’s photo team.

rows.title: Salary negotiations: a guide for scientists
rows.summary: Seasoned negotiators share tips on how to handle conversations around pay, bonuses, benefits and contract length.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The sweet smell of outer space
rows.summary: How the smells of outer space could lead us to extraterrestrial life. Plus, an ancient ‘ambidextrous’ protein that can function in both mirror-image forms and the month’s best science images.

rows.title: NIH grant cuts will axe clinical trials abroad — and could leave thousands without care
rows.summary: US agency’s new policy could abruptly end studies of infectious diseases and cancer, leaving researchers scrambling for funds.

rows.title: Forehead ‘e-tattoo’ tracks how hard you’re thinking
rows.summary: Temporary device records eye movement and brain activity to monitor mental strain.

rows.title: Black Death bacterium has become less lethal after genetic tweak
rows.summary: Reducing the number of copies of one gene in the pathogen could also make it more transmissible.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Immune cell ‘spies’ give the brain information about the gut
rows.summary: Specialized immune cells in mice can act as ‘spies’ that help the brain control behaviours such as pursuit of food. Plus, publishing outside of your research field comes with a ‘pivot penalty’ and AI tools that can ‘hear’ signs of illness in a person’s voice.

rows.title: ‘Scienticide’ in Argentina sparks huge protest by researchers
rows.summary: Hundreds of activists, some wearing gas masks, took to the streets to denounce the government for slashing science funding.

rows.title: Rare ‘ambidextrous’ protein breaks rules of handedness
rows.summary: Most proteins are left-handed, but scientists have found an ancient molecule that works in both mirror-image forms.

rows.title: How the natural world is inspiring the robot eyes of the future
rows.summary: Intelligent machine vision could get a boost from unconventional hardware design.

rows.title: Researchers who ‘pivot’ into new fields should not be given a citation penalty
rows.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic showed the value of changing direction in research. It should be incentivized, encouraged and celebrated.

rows.title: Mouse liver assembloids model periportal architecture and biliary fibrosis
rows.summary: An organoid system comprising adult mouse hepatocytes, cholangiocytes and mesenchymal cells recapitulates liver morphology, biliary function and fibrotic pathology, providing a new model for studies of hepatic biology.

rows.title: The perfect storm for dust storms, thanks to global warming
rows.summary: Climate change is lengthening the gap between snowmelt and vegetation growth.

rows.title: AI linked to boom in biomedical papers, infrared contact lenses, and is Earth’s core leaking?
rows.summary: We round up some recent stories from the Nature Briefing .

rows.title: How a freezing pond could kick-start life’s self-replication
