rows.summary: Freeze–thaw cycles in an icy pond could let an enzyme copy RNA double helices indefinitely — suggesting one way in which evolution could have begun.

rows.title: Bed bugs boomed as the world’s first cities did
rows.summary: Genomic evidence suggests that the bloodsuckers might have been among the first urban insect pests.

rows.title: Origins of the ‘vampire fungus’ that causes white-nose syndrome in bats
rows.summary: An emerging fungal infection is endangering bats in America. DNA analysis reveals that the infection first arose in Europe, mediated by two fungal culprits.

rows.title: Europe can capture the US brain drain — if it acts fast
rows.summary: Countries must cooperate to seize a once-in-a-generation opportunity to become the top destination for scientists.

rows.title: Archaeology field notebook
rows.summary: Digging for clues.

rows.title: Reverse electron transport drives metabolic changes in obesity
rows.summary: Mitochondria, best known for converting nutrients into energy, also generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide — redox signalling molecules that become harmful when overproduced. Research reveals that such overproduction is not random, but rather occurs at a specific site in one mitochondrial enzyme, opening the door to targeted therapies for metabolic diseases.

rows.title: The ‘pivot penalty’: scientists get cited less after switching fields, analysis finds
rows.summary: Massive study of nearly 26 million research papers measures the consequences of striking out in another research area.

rows.title: How the brain spies on the gut: with help from newfound immune cells
rows.summary: The body’s pathogen fighters can act as surveillance forces that ferry information from the gut and fat deposits to the brain.

rows.title: Light reflects as a vortex off a metamaterial with unusual optical properties
rows.summary: Metamaterials made of magnetic photonic crystals have been generated and tuned to a theoretically predicted transition point at which peculiar optical properties emerge. For example, when light is shone on a slab of the material, some of it is reflected back as a spatio-temporal vortex.

rows.title: Shifting research focus comes with the risk of reduced impact
rows.summary: An analysis of millions of scientific papers and patents shows that the further a researcher or inventor moves from their previous work, the less cited their latest work will be.

rows.title: First Chinese mission to sample an asteroid starts its journey
rows.summary: Over a decade, Tianwen-2 will sample rocks from a near-Earth asteroid, return them to Earth and then visit a comet.

rows.title: Singapore’s fight to save its green spaces from development
rows.summary: Despite sophisticated conservation strategies, vast resources and an engaged civil society, economic growth might come at the expense of the city’s natural environment.

rows.title: ‘A funeral for our careers’: Trump’s science cuts spill onto Canadian turf
rows.summary: Researchers in Canada prepare for turbulence in the wake of US funding changes — but there’s a silver lining.

rows.title: Molecular blueprint of a cellular sorting centre
rows.summary: Endosomes are sorting centres inside cells that decide where to deliver materials that are taken from outside or from other parts of the cell. A comprehensive map of endosomal proteins uncovers new components, and reveals the assembly and architecture of hundreds of molecular machines that work together in the endosomal system.

rows.title: Trump’s call for ‘gold-standard science’ has prompted an outcry: here’s why
rows.summary: Thousands have signed an open letter against the US president’s latest order, anxious about political interference in science and more.

rows.title: Brain drugs can now cross the once impenetrable blood–brain barrier
rows.summary: New technologies to shuttle drugs into the brain are showing promise in Alzheimer’s disease, cancer and more.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Chemical ‘shuttles’ carry large drugs across the blood–brain barrier
rows.summary: Molecules that take advantage of natural transport systems are making it possible to deliver large drugs to the brain. Plus, climbers have reached Mount Everest using xenon gas and a landmark air-pollution lab faces threat of closure.

rows.title: Cross-tissue multicellular coordination and its rewiring in cancer
rows.summary: Comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic analysis of 35 human tissues reveals 12 cross-tissue coordinated cellular modules that exhibit intramodule communication and dynamic changes with ageing, and whose organization is perturbed during cancer progression.

rows.title: CoQ imbalance drives reverse electron transport to disrupt liver metabolism
rows.summary: Reverse electron transport is the mechanism behind excess mitochondrial reactive oxygen species in the livers of obese mice, which has implications for developing therapeutics for fatty liver disease in humans.

rows.title: Detection of X-ray emission from a bright long-period radio transient
rows.summary: A long-period radio transient with coincident radio and X-ray emission and observational properties unlike any known Galactic object has been observed by the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder.

rows.title: Two distinct host-specialized fungal species cause white-nose disease in bats
rows.summary: The identification of two cryptic species of the fungal pathogen that causes white-nose disease in bats highlights the need to integrate studies of genetic variability in pathogens into disease surveillance, management and prevention strategies.

rows.title: Astrocyte morphogenesis requires self-recognition
rows.summary: Human and mouse astrocytes express the protocadherin PcdhγC3, which promotes self-recognition of individual astrocytes, thereby contributing to normal astrocyte and brain development.

rows.title: Preoptic EP3R neurons constitute a two-way switch for fever and torpor
rows.summary: Neurons in the median preoptic nucleus that express the prostaglandin EP3 receptor produce prolonged hypothermic responses or hyperthermic responses, respectively, following brief activation or inhibition.

rows.title:
Radiative forcing reduced by early twenty-first century increase in land
            albedo
rows.summary: Effects of snow cover dynamics, land use or land cover conversions and non-conversion regions on albedo variations during 2001–2020 are quantified and their induced radiative forcing estimated, highlighting the role of land surface dynamics in modulating global warming.

rows.title: The shaping of terrestrial planets by late accretions
rows.summary: Differences in the role of late accretion in the long-term evolution of terrestrial planets are shown to possibly lead to distinct geophysical and chemical properties, as well as pathways conducive to prebiotic chemistry.

rows.title: Air pollution modulates trends and variability of the global methane budget
rows.summary: An integrated observation-driven and model-driven approach demonstrates that, from 2005 to 2021, periods of high atmospheric methane growth were linked to trends and variations in OH levels driven by fluctuations in air pollutants, especially during extreme events.

rows.title: In vivo haemopoietic stem cell gene therapy enabled by postnatal trafficking
rows.summary: In vivo gene delivery to haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells in newborn mice using engineered lentiviral vectors shows promise as an effective treatment for genetic diseases.

rows.title: Dating the evolution of oxygenic photosynthesis using La-Ce geochronology
rows.summary: 138 La- 138 Ce geochronology shows that La/Ce fractionation, and Ce oxidation, occurred at the time of deposition, placing the origin of oxygenic photosynthesis in the Mesoarchaean or earlier.

rows.title: Light-triggered regionally controlled n-doping of organic semiconductors
rows.summary: A facile light-triggered doping strategy involving a series of inactive photoactivable dopants is described that facilitates tunable regionally controlled n-doping of organic semiconductors, resulting in stable patterning of the doping profile at record high resolutions.

rows.title: Protein-primed homopolymer synthesis by an antiviral reverse transcriptase
rows.summary: A bacterial reverse transcriptase synthesizes polydeoxyadenylate to provide population-level immunity against viral infection.

rows.title: Unconventional solitonic high-temperature superfluorescence from perovskites
rows.summary: Exciton–lattice interactions suppress thermal noise through vibration isolation, enabling unconventional solitonic superfluorescence at unusually high temperatures in lead halide perovskites.

rows.title: Observing anyonization of bosons in a quantum gas
rows.summary: Emergent anyonic correlations via spin–charge separation are observed in a one-dimensional strongly interacting quantum gas, enabling the exploration of non-equilibrium anyonic phenomena in a highly controllable setting.

rows.title: EndoMAP.v1 charts the structural landscape of human early endosome complexes
rows.summary: A study presents EndoMAP.v1, a resource that combines information on protein interactions and crosslink-supported structural predictions to map the interaction landscape of early endosomes.

rows.title: Dynamic basal ganglia output signals license and suppress forelimb movements
rows.summary: Basal ganglia output neurons fire dynamically in bidirectional and movement-specific patterns to license forelimb movements.

rows.title: The pivot penalty in research
rows.summary: An analysis of millions of scientific papers and patents reveals a ‘pivot penalty’ when researchers shift direction, with the impact of studies decreasing rapidly the further they move from their previous work.

rows.title: Pt migration–lockup in zeolite for stable propane dehydrogenation catalyst
rows.summary: Tuning the b -axis length of silicalite-1 crystals allows control over the migration–agglomeration–lockup of active metal species in zeolites, which enables the creation of stable and durable catalysts for propane dehydrogenation in industrial applications.

rows.title: The subfornical organ is a nucleus for gut-derived T cells that regulate behaviour
rows.summary: A distinct population of CD4 T cells resides in specific regions of the steady-state brain, and these T cells are programmed in the periphery by the microbiome to coordinate adaptive behaviour.

rows.title: The history and future of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging
rows.summary: This Review provides an overview of the history of resting-state functional MRI research, which has helped to reveal the spatiotemporal organization of the brain, and discusses how it can contribute further to neuroscience research and precision psychiatry.

rows.title: Global dominance of seasonality in shaping lake-surface-extent dynamics
rows.summary: Monthly mapping of multisource remote-sensing data for 1.4 million lakes reveals that seasonality is the dominant driver of lake-surface-extent variations globally.

rows.title: Domesticated cannabinoid synthases amid a wild mosaic cannabis pangenome
rows.summary: A pangenome of the Cannabis genus including 193 genomes demonstrates high variability in most of the genome but low diversity in cannabinoid synthesis genes and provides a resource for future genetic studies and crop optimization.

rows.title: Electricity-driven enzymatic dynamic kinetic oxidation
rows.summary: Reshaping of thiamine-dependent enzymes with ferrocene-mediated electrocatalysis can unlock an unnatural dynamic kinetic oxidation of α-branched aldehydes, providing new opportunities for making molecules.

rows.title: Electrical switching of a p -wave magnet
rows.summary: Experimental observations and theoretical analysis provide evidence that the spin polarization of the spin-spiral type II multiferroic NiI 2 exhibits p -wave magnetism and its spin chirality is related to ferroelectric polarization, which can be electrically controlled.

rows.title: Taking common medicines might matter for cancer treatment
Address academic bullying through structural reform
The forest space age needs eyes on the ground
The diet crazes of the nineteenth century
rows.summary: Far-out food fads, and scientists commemorate the discovery of benzene in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

rows.title: Global measles eradication goal is urgently needed
Daily briefing: Harvard has had nearly 1,000 research grants cancelled
rows.summary: Harvard University has had grants worth more than US$2.4 billion cancelled by the Trump administration. Plus, why scientists across the United States are chasing hailstorms and the science behind The Last of Us.

rows.title: Time-management skills I honed as a PhD student now serve me well in industry
rows.summary: In her new role as a biotechnology entrepreneur, Maya Gosztyla relies on tried-and-tested strategies to plan ahead and avoid burnout.

rows.title: ‘Science saved my life’ — and it must save other at-risk scholars
rows.summary: The global scientific community must do more to offer safety and support to displaced academics and others.

rows.title: End racism in science: there shouldn’t be any argument about this goal
rows.summary: Five years after the murder of George Floyd spurred global protests, it is imperative that institutions continue to confront racism and discrimination.

rows.title: Fake AI images will cause headaches for journals
rows.summary: The race is on to build tools that can detect fradulent AI-generated images in research.

rows.title: Cancer-fighting immune cells could soon be engineered inside our bodies
rows.summary: Manufacturing CAR T cells in the laboratory is expensive and time-consuming. An in vivo approach could get the powerful therapy to more people.

rows.title: Gripping account of psychology’s cautionary tale is marred by flawed assumptions
rows.summary: A dissection of the field of ‘social priming’ asks what this controversy can teach us about how to study human behaviour.

rows.title: A coordinated cellular network regulates tolerance to food
rows.summary: Immune tolerance to dietary antigens is mediated by a circuit of dedicated antigen-presenting cells and T cells, ensuring protective effector responses without compromising the overall strategy of tolerance that ensures safe food consumption.

rows.title: Hong Kong universities woo Harvard international students targeted by Trump
rows.summary: Offers follow the US administration’s decision last week to prevent the prestigious university from enrolling foreign students.

rows.title: Scientists with ADHD speak up: when fire meets focus
rows.summary: Researchers with the neurodevelopmental condition discuss its peaks and valleys and how they structure their work lives to succeed.

rows.title: Scaling and logic in the colour code on a superconducting quantum processor
rows.summary: Colour code on a superconducting qubit quantum processor is demonstrated, reporting above-breakeven performance and logical error scaling with increased code size by a factor of 1.56 moving from distance-3 to distance-5 code.

rows.title: Author Correction: Chromosome end protection by RAP1-mediated inhibition of DNA-PK
A walk down memory lane and other stirring stories: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: I apply my aquatic-science training to empower Tanzania’s seaweed farmers
rows.summary: Amenipa Kyando supports coastal communities to enhance their livelihoods while protecting their environment.

rows.title: These contact lenses let humans see invisible infrared light
rows.summary: An infrared LED was visible even through closed eyelids

rows.title: I didn’t find AI useful. Then I let it teach me to code
rows.summary: Artificial intelligence is perfect for teaching novices, but less good for experts. Use it with that in mind, says Hannah Hackney.

rows.title: Harvard researchers devastated as Trump team cuts nearly 1,000 grants
rows.summary: Nature talks to scientists about an uncertain future as the US government lays siege to their university.

rows.title: How to delight your future boss at a science job interview
rows.summary: Two lab leaders discuss what they look for in candidates, and how their own values and cultural backgrounds influence their approach.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Contact lenses give people infrared vision
rows.summary: New contact lenses allow people to see multi-coloured infrared images — even with their eyes closed. Plus, why some conferences are abandoning the United States and evidence challenging the dominance of ‘natural selection’ as the sole adaptive force in evolution.

rows.title: The Last of Us science adviser: COVID changed our appetite for zombies
rows.summary: Behavioural ecologist David Hughes, who consulted on the video game that inspired the hit TV series, speaks to Nature ahead of the show’s second-season finale.

rows.title: Why do hailstones get so big? Scientists are chasing storms to find answers
rows.summary: Dozens of scientists have descended on the US Great Plains to study hail, which can inflict damage on property and even take lives.

rows.title: How artificial intelligence is transforming pathology
rows.summary: Some researchers say that deep-learning ‘foundation’ models will revolutionize the field — but others are not so sure.

rows.title: Landmark air-pollution lab under threat from Trump cuts — can it be saved?
rows.summary: The US government is shutting down a state-of-the-art facility that has provided data to inform health and environment regulations for decades.

rows.title: Don’t feel the pain — these brain cells help with managing opioid withdrawal
rows.summary: Neurons in a brain region linked with substance-use disorders can affect how much pain is felt when stopping chronic opioid use.

rows.title: Rare ‘spider star’ spotted consuming its companion
rows.summary: A spinning neutron star orbits the remnants of a once-massive stellar partner it has stripped to its core.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Imaging surface structure and premelting of ice Ih with atomic resolution
Publisher Correction: Multi-zonal liver organoids from human pluripotent stem cells
How and when North America’s deepest river gorge formed
rows.summary: An analysis of landscape features and of river deposits preserved in caves point to an event 2.1 million years ago that triggered the formation of Hells Canyon.

rows.title: Author Correction: A human brain map of mitochondrial respiratory capacity and diversity
Author Correction: Global methane emissions from rivers and streams
These contact lenses give people infrared vision — even with their eyes shut
rows.summary: Sci-fi-style technology uses nanoparticles to convert infrared light into visible light that humans can see.

rows.title: ‘Landmark’ evolution study shows how rice inherits tolerance to cold without DNA changes
rows.summary: The study adds to evidence challenging the dominance of ‘natural selection’ as the sole adaptive force in evolution.

rows.title: Why space exploration must not be left to a few powerful nations
rows.summary: Indigenous people and others need a say in space-industry decisions. Here’s how that can happen.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Ageing limits stemness and tumorigenesis by reprogramming iron homeostasis
AI listens for health conditions
rows.summary: Voice recordings, examined by artificial intelligence, might provide new biomarkers for conditions such as heart disease and Alzheimer’s.

rows.title: ‘Powerful and horrifying’ — David Attenborough’s latest film is a cry to protect our oceans
rows.summary: The seas could save us from climate change, but only if we save them first, legendary naturalist and broadcaster argues in a vivid film.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Earth’s core could be leaking
rows.summary: Hot magma might’ve pushed material from Earth’s dense metallic core all the way to the surface. Plus, the absence of just one amino acid helps mice shed weight and groundbreaking scientific discoveries might be getting harder to come by.

rows.title: This ancient pathogen became deadlier when humans started wearing wool
rows.summary: Ancient genomes reveal that a bacterial fever jumped from human-borne ticks to lice around the time wool textiles became common.

rows.title: Scientific conferences are leaving the US amid border fears
rows.summary: Some meetings have been put on hold in response to foreign researchers’ travel concerns.

rows.title: Author Correction: Structure and topography of the synaptic V-ATPase–synaptophysin complex
Nations urged to ‘pick up the ball’ after DEI research cuts
rows.summary: Researchers say a lack of funding for studies that focus on sex and gender might also hasten a US brain drain.

rows.title: Signatures of chiral superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene
rows.summary: Observations indicating the chiral nature of superconducting states in five rhombohedral tetralayer and pentalayer graphene devices without moiré superlattice effects are reported, establishing a pure carbon material for the study of topological superconductivity.

rows.title: These malaria drugs treat the mosquitoes — not the people
rows.summary: Tackling malaria in the insect stage could help control its spread — plus, new research on the complex genetics of pregnancy loss.

rows.title: Antimalarial-treated bed nets could stop parasites developing in mosquitoes
rows.summary: In a fresh approach to blocking transmission of the malaria parasite by mosquitoes, potent antimalarial compounds that kill parasites in mosquitoes are incorporated into bed-net prototypes. Exposure to the compounds through bed-net contact prevents parasite development, even when infection takes place four days later.

rows.title: Early barred galaxy raises questions about cosmic evolution
rows.summary: Observations of a galaxy from an early period of the Universe’s history reveal a bar-shaped structure and gas dynamics thought not to have been possible at that time.

rows.title: Are groundbreaking science discoveries becoming harder to find?
rows.summary: Researchers are arguing over whether ‘disruptive’ or ‘novel’ science is waning – and how to remedy the problem.

rows.title: Daily briefing: ‘I used AI to design an awful protein’
rows.summary: This is what happened when a Nature reporter designed his own protein using AI. Plus, the ‘Gollum effect’ that makes researchers hoard data and hopeful results for the first mRNA bird-flu vaccine for cattle.

rows.title: The path for AI in poor nations does not need to be paved with billions
rows.summary: Researchers in low- and middle-income countries show that home-grown artificial-intelligence technologies can be developed, even without large external investments.

rows.title: How axolotl cells ‘remember’ development to rebuild a lost limb
rows.summary: The molecular feedback loops that program positional identity as salamander limbs develop and regrow could be harnessed for regenerative medicine.

rows.title: #OpenToWork: how laid-off US scientists are coping with shattered careers
rows.summary: Unemployed researchers face some tough career choices as they flood the job market after the Trump administration’s cuts to science.

rows.title: Dying stars give a second wind to exoplanet formation
rows.summary: The binary star system ν Octantis has long been considered hostile to planet formation. The discovery of a white dwarf in the system offers an alternative view.

rows.title: The evolutionary origin of sensitive dental structures
rows.summary: Fossil data shed light on a debate about when vertebrate dental tissues arose by assigning an early sensory structure to arthropods rather than to vertebrates.

rows.title: Is Earth’s core leaking? Volcanic rocks provide strongest evidence yet
rows.summary: Samples from Hawaii seem to contain material that passed across the boundary between the planet’s core and its mantle, nearly 3,000 kilometres below the surface.

rows.title: Projections of Earth’s health under different environmental policies
rows.summary: Model-based scenarios of Earth’s future suggest that in the next few decades, eight of the nine planetary boundaries — safety limits for environmental pressure — could be crossed. However, targeted interventions, such as stringent climate policies and dietary shifts, could halt further degradation. Urgent action and time would be needed to return within all planetary boundaries.

rows.title: NIH killed grants on orders from Elon Musk’s DOGE
rows.summary: Court documents and internal correspondence show the cost-cutting force has broad control over the world’s largest public biomedical funder.

rows.title: The Age of Reason
rows.summary: Seeds of hope.

rows.title: Before studying parasites, this PhD researcher was their host
rows.summary: Kevin Liévano-Romero abandoned a veterinary career in Colombia to move to the United States, where he studies feared but fascinating creatures.

rows.title: AI linked to explosion of low-quality biomedical research papers
rows.summary: Analysis flags hundreds of studies that seem to follow a template, reporting correlations between complex health conditions and single variables based on publicly available data sets.

rows.title: Patterns of DNA modifications provide a ‘barcode’ for cell-lineage tracing
rows.summary: Differences in the pattern of a biochemical modification called DNA methylation in blood-generating cells and their progeny can be used to accurately track clones through differentiation. This approach identified biased expansions of blood stem cells giving rise to myeloid-type cells as a characteristic of ageing in mice and humans.

rows.title: Under the microscope: DNA damage tracked through cell generations
rows.summary: An ingenious technique reveals how stressed cells divide to produce progeny that have different traits — a phenomenon that can initiate cancer.

rows.title: Mice lacking this amino acid lost 30% of their body weight
rows.summary: But eliminating cysteine, which is found in high-protein foods, from human diets would be challenging.

rows.title: Unravelling cysteine-deficiency-associated rapid weight loss
rows.summary: Conditional cysteine restriction in mice causes substantial weight loss, exceeding that seen with essential amino acid restriction, by activating the integrated stress and oxidative stress responses, and by unexpectedly depleting coenzyme A, leading to metabolic inefficiency.

rows.title: A retrograde planet in a tight binary star system with a white dwarf
rows.summary: A planet in a retrograde orbit around a star with a close-in white dwarf companion reveals the role of binary stellar evolution in the formation and evolution of planets.

rows.title: Clonal tracing with somatic epimutations reveals dynamics of blood ageing
rows.summary: The discovery that DNA methylation of different CpG sites can serve as digital barcodes of clonal identity led to the development of EPI-Clone, an algorithm that enables single-cell lineage tracing through cellular differentiation at scale.

rows.title: Programmable control of spatial transcriptome in live cells and neurons
rows.summary: CRISPR-TO, a system for programmable control of spatial localization of cellular RNAs, is presented and enables functional investigation of endogenous RNA localization in diverse living cells.

rows.title: Large gas inflow driven by a matured galactic bar in the early Universe
rows.summary: Gas distribution and motion patterns driven by a galactic bar of the J0107a dusty star-forming galaxy have analogues in local bars, indicating that similar processes of active star formation were already operating 11.1 billion years ago.

rows.title: Quasar radiation transforms the gas in a merging companion galaxy
rows.summary: We demonstrate that in a major merging system, radiation from the quasar in one galaxy directly alters the gas properties in the companion galaxy.

rows.title: Closed-loop vagus nerve stimulation aids recovery from spinal cord injury
rows.summary: Following spinal cord injury, gamified physical therapy that incorporates closed-loop vagus nerve stimulation can aid restoration of arm and hand function.

rows.title: The structure of liquid carbon elucidated by in situ X-ray diffraction
rows.summary: A precise structure measurement of liquid carbon at pressures of around 1 million atmospheres obtained by in situ X-ray diffraction at an X-ray free-electron laser shows a complex fluid with transient bonding and approximately four nearest neighbours on average.

rows.title: Glioblastoma-instructed astrocytes suppress tumour-specific T cell immunity
rows.summary: A population of TRAIL-positive astrocytes in glioblastoma contributes to an immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment and this mechanism can be targeted with an engineered oncolytic virus to improve outcomes.

rows.title: C-to-N atom swapping and skeletal editing in indoles and benzofurans
rows.summary: C to N atom swapping in indoles is introduced that gives indazoles through oxidative cleavage of the indole heteroarene core and subsequent ring closure, adding another method to the field of skeletal editing.

rows.title: Stepwise ATP translocation into the endoplasmic reticulum by human SLC35B1
rows.summary: SLC35B1, initially thought to be a nucleotide sugar transporter, is an essential ATP/ADP exchanger that imports ATP into the endoplasmic reticulum through a unique stepwise translocation mechanism.

rows.title: A foundation model for the Earth system
rows.summary: Aurora, a new large-scale foundation model trained on more than one million hours of diverse geophysical data, outperforms operational forecasts in predicting air quality, ocean wave dynamics, tropical cyclone tracks and high-resolution weather.

rows.title: Multigenerational cell tracking of DNA replication and heritable DNA damage
rows.summary: A multigenerational single-cell tracking approach provides a framework to dissect phenotypic plasticity at the single-cell level, offering insights into cellular processes that may resemble early events during cancer development.

rows.title: Ru and W isotope systematics in ocean island basalts reveals core leakage
rows.summary: Ru isotopes are proposed as tracers for core–mantle interaction on Earth, and anomalies for ocean island basalts from Hawaii are reported that have higher ε 100 Ru than the ambient mantle.

rows.title: Sequence diversity lost in early pregnancy
rows.summary: Around 1 in 136 pregnancies is lost due to a pathogenic small sequence variant genotype in the fetus.

rows.title: PCSK9 drives sterol-dependent metastatic organ choice in pancreatic cancer
rows.summary: PCSK9 regulates low density lipoprotein-cholesterol import and determines organ preference of metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, with PCSK9-low cells metastasizing to the liver and PCSK9-high cells preferring the lung.

rows.title: Molecular basis of positional memory in limb regeneration
rows.summary: A molecular analysis of axolotl limb regeneration has identified a positive genetic circuit that maintains posterior cell identity and can be used to reprogramme anterior cells into posterior cells.

rows.title: Effect of phosphorylation barcodes on arrestin binding to a chemokine receptor
rows.summary: Different phosphorylation patterns created by GRK2 and GRK5 on the C-terminal tail of ACKR3 lead to distinct structural arrangements and dynamics of G-protein-coupled receptor–arrestin complexes, potentially explaining diverse cellular outcomes.

rows.title: In vivo screen of Plasmodium targets for mosquito-based malaria control
rows.summary: An in vivo screen of small-molecule compounds to inhibit the mosquito-stage development of Plasmodium identified hits that can be incorporated into bed nets and led to effective parasite killing in the insect host.

rows.title: Unexpected clustering pattern in dwarf galaxies challenges formation models
rows.summary: Unexpected large-scale clustering of isolated, diffuse and blue dwarf galaxies, comparable to that seen for massive galaxy groups, challenges current models of cosmology and galaxy evolution.

rows.title: The origin of vertebrate teeth and evolution of sensory exoskeletons
rows.summary: Re-examination of the presumed Cambrian fossil fish Anatolepis reveals previous misidentification of aglaspidid sensory structures as dentine, a vertebrate sensory tissue, showing it to be an arthropod, and shifting the origin of vertebrate hard tissues to the Middle Ordovician.

rows.title: AI bots threaten online scientific infrastructure
Telescope team reads the fine print — from more than a kilometre away
rows.summary: A pair of telescopes picking up reflected light achieve a performance 14 times better than a single telescope can manage alone.

rows.title: Does lightning make trees swish?
rows.summary: Noises in nearby greenery heard before a thunderbolt, and the physics of a peculiar echo made by fences in our weekly dip into Nature’ s archive.

rows.title: AI-generated literature reviews threaten scientific progress
Data resources must be protected from political interference
What big eyes this whale has — but not the better to see you with
rows.summary: The humpback whale has the whale equivalent of nearsightedness, which puts it at risk of being snarled in fishing gear.

rows.title: Don’t forget the lessons of the McCarthy era
How ‘organized looting and plunder’ drove Britain’s second scientific revolution
rows.summary: Manuscripts and specimens accumulated by the colonial East India Company lie at the roots of modern science and museums.

rows.title: I told AI to make me a protein. Here’s what it came up with
rows.summary: A new crop of artificial-intelligence models allows users to create, manipulate and learn about biology using ordinary language.

rows.title: How much ultra-processed food do you eat? Blood and urine record it
rows.summary: Samples could provide an objective measure of diets and help to unravel their contribution to disease.

rows.title: Who were the ancient Denisovans? Fossils reveal secrets about the mysterious humans
rows.summary: Clues are emerging about the ghostly clan that settled eastern Asia and left a genetic legacy in people today.

rows.title: Bird-flu vaccine for cattle aces early test
rows.summary: Vaccines for livestock could reduce the risk of human outbreaks, but hurdles remain.

rows.title: Trump’s cuts to international aid are stifling Africa’s HIV research
rows.summary: African scientists must find ways to mobilize alternative resources to maintain hard-won gains.

rows.title: Philanthropic funders: team up to jump-start innovative science
rows.summary: Collaborations between privately run foundations provide an opportunity to fund risky science that governments cannot take on.

rows.title: Author Correction: Earth’s ambipolar electrostatic field and its role in ion escape to space
NSF plan to slash ‘indirect’ science funding: will it stick?
rows.summary: As it awaits a court ruling, the US National Science Foundation has paused its attempt to cap indirect-cost payments on research grants.

rows.title: Richard Garwin obituary: designer of the hydrogen bomb who advocated for arms control
rows.summary: The particle physicist and inventor advised 13 US presidents — whether they asked him to or not.

rows.title: Daily briefing: What a precious handful of fossils is teaching us about Denisovans
rows.summary: It started with a tiny fingerbone; now more fossils are revealing what exactly is a Denisovan. Plus, a world-first trial of ‘prime editing’ in a person and capuchin monkeys are ‘kidnapping’ babies from another species.

rows.title: Turning the tide on ocean conservation
rows.summary: The UN Ocean Conference offers a rare opportunity for countries to correct their course on ocean health.

rows.title: Science’s ‘Gollum effect’: PhDs bear brunt of territorial behaviour
rows.summary: Survey respondents at all career stages report colleagues engaging in territorial and possessive behaviours — but early-career researchers are most often affected.

rows.title: One-carbon homologation of alkenes
rows.summary: A new method for extending alkenes by one or two carbons is shown to be useful in attenuating the immunosuppressive properties of a medicine, making it potentially applicable for targeting disease areas where immunosuppresion is unwanted.

rows.title: AI tool flags people at high risk of post-partum depression
rows.summary: Model could be used by hospitals to identify people who would benefit from preventive measures.

rows.title: People and dogs team up to protect sea turtles in Cabo Verde
rows.summary: João José Mendes de Oliveira and the Turtle Foundation catch poachers with the help of trained dogs.

rows.title: Mother–infant bonds in wild chimpanzees resemble those of humans
rows.summary: The observation of bonding behaviours in wild chimpanzees suggests that some aspects of human attachment have a deep evolutionary origin.

rows.title: Author Correction: Soft–hard zwitterionic additives for aqueous halide flow batteries
Daily briefing: The world’s first human bladder transplant
rows.summary: A 41-year-old man has become the first person to receive a bladder transplant in an eight-hour operation. Plus, a ‘minimalist’ approach to quantum computing and meet the dog who helps stop turtle poachers.

rows.title: Exclusive: NIH grant rejections have more than doubled amid Trump chaos
rows.summary: At least 2,500 applications for research funding have been denied so far this year.

rows.title: World first: ultra-powerful CRISPR treatment trialled in a person
rows.summary: Immune-cell function improved in a teenager whose DNA was altered using prime editing.

rows.title: Mighty microbes — the invisible forces that can save the world
rows.summary: A call to arms argues that emerging microbial technologies can not only improve planetary health and preserve biodiversity — but also be the cornerstone of a thriving economy.

rows.title: When the government cancels your research grant, here’s what you can do
rows.summary: The mass cancellation of US federal grants marks yet another escalation in political interference in science, but there are ways to keep crucial research going.

rows.title: AI is more persuasive than people in online debates
rows.summary: When given information about its human opponents, the large language model GPT-4 could make particularly convincing arguments.

rows.title: Hurricane risk in a changing climate — the role of uncertainty
rows.summary: When it comes to modelling how global warming will affect storms hitting the United States, some factors are better understood than others.

rows.title: Author Correction: Inhibitory specificity from a connectomic census of mouse visual cortex
Genomics reveals zoonotic and sustained human mpox spread in West Africa
rows.summary: Monkeypox virus genomic data from Nigeria and Cameroon, sampled between 2018 and 2023, indicate that the virus spread through repeated zoonoses in Cameroon, whereas in Nigeria, it spread mainly through human–human transmission, predominantly originating in Rivers State.

rows.title: Atacama sunshine helps to pull water from thin air
rows.summary: A device involving solar panels and a gel produces substantial amounts of water in one of the world’s driest deserts.

rows.title: Single particle acts as a quantum computer to simulate molecules
rows.summary: A trapped ytterbium ion can be used to model complex changes in the energy levels of organic molecules interacting with light.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Meet the baby who received the world’s first personalized CRISPR therapy
rows.summary: A baby boy is thriving after receiving a CRISPR therapy to treat his specific disease-causing mutation. Plus, the FDA plans to phase out animal toxicity testing and physicists are trialling a portable antimatter containment system.

rows.title: Can NIH-funded research on racism and health survive Trump’s cuts?
rows.summary: The US administration has cancelled ‘DEI grants’ without defining DEI, leaving health-equity researchers in the dark.

rows.title: US brain drain: Nature ’s guide to the initiatives drawing scientists abroad
rows.summary: In response to US turmoil, premier establishments such as the European Research Council have sweetened incentives to attract talent.

rows.title: Can AI help us talk to dolphins? The race is now on
rows.summary: Lucrative prizes are offered for an AI-powered breakthrough in communications between humans and other species.

rows.title: How CAR-T cancer therapies could harm the brain
rows.summary: Immune-system responses to cell therapies produce long-term effects on cognition in mice.

rows.title: PhD students in STEM: Nature wants to hear from you
rows.summary: Buried in lab work or drowning in data? Take a break and help shape the future of PhD education.

rows.title: The world’s richest people have an outsized role in climate extremes
rows.summary: The consumption and investments of the wealthiest 10% contribute disproportionately to the emissions that drive heat waves and drought.

rows.title: Stem cells coaxed into most advanced amniotic sacs ever grown in the lab
rows.summary: The sacs grew to roughly 2 centimetres wide and could be used to study early pregnancy.

rows.title: Explosive volcanoes can bury carbon —a climate boon
rows.summary: Ash spread by violent eruptions in South American sequester carbon in the soil.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Yes, you can find love during your PhD
rows.summary: The highs and lows of looking for ‘the one’ during a PhD. Plus, mice with a human gene grow bigger-than-usual brains and reptiles might have evolved 35 million years earlier than we thought.

rows.title: World’s first personalized CRISPR therapy given to baby with genetic disease
rows.summary: Treatment seems to have been effective, but it is not clear whether such bespoke therapies can be widely applied.

rows.title: Powerful CRISPR system inserts whole gene into human DNA
rows.summary: ‘Directed’ evolution in the laboratory creates an editing tool that outperforms classic CRISPR systems.

rows.title: Seeking a job in science? How hiring practices across industry and academia compare
rows.summary: Why is recruitment often speedier in industry? Julie Gould investigates what the two sectors can learn from each other in the race to source top talent.

rows.title: AI language models develop social norms like groups of people
rows.summary: When LLMs are grouped together, they exhibit similar characteristics to human societies.

rows.title: Ku limits RNA-induced innate immunity to allow Alu expansion in primates
rows.summary: Studies on the essentiality of Ku in human cells reveal that Ku interacts with diverse double-stranded RNA molecules, including antisense Alu , and enables tolerance of Alu sequence expansion in primates.

rows.title: How to transport antimatter — stick it on the back of a van
rows.summary: Researchers put a portable antimatter containment system through its paces at CERN — plus, the maths of a black hole fly-by.

rows.title: Brain tissues, assemble! Inside the push to build better brain models
rows.summary: With organoids, assembloids and a growing toolkit of bioengineering tricks, scientists are stitching together models of the developing human brain — and pushing the limits of realism and control.

rows.title: ‘I don’t have the bandwidth’: how to juggle dating alongside a PhD
rows.summary: Is lasting love more likely if you date only other scientists? How much should you talk about your research on a first date? Researchers lift the lid on their experiences of when science meets affairs of the heart.

rows.title: Daily briefing: These award-winning photos show scientists at work
rows.summary: The best of scientists’ photos from the field. Plus, researchers are split about whether it’s OK for AI to write science papers and bad philosophy is stopping progress in physics, says Carlo Rovelli.

rows.title: Is it OK for AI to write science papers? Nature survey shows researchers are split
rows.summary: Poll of 5,000 researchers finds contrasting views on when it’s acceptable to involve AI and what needs to be disclosed.

rows.title: Mice grow bigger brains when given this stretch of human DNA
rows.summary: Finding adds to the bigger picture of how humans developed such large brains.

rows.title: Fossil claw marks show reptiles arose much earlier than thought
rows.summary: Tracks in Australia seem to be the earliest known prints of amniotes — a group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals.

rows.title: Dear editors, your publication delays are damaging our careers
rows.summary: Chia-Hsuan Hsu waited 18 months before chasing an editor for a decision on a paper. The answer surprised him.

rows.title: Do look up: how science and international cooperation closed the ozone hole
rows.summary: Forty years ago this month, scientists reported that human activities had punctured Earth’s protective ozone layer. What happened next offers a masterclass in international science-diplomacy.

rows.title: Immune control of metastatic cancer at the edge of the central nervous system
rows.summary: Leptomeningeal metastasis is a deadly consequence of cancer that creates an unusually inflamed environment around the brain and spinal cord. One of the inflammatory signalling molecules found in cerebrospinal fluid, interferon-γ, induces an antitumour immune response through an unexpected series of cell–cell interactions.

rows.title: Black hole fly-by modelled with landmark precision
rows.summary: A prediction of the gravitational waves produced by interacting black holes achieves high precision and demonstrates the link between general relativity and geometry.

rows.title: Black hole flings out clumps of gas
rows.summary: Measurements of wind in a luminous galactic core reveal dense pockets of gas — a finding that calls for a rethink of how black holes interact with their host galaxies.

rows.title: Track record: unexpectedly early reptile claw prints found
rows.summary: Fossil evidence points to an earlier-than-expected timeline for when reptiles, members of the four-limbed group of animals called tetrapods, began to evolve.

rows.title: The visitors
rows.summary: A place to remember.

rows.title: DeepMind unveils ‘spectacular’ general-purpose science AI
rows.summary: System improves chip designs and tackles unsolved maths problems, but has not been rolled out to researchers outside the company.

rows.title: Genomes from a four-generation family reveal the rate of new mutations
rows.summary: The rate at which mutations arise can be estimated by studying multigenerational human families. Reference genomes have been assembled for 28 people from four generations of the same family. This publicly available resource provides insight into the mechanisms that underlie mutations in the most complex regions of the genome.

rows.title: Marsupial embryos lack the epigenetic reset seen in placental mammals
rows.summary: Biochemical ‘DNA methylation’ marks are found across the genome in vertebrate animals, but in the early embryos of placental mammals, such as mice and humans, they are largely erased in a ‘system reset’. Surveying DNA methylation in opossum embryos reveals that, in marsupials, such marks are retained.

rows.title: Take Nature ’s AI research test: find out how your ethics compare
rows.summary: What’s your view on using AI for peer review and for writing research papers?

rows.title: Earth’s climatic past illuminates future South Asian monsoon patterns
rows.summary: An analysis of warm periods in Earth’s history helps to clarify an apparent anomaly in projections of the future behaviour of the South Asian summer monsoon.

rows.title: Structured ionized winds shooting out from a quasar at relativistic speeds
rows.summary: Observations of a luminous quasar from the high-resolution spectrometer Resolve aboard XRISM revealed highly inhomogeneous wind structure outflowing from a supermassive black hole, which probably consists of up to a million clumps.

rows.title: Past warm intervals inform the future South Asian summer monsoon
rows.summary: Proxy records and climate simulations show that in past warm intervals, the South Asian summer monsoon was characterized by an increase in monsoon rainfall, and weakening and strengthening of different parts of the monsoon circulation, consistent with future projections.

rows.title: Exploring pathways for world development within planetary boundaries
rows.summary: Current trends imply that we will transgress most of the planetary boundaries by 2050; however, ambitious, urgent and universal action to ameliorate climate change and increase resource efficiency can effectively reduce the degree of transgression.

rows.title: Radiation-induced amphiregulin drives tumour metastasis
rows.summary: Radiotherapy induces expression of the EGFR ligand amphiregulin, which promotes metastasis growth at remote sites in mouse models and human patients by shifting myeloid cells towards an immunosuppressive state.

rows.title: Taurine from tumour niche drives glycolysis to promote leukaemogenesis
rows.summary: The taurine–taurine transporter axis is a critical dependency of aggressive myeloid leukaemias.

rows.title: Encapsulated Co–Ni alloy boosts high-temperature CO 2 electroreduction
rows.summary: An optimized Co–Ni alloy catalyst encapsulated with Sm 2 O 3 -doped CeO 2 shows both high activity and stability for high-temperature CO 2 -to-CO conversion, overcoming the limitations of such catalysts typically used in industrial applications.

rows.title: Proton transport from the antimatter factory of CERN
rows.summary: The successful transport of a trapped proton cloud from the antimatter factory of CERN using a transportable, superconducting, autonomous and open Penning-trap system that can distribute antiprotons into other experiments is reported.

rows.title: Divergent DNA methylation dynamics in marsupial and eutherian embryos
rows.summary: A study reports on the DNA methylation dynamics during embryogenesis in marsupials, showing that these differ from those occurring during embryogenesis in eutherian mammals.

rows.title: A human-specific enhancer fine-tunes radial glia potency and corticogenesis
rows.summary: HARE5 , a human accelerated region enhancer, modulates cortical development by influencing neural progenitor cell behaviour, leading to an enlarged neocortex with increased functional independence between cortical regions through amplified WNT signalling.

rows.title: Chicago Archaeopteryx informs on the early evolution of the avian bauplan
rows.summary: Analysis of the 'Chicago' Archaeopteryx , a nearly complete and uncrushed specimen, reveals details of the skeleton, soft tissues and plumage of this taxon, providing information on the evolution to avian dinosaur.

rows.title: Earliest amniote tracks recalibrate the timeline of tetrapod evolution
rows.summary: Analysis of a fossil trackway from the earliest Carboniferous of Australia shows prints of toes with claws, suggesting that the origin of amniotes was at least 35–40 million years earlier than previously thought.

rows.title: Wireless transmission of internal hazard signals in Li-ion batteries
rows.summary: A miniaturized and low-power-consumption system is designed to allow the accurate sensing and wireless transmission of internal temperature and strain signals inside lithium-ion batteries with negligible influence on their performance, improving their safety.

rows.title: Ultrahigh-pressure crystallographic passage towards metallic hydrogen
rows.summary: The observation of the transition from hcp H 2 to a post- hcp structure with a six-fold larger supercell at pressures above 212 GPa is reported, indicating the trend of H 2 polymerization through molecular association.

rows.title: Targeting symbionts by apolipoprotein L proteins modulates gut immunity
rows.summary: APOL9a/b proteins coat mouse intestinal bacteria with high specificity, and genetic abolition of ceramide-1-phosphate synthesis pathways in the symbiote Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron significantly decreases this binding of APOL9a/b to the bacterium.

rows.title: STAT5 and STAT3 balance shapes dendritic cell function and tumour immunity
rows.summary: Immune checkpoint blockade activates T cell immunity by reprogramming the STAT3 and STAT5 transcriptional pathways in dendritic cells, and STAT3 degradation is effective for treating tumours of multiple cancer types in mouse models.

rows.title: Bulk–spatiotemporal vortex correspondence in gyromagnetic zero-index media
rows.summary: Realization of a gyromagnetic double-zero-index metamaterial results in unconventional optical and topological properties, suitable to be used for the generation of light pulses shaped as a vortex both in time and space.

rows.title: Interferon-γ orchestrates leptomeningeal anti-tumour response
rows.summary: Independent of antigen presentation, migratory CCR7 + dendritic cells orchestrate the influx, proliferation and cytotoxic action of natural killer cells to control cancer cell growth in the leptomeninges.

rows.title: Systems consolidation reorganizes hippocampal engram circuitry
rows.summary: A study shows that loss of memory precision associated with systems consolidation can be explained by neurogenesis-dependent reorganization of engram circuitry within the hippocampus over time.

rows.title: Tunable vacuum-field control of fractional and integer quantum Hall phases
rows.summary: Using a system to adjust the strength of cavity vacuum fields penetrating a Hall bar, a study describes the effect of the vacuum field of a cavity on electronic correlations in quantum Hall systems.

rows.title: Genome diversity and signatures of natural selection in mainland Southeast Asia
rows.summary: Analysis of whole-genome sequencing data from 3,023 human genomes from mainland Southeast Asia identifies high genetic heterogeneity among populations in the region and many unique small and structural variants.

rows.title: Quantum error correction of qudits beyond break-even
rows.summary: Quantum error correction of a logical qutrit and ququart were experimentally realized beyond the break-even point with the Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill bosonic code.

rows.title: Oncogenic fusions converge on shared mechanisms in initiating astroblastoma
rows.summary: The molecular mechanisms of astroblastoma development are identified, whereby distinct gene fusions upregulate shared transcriptional networks to disrupt the normal development of ventral telencephalon neural progenitors, which leads to oncogenesis.

rows.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals human cortical layer and area specification
rows.summary: Multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) together with deep-learning-based nucleus segmentation enabled the construction of a highly detailed and informative spatially resolved single-cell atlas of human fetal cortical development.

rows.title: Solid phase transitions as a solution to the genome folding paradox
rows.summary: In vitro reconstitution and in vivo live-cell imaging of LHX2–EBF1–LDB1 enhancer hubs in olfactory sensory neurons reveals that these transcription factors form condensates with solid, rather than liquid, phase properties.

rows.title: Unconventional domain tessellations in moiré-of-moiré lattices
rows.summary: Examination of a complete structural phase diagram of twisted trilayer graphene shows that several large-scale moiré domain lattices can be formed, the physical properties of which can be tuned by the twist angles between layers.

rows.title: Emergence of Calabi–Yau manifolds in high-precision black-hole scattering
rows.summary: A new, highest-precision analytical result for solving the gravitational two-body problem of black hole or neutron star scattering reveals the emergence of Calabi–Yau manifolds in the solution to the radiated energy in these encounters.

rows.title: Dopaminergic action prediction errors serve as a value-free teaching signal
rows.summary: Dopaminergic action prediction error signals are used by mice as a value-free teaching signal to reinforce stable sound–action associations in the tail of the striatum.

rows.title: Water ice in the debris disk around HD 181327
rows.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has detected water ice in the cold debris disk (analogous to the Kuiper belt) around the star HD 181327.

rows.title: Prefrontal encoding of an internal model for emotional inference
rows.summary: Neurons in the rodent dorsomedial prefrontal cortex encode a flexible internal model of emotion by linking directly experienced and inferred associations with aversive experiences.

rows.title: Thermal asymmetry in the Moon’s mantle inferred from monthly tidal response
rows.summary: Data from the NASA GRAIL spacecraft recover the lunar gravity field suggesting preservation of a predominantly thermal anomaly in the nearside mantle, which could influence the spatial distribution of deep moonquakes.

rows.title: China needs to deal with discarded electric-vehicle batteries
‘Loss and damage fund’ for climate change needs broader remit
Empower communities to fight climate change at grassroots level
Do universities serve their community?
Where do comets come from?
rows.summary: The interstellar origins of space’s dirty snowballs, and debunking a myth about maternal crustaceans, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Five secrets of super-healthy seniors
rows.summary: How to become (and remain) unusually healthy old people. Plus, all living things emit a very slight glow and a promising drug for early migraine symptoms.

rows.title: Six striking images showcase scientific fieldwork
rows.summary: The winners of Nature ’s 2025 photo competition braved crashing waves and misty mountains to capture their science.

rows.title: My PhD adviser was fired and I was collateral damage. I learnt how to build resilience into graduate school
rows.summary: Students and institutions should treat PhD degrees as they would a job.

rows.title: US researchers must stand up to protect freedoms, not just funding
rows.summary: Curtailment of freedoms and disregard for the rule of law in the United States is destroying the ability of science to serve the nation’s, and the world’s, interests. Researchers can take action.

rows.title: What an angry exchange with a reviewer taught me about arrogance and humility
rows.summary: I should have paused and asked myself some tough questions. Instead, I started to type.

rows.title: Author Correction: Microbiota-derived 3-IAA influences chemotherapy efficacy in pancreatic cancer
Nature project to encourage early-career researchers in peer review is working
rows.summary: Science stands to benefit from a project in which experienced academics and early-career researchers co-review studies.

rows.title: US brain drain: the scientists seeking jobs abroad amid Trump’s assault on research
rows.summary: Five US-based researchers tell Nature why they are exploring career opportunities overseas.

rows.title: NSF terminates huge number of grants and stops awarding new ones
rows.summary: In this podcast we get an overview of recent developments at the US research funder, and what proposed budget cuts could mean for US science.

rows.title: Scientists turn lead into gold
rows.summary: The transmuted metal only lasted a fraction of a second before it was obliterated but can tell researchers more about how atoms change.

rows.title: What language do bats speak? I’m trying to find out
rows.summary: Cesária Huó is collecting bat vocalizations to understand how the sounds they make evolve.

rows.title: North America’s birds are declining where they should be thriving
rows.summary: The steepest drops in number are seen in areas that host the largest populations — a trend observed for more than 80% of bird species across the continent.

rows.title: Migraine drug is first to tackle debilitating early symptoms
rows.summary: Results from a phase III clinical trial suggest that taking ubrogepant at the first sign of an oncoming migraine can prevent pre-headache fatigue and light sensitivity.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Chimp societies drum to a distinct beat
rows.summary: The drumming cultures of chimpanzees differ between subspecies. Plus, the EPA and NOAA are being hobbled by DOGE red tape and how fast the human genome mutates.

rows.title: ‘AI models are capable of novel research’: OpenAI’s chief scientist on what to expect
rows.summary: Jakub Pachocki, who leads the firm’s development of advanced models, is excited to release an open version to researchers.

rows.title: Hunting extreme microbes that redefine the limits of life
rows.summary: An adventurous survey of inhospitable habitats unearths extraordinary organisms that pose challenging research questions.

rows.title: The scars of war last for centuries: how we understand collective trauma needs to change
rows.summary: Researchers looking to study the social ramifications of mass traumas must not overlook the histories of affected communities in the search for healing.

rows.title: Why bad philosophy is stopping progress in physics
rows.summary: Theoretical physicists are in thrall to a misguided mindset that allows viable ideas to be advanced only by overturning what already exists.

rows.title: A pope, a polymath and plucky women: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: China’s dementia incidence is rising fast ― outpacing the global average
rows.summary: Public-health measures to curb high blood-sugar levels, smoking and obesity could help to rein in the trend.

rows.title: Rice paddies produce food for billions ― and lots of methane
rows.summary: Just five nations account for more than three-quarters of the emissions of this potent greenhouse gas that stem from rice cultivation.

rows.title: Author Correction: 2023 summer warmth unparalleled over the past 2,000 years
A ‘hidden gem’ of the Amazon is a frog with odd habits
rows.summary: A newly identified species of poison-dart frog seems to be monogamous, making it a rarity of its kind.

rows.title: Physicists turn lead into gold — for a fraction of a second
rows.summary: Colliding beams of lead create fast-moving, short-lived gold ions. Understanding the process could help to refine particle-accelerator experiments.

rows.title: US environmental agency halts funding for its main science division
rows.summary: E-mails reveal the stoppage at the US Environmental Protection Agency, which is encouraging workers to resign ahead of a reorganization.

rows.title: Daily briefing: How skunk cabbages get their stink
rows.summary: A small tweak to a common enzyme lets stinky plants make their distinctive scents. Plus, physicists turned lead into gold for a fraction of a second and the migrations of herrings are being altered by the loss of elders’ knowledge.

rows.title: ‘Orwellian’: planetary scientists outraged over deletion of research records
rows.summary: Researchers say that a NASA-funded institute is over-interpreting Trump’s anti-DEI order.

rows.title: How political attacks could crush the mRNA vaccine revolution
rows.summary: Drug makers are scrambling to navigate an ‘existential threat’ to a once-celebrated technology.

rows.title: Google AI better than human doctors at diagnosing rashes from pictures
rows.summary: Chatbot can analyse health-care imagery, such as PDFs of test results, to accurately diagnose a range of medical conditions.

rows.title: How quickly do humans mutate? Four generations help answer the question
rows.summary: DNA sequencing of a family from children to great-grandparents reveals more mutations than previously seen.

rows.title: Microbe that infests hospitals can digest medical-grade plastic ― a first
rows.summary: The bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces an enzyme that breaks down biodegradable plastics.

rows.title: Guess how much of the ocean floor humans have explored
rows.summary: Hint: it’s less than 1% — a lot less.

rows.title: Exclusive: documents reveal how NIH will axe climate studies
rows.summary: US agency guidelines nix funding for studies on climate anxiety and more, but allow it for work on extreme weather and health.

rows.title: Daily briefing: How we taste sweetness
rows.summary: The structure of the taste receptor responsible for sweetness has finally been mapped out. Plus, the intricate patterns of cells in mouse brains illuminated with just a light microscope and a class of drugs offering hope for rare children's cancers.

rows.title: Curiosity, drive, willingness to learn: three qualities to display at science job interviews
rows.summary: Recruiters want to see evidence of your potential to grow and develop, learn from mistakes, and how well you will fit into the team, says entrepreneur Ilana Wisby.

rows.title: P hacking — Five ways it could happen to you
rows.summary: Some data practices can lead to statistically dubious findings. Here’s how to avoid them.

rows.title: How skunk cabbages and other smelly plants brew their foul odour
rows.summary: A small tweak to a common enzyme gives plants the ability to make smelly sulfurous molecules.

rows.title: Renewal of NIH grants linked to more innovative results, study finds
rows.summary: Survey of hundreds of scientists’ work suggests that cutting off funding disrupts focus and reduces the novelty of research.

rows.title: Herring population loses migration 'memory' after heavy fishing
rows.summary: Removal of experienced fish results in younger members not knowing migration routes — plus, how AI companion apps may affect our mental health.

rows.title: How Korea’s female divers have adapted to cold plunges
rows.summary: The Haenyeo divers of the Korean island of Jeju have a genetic variant linked to pain tolerance, as do other people living on Jeju.

rows.title: ‘Forever’ molecules arrange themselves into cell-like structures
rows.summary: At sufficiently high concentrations, some of the compounds called per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances self-organize into two-layered membranes.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Stress dynamically modulates neuronal autophagy to gate depression onset
Climate risk for younger generations is set to soar
rows.summary: An analysis shows that large fractions of future generations will be exposed to extreme climate events that would occur only once every 10,000 years in the absence of global warming.

rows.title: Engineered bacteria can degrade five wastewater pollutants at the same time
rows.summary: Five gene clusters have been integrated into the bacterium Vibrio natriegens to engineer a strain that can remediate five organic pollutants — toluene, phenol, naphthalene, biphenyl and dibenzofuran — in industrial waste water and saline soil.

rows.title: Trump freezes ‘gain of function’ pathogen research ― threatening all US virology, critics say
rows.summary: An executive order suspends the use of federal funds for certain experiments on pathogens with pandemic potential. Critics say low-risk science could be affected too.

rows.title: How protein-slayer drugs could beat some of the cruellest cancers
rows.summary: Momentum is building for PROTAC treatments that eliminate disease-causing proteins, including those responsible for difficult-to-treat childhood cancers.

rows.title: Blocking a key node in cancer signalling unlocks therapeutic potential
rows.summary: Mutations in RAS enzymes commonly drive cancer. Targeting an overlooked protein complex that works with RAS offers a fresh avenue to cancer therapy.

rows.title: Superb starlings swap helper and breeder roles with kin and non-kin
rows.summary: A 20-year field study of the African superb starling ( Lamprotornis superbus ) found striking evidence that birds often switch breeding roles from year to year by taking turns as ‘breeders’ or each other’s ‘helpers’. This reciprocal assistance was not explained by genetic relatedness (kinship) and required decades of observation to be detected.

rows.title: How climate change will burden our children: data reveal a lifetime of extreme heat
rows.summary: Young people will be exposed to a number of heatwaves that no one would have experienced in pre-industrial times.

rows.title: Author Correction: Matrix-producing neutrophils populate and shield the skin
Controversial geoengineering projects to test Earth-cooling tech funded by UK agency
rows.summary: The Advanced Research and Invention Agency is investing £57 million to study climate-manipulating technologies, but says it is taking a cautious approach.

rows.title: Leviathan
rows.summary: Contact has not been made.

rows.title: How we taste sweetness: long-sought structure of human receptor mapped at last
rows.summary: 3D structure of the tongue’s sweet-sensing protein could guide future food designs.

rows.title: Lipid-degrading small molecule kills cancer cells by ferroptosis
rows.summary: A molecule designed to activate iron locked up in organelles called lysosomes and thereby induce cell death might offer a way to tackle treatment-resistant cancer.

rows.title: Why you should write your PhD thesis backwards
rows.summary: By considering the central statement of your entire PhD, you can structure your writing around it, says Tuuli Toivonen.

rows.title: Uncovering a key enzyme opens possible therapeutic avenues for lysosomal diseases
rows.summary: Lipid recycling in organelles called lysosomes depends on the lipid BMP, which was thought to be resistant to degradation by lysosomal enzymes. It emerges that the enzyme PLA2G15 breaks down BMP, and inhibiting PLA2G15 extends lifespan in a mouse model of Niemann–Pick type C1, a neurodegenerative disorder marked by impaired lysosomal lipid metabolism.

rows.title: Daily briefing: A spinal tumour was removed through a person’s eye socket for the first time
rows.summary: A nineteen-year-old has become the first person to undergo a ‘third nostril’ surgery to remove a spinal tumour. Plus, generations of cold-water diving has influenced the genetics of an entire island and the UK geoengineering projects awarded £57 million of funding.

rows.title: ‘Second chance’: convicted US chemist Charles Lieber moves to Chinese university
rows.summary: Former Harvard scientist convicted of making false statements says he wants to do research that benefits humanity — and cannot do that in the United States.

rows.title: Why China needs to review its approach to research evaluation
rows.summary: The country’s publication policies should balance the need to promote science locally with the benefits of disseminating research internationally.

rows.title: Tracking older LGBTQ+ people’s health: ‘I hear their voices and their stories’
rows.summary: Undeterred by US funding cuts, behavioural-health researcher Jason Flatt studies how dementia affects people from sexual and gender minorities.

rows.title: Detailed mouse brain map created with off-the-shelf microscope
rows.summary: Sample-enlarging trick helps researchers to untangle brain connectivity using readily available equipment.

rows.title: Time for adults to finally act like adults on climate change
rows.summary: A report detailing how climate inaction will consign people born today to a lifetime of weather extremes must awaken a sense of responsibility.

rows.title: Brain tissue artificially expanded to show how neurons wire together
rows.summary: A fluorescence-microscopy method for tracing neuronal connections in the brain could make connectomics studies more widely accessible for neuroscientists.

rows.title: Global emergence of unprecedented lifetime exposure to climate extremes
rows.summary: Climate models, impact models and demographic data are used to estimate the number of people projected to experience unprecedented lifetime exposure to extreme climate events across multiple dimensions, including birth year, warming scenario and vulnerability.

rows.title: Twist-programmable superconductivity in spin–orbit-coupled bilayer graphene
rows.summary: The superconductivity in Bernal bilayer graphene that emerges from the spin–orbit coupling induced by proximal tungsten diselenide can be tuned by modulating the twist angle between the two materials.

rows.title: PLA2G15 is a BMP hydrolase and its targeting ameliorates lysosomal disease
rows.summary: Lysosomal phospholipase PLA2G15 was identified as a physiological BMP hydrolase whose activity depends on unique esterification and stereochemistry of BMP and offers a potential therapeutic target for Niemann–Pick disease type C1 and other neurodegenerative conditions.

rows.title: Bioremediation of complex organic pollutants by engineered Vibrio natriegens
rows.summary: A synthetic biology approach was used to engineer Vibrio natriegens into a strain capable of bioremediating complex organic pollutants in saline wastewater and soils, thereby addressing notable threats to marine biosecurity.

rows.title: Intragrain 3D perovskite heterostructure for high-performance pure-red perovskite LEDs
rows.summary: To increase the efficiency, brightness and stability of next-generation light-emitting diodes (LEDs), the microstructure of CsPbI 3- x Br x metal-halide perovskite, a good pure-red emitter, was altered to fix hole leakage, which was identified as decreasing efficiencies in overworked LEDs.

rows.title: Light-microscopy-based connectomic reconstruction of mammalian brain tissue
rows.summary: A technique called LICONN (light-microscopy-based connectomics) allows mapping of brain tissue at synapse level and simultaneous measurement of molecular information, thus enabling quantification of cellular properties and multimodal analysis of brain tissue.

rows.title: Oncogene aberrations drive medulloblastoma progression, not initiation
rows.summary: A large-scale multi-omics analysis reports oncogenic alterations that drive medulloblastoma progression, rather than initiation, and the findings show how single-cell technologies can be used for early detection and diagnosis of medulloblastoma.

rows.title: Striatum supports fast learning but not memory recall
rows.summary: Activity in the striatum is necessary for trial-to-trial improvements in learning sensory–motor tasks but not memory recall.

rows.title: Heterogeneous pericoerulear neurons tune arousal and exploratory behaviours
rows.summary: A set of neurons in the peri-locus coeruleus region controls arousal and avoidance states, providing an understanding of the neurobiological basis of arousal and exploratory behaviours.

rows.title: Dopamine D1–D2 signalling in hippocampus arbitrates approach and avoidance
rows.summary: Approach versus avoidance responses are driven by D1 and D2 neurons in the ventral hippocampus.

rows.title: Targeting the SHOC2–RAS interaction in RAS-mutant cancers
rows.summary: A study of dependencies associated with cancer-causing mutations has identified a small molecule that binds to SHOC2 and inhibits RAS signalling in cells carrying NRAS Q61 mutations, a common oncogenic driver in melanoma.

rows.title: Herring spawned poleward following fishery-induced collective memory loss
rows.summary: A critically low abundance of older herring due to age-selective fisheries resulted in an approximately 800-km poleward shift in main spawning.

rows.title: Trends in the seasonal amplitude of atmospheric methane
rows.summary: Model simulations show that the observed trends in the seasonal amplitude of methane can be attributed to changes in emissions and the atmospheric sink from reaction with the hydroxyl radical.

rows.title: Native nucleosomes intrinsically encode genome organization principles
rows.summary: A technique called condense-seq has been developed to measure nucleosome condensability and used to show that mononucleosomes contain sufficient information to condense into large-scale compartments without requiring any external factors.

rows.title: Superconductivity and spin canting in spin–orbit-coupled trilayer graphene
rows.summary: Introducing spin–orbit coupling by substrate proximity effect leads to an enhancement of superconducting phases in rhombohedral trilayer graphene.

rows.title: Deep origin of eukaryotes outside Heimdallarchaeia within Asgardarchaeota
rows.summary: Ancestral reconstruction together with molecular dating of the last Asgard archaea and eukaryote common ancestor suggest that eukaryotes arose from the fusion of a H 2 -consuming archaeal host and a H 2 -producing protomitochondrion.

rows.title: Activation of lysosomal iron triggers ferroptosis in cancer
rows.summary: Some cancer cells exhibit high loads of reactive iron in lysosomes, and this feature is exploited by using fentomycin-1, a newly developed small molecule, to induce ferroptosis.

rows.title: Nasal vaccines for respiratory infections
rows.summary: This Review provides an overview of progress and future directions in the development of nasally administered vaccines for respiratory infections.

rows.title: Motor learning refines thalamic influence on motor cortex
rows.summary: Imaging and optogenetics in mice provide insight into the interplay between the primary motor cortex and the motor thalamus during learning, showing that thalamic inputs have a key role in the execution of learned movements.

rows.title: A cryptic role for reciprocal helping in a cooperatively breeding bird
rows.summary: A study of the cooperative breeding behaviour of superb starlings during 40 consecutive breeding seasons over 20 years reveals long-term reciprocal helping between both related and unrelated individuals.

rows.title: Chromatin loops are an ancestral hallmark of the animal regulatory genome
rows.summary: The physical organization of the genome in non-bilaterian animals and their closest unicellular relatives is characterized; comparative analysis shows chromatin looping is a conserved feature of genome architecture and spatial genome regulation emerged early in animal evolution.

rows.title: In science-for-policy design, one size doesn’t fit all
AI reveals title of ‘unreadable’ Vesuvius scroll for first time
rows.summary: Team scoops US$60,000 prize for identifying a Greek work on vices from scans of a 2,000-year-old papyrus charred by volcanic eruption.

rows.title: Avian vandals demolish spring flowers
rows.summary: Hungry house-sparrows destroy primroses and bees dance to direct others to sweetness, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: USAID’s shutdown: a crisis for sub-Saharan Africa
Next CERN collider has community input
Manage releases of ‘forever chemicals’ in lab waste
Cuts to US science will take a generation to repair — leaders must speak up now
rows.summary: There’s no mystery to innovation and economic growth; the US must nurture its scientists or find out the hard way.

rows.title: Daily briefing: AI companions — friend or frenemy?
rows.summary: How increasingly sophisticated ‘AI companions’ can impact our mental health. Plus, the blood of a man who’s been bitten by snakes 200 times is used to make a potent antivenom and a timeline of Trump’s attack on US science.

rows.title: Make science more collegial: why the time for ‘adversarial collaboration’ has come
rows.summary: Bringing together proponents of rival theories to test their ideas against each other can advance science — but only if all sides can accept that they might be wrong.

rows.title: Can Germany rein in its academic bullying problem?
rows.summary: Researchers and administrators are exploring ways to restructure a rigid hierarchy that can breed power abuses.
