rows.title: Supportive? Addictive? Abusive? How AI companions affect our mental health
rows.summary: Studies suggest benefits as well as harms from digital companion apps — but scientists worry about long-term dependency.

rows.title: Medical AI trained on whopping 57 million health records
rows.summary: Researchers fed an artificial-intelligence model called Foresight with anonymized data from a huge swathe of patients in England’s National Health Service.

rows.title: How I honed my biopharma dealmaking and business-development skills after my PhD
rows.summary: What does a chief business officer do, and how do you become one? Filippo Mulinacci describes his corporate career, the importance of on-the-job training and why he doesn’t miss the bench.

rows.title: Naturally ornate RNA-only complexes revealed by cryo-EM
rows.summary: Cryo-electron microscopy structures of three large ornate natural bacterial RNA molecules reveal their quaternary structures and intra- and intermolecular interactions that stabilize them.

rows.title: A kinase mediator of rhizobial symbiosis and immunity in Medicago
rows.summary: A plant kinase mediates symbiotic signalling and suppress host immunity to enable legume–rhizobium symbiosis.

rows.title: Molecular basis of SIFI activity in the integrated stress response
rows.summary: To efficiently silence the integrated stress response, SIFI detects many diverse substrates that include stress indicators and stress response components through flexible domains within an easily accessible scaffold, before building linkage-specific ubiquitin chains at separate, sterically restricted elongation modules.

rows.title: I climb mountains in search of sustainable agricultural systems
rows.summary: Jiraporn Inthasan studies soils in Thailand’s plantations to identify farming methods that best absorb carbon.

rows.title: Don’t need much sleep? Mutation linked to thriving with little rest
rows.summary: The genetic variant is one of a handful that have been identified in people who don’t need a lot of sleep.

rows.title: Want to supercharge your science? Turn to technicians
rows.summary: To foster research excellence, institutions should value both researchers and technicians — and facilitate collaborations between them.

rows.title: Teens with anxiety and depression spend more time on social media
rows.summary: Survey of thousands of young people shows that those with mental-health conditions spend more time on social-networking sites but are less happy with their online experience than their peers.

rows.title: Author Correction: Parvalbumin-expressing basket-cell network plasticity induced by experience regulates adult learning
Fungus from the human gut slows liver disease in mice
rows.summary: The disease affects almost one-third of adults and treatments are limited.

rows.title: Searching for dark photons in the Sun’s atmosphere
rows.summary: Satellite observations of solar radiation have narrowed down the possible properties of dark photons — a proposed dark-matter particle.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The unusual mathematics that gives rose petals their shape
rows.summary: Unusual ‘extrinsic’ geometries give rose petals their curled edges and pointed corners. Plus, a new technique that can directly edit proteins in living cells and how India rewrote the rules of space travel when it launched its first satellite.

rows.title: AI scientist ‘team’ joins the search for extraterrestrial life
rows.summary: The collaborative system generated more than 100 hypotheses relating to the origins of life in the Universe.

rows.title: Trump gutted two landmark environmental reports — can researchers save them?
rows.summary: Scientists working on disrupted national climate and nature assessments aren’t giving up.

rows.title: Blood of man who’s had 200 snake bites helps make a potent antivenom
rows.summary: Treatment combines existing drug with antibodies from hyper-immune reptile collector, raising both hopes and ethical concerns.

rows.title: Star ecologist ‘blurred boundaries’ in lab — but colleagues criticize investigation
rows.summary: A report into Thomas Crowther’s conduct at ETH Zurich finds that the professor breached some internal rules, but clears him of misusing funds.

rows.title: Walking in two worlds: how an Indigenous computer scientist is using AI to preserve threatened languages
rows.summary: Michael Running Wolf leads artificial-intelligence initiatives to revive lost languages and empower Indigenous people.

rows.title: Trump proposes unprecedented budget cuts to US science
rows.summary: Huge reductions, if enacted, could have ‘catastrophic’ effects on US competitiveness and the scientific pipeline, critics say.

rows.title: Storm of seizures in a baby’s brain calms after trial therapy
rows.summary: The treatment, which aimed to block production of a mutant protein, reduced the frequency of infant’s seizures, but did not improve neurological impairments.

rows.title: Powerful protein editors offer new ways of probing living cells
rows.summary: Scientists deploy self-splicing protein subunits to insert strange new additions into target proteins.

rows.title: Exclusive: NSF stops awarding new grants and funding existing ones
rows.summary: US science funder also plans to screen grant applications for compliance with ‘agency priorities’.

rows.title: Whale earwax, fungal fertilizer and chocolate emissions: exhibition explores biodiversity research
rows.summary: The Natural History Museum’s new gallery, Fixing our Broken Planet, examines Earth’s changing ecosystems and how to protect them.

rows.title: Daily briefing: A supersingular elliptic curve brought to life — the month’s best science images
rows.summary: Marvel at the month’s best science images. Plus, how a high-fibre diet was able to fix a disrupted mouse gut microbiome and an Indigenous American tribe who’ve forged an unprecedented collaboration with a genomics lab.

rows.title: Revealed: the unusual mathematics that gives rose petals their shape
rows.summary: Petals’ pointy edges rely on a type of geometric feedback never before seen in nature.

rows.title: Why the green-technology race might not save the planet
rows.summary: The emerging global competition for green innovation, markets and investments might boost prosperity without improving environmental sustainability.

rows.title: The dismantling of US science: can it survive Trump 2.0?
rows.summary: In the face of massive upheaval, what is the long-term outlook for science in the US and beyond?

rows.title: One of the world’s richest lithium deposits began inside a mega-volcano
rows.summary: Lithium that pooled in a volcanic caldera in the western United States had no way out, thanks to a lack of rivers.

rows.title: Nickel production is notoriously dirty — here’s how to make it greener
rows.summary: If scaled up, a method for extracting nickel without using carbon-rich coke could reduce emissions considerably.

rows.title: How to protect research data
rows.summary: Contingency plans are needed to shore up important information.

rows.title: The cell-division cycle is faster in cell types prone to forming cancer
rows.summary: Some types of cell are more likely than others to give rise to tumours. A rapid cell cycle is a newly identified predictor of cancer susceptibility.

rows.title: The end of AIDS is in sight: don’t abandon PEPFAR now
rows.summary: The US administration should clear up the confusion over the future of a widely admired AIDS fund and push for Congress to reauthorize it.

rows.title: Native American tribe teams up with genomicists to confirm link to iconic ancient site
rows.summary: DNA from ancient and present-day members of Picuris Pueblo confirm oral histories linking the tribe to the famed Chaco Canyon centre.

rows.title: Why we need to measure people’s well-being — lessons from a global survey
rows.summary: Greater insights into what makes people happy, secure and hopeful will make for a better world.

rows.title: Metal-centred planar [15]annulenes
rows.summary: An aromatic metallo-annulene, comprising a 15-carbon macrocycle enclosing an osmium complex, with the metal residing within the plane of the macrocycle is reported.

rows.title: Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?
rows.summary: An ambitious plan to stop the global threat of AIDS has been derailed. But many are hopeful that progress can be salvaged.

rows.title: Inflammatory bowel disease has stages of epidemiology that can be tracked across global regions
rows.summary: The spatio-temporal evolution of inflammatory bowel disease across the world follows four epidemiological stages: emergence, acceleration in incidence, compounding prevalence and prevalence equilibrium. Classifying regions by epidemiological stage enables health-care systems to prepare for the evolving global burden.

rows.title: Romeo and the robots
rows.summary: A droid by any other name.

rows.title: Did a tardigrade get the world’s tiniest tattoo? April’s best science images
rows.summary: The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature ’s photo team.

rows.title: Daily briefing: 17 ways to ward off stroke, dementia or depression later in life
rows.summary: Researchers have identified a suite of risk factors that contribute to the chance of developing several conditions related to damaged blood vessels in the brain. Plus, dopamine helps the brain overwrite fearful memories and how we might salvage progress in the global fight against AIDS.

rows.title: Indigenous American tribe’s ancestral history confirmed by genomes
rows.summary: Ancient and present-day genomes from members of the Indigenous American tribe Picuris Pueblo in the US Southwest show genetic continuity with Ancestral Pueblo individuals from the Chaco Canyon, New Mexico. These results confirm traditional knowledge and contest previous accounts that suggested that the population in the region collapsed before European colonization.

rows.title: How we call out the infuriating mistakes we spot in school science textbooks
rows.summary: Two scientist parents who often help their children with homework deal with acceptable — and unacceptable — errors in course materials.

rows.title: Trump team’s science cuts threaten tenure hopes for early-career academics
rows.summary: As funding dries up, US universities will need to reconsider traditional tenure requirements.

rows.title: Exclusive: NIH to end billions of dollars in foreign research grants
rows.summary: Move by US biomedical agency jeopardizes thousands of projects on infectious diseases, cancer and more.

rows.title: Metal-cored molecule is the first of its kind
rows.summary: A new class of organometallic compound has been made that has a distinctive geometry and electronic structure — with potential for catalysis and materials science.

rows.title: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness
rows.summary: Multimodal results (iEEG, fMRI and MEG) of predictions from integrated information theory and global neuronal workspace theory align with some predictions of both theories on visual consciousness, but also critically challenge key tenets of both theories.

rows.title: Diet outperforms microbial transplant to drive microbiome recovery in mice
rows.summary: Experiments in mouse models show that proper recovery of the intestinal microbiota following depletion, with or without faecal microbiota transplant therapy, is dependent on syntrophic interactions that occur only with specific dietary interventions.

rows.title: A DNA-gated molecular guard controls bacterial Hailong anti-phage defence
rows.summary: Hailong, an anti-phage defence system, synthesizes an oligodeoxyadenylate signal that blocks effector activity in the absence of phage infection but is degraded by phage-encoded DNA exonucleases, leading to protective growth arrest of infected cells.

rows.title: TIR domains produce histidine-ADPR as an immune signal in bacteria
rows.summary: In response to phage infection, the Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain protein ThsB of the type II Thoeris defence system produces histidine conjugated to ADP-ribose, which stimulates bacterial defence by interacting with the Macro domain of the ThsA membrane effector protein.

rows.title: Cell cycle duration determines oncogenic transformation capacity
rows.summary: Total cell cycle duration is a key hallmark of cancer initiation, and determines whether defects in apoptosis, senescence, immune surveillance, angiogenesis, DNA repair, polarity and proliferation lead to cancer development.

rows.title: Structurally complex phase engineering enables hydrogen-tolerant Al alloys
rows.summary: A size-sieved complex precipitation in Sc-added Al–Mg alloys achieves a high-density dispersion of both fine Al 3 Sc nanoprecipitates and in situ formed core-shell Al 3 (Mg, Sc) 2 /Al 3 Sc nanophases with high hydrogen-trapping ability.

rows.title: Picuris Pueblo oral history and genomics reveal continuity in US Southwest
rows.summary: A collaborative study initiated by the sovereign nation of Picuris Pueblo in the Northern Rio Grande region of New Mexico addresses gaps in traditional knowledge and furthers understanding of their population history and ancestry.

rows.title: Global evolution of inflammatory bowel disease across epidemiologic stages
rows.summary: An analysis of data from 522 population-based studies encompassing 82 global regions and spanning more than a century (1920–2024) shows spatiotemporal transitions across epidemiologic stages 1 to 3 of inflammatory bowel disease, and models stage 4 progression.

rows.title: The distribution of subsurface microplastics in the ocean
rows.summary: Global data collected between 2014 and 2024 provide insights into the distribution and potential transport mechanisms of subsurface microplastics throughout the oceanic water column.

rows.title: A MERS-CoV-like mink coronavirus uses ACE2 as an entry receptor
rows.summary: A newly identified coronavirus isolated from farmed minks can use the receptor ACE2 to infect cells of different mammalian species, including human cells, which has implications for potential zoonotic spillover events.

rows.title: Pacific hotspots reveal a Louisville–Ontong Java Nui tectonic link
rows.summary: Geochemistry and geochronology show that Samoa and Rurutu–Arago are the longest-lived Pacific hotspots, providing better constraints on plate rotation and support for a link between the Louisville volcanic track and the Ontong Java Nui Plateau.

rows.title: Regulation of PV interneuron plasticity by neuropeptide-encoding genes
rows.summary: Increasing the activity of individual parvalbumin-expressing interneurons in the mouse brain modulates the number and strength of inhibitory parvalbumin synapses received by these cells through changes in the expression of the neuropeptide-encoding genes Vgf and Scg2 .

rows.title: Using life cycle assessment to drive innovation for sustainable cool clouds
rows.summary: A life cycle assessment study is used to examine the impacts of advanced cooling technologies on cloud infrastructure, from virtual machines to server architecture, data centre buildings and the grid.

rows.title: Selective inhibition of stromal mechanosensing suppresses cardiac fibrosis
rows.summary: Inhibition of a cardiac stroma-enriched mechanosensor, SRC—in concert with suppression of the TGFβ pathway—potentiates the reversal of fibroblast activation and alleviates contractile dysfunction in fibrotic hearts.

rows.title: Serotonin and neurotensin inputs in the vCA1 dictate opposing social valence
rows.summary: Aversive and rewarding social experiences are linked to conspecific identity through converging dorsal raphe 5-HT and paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus neurotensin signals in the vCA1 that instruct opposing valence, representing a synaptic switch for flexible social valence computation.

rows.title: A battery-free nanofluidic intracellular delivery patch for internal organs
rows.summary: A nanofluidic intracellular delivery (NanoFLUID) patch provides a versatile, biocompatible and efficient method for the targeted delivery of payloads to internal organs for therapeutic purposes and for biomolecular investigations.

rows.title: An asymmetric fission island driven by shell effects in light fragments
rows.summary: Measurements of fission fragments for 100 fissioning systems are used to map an asymmetric fission island, providing evidence for the role played by the deformation induced by a closed 36-proton shell.

rows.title: Single-cell transcriptomics reveal how root tissues adapt to soil stress
rows.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic approaches reveal major expression changes in outer root cell types when grown in soil versus gel conditions, and also uncover how root tissues communicate and adapt to contrasting soil conditions at single-cell resolution.

rows.title: Plant diversity dynamics over space and time in a warming Arctic
rows.summary: Warming temperatures and interactions between plants are the main drivers of changes in Arctic plant communities in response to climate change, and there is no evidence of overall biotic homogenization.

rows.title: Sustainable nickel enabled by hydrogen-based reduction
rows.summary: A one-step process using fossil-free hydrogen-plasma-based reduction is used to extract nickel from low-grade ore and create high-grade ferronickel alloys, providing a more sustainable and environmentally friendly method for obtaining nickel.

rows.title: Comparative connectomics of Drosophila descending and ascending neurons
rows.summary: Three electron microscopy datasets are combined to provide a complete connectomic description of the neural circuitry that makes up the neck connective in Drosophila , including the descending neurons, ascending neurons and sensory ascending neurons.

rows.title: Observation of edge and bulk states in a three-site Kitaev chain
rows.summary: An artificial Kitaev chain is realized by engineering three coupled quantum dots in a two-dimensional electron gas, which enables the manipulation and observation of both the edge and bulk states.

rows.title: Tattoo-making tools used by ancient Maya revealed
rows.summary: The stone fragments had been discovered inside ‘Handprint Cave’ in Belize alongside other artefacts suggestive of ritual use.

rows.title: When a great ball of fire came crashing down
rows.summary: First-hand accounts of luminous objects falling in a storm, and a warning against the exploitative trade of tropical butterflies, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Cell classification should be based on more than just DNA
The use of AI in peer review could undermine science
Preserve access to crucial climate data
For these bats, eavesdropping is a valuable learnt skill
rows.summary: Over time, young fringe-lipped bats learn how to distinguish the calls of palatable frogs from those of toxic ones.

rows.title: Debris from rockets is polluting the Caribbean
Canada’s election: what Mark Carney’s win means for science
rows.summary: In turbulent economic times, the prime minister’s Liberal party has promised funding to attract research talent to Canada.

rows.title: The do’s and don’ts of scientific image editing
rows.summary: Acceptable image-editing practices are partly a matter of common sense. But researchers say journals and funders could help scientists by standardizing policies.

rows.title: Will US science survive Trump 2.0?
rows.summary: President Donald Trump and his administration have gutted science agencies, terminated research programmes and cancelled billions of dollars in grants to universities. What are the long-term impacts for the United States and the world?

rows.title: Historic pandemic treaty is a triumph in a world being torn apart
rows.summary: Global agreement on a pandemic preparedness plan came against all the odds. Now all parties must follow good intentions with concrete actions.

rows.title: COVID vaccine works faster with both doses in the same arm
rows.summary: Quick immune responses could be key to establishing herd immunity in future pandemics.

rows.title: Daily briefing: COVID booster jabs given in the same arm as the original work faster
rows.summary: Receiving a COVID-19 booster vaccine in the same arm as the first vaccine dose leads to a more effective immune response. Plus, how the sounds spiders are used to can shape their webs and whether US science can survive a second Trump term.

rows.title: A forensic investigator of glacier change
rows.summary: Jemma Wadham analyses the ever-changing glaciers of the Arctic.

rows.title: ‘Fear extinction’ signal in mouse brain offers clues about how to treat PTSD
rows.summary: Mechanism involving neurons that stimulate fear, and ones that suppress it, could help to explain conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: irCLIP-RNP and Re-CLIP reveal patterns of dynamic protein assemblies on RNA
How the world’s largest language family spread — and why others go extinct
rows.summary: Three books that take on the history of languages have something for everyone.

rows.title: Academia needs a more honest, scientific approach to DEI
rows.summary: Universities must be frank about barriers to equity, devise clear metrics for what they are trying to achieve and measure progress transparently.

rows.title: Microbial molecule of ageing gut nudges blood stem cells towards cancer
rows.summary: The risk of developing blood cancer increases with age. The finding that a molecule from gut bacteria plays a part points to new ways to intervene.

rows.title: My fight to unlock cannabis and psychedelic drugs for use in medical research
rows.summary: Physician Sue Sisley battles to study cannabis and psilocybin mushrooms for pain, addiction and PTSD.

rows.title: ‘Tatooine’-like planet orbits two stars ― but at a weird angle
rows.summary: Like the Star Wars planet, a distant world follows a path around two stars, both of them small, cool bodies called brown dwarfs.

rows.title: Audio long read: Do smartphones and social media really harm teens’ mental health?
rows.summary: While researchers agree that adolescents are struggling with mental health, there is fierce debate about how much technology is to blame.

rows.title: This is not the new colour that scientists have created
rows.summary: Firing tiny doses of laser light into people’s eyes allowed them to perceive a never-seen-before hue.

rows.title: My ‘woke DEI’ grant has been flagged for scrutiny. Where do I go from here?
rows.summary: My work in making artificial intelligence fair has been noticed by US officials intent on ending ‘class warfare propaganda’.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Bite marks on bones hint that Romans really did fight lions
rows.summary: Marks on a pelvic bone excavated from a gladiator graveyard are the first physical evidence of lion–human combat in the Roman empire. Plus, hundreds of papers use artificial intelligence without disclosing it and how whole-genome sequencing is changing the game for rare genetic diseases.

rows.title: Hundreds more NSF grants terminated after agency director resigns
rows.summary: Sethuraman Panchanathan abruptly leaves helm of US funding agency after Elon Musk’s DOGE arrives.

rows.title: Huge reproducibility project fails to validate dozens of biomedical studies
rows.summary: Unique reproducibility effort in Brazil focuses on common methods rather than a single field ― and prompts call for reform.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Fibromyalgia eases after doses of gut microbes
rows.summary: A small trial hints that gut microbes might help treat the symptoms of fibromyalgia. Plus, what it’s like to see a colour no one else has seen and a cri de cœur from a physician who says we are facing a second, preventable wave of the HIV pandemic.

rows.title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Essential roles of PI(3)K–p110β in cell growth, metabolism and tumorigenesis
Editorial Expression of Concern: A melanocyte lineage program confers resistance to MAP kinase pathway inhibition
Science sleuths flag hundreds of papers that use AI without disclosing it
rows.summary: Telltale signs of chatbot use are scattered through the scholarly literature — and, in some cases, have disappeared without a trace.

rows.title: How Trump’s attack on universities is putting research in peril
rows.summary: Scientists have little information as the US government freezes and cancels their funding.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Ancient Phoenicians spread their culture — but not their DNA
rows.summary: People from Mediterranean outposts of Phoenician culture shared no ancestry with ancient Middle Easterners. Plus, Mendel’s last pea-plant mysteries have finally been solved and an origami-inspired material can make ‘dancing’ robots.

rows.title: Eugenics is on the rise again: human geneticists must take a stand
rows.summary: Scientists must push back against the threat of rising white nationalism and the dangerous and pseudoscientific ideas of eugenics.

rows.title: Major European institutes join race to save US science data
rows.summary: As the administration of US President Donald Trump slashes budgets, crucial data sets on climate and other subjects could disappear.

rows.title: Baffling chronic pain eases after doses of gut microbes
rows.summary: A small, preliminary trial and studies in mice draw links between fibromyalgia and alterations of the gut microbiome.

rows.title: How Democrats and Republicans cite science: study reveals stark differences
rows.summary: Democratic-led congressional committees and left-wing think tanks reference research papers more often than their right-wing counterparts.

rows.title: Parkinson’s gut-microbiota links raise treatment possibilities
rows.summary: The relationship between pathology in the brain and alterations in the gut microbiome could lead to therapies — even if it’s not clear which changes come first.

rows.title: Author Correction: Global influence of soil texture on ecosystem water limitation
An origami design for metamaterial robots
rows.summary: Bendy, twisty and collapsable origami towers could make temperature controlling panels, or, dancing robots.

rows.title: A front-line antiviral drug disappoints against worrisome monkeypox strain
rows.summary: Tecovirimat, which has been approved to treat mpox, was no better than a placebo in a large trial.

rows.title: Why US police shootings are so deadly ― and why some police forces do better
rows.summary: Two studies show the extent of gunshot wounds inflicted by police and link certain police-department policies with a lower death toll.

rows.title: Ancient DNA reveals Phoenicians’ surprising genetic ancestry
rows.summary: Phoenician civilization thrived across the Mediterranean for more than 1,000 years.

rows.title: A brand-new colour created by lasers, a pig-liver transplant trial gets the green light, and a nugget-sized chunk of lab-grown meat
rows.summary: We round up some recent stories from the Nature Briefing .

rows.title: China overtakes the United States in cancer research output
rows.summary: China takes pole position in cancer-related research in the Nature Index, with a massive jump in output.

rows.title: Tracking the evolution and persistence of antibiotic resistance in the human gut
rows.summary: Bacterial resistance to antibiotics is a growing health threat, but its evolution outside laboratory settings is poorly understood. Bacteria living in the human gut are now found to evolve persistent resistance after brief exposure to antibiotics, and factors that promote this evolution have been identified, highlighting the gut as a potential hotspot for this process.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Sea-turtle conservation is working
rows.summary: Endangered sea turtle populations are bouncing back around the world — but there are still significant challenges. Plus, chimpanzees like to share fermented fruit and three ways to cool Earth by pulling carbon from the sky.

rows.title: Answers to a 160-year-old riddle about the genetics of Mendel’s pea traits
rows.summary: The genetic bases of the seven pairs of contrasting traits in the garden pea that were described by the ‘father of genetics’, Gregor Mendel, have long puzzled scientists. The discovery of the genetic variants underlying these traits sheds light on the ‘inherited factors’ that Mendel proposed and how they shape biological differences.

rows.title: Psychedelics reduce fear by targeting immune cells that modulate brain cells
rows.summary: Immune cells boost stress-linked fear responses by communicating with brain cells. One way that psychedelics lessen such fear is by modulating this interaction.

rows.title: Clinical trials by the numbers
rows.summary: Emerging companies and an evolving market are changing the dynamics of cancer trials.

rows.title: How we’re battling Trump’s science cuts across small-town America
rows.summary: Neuroscientist Jessica Cantlon is urging scientists to use the power of local newspapers in the fight against US research-funding cuts.

rows.title: Shapeshifting origami material shrinks when twisted
rows.summary: An origami-inspired ‘metamaterial’ has been engineered to have properties not found in natural materials — enabling it to undergo large, reversible deformations.

rows.title: Four rising stars at the forefront of cancer research
rows.summary: These scientists are coming at cancer from all angles.

rows.title: Scientific naming conventions should keep in step with contemporary science
rows.summary: A three-part Nature Podcast series explores the importance of scientific naming conventions — and talks to researchers looking at how to make them more inclusive.

rows.title: A protein tunnel that shuttles lipids around the cell
rows.summary: The high-resolution structure of a bridge-like lipid-transfer protein that moves lipids between cellular compartments shows how these ‘lipid superhighways’ operate.

rows.title: Cancer vaccine momentum builds, but US funding cuts raise concerns
rows.summary: Vaccine scepticism could undermine important progress in cancer research.

rows.title: Inside the quest to digitally unroll ancient scrolls burnt by Vesuvius
rows.summary: Mission to decipher Herculaneum scrolls using high-resolution scanning and artificial intelligence scales up rapidly.

rows.title: Heart-attack outcomes are worse in the morning when activity of protein duo dips
rows.summary: A protein pair that influences how damage to cardiac muscle fluctuates with circadian rhythm could be the key to optimizing heart-attack recovery.

rows.title: How to fix a gut microbiome ravaged by antibiotics
rows.summary: A diet rich in diverse carbohydrates outperforms faecal transplants in mice at restoring microbial diversity, which has been linked to a range of health conditions.

rows.title: Three ways to cool Earth by pulling carbon from the sky
rows.summary: With the world set to blow past its temperature targets, efforts are growing to remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere.

rows.title: How AI is helping to boost cancer screening
rows.summary: Cancer blood tests and AI-powered scans look promising for quicker and more accurate detection of disease.

rows.title: Memories of a cold place trigger bodily responses to warm up
rows.summary: Neurons involved in forming memories of a cold environment communicate with the part of the brain that regulates metabolic responses to cold stress.

rows.title: A guide to the Nature Index
rows.summary: A description of the terminology and methodology used in this supplement, and a guide to the functionality that is available free online at natureindex.com.

rows.title: Century-old genetics mystery of Mendel’s peas finally solved
rows.summary: Researchers pinpoint the genes responsible for the final three pea traits studied by the famed citizen scientist.

rows.title: Wild strawberries on Mars
rows.summary: Seeing red.

rows.title: mRNA technology helps reinvigorate the hunt for cancer vaccines
rows.summary: Fresh optimism surrounds initiatives to treat existing disease.

rows.title: Blood cancer driven by ‘one hit’ mutation event undergoes rapid growth
rows.summary: Reconstructions of the ‘evolutionary’ relationships among blood-cell clones from individuals with the blood cancer chronic myeloid leukaemia reveal that the cancer clone grows exceptionally quickly, reaching rates of between 10,000% and 1,000,000% per year. This variability in growth rate could explain differences in responses to cancer treatments.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Oncolytic virus VG161 in refractory hepatocellular carcinoma
Quantum communication across a 250-kilometre optical-fibre network
rows.summary: Quantum communication over long distances can be achieved by exploiting a property of light called coherence. The coherence-based exchange of a ‘quantum encryption key’ over an optical telecommunications network demonstrates the feasibility of implementing a large-scale quantum network in existing telecommunications infrastructure.

rows.title: Psychedelic control of neuroimmune interactions governing fear
rows.summary: Inflammatory monocytes in the brain meninges promote stress-induced fear behaviour, and the pathways involved can be modulated using psychedelic compounds.

rows.title: Superconducting gap of H 3 S measured by tunnelling spectroscopy
rows.summary: Characterizing the superconducting gap structure in the high-temperature superconductor H 3 S by means of tunnelling spectroscopy reveals that it, as well as D 3 S, has a fully gapped structure, confirming the phonon-mediated mechanism of superconducting pairing.

rows.title: Carbon majors and the scientific case for climate liability
rows.summary: A transparent and reproducible scientific framework is introduced to formalize how trillions in economic losses are attributable to the extreme heat caused by emissions from fossil fuel companies, which could inform climate liability claims.

rows.title: Geographic and age variations in mutational processes in colorectal cancer
rows.summary: Analysis of genomic data from 981 colorectal cancers from participants in 11 countries reveals variations in mutational signatures of microsatellite-stable cancers that are dependent on geographical origin and age at which the cancer was diagnosed.

rows.title: Deciphering disordered regions controlling mRNA decay in high-throughput
rows.summary: Using high-throughput functional profiling, how disordered regions control mRNA stability and translation is explored.

rows.title: Cold memories control whole-body thermoregulatory responses
rows.summary: Cold-sensitive engrams contribute to learned thermoregulation in mice that are returned to an environment in which they previously experienced a cold challenge, through a network formed between the hippocampus and hypothalamus that enables the recall of cold-related memories.

rows.title: Atomic lift-off of epitaxial membranes for cooling-free infrared detection
rows.summary: Atomic precision lift-off of ultrathin membranes without artificial release layers can be achieved to facilitate the high-throughput production of scalable, ultrathin, single-crystalline, freestanding perovskite systems.

rows.title: Effects of glacial forcing on lithospheric motion and ridge spreading
rows.summary: Realistic-lithosphere numerical models suggest glacial forcing in the last glacial cycle notably affected plate motions and mid-ocean-ridge spreading rates near major ice sheets, with implications for modern polar deglaciation enhancing magmatism and markedly impacting climate.

rows.title: Long-distance coherent quantum communications in deployed telecom networks
rows.summary: A twin-field quantum key distribution protocol based on optical coherence is deployed over a 254-kilometre commercial telecom network, demonstrating that coherence-based quantum communication can be aligned with existing telecommunication infrastructure.

rows.title: BMAL1–HIF2A heterodimer modulates circadian variations of myocardial injury
rows.summary: The core circadian transcription factor BMAL1 regulates circadian-dependent myocardial injury.

rows.title: Quantum twisting microscopy of phonons in twisted bilayer graphene
rows.summary: Generalization of a quantum twisting microscope to cryogenic temperatures in twisted bilayer graphene shows the ability to map phononic dispersions through inelastic momentum-conserving tunnelling and reveals an angle-dependent coupling between electrons and phonons.

rows.title: Microbial metabolite drives ageing-related clonal haematopoiesis via ALPK1
rows.summary: ADP-heptose binds to ALPK1, triggering transcriptional reprogramming and NF-κB activation, endowing pre-leukaemic cells with a competitive advantage due to excessive clonal proliferation.

rows.title: Modular chiral origami metamaterials
rows.summary: A versatile origami-inspired modular chiral mechanical metamaterial structure facilitates dual-mode actuation, converting compression into rotational motion and torsion into extension or compression.

rows.title: Melt focusing along lithosphere–asthenosphere boundary below Axial volcano
rows.summary: 3D seismic reflection images of the lithosphere–asthenosphere boundary beneath Axial volcano show a magma assimilation front that focuses magmatism towards the centre of the volcano, controlling both eruption and hydrothermal processes.

rows.title: Targeting PIKfyve-driven lipid metabolism in pancreatic cancer
rows.summary: A study of human and mouse models of pancreatic cancer finds that inhibiting the lipid kinase PIKfyve interferes with the cancer’s lipid homeostasis, making it a potential target for drug development.

rows.title: Genomic and genetic insights into Mendel’s pea genes
rows.summary: Characterization of the genetic architecture underlying the 7 pairs of contrasting traits studied by Mendel and the over 70 additional agronomic traits in pea ( Pisum sativum ) reveals their molecular details and provides tools for further studies in pea genetics, functional genomics and crop improvement.

rows.title: Human de novo mutation rates from a four-generation pedigree reference
rows.summary: Analysis of more than 95% of each diploid human genome of a four-generation, twenty-eight-member family using five complementary short-read and long-read sequencing technologies provides a truth set to understand the most fundamental processes underlying human genetic variation.

rows.title: Whole-body physics simulation of fruit fly locomotion
rows.summary: A detailed whole-body model of the fruit fly, developed using a physics-based simulation and deep reinforcement learning, accurately replicates real fly behaviour.

rows.title: A distributed coding logic for thermosensation and inflammatory pain
rows.summary: Functional imaging and multiplexed in situ hybridization were combined to investigate how trigeminal neurons encode heat and mechanical stimuli, revealing distinct cellular mechanisms for continuing pain, heat hypersensitivity and tactile allodynia during inflammation.

rows.title: Spatial mapping of transcriptomic plasticity in metastatic pancreatic cancer
rows.summary: Spatially resolved transcriptomic profiling of primary tumours and metastases from patients with pancreatic cancer provides insight into the evolutionary progression to metastasis, and the variation in clonal architecture within and between individuals.

rows.title: Punic people were genetically diverse with almost no Levantine ancestors
rows.summary: Levantine Phoenicians made little genetic contribution to Punic settlements in the central and western Mediterranean between the sixth and second centuries bce ; instead, the Punic people derived most of their ancestry from a genetic profile similar to that of Sicily and the Aegean, with notable contributions from North Africa as well.

rows.title: Brief antibiotic use drives human gut bacteria towards low-cost resistance
rows.summary: Brief ciprofloxacin exposure in humans drives antibiotic resistance evolution in gut bacteria through selective sweeps, particularly involving DNA gyrase mutations, which persist long after exposure and demonstrate the human gutʼs capacity to promote resistance evolution.

rows.title: Structural basis of lipid transfer by a bridge-like lipid-transfer protein
rows.summary: The LPD-3 complex structure reveals protein–lipid interactions that suggest a model for how the native LPD-3 complex mediates bulk lipid transport and provides a foundation for mechanistic studies of bridge-like lipid-transport proteins.

rows.title: ‘Dark matter’, 'Big Bang' and ‘spin’: how physics terms can confuse researchers
rows.summary: In episode three of What's in a name we look at how ideas can be lost in translation when physicists try to name the unknown.

rows.title: Europe must become a research epicentre as US system gets undermined
Author Correction: Structure of the human dopamine transporter in complex with cocaine
Top of the crops: rice scientists seek to meet global food demands
rows.summary: Work from the International Rice Research Institute to develop high-yield rice that survives deep waters, and a holistic view of physiology, in this week’s dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Defend scientific integrity and academic freedom
Trade tariffs could worsen deforestation in South America
The global assault on universities is an attack on democracy
Kidney disease is a worldwide killer. Treat it that way
rows.summary: The international community has a golden opportunity to start reining in the escalating, mostly ignored global burden of chronic kidney disease.

rows.title: Exclusive: a Nature analysis signals the beginnings of a US science brain drain
rows.summary: A trawl of job views and application data suggests jobseekers are looking abroad as the Trump administration’s cuts to science take hold.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Potato pangenome reveals the complex genetics of the humble spud
rows.summary: Trove of potato genomes reveals genetic bottlenecks and past flirtations with wild varieties. Plus, scientists have used lasers to create the perception of a brand-new colour and physicists express doubt over a ‘biosignature’ from a distant planet.

rows.title: Sexual harassment thrives in silence, even in gender-equality hotspots
rows.summary: ‘There are no model countries’ when it comes to creating environments that encourage victims of sexual harassment to come forward, shows a study of one Swedish university.

rows.title: Arctic researchers need to find ways to keep working together
rows.summary: Geopolitical events must not stall crucial research in the fastest-warming place on Earth.

rows.title: Which programming language should I use? A guide for early-career researchers
rows.summary: Computer scientists and bioinformaticians address four key questions to help rookie coders to make the right choice.

rows.title: Stereoretentive radical cross-coupling
rows.summary: Readily accessible enantioenriched sulfonylhydrazides and low loadings of an inexpensive achiral Ni catalyst can be used to control the stereochemical outcome of radical cross-coupling.

rows.title: Substrate recognition and cleavage mechanism of the monkeypox virus core protease
rows.summary: Structural and biochemical studies of the monkeypox virus core protease show that it exists as an active homodimer and indicate that the substrate-binding sites of core proteases are a promising target for antiviral drugs.

rows.title: Custom CRISPR–Cas9 PAM variants via scalable engineering and machine learning
rows.summary: Combined high-throughput protein engineering with machine learning to curate libraries of CRISPR genome-editing enzymes with distinct genome targeting properties is described.

rows.title: How India rewrote the rules of space travel when it launched its first satellite
rows.summary: Fifty years ago, a spacecraft designed and built by young Indian scientists redefined what a low-income country could achieve.

rows.title: Brand-new colour created by tricking human eyes with laser
rows.summary: The ‘off-the-charts saturated’ greenish hue — called olo — has been seen by only five study participants.

rows.title: Microplastic pollution found in insect casing from 1971
rows.summary: Freshwater insects used ‘microplastic’ as a building material long before scientists coined the term.

rows.title: The lunatic is on the grass: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: Sowing solutions: my quest to save Kenya’s maize from a devastating invader
rows.summary: Henry Sila Nzioki has developed a weed-killing fungus to improve food security.

rows.title: Martian rock hints at ancient dense atmosphere
rows.summary: Carbonate mineral is long-sought evidence of conditions that supported liquid water.

rows.title: Author Correction: Continued Atlantic overturning circulation even under climate extremes
Exclusive: Trump team freezes new NSF awards — and could soon axe hundreds of grants
rows.summary: The National Science Foundation is the latest US agency to be disrupted by Elon Musk’s DOGE.

rows.title: Whole-genome sequencing susses out rare diseases
rows.summary: Conventional tests that look only at a small subset of genetic code often miss variations hiding outside the protein-coding genome.

rows.title: ‘Totally broken’: how Trump 2.0 has paralysed work at US science agencies
rows.summary: Researchers who spoke to Nature say they don’t have the money or staff to do fieldwork or process samples.

rows.title: Invasion of the ‘journal snatchers’: the firms that buy science publications and turn them rogue
rows.summary: Study finds dozens of journals that have hiked their fees and started churning out papers after being acquired by small, recently formed companies.

rows.title: Signs of life on a distant planet? Not so fast, say these astronomers
rows.summary: Bold claims of ‘biosignature’ molecules trigger an outpouring of scepticism.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The biggest single piece of meat ever grown in the lab
rows.summary: A nugget-sized chunk of chicken is the biggest single piece of lab-grown meat to date. Plus, the up-and-coming world of stem-cell therapies and how cuts to US foreign aid could cause millions of deaths by 2040.

rows.title: 25 million deaths: what could happen if the US ends global health funding
rows.summary: Models estimate the ginormous potential impact of foreign-aid cuts.

rows.title: Why politicians manipulate statistics — and what to do about it
rows.summary: Understanding the playbook that those in power use to twist numbers, and how they make others complicit, is only becoming more important in the post-truth world.

rows.title: Reframe perspectives on Alzheimer’s disease
rows.summary: Advances in diagnosis and treatment mean that rapid cognitive decline won’t necessarily follow hot on the heels of a diagnosis.

rows.title: What a trove of potato genomes reveals about the humble spud
rows.summary: Potato ‘pangenome’ could allow easier sequencing of new varieties — plus, a Nature analysis reveals the most cited paper written in the twenty-first century.

rows.title: Print, melt, repeat: 3D-printing formula yields sturdy objects time after time
rows.summary: Complex shapes made of a specially formulated resin are easily recycled into other, equally durable objects.

rows.title: Roses are red — but their ancestors were yellow
rows.summary: A genomic analysis of 84 species in the genus Rosa traces the evolutionary history of the beloved flower.

rows.title: The first observation of ‘plastic ice’ reveals unusual behaviour of water molecules
rows.summary: Neutron-scattering experiments have revealed a predicted high-pressure phase of ice called ‘plastic ice VII’, in which molecules form crystals, as they do in normal ice, but rotate as in liquid water. These data highlight the role of hydrogen dynamics in defining exotic ice phases and could have implications for the geodynamics of icy planets.

rows.title: Faster, cheaper, better: the rise of blood tests for Alzheimer’s
rows.summary: Circulating biomarkers are quickly becoming a crucial part of diagnosis and disease monitoring for physicians, researchers — and even some consumers.

rows.title: How a hydrogen lab is helping to power Spain’s green-energy shift
rows.summary: Cost is key in the drive to ‘defossilize’ Spain’s energy needs as the country faces the devastating impacts of climate change.

rows.title: Age-related blood condition counteracted with a common diabetes drug
rows.summary: Metformin could reduce people’s risk of certain age-associated blood cancers, but more work is needed to identify who is likely to benefit.

rows.title: Don’t rush promising stem-cell therapies
rows.summary: Potential treatments need to be subject to the highest standards of safety and efficacy.

rows.title: The unusual genetic inheritance that could change Alzheimer’s treatment
rows.summary: The genes of a Colombian woman who beat the odds might lead to a new way to tackle the disease.

rows.title: First global pandemic treaty agreed — without the US
rows.summary: The World Health Organization accord promotes sharing scientific data in exchange for more-equitable distribution of drugs and vaccines.

rows.title: Receptor-binding specificity of a bovine influenza A virus
Clinical trials test the safety of stem-cell therapy for Parkinson’s disease
rows.summary: Transplanting dopamine-releasing neurons into the brain is a promising regenerative therapy for Parkinson’s disease. Two clinical trials show that it is safe, but more evidence is needed to prove its effectiveness.

rows.title: Japan’s big bet on stem-cell therapies might soon pay off with medical breakthroughs
rows.summary: Induced pluripotent stem cells are being tested to treat blindness, paralysis, Parkinson’s disease and more. Approvals might be around the corner.

rows.title: Reply to: Natively expressed AcrIII-1 does not function as an anti-CRISPR protein
Unlocking the diversity of wild and domesticated rice
rows.summary: The construction of a ‘pangenome’ sequence collection that incorporates the genomes of nearly 150 wild and cultivated rice varieties captures all the genetic diversity found in this plant. It reveals genes associated with disease resistance that are unique to wild rice, and provides insights into the origins of domesticated rice.

rows.title: Highly sensitive method captures rare RNAs in blood to search for disease
rows.summary: A method for examining RNAs in blood samples offers a clinical tool to detect and monitor cancer and to assess immune responses to vaccination.

rows.title: Alzheimer’s disease: highlights from research
rows.summary: The ‘dark’ cells behind disease, how diabetes drugs might protect cognitive function, and other studies and trials.

rows.title: Natively expressed AcrIII-1 does not function as an anti-CRISPR protein
Why women experience Alzheimer’s disease differently from men
rows.summary: Sex and gender research could lead to better, more equitable treatments — if it is allowed to continue without political interference.

rows.title: SWOT satellite provides a finer view of climate-driving ocean dynamics
rows.summary: High-resolution observations of ocean topography from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission reveal that small surface structures have a larger-than-expected impact on the ocean’s total energy budget.

rows.title: Science on our sleeves: the research that inspires our tattoos
rows.summary: Inked scientists choose scientific images to mark career accomplishments and illustrate their research passion.

rows.title: Healthy soil is the hidden ingredient — here’s how I’m fighting to save it
rows.summary: Around 60% of the European Union’s soils are considered unhealthy, but geographer Jesús Rodrigo Comino is determined to help change that in his native Spain.

rows.title: Meet the researchers pioneering Spanish climate solutions
rows.summary: Spain is feeling the heat. Four researchers share how climate change shapes their work and their fight for a sustainable future.

rows.title: Do infections have a role in Alzheimer’s disease?
rows.summary: The suggestion that pathogens play a part in driving dementia is not as niche as it once was, but the evidence remains inconclusive.

rows.title: A. J. Eisfeld et al. reply
You’re only human: a six-step strategy to surviving your PhD
rows.summary: Graduate students are not machines. Behaving like one during your programme will leave you frustrated and unfulfilled, says Gauthier Weissbart.

rows.title: ‘Big leap’ for Parkinson’s treatment: symptoms improve in stem-cell trials
rows.summary: Studies show the therapy is safe, but bigger trials are needed to prove its efficacy.

rows.title: Winner, winner, lab-made dinner! Team grows nugget-sized chicken chunk
rows.summary: Artificial circulatory system enables feat by delivering nutrients to growing tissue.

rows.title: The future of Alzheimer’s treatment
rows.summary: Drugs that clear away brain plaques are a welcome arrival, but targeting amyloid alone might not be enough to halt the disease.

rows.title: Spain adapts to new reality as climate crisis hits home
rows.summary: Country doubles down on climate pledges in the wake of devastating floods.

rows.title: Bovine H5N1 binds poorly to human-type sialic acid receptors
Daily briefing: The first colossal squid caught on camera in its natural habitat
rows.summary: Scientists have captured a colossal squid in the deep sea for the first time. Plus, crows have surprising geometry skills and the world now has a plan in place for pandemics.

rows.title: Don’t believe the hype — quantum tech can’t yet solve real-world problems
rows.summary: Investors and the public should know what quantum devices can and, more importantly, can’t do.

rows.title: Within dead branches
rows.summary: Treading familiar ground.

rows.title: The phased pan-genome of tetraploid European potato
rows.summary: A haplotype-resolved pan-genome of autotetraploid European potato founder lines shows high nucleotide diversity at remarkably low haplotype diversity, which is probably the result of hybridization events with wild potato species, followed by population bottlenecks during domestication and transition to Europe.

rows.title: Metformin reduces the competitive advantage of Dnmt3a R878H HSPCs
rows.summary: Dnmt3a mutations in mouse haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells equivalent to R882 mutations in human cause increased mitochondrial respiration, suggesting that this is a mechanism of clonal haematopoiesis and a potential therapeutic target.

rows.title: Electric-field-induced domain walls in wurtzite ferroelectrics
rows.summary: Experimental and theoretical exploration of domain walls forming in wurtzite ferroelectrics following the application of electric fields demonstrates their reconfigurable conductivity as well as tunability, showing potential for use in ultrascaled devices.

rows.title: Multi-zonal liver organoids from human pluripotent stem cells
rows.summary: Liver organoids derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells populations grown with ascorbate and bilirubin can be used to recapitulate differential zonal functions of human hepatocytes and for transplantation in animal models of liver dysfunction.

rows.title: A pangenome reference of wild and cultivated rice
rows.summary: A pangenome of wild and cultivated rice accessions captures the entire set of non-redundant genes and diversity in rice, and provides insights into the pathways involved in the evolution of rice.

rows.title: Structure of the ATP-driven methyl-coenzyme M reductase activation complex
rows.summary: The structure and function of the MCR activation complex from Methanococcus maripaludis were revealed, demonstrating its ATP-dependent ability to activate MCR and form methane while uncovering a unique electron transfer pathway involving iron–sulfur clusters similar to the nitrogenase cofactor intermediates.

rows.title: An ultrasensitive method for detection of cell-free RNA
rows.summary: A method, RARE-seq, for sensitive detection of cell-free RNAs in blood is demonstrated to have diverse clinical applications including diagnosing and characterizing human cancers, and tracking response to RNA therapeutics.

rows.title: Observation of the axion quasiparticle in 2D MnBi 2 Te 4
rows.summary: The dynamical axion quasiparticle, which is directly analogous to the hypothetical fundamental axion particle, is observed in two-dimensional MnBi 2 Te 4 , and has implications for quantum chromodynamics, cosmology and string theory.

rows.title: Subnanosecond flash memory enabled by 2D-enhanced hot-carrier injection
rows.summary: A two-dimensional Dirac graphene-channel flash memory based on a two-dimensional-enhanced hot-carrier-injection mechanism that supports both electron and hole injection is used to make devices with a subnanosecond program speed.

rows.title: A sharp volatile-rich cap to the Yellowstone magmatic system
rows.summary: Seismic reflection imaging beneath the northeastern Yellowstone caldera reveals a sharp boundary at about 3.8 km depth, which is inferred to result from a mixture of supercritical fluid and magma filling the pore space.

rows.title: Mitochondrial metabolism sustains DNMT3A -R882-mutant clonal haematopoiesis
rows.summary: Metformin may serve as a non-toxic intervention to inhibit mitochondrial metabolism and slow DNMT3A -R882 clonal haematopoiesis expansion, thus delaying or averting progression to acute myeloid leukaemia.

rows.title: Driven bright solitons on a mid-infrared laser chip
rows.summary: New fully integrated semiconductor laser architectures are shown to be able to generate bright and background-free picosecond solitons at GHz repetition rates in the mid-infrared range.

rows.title: Phase I/II trial of iPS-cell-derived dopaminergic cells for Parkinson’s disease
rows.summary: After transplantation into the brain of patients with Parkinson’s disease, allogeneic dopaminergic progenitors derived from induced pluripotent stem cells survived, produced dopamine and did not form tumours, therefore suggesting safety and potential clinical benefits for Parkinson’s disease.

rows.title: Chromosome end protection by RAP1-mediated inhibition of DNA-PK
rows.summary: Biochemical, structural and genetic analysis of the shelterin complex reveal that by recruiting RAP1 to DNA, TRF2 directly inhibits DNA-dependent protein kinase to regulate classical non-homologous end joining at telomeres.

rows.title: The growing memristor industry
rows.summary: The status and prospects of the memristor industry are analysed and the obstacles and pathways to their implementation are discussed.

rows.title: Antiferromagnetic quantum anomalous Hall effect under spin flips and flops
rows.summary: A new device based on 7-septuple-layer MnBi 2 Te 4 covered with an AlO x capping layer enables the investigation of antiferromagnetic quantum anomalous Hall effect over wide parameter spaces.

rows.title: Perturbing LSD1 and WNT rewires transcription to synergistically induce AML differentiation
rows.summary: Simultaneous inhibition of LSD1 and GSK3 kinase promotes cell differentiation, providing a therapeutic strategy for treating acute myeloid leukaemia.

rows.title: Histone H1 deamidation facilitates chromatin relaxation for DNA repair
rows.summary: Insights into how the linker histone H1 promotes chromatin alterations and allows repair of DNA damage are described.

rows.title: Re-adenylation by TENT5A enhances efficacy of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines
rows.summary: Upon intramuscular administration, COVID-19 mRNA vaccines are primarily taken up by macrophages, in which the cellular machinery extends their poly(A) tails, thereby increasing mRNA stability and translation, providing an explanation for the efficacy of these vaccines.

rows.title: Towards multimodal foundation models in molecular cell biology
rows.summary: The development of multimodal foundation models, pretrained on diverse omics datasets, to unravel the intricate complexities of molecular cell biology is envisioned.

rows.title: Generation of human adult hepatocyte organoids with metabolic functions
rows.summary: The combined activation of Wnt and STAT3 signalling enables long-term self-renewal of human hepatocyte organoids, maintaining hepatic identity, supporting gene editing and offering therapeutic potential for liver disease through enhanced functionality, structure and metabolic competency.

rows.title: Deep Visual Proteomics maps proteotoxicity in a genetic liver disease
rows.summary: High-resolution spatial proteomics were used to map molecular events during hepatocyte stress in pseudotime across all fibrosis stages, recapitulating known disease progression markers and revealing early peroxisomal activation and late-stage proteotoxic phenotypes.

rows.title: Wide-swath satellite altimetry unveils global submesoscale ocean dynamics
rows.summary: Data from the recently launched Surface Water and Ocean Topography satellite reveal the characteristics of submesoscale eddies and waves and suggest that their potential impacts on overall ocean circulation is much larger than previously thought.

rows.title: Low overlap of transcription factor DNA binding and regulatory targets
rows.summary: A near-complete survey of transcription factor activities in Saccharomyces cerevisiae reveals that most transcription factors have both activator and repressor activities and limited overlap between their binding sites on DNA and regulation of nearby genes.

rows.title: Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease
rows.summary: Bilateral grafts of cryopreserved human embryonic stem cell-derived dopaminergic neuron progenitor cells into the putamen of patients with Parkinson’s disease in a phase I clinical trial showed safety, improvements in off-drug motor function and graft survival at 18 months after transplant.

rows.title: Negative thermal expansion and oxygen-redox electrochemistry
rows.summary: Using operando electrochemical processes, we found a way to restore oxygen-redox active materials exhibiting structural and voltage decay to their pristine state, providing a framework for the design of functional materials with zero thermal expansion.

rows.title: Ensuring that conferences are inclusive requires diverse organizers
Pig livers for people: US regulator greenlights first safety trial
rows.summary: Four people with liver failure will be connected to an external organ from genetically modified pigs.

rows.title: Scientists must regain trust
Discussions of technologies’ societal impacts are still too limited
Africa CDC must become financially independent
Early air-pollution activists fight against city smoke
rows.summary: A 250,000-year-old footprint preserved in ash, and the effect of a polluted atmosphere on health and the economy, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Science’s golden oldies: the decades-old research papers still heavily cited today
rows.summary: An analysis for Nature reveals the studies that appear most in the reference lists of current publications.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Leaked documents reveal the next science funding on Trump’s chopping block
rows.summary: Documents obtained by Nature reveal that the Trump administration intends to propose cuts to the 2026 budgets of NASA and NOAA. Plus, AI-enhanced glasses could help visually impaired people navigate their surroundings and the most-cited research papers of the twenty-first century.

rows.title: These are the most-cited research papers of all time
rows.summary: Some studies have received hundreds of thousands of citations, Nature ’s updated analysis shows.

rows.title: The fight to keep big tech in check: digital researchers are in ‘David and Goliath’ battle
rows.summary: Resource constraints hobble analyses of how digital technologies affect mental health, and take a huge toll on the scientists working to make the online world safer.

rows.title: High time to tackle drug-resistant fungal infections
rows.summary: To combat long-overlooked fungal pathogens, researchers and regulators must embrace innovative science and policy.

rows.title: Exclusive: the most-cited papers of the twenty-first century
rows.summary: A Nature analysis reveals the 25 highest-cited papers published this century and explores why they are breaking records.

rows.title: Richard Fortey obituary: palaeontologist, author and TV presenter who traced continents through fossils
rows.summary: The fossil expert found love at first sight with trilobites.

rows.title: Twenty years of genome-wide association studies
rows.summary: A powerful and unbiased way to identify links between genetic variants and biological traits has changed scientists’ understanding of complex diseases and how to treat them.

rows.title: Should I return to my home country after my PhD abroad?
rows.summary: A graduate student from southeast Asia, now based in a European country and missing her homeland, agonizes over her next career move.

rows.title: Lung signals drive cancer-associated blood clots
rows.summary: Fatal blood clots can arise in people who have cancer. The discovery of a cue that underlies these clots offers a therapeutic target and a way to assess clot risk.

rows.title: Understanding bones from the remote wilderness of Wyoming
rows.summary: Digging in overlooked regions has opened up a world of discovery for palaeontologist David Lovelace.

rows.title: The dangerous fantasies driving the quest for super-intelligent AI
rows.summary: More Everything Forever dissects the techno-utopian vision gripping Silicon Valley and Washington DC.

rows.title: Radical approach to shrink particle colliders gains momentum
rows.summary: Plans are taking off to use an unconventional technique to accelerate particles in a future collider.

rows.title: Five years on: how Brexit changed three scientists’ careers
rows.summary: How did the United Kingdom’s formal departure from the European Union in January 2020 affect scientists who had moved there from mainland Europe?

rows.title: How the United States became a science superpower — and how quickly it could crumble
rows.summary: US global dominance in science was no accident, but a product of a far-seeing partnership between public and private sectors to boost innovation and economic growth.

rows.title: AI-boosted cameras help blind people to navigate
rows.summary: A prototype wearable system uses machine-learning to guide users around obstacles.

rows.title: Dear US researchers: break the outrage addiction. I survived the besieging of science. So can you
rows.summary: As I watch US researchers respond to threats against science, I’m reminded of when scientists in Brazil navigated a similar storm.

rows.title: Five key climate and space projects on Trump’s chopping block
rows.summary: Leaked budget documents indicate which research programmes are at risk of losing their funding in 2026.

rows.title: ‘I’m touching space’: the fascinating insights meteorites can bring us
rows.summary: Two books discuss how these space rocks are entwined with science, commerce, policy and life.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Five lawsuits have been filed in response to NIH cuts — what now?
rows.summary: Scientific bodies, academics and state attorneys have filed five lawsuits against the US National Institutes of Health, with more likely to follow. Plus, physicists have a new estimate for the maximum mass of a neutrino and a planet was spotted falling into its host star.

rows.title: How a ‘boring administrative task’ transformed my PhD career
rows.summary: Good ideas — and impactful tools — don’t just come from rich, Western nations, says Aleksandra Lazić, a social scientist in Serbia.

rows.title: PRDM16-dependent antigen-presenting cells induce tolerance to gut antigens
rows.summary: A subset of antigen-presenting cells of myeloid origin that require PRDM16 and RORγt regulates T cell function to enable immune tolerance of food and commensal gut microorganisms.

rows.title: Author Correction: Sulfide-rich continental roots at cratonic margins formed by carbonated melts
Mystery of medieval manuscripts revealed by ancient DNA
rows.summary: Biomolecular analysis shows that unusual book coverings are made of sealskin, hinting at far-flung trade networks.

rows.title: Liquids in a glass recover a graceful shape even after being shaken
rows.summary: Oil and water contained in a cylinder with magnetic nickel particles form the shape of a Grecian urn.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Mysterious Taiwan fossil is Denisovan
rows.summary: A fossilized jawbone discovered more than 20 years ago belonged to a Denisovan. Plus, the states hit hardest by NIH cuts in charts and an acoustics lab inside an abandoned nuclear plant.

rows.title: NIH cuts triggered a host of lawsuits: Nature ’s guide to what’s next
rows.summary: A host of legal claims aim to roll back the Trump administration’s grant terminations, indirect-cost cap and more.

rows.title: Physicists narrow down neutrino’s mysterious mass
rows.summary: Blimp-shaped experiment shows the particle is at least one million times lighter than an electron.

rows.title: Allergic reactions flare in the gut after cuts to the skin, mouse research shows
rows.summary: Damage done to the skin can increase the risk of an allergic reaction in other organs.

rows.title: Top quarks spotted at mega-detector could reveal clues to early Universe
rows.summary: Heaviest known elementary particles and their antimatter counterparts are detected after nuclear smash-ups at the Large Hadron Collider.

rows.title: Data centres will use twice as much energy by 2030 — driven by AI
rows.summary: These facilities accounted for roughly 1.5% of global electricity consumption in 2024.

rows.title: ‘Mind blowing’: quantum computer untangles the mathematics of knots
rows.summary: Algorithms for studying knots and other topological objects could have a quantum advantage.

rows.title: How Trump 2.0 is slashing NIH-backed research — in charts
rows.summary: Nature analyses which fields of science and US states are being hit hardest by grant terminations.

rows.title: Brain cells given an ‘invisibility cloak’ fix Parkinson’s symptoms in rats
rows.summary: Neurons engineered to evade the immune system could work as cell-replacement therapy.

rows.title: Can peer-reviewed podcasts fast-track science?
rows.summary: Researchers are experimenting with audio formats, and debating how to handle reviewer feedback.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Dogs have a serious environmental impact — but owners can mitigate it
rows.summary: How we can reduce our dogs’ surprisingly large environmental footprint. Plus, the most detailed wiring diagram of a mammalian brain to date and the complete sequenced genomes of not one, but six ape species.

rows.title: Mysterious human fossil found in Taiwan was a Denisovan
rows.summary: Analysis of ancient proteins identifies jawbone as belonging to archaic human group.

rows.title: Long-awaited ape genomes give new insights into their evolution — and ours
rows.summary: New sequencing analyses fill in long-awaited gaps in the genomes of six ape species — plus, evidence that laser-plasma particle accelerators could work as well as conventional kinds.

rows.title: These 4,200-year-old cymbals show music’s far-reaching power
rows.summary: People from modern Pakistan imported their musical technology all the way to what is now Oman.

rows.title: Hunter-gatherers journeyed by sea to Malta
rows.summary: Evidence reveals that people reached Malta 8,500 years ago. Hunter-gatherers made the long trip there 1,000 years before agricultural societies arrived.

rows.title: The infuriating, expensive road to a good night’s sleep
rows.summary: Finding an effective treatment for insomnia is one thing — getting an insurance company to pay for it is another, says Rachel Nuwer.

rows.title: Airborne microplastics enter plant leaves and end up in our food
rows.summary: Evidence for a previously overlooked route for microplastics to enter crops and reach plant tissues has implications for ecology and human health.

rows.title: The hunt for the next CRISPR: how warring microbes are inspiring new technology
rows.summary: Gene editing and many other useful biotechnology tools came from studies of bacteria fighting off viral invaders. But scientists have only begun to unlock the secrets of this ancient arms race.

rows.title: New treatments to put insomnia to bed
rows.summary: Drugs that eliminate wakefulness, molecules in cannabis and wearable devices that modulate brain activity could help those with the condition.

rows.title: Cancer vulnerabilities exposed by finding interactions among DNA repair factors
rows.summary: A screen of interactions between genes involved in the cell’s response to DNA damage has revealed several previously unreported ‘synthetic lethalities’, in which disrupting a pair of genes, but not either gene alone, causes cell death. The resulting map of genetic interactions could help to identify therapeutic targets for cancer.

rows.title: Docking stations in porous crystals unlock elusive molecular structures
rows.summary: Porous crystals have been engineered to trap ‘oily’ molecules — enabling X-ray structures to be determined for these compounds that defy standard crystallographic analysis.

rows.title: How do I explain the publication gap I ended up with after a hostile manager?
rows.summary: A poor working relationship with a supervisor or manager can result in lost opportunities, creating an unexplained gap in an early-career researcher’s publication record.

rows.title: Photonic chips provide a processing boost for AI
rows.summary: Computer processors that exploit both electricity and light could improve the performance of artificial-intelligence systems while consuming less energy.

rows.title: Unlocking the secrets of sleep
rows.summary: The activity that consumes roughly one-third of our lives affects health in ways scientists are only beginning to fully understand.

rows.title: Research round-up: sleep
rows.summary: The academic impact of early morning lectures, alcohol’s effects on sleep and other highlights from sleep studies.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Tonka bean trees survive lightning strikes that kill their competitors
rows.summary: Tonka bean trees might make themselves into lightning rods to edge out the competition. Plus, Trump cuts threaten US scientific leadership in Antarctica and how to build a broader, more inclusive defence of science.

rows.title: The life aquatic: this board game lets you dip into marine ecology
rows.summary: Finspan is visually stunning and brilliantly captures the intricacies of the ocean’s ecosystems.

rows.title: Sleep is essential — researchers are trying to work out why
rows.summary: A typical person spends more than 20 years in a state of dreamy semi-consciousness. But surprisingly little is known about why we need this down time.

rows.title: A wetter ancient Arabia could have enabled easier intercontinental species dispersal
rows.summary: Recurrent humid phases in Arabia over the past seven million years could have influenced how species, including human ancestors, moved between continents.

rows.title: Complete ape genomes offer a close-up view of human evolution
rows.summary: Scientists have fully sequenced the genomes of six living ape species, enabling long-awaited comparisons of hard-to-assemble genomic regions.

rows.title: A map of neural signals and circuits traces the logic of brain computation
rows.summary: A large consortium of scientists adds functional data to neuronal wiring maps, seeking to crack the computational circuitry of the mouse brain.

rows.title: Chronic stress drives depression by disrupting cellular housekeeping
rows.summary: Boosting the recycling process known as autophagy — impaired in the brain during prolonged stress — has the potential to restore normal neuronal activity and treat depression.

rows.title: Losing weight through better sleep
rows.summary: Sleep-medicine specialist Esra Tasali explains the science behind maintaining a healthy weight without the need for expensive drugs.

rows.title: A mental-health crisis plagues PhDs — these evidence-led initiatives offer help
rows.summary: Communities of researchers worldwide are taking on the toxic research cultures that drive poor psychological health among academics.

rows.title: The great brain clearance and dementia debate
rows.summary: An established theory for how good sleep reduces a person’s risk of neurodegenerative disease has been called into question. The ensuing argument could have enormous consequences for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease.

rows.title: Jurassic fossil reveals the origin of parasitic thorny-headed worms
rows.summary: A body fossil of a thorny-headed worm (Acanthocephala) has been dated to the Jurassic period, about 165 million years ago. It has characteristics of both Acanthocephala and tiny animals called Rotifera, thus casting light on the origin of the acanthocephalans and bridging the evolutionary gap between jawed rotifers and parasitic, jawless acanthocephalans.

rows.title: Biggest brain map ever details huge number of neurons and their activity
rows.summary: 3D reconstruction is the first to overlay neuronal activity on a large-scale map of brain cells.

rows.title: Will AI improve your life? Here’s what 4,000 researchers think
rows.summary: Scientists working on artificial intelligence are more confident than the public that the technology will benefit people.

rows.title: Why it’s time the United Nations is led by a woman
rows.summary: With efforts towards gender equality stalling, voting in a first female head of the UN would provide powerful representation for half the world’s population — and be good for all of it.

rows.title: Skin wound healing measured remotely through molecular flux
rows.summary: A non-contact wearable device measures the skin’s ‘microclimate’ for continuous, real-time monitoring of wounds and wound healing.

rows.title: Relics
rows.summary: The rhythm of life.

rows.title: What makes us human? Milestone ape genomes promise clues
rows.summary: DNA sequences for chimpanzees, orangutan and more will help scientists to determine what sets humans apart from other apes.

rows.title: Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models
rows.summary: Diagnostic reasoning using an optimized large language model with a dataset comprising real-world medical cases exhibited improved differential diagnostic performance as an assistive tool for clinicians over search engines and standard medical resources.

rows.title: Connectomics of predicted Sst transcriptomic types in mouse visual cortex
rows.summary: The authors use Patch-seq and electron microscopy datasets to relate synaptic connectivity to the transcriptomic cell type of different types of inhibitory neuron.

rows.title: Ultra-broadband optical amplification using nonlinear integrated waveguides
rows.summary: An integrated optical parametric amplifier with an ultra-wide bandwidth was implemented using geometrically optimized low-loss nonlinear rib silicon nitride waveguides including the demonstration of broadband all-optical wavelength conversion.

rows.title: Immune checkpoint TIM-3 regulates microglia and Alzheimer’s disease
rows.summary: The immune-checkpoint molecule TIM-3 regulates microglial homeostasis, and its microglial-specific deletion reduced cognitive impairment in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease.
