rows.title: Author Correction: Endocytosis in the axon initial segment maintains neuronal polarity
Swarms of satellites are harming astronomy. Here’s how researchers are fighting back
rows.summary: SpaceX and other companies plan to launch tens of thousands of satellites, which could mar astronomical observations and pollute the atmosphere.

rows.title: Space debris is falling from the skies. We need to tackle this growing danger
rows.summary: Why failing to control defunct satellites leaves everyone at risk from their impacts.

rows.title: Catchy, clear, concise: three-part phrases boost research paper citations
rows.summary: Memorable ‘tripartite’ phrases in titles make studies more likely to be read and cited.

rows.title: Governments must stop hoarding climate data
rows.summary: National agencies too often use spurious reasons to deny researchers unfettered access to resources that are key to understanding past and future climate change.

rows.title: Cleaning up space: how satellites and telescopes can live together
rows.summary: Satellites connect people around the world but they also interfere with astronomers’ views of the cosmos. There are ways to reduce these tensions.

rows.title: Structures and mechanism of the human mitochondrial pyruvate carrier
rows.summary: Cryo-electron microscopy structures of the human mitochondrial pyruvate carrier provide insights into its architecture, substrate transport mechanism and inhibition by the drug UK5099, with implications for the development of treatments for various metabolic diseases.

rows.title: How I connect Colombia’s remote communities to safer water
rows.summary: Alba Graciela Ávila Bernal’s research focuses on power-storage technologies, but she also builds custom probes to test water quality.

rows.title: The untamed river and the Moog: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: How researchers can work fairly with Indigenous and local knowledge
rows.summary: Scientists around the world are recognizing that their research method isn’t the only way.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Mice give unconscious friends first aid
rows.summary: ‘Microlightning’ might have sparked life on Earth. Mice who find a friend unconscious will give them friends first aid.

rows.title: ‘Science is happening’: Israeli and Palestinian scientists continue collaborations amid conflict
rows.summary: From owl surveys to peer review, Israel’s researchers are maintaining regional and international ties despite boycotts and the risk of war resuming.

rows.title: I spent two years organizing an international conference. How do I get compensated for my work?
rows.summary: It can be hard to say no to service requests in academia. Nature ’s Careers team sought advice on how to ensure researchers don’t get stuck doing unpaid labour.

rows.title: Don’t wait out four hard years: speak truth to power
rows.summary: The importance of diversity in science is an unshakeable reality that the scientific community must stand by.

rows.title: What’s in store for US science as funding bill averts government shutdown
rows.summary: Spending on research, including at the NIH, will see modest cuts this year. But the threat of big reductions in future remain.

rows.title: A radical manifesto for truth
rows.summary: Is a revolution of standards in public life the key to tackling our intertwined environmental crises? A compelling book argues it is.

rows.title: How a PhD travel fellowship enriched an international cell-biology meeting
rows.summary: The recipients, all from African countries, were not the only beneficiaries, says Rafiou Agoro.

rows.title: Author Correction: B-cell-specific checkpoint molecules that regulate anti-tumour immunity
Fossilized dinosaur cells that defied the ravages of time — 20 years since a key discovery
rows.summary: The 2005 finding of cells and blood vessels in dinosaur bone launched a systematic search for fossil remnants of biomolecules, creating innovations in methods and applications.

rows.title: The early origins of bone-tool manufacturing traditions by hominins 1.5 million years ago
rows.summary: Excavations at Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, reveal evidence of the systematic use of animal bones as a raw material for prehistoric tools.

rows.title: Errors in the Huntington’s disease gene accumulate slowly and then all at once
rows.summary: Inherited repeat mutations in the HTT gene expand in neurons over decades before crossing a toxic threshold, revealing a long time window for therapy.

rows.title: Strong, flexible ‘nylon’ made by engineered bacteria for the first time
rows.summary: The bioplastic was malleable, but is more expensive to produce than are plastics made from fossil fuels.

rows.title: Drugs that target ‘zombie’ cells soothe an aching back
rows.summary: Research on mice show promise for agents that attack senescent cells, which contribute to the degradation of spinal discs.

rows.title: How extreme lethargy can promote healthy ageing
rows.summary: The drop in body temperature that occurs during a torpid state is linked to molecular markers of longer life in mice.

rows.title: ‘My career is over’: Columbia University scientists hit hard by Trump team’s cuts
rows.summary: The US government has begun slashing US$400 million in research grants at Columbia University over pro-Palestinian campus protests.

rows.title: Protect yourself — and your data — with these cybersecurity tips
rows.summary: In this era of anti-science activism, it‘s wise to take steps to stay safe from online hate.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Jurassic mammals had dark fur
rows.summary: First glimpse of the colour of mammals who lived alongside dinosaurs. Plus, what anti-vaccine rhetoric in the US government will mean for the country’s health and, in a world first, a man has survived with a titanium heart for 100 days.

rows.title: Your lab pollutes: here’s how to stop it
rows.summary: Single-use plastics are everywhere — but two researchers are redefining the norm and championing sustainability.

rows.title: A century of quantum physics
rows.summary: A Nature special.

rows.title: Mega-storm dumps 11 billion tonnes of snow ― and builds up a melting ice sheet
rows.summary: A well-timed atmospheric river dropped enough snow on Greenland for its ice sheet to lose 8% less mass than expected.

rows.title: Why coalitions of wealthy nations should fund others to decarbonize
rows.summary: Failure to agree on global grants to help low- and middle-income countries to achieve net-zero emissions cannot be the end of the story. An urgent solution is needed.

rows.title: Man survives with titanium heart for 100 days — a world first
rows.summary: The device, to be tested in more people, could be used as a temporary measure for those waiting for a donor organ.

rows.title: Will RFK Jr’s vaccine agenda make America contagious again?
rows.summary: Fears are rising that infectious diseases such as measles could make a comeback now that the anti-vaccine advocate is in charge of the US public-health system.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Should the Stanford Prison Experiment be retracted?
rows.summary: Leopard-spotted rocks are ‘an intriguing signal’ of microbial life on Mars. Plus, should the infamous Stanford Prison Experiment be retracted more than 50 years on?

rows.title: These frustrated scientists want to leave the United States — do you? Take Nature’s poll
rows.summary: In the wake of the Trump administration’s funding freezes and job cuts, some researchers are planning their next move.

rows.title: Saturn has a whopping 274 moons ― scientists want to know why
rows.summary: A huge haul of 128 newfound satellites might be a hint of past collisions in the planet’s orbit, or something else.

rows.title: Robotic fingers can tell objects apart by touch
rows.summary: Prosthetic appendage uses three layers of touch sensors to accurately differentiate between textures.

rows.title: Watch DeepMind’s AI robot slam-dunk a basketball
rows.summary: The firm has incorporated its Gemini artificial-intelligence model into robots to perform fiddly tasks.

rows.title: How fast your brain ages is affected by these 64 genes
rows.summary: Scientists also identified anti-ageing drugs and experimental compounds that could target the genes to reverse decline.

rows.title: Author Correction: Observation of Nagaoka polarons in a Fermi–Hubbard quantum simulator
Sapphire anvils squeeze metals atomically-thin
rows.summary: Technique could help researchers probe strange properties of 2D metals — plus, five years after the pandemic, how did COVID change virology?

rows.title: Liver cancer recurrence predicted by immune-cell location and gene expression
rows.summary: Immune cells called natural killer cells can target and eliminate tumours. The gene expression and spatial distribution of the immune cells in the tumour microenvironment indicates whether liver cancer will recur after surgery.

rows.title: Reply to: Weather anomalies cannot explain insect decline
Did Mars harbour life? One of the strongest signs yet is spotted in a peculiar rock
rows.summary: The intriguing chemistry of a rock collected by the Perseverance rover could trace to microbial activity — or not.

rows.title: Medical records from the Center for the Study of Temporal Disorders, Pediatric Department
rows.summary: The doctor will see you now (and then).

rows.title: An archaic European face more than one million years old
rows.summary: The partial midface of a hominin fossil has been found in the Sima del Elefante cave site near Burgos, northern Spain, and dates to between 1.4 million and 1.1 million years ago. Its discovery enables the exploration of the facial features of early Europeans and enhances our understanding of the evolutionary history of European ancestors.

rows.title: So you’ve made a lab website. What should go on it?
rows.summary: William Mills aims to make the website for his laboratory more than just a channel for promoting publications and research projects to the outside world.

rows.title: Move over graphene! Scientists forge bismuthene and host of atoms-thick metals
rows.summary: Tiny anvil squeezes metal atoms into super-thin sheets with strange properties.

rows.title: Four ways COVID changed virology: lessons from the most sequenced virus of all time
rows.summary: After 150,000 articles and 17 million genome sequences, what has science taught us about SARS-CoV-2?

rows.title: Immune molecule links COVID‑19 with severe inflammatory disorder in children
rows.summary: The immune molecule TGFβ has been found to weaken immune defences against latent viruses, triggering reactivation of the Epstein–Barr virus. This mechanism links TGFβ release in SARS-CoV-2 infection to multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, and could inform the development of therapies for managing this serious condition.

rows.title: Elisabeth Vrba obituary: palaeontologist who solved a problem that vexed Darwin
rows.summary: The biologist’s theories about how environments prompt rapid species evolution and extinction propelled her onto the world stage.

rows.title: Weather anomalies cannot explain insect decline
The brain’s building blocks for understanding social interactions
rows.summary: The human brain not only remembers who other people are, it also uses basic mathematical functions called basis functions to store information about how people interact — for example, how they work together or compete. Each basis function specifies part of an interaction pattern, and combinations of them specify complex interactions.

rows.title: An operating system for networked quantum computers is a huge practical step forward
rows.summary: Quantum computers have gained the powerful abstractions that allow programmers of classical computers to design and integrate new apps and hardware, and connect devices into networks with ease.

rows.title: Ancient DNA shows Stone Age Europeans voyaged by sea to Africa
rows.summary: Roughly 8,000-year-old remains unearthed from present-day Tunisia held a surprise: European hunter-gatherer ancestry.

rows.title: Biodiversity declines across fragmented forests
rows.summary: A global analysis of species in fragmented-forest landscapes reveals species losses in fragments, and that the changes in species composition across fragments is not enough to benefit biodiversity over entire landscapes.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Saturn has 128 new moons
rows.summary: Blue-lined octopuses immobilize their partners with venom to avoid being eaten after sex. Plus, astronomers have discovered 128 new moons orbiting Saturn.

rows.title: Why are proponents of ‘smart cities’ neglecting research?
rows.summary: Despite the buzz surrounding smart cities in urban-policy circles, studies are lacking on the evidence for what works, what doesn’t — and who benefits.

rows.title: Metals squeezed to thickness of just two atoms
rows.summary: Ultrathin metals have been prepared using a benchtop hydraulic press — allowing the fascinating properties of the resulting 2D materials to be observed.

rows.title: Fresh ‘quantum advantage’ claim made by computing firm D-Wave
rows.summary: The company says it has solved the first problem of scientific relevance with a quantum processor faster than would be done using classical computers.

rows.title: High temporal variability not trend dominates Mediterranean precipitation
rows.summary: Our assessment of a 27-country weather station dataset in the Mediterranean region revealed long-term stability in precipitation over 150 years, along with substantial short-term variability on annual to decadal scales driven by atmospheric circulation; these findings align with the precipitation trends seen in CMIP6 models.

rows.title: Genomic determinants of antigen expression hierarchy in African trypanosomes
rows.summary: A highly sensitive single-cell RNA sequencing approach reveals genomic features controlling the order of antigen activation in the model protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei .

rows.title: Perception of viral infections and initiation of antiviral defence in rice
rows.summary: Viral coat proteins are perceived by the RING1–IBR–RING2-type ubiquitin ligase, initiating the first step of the natural antiviral response in rice.

rows.title: TGFβ links EBV to multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children
rows.summary: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome following SARS-CoV-2 infection results from increased serum levels of TGFβ, which impairs the reactivation of virus-specific T cells.

rows.title: An operating system for executing applications on quantum network nodes
rows.summary: A new quantum operating system architecture is described that is capable of executing applications on quantum networks in high-level software, which is a step towards bringing quantum network technology to society.

rows.title: A robustly rooted tree of eukaryotes reveals their excavate ancestry
rows.summary: The root of the eukaryote Tree of Life is estimated from a new, larger dataset of mitochondrial proteins including all known eukaryotic supergroups, showing it lies between two multi-supergroup assemblages.

rows.title: Realization of 2D metals at the ångström thickness limit
rows.summary: Melting and squeezing pure metals between two sapphires covered in molybdenum disulfide produces diverse two-dimensional metals at the ångström thickness limit.

rows.title: Species turnover does not rescue biodiversity in fragmented landscapes
rows.summary: An analysis of habitat fragmentation using a dataset of more than 4,000 species worldwide shows that fragmentation reduces biodiversity at all scales, and that increases in β diversity do not compensate for the loss of α diversity.

rows.title: The earliest human face of Western Europe
rows.summary: A Homo aff. erectus individual dated to 1.4 million to 1.1 million years ago found at Sima del Elefante (Sierra de Atapuerca, Spain) does not display the modern-human-like aspect of Homo antecessor found at the neighbouring Gran Dolina site (900,000–800,000 years ago).

rows.title: Adaptive locomotion of active solids
rows.summary: The development of active solids based on centimetre-scale building blocks incorporating odd elasticity shows that they can spontaneously undergo limit cycles of shape changes, leading to adaptive locomotion such as rolling and crawling.

rows.title: Record sea surface temperature jump in 2023–2024 unlikely but not unexpected
rows.summary: Observations and climate models suggest that the global sea surface temperature jump in 2023–2024 was not unexpected and would have been nearly impossible without anthropogenic warming.

rows.title: MYC ecDNA promotes intratumour heterogeneity and plasticity in PDAC
rows.summary: In a model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, extrachromosomal DNAs are shown to be a source of high-level focal amplification driving MYC heterogeneity and phenotypic adaptation.

rows.title: Natural behaviour is learned through dopamine-mediated reinforcement
rows.summary: Studies in zebra finches show that dopamine has a key role as a reinforcement signal in the trial-and-error process of learning that underlies complex natural behaviours.

rows.title: Large recoverable elastic energy in chiral metamaterials via twist buckling
rows.summary: High-enthalpy elastic metamaterials constructed from freely rotatable chiral metacells have high stiffness, large recoverable strain and improved buckling strength.

rows.title: Magnetically and optically active edges in phosphorene nanoribbons
rows.summary: Phosphorene nanoribbons demonstrate extraordinary magnetic properties, ranging from large internal fields in films to macroscopic alignment in solution, which can be coupled to photoexcitations that localize to the magnetic edge of these ribbons.

rows.title: Hepatic stellate cells control liver zonation, size and functions via R-spondin 3
rows.summary: Hepatic stellate cells regulate hepatocyte functions via R-spondin 3.

rows.title: Basis functions for complex social decisions in dorsomedial frontal cortex
rows.summary: A study combining group decision-making tasks with fMRI shows that the brain’s dorsomedial prefrontal cortex uses basis functions, similar to those in the visual, motor and spatial domains, to represent patterns of social interaction.

rows.title: Structure and mechanism of the plastid/parasite ATP/ADP translocator
rows.summary: ATP/ADP translocators in obligate intracellular parasites and plastids facilitate energy parasitism and endosymbiosis by mediating ATP import and ADP export, with their cryo-EM structures and mechanisms revealed, providing insights for drug development against intracellular pathogens.

rows.title: Spatial immune scoring system predicts hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence
rows.summary: A publicly accessible tool—the TIMES score—for predicting the risk of recurrence of hepatocellular carcinoma is revealed, providing mechanistic insights into the prognostic patterns for hepatocellular carcinoma.

rows.title: Increasing hourly heavy rainfall in Austria reflected in flood changes
rows.summary: Long-term increases in heavy daily and hourly precipitation in Austria from different climatic mechanisms emphasize the need for flood management adaptation, especially in smaller catchments affected by the increased hourly rainfall.

rows.title: Unconventional magnons in collinear magnets dictated by spin space groups
rows.summary: Spin space group theory is applied to identify more than 200 collinear magnets with unconventional magnons; high-throughput calculations with spin–orbit coupling find that most of these unconventional magnets are dictated by the Heisenberg exchange interaction.

rows.title: High continuity of forager ancestry in the Neolithic period of the eastern Maghreb
rows.summary: Ancient DNA from the eastern Maghreb (Tunisia and Algeria) dating between 15,000 and 6,000 years ago shows that this region was far less affected by external gene flow than the rest of the Neolithic Mediterranean, including not only Europe but also the western Maghreb (Morocco).

rows.title: Sliding and healing of frictional interfaces that appear stationary
rows.summary: Digital image correlation measurements show that nominally stationary interfaces subjected to constant shear and normal loads are sliding at extremely small rates, confirming the predictions of rate-and-state friction formulations.

rows.title: Dual neuromodulatory dynamics underlie birdsong learning
rows.summary: Dopamine release in the basal ganglia of the zebra finch is driven by neurons associated with reinforcement learning and by cholinergic signalling, and tracks performance quality during long-term learning of its song.

rows.title: An ultra-broadband photonic-chip-based parametric amplifier
rows.summary: An optical parametric amplifier based on integrated photonic circuits fabricated using low-loss gallium phosphide-on-silicon dioxide demonstrates improved bandwidth and gain performance over state-of-the-art erbium-doped fibre amplifiers while maintaining a low noise figure.

rows.title: Fate of pistachio production in Iran holds lessons for the world
An organ that stores red blood cells for emergencies
rows.summary: A new ‘storehouse’ function ascribed to the spleen, and reducing laboratory waste by reusing vials, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Similar chiral phenomena occur in cell cultures and human crowds
Author Correction: Classification with a disordered dopant atom network in silicon
COP30 must deliver binding mechanisms to address climate change, not empty promises
Author Correction: Transforming a head direction signal into a goal-oriented steering command
Bad romance: male octopuses inject deadly venom into their mates
rows.summary: The paralysing toxin deployed by the male blue-lined octopus might help to protect him from being eaten.

rows.title: For more reliable AI, academics should edit Wikipedia
How a vast digital twin of the Yangtze River could prevent flooding in China
rows.summary: A project that intertwines data on weather, water flow and energy demand to create a 3D model of the whole river basin would enable researchers and others to make water-management decisions in real time.

rows.title: NASA begins mass firings of scientists ahead of Trump team’s deadline
rows.summary: Top advisers in the Office of the Chief Scientist are among the first to go amid downsizing effort.

rows.title: Public-health experts should be more political, not less
rows.summary: Health has always been political, long before Donald Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr took power. Denying this is what’s been killing us.

rows.title: Alcohol and cancer risk: what you need to know
rows.summary: Experts weigh in on the risks of moderate drinking — and how people should assess them.

rows.title: Daily briefing: NASA begins mass firings of scientists
rows.summary: NASA has become the first US agency to pre-emptively fire career employees as part of a radical downsizing of the federal government. Plus, the activity of a certain gene variant is linked to obesity in Labrador retrievers.

rows.title: Preprint sites bioRxiv and medRxiv launch new era of independence
rows.summary: The popular repositories, on which life scientists post research before peer review, will be managed by a new organization called openRxiv.

rows.title: Complex water networks visualized by cryogenic electron microscopy of RNA
rows.summary: Using cryogenic electron microscopy and a modelling approach, complex water networks in a ribozyme are visualized.

rows.title: #ScientistAtWork 2025: Nature is seeking stunning photographic images that capture researchers’ working lives
rows.summary: Winners get a cash prize, and will have their image featured in Nature in print and online.

rows.title: I create buildings from mushroom components
rows.summary: Mtamu Kililo creates alternative construction materials to confront Kenya’s housing crisis.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Thousands protest Trump cuts at #StandUpForScience rallies
rows.summary: Thousands of researchers and science supporters in the United States and in Europe protested under the banner of ‘Stand Up for Science’ on Friday. Plus, how ‘resilience’ can mask a toxic lab culture.

rows.title: Are microplastics bad for your health? More rigorous science is needed
rows.summary: Tiny plastic particles are being found everywhere, including in the human brain. But it is not yet clear which findings can be trusted and what they might mean.

rows.title: How the NIH dominates the world’s health research — in charts
rows.summary: Abrupt cuts by the Trump administration to the US National Institutes of Health threaten progress in medical research globally.

rows.title: Science diplomacy can help to heal global rifts — if research is respected
rows.summary: The universal language of science allows nations to reach a mutual understanding of shared problems. But that requires politicians not to meddle in how science is done.

rows.title: Our experience of teaching neuroscience in a maximum-security prison
rows.summary: Making our way through security each week is a slog, but teaching incarcerated people has been an incredible career experience.

rows.title: The ‘quantum’ principle that says why atoms are as they are
rows.summary: From strange beginnings, the 100-year-old Pauli exclusion principle has become a gift that keeps on giving for scientists who aim to understand the workings of matter.

rows.title: Author Correction: Warming and cooling catalyse widespread temporal turnover in biodiversity
The surprising culprit for the loss of huge swathes of tropical forest
rows.summary: Analysis of satellite imagery of the Brazilian Amazon, the Congo Basin and New Guinea helps to show that ‘secondary’ roads take an outsized toll.

rows.title: Rock hunters, tree huggers and taxi drivers: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: Who’s likely to wake up from a coma? Brainwaves provide a clue
rows.summary: The presence of a pattern called a sleep spindle helps to predict which people will recover from an unresponsive state.

rows.title: ‘I was told to toughen up’: is academia getting resilience all wrong?
rows.summary: Being repeatedly told to bounce back and develop a thicker skin can mask a toxic lab culture.

rows.title: ‘Scientists will not be silenced’: thousands protest Trump research cuts
rows.summary: Researchers at Stand Up for Science rallies voice defiance against the policies of US President Donald Trump’s administration.

rows.title: Microsoft quantum computing ‘breakthrough’ faces fresh challenge
rows.summary: Analysis pokes holes in protocol that underpins Microsoft’s claim to have created the first topological qubits.

rows.title: Daily briefing: This key protein could be responsible for brain ageing
rows.summary: A key protein that could be responsible for brain ageing. Plus, researchers organize a day of action to #StandUpForScience.

rows.title: AI tools are spotting errors in research papers: inside a growing movement
rows.summary: Large language models are being used to check papers, but researchers warn they come with risks.

rows.title: Ice-hunting Moon lander runs into trouble ― leaving scientists in suspense
rows.summary: The Athena lander seems to be in the wrong orientation, but some of its science might be salvaged.

rows.title: How a PhD student’s lab size affects their chance of future academic success
rows.summary: Trainees in big research groups tend to go on to greater academic success than their small-group counterparts — but are more likely to quit academia altogether.

rows.title: Ancient puppets that smile or scowl hint at shared rituals
rows.summary: Clay figurines found on top of the remnants of a pyramid in what is now El Salvador might have been used in public ceremonies.

rows.title: Trump’s nominee for NIH chief talks frozen grants and fostering ‘scientific dissent’
rows.summary: Health economist Jay Bhattacharya, who drew censure for controversial views on COVID-19, vows to provide funding but is short on details.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The second X chromosome isn’t so silent after all
rows.summary: The US National Institutes of Health is terminating swathes of diversity- and climate-related grants. Plus, the second X chromosome in female cells might explain why women tend to be more resilient to cognitive decline than men.

rows.title: The financial shackling of historically Black universities in the United States
rows.summary: Evolutionary biologist Joseph L. Graves Jr argues that — now more than ever — the United States should honour its commitments to Black higher education to diversify the science workforce.

rows.title: Exclusive: NIH to terminate hundreds of active research grants
rows.summary: Studies that touch on LGBT+ health, gender identity and DEI in the biomedical workforce could be terminated, according to documents obtained by Nature .

rows.title: Trans researchers under attack: LGBTQ+ biologists face hostile work environment
rows.summary: Largest survey of LGBTQ+ biologists finds 40% of trans and gender-nonconforming, and 20% of lesbian, gay, bisexual and queer researchers, experience hostility, intimidation or offensive behaviour at work.

rows.title: Foreign researchers in China face tightening restrictions
rows.summary: Data and security laws are affecting scientists who stayed in China after COVID — but for some it’s still a great place to do research.

rows.title: Sensing ceramides by CYSLTR2 and P2RY6 to aggravate atherosclerosis
rows.summary: CYSLTR2 and P2RY6 are identified as endogenous ceramide receptors, and inhibition of these ameliorates atherosclerosis, particularly in chronic-kidney-disease-associated cardiovascular disease.

rows.title: Vision: protecting and restoring a prized sense
rows.summary: The scale of work to improve therapies for eye disease reflects the importance people place on sight.

rows.title: A super-gel stays supple from −115 ºC to 143 ºC
rows.summary: A network of two polymers plus sulfuric acid allows a hydrogel to keep its elasticity and softness at extreme temperatures.

rows.title: Earliest systematically crafted bone tools date back 1.5 million years
rows.summary: Evidence suggests deliberate production of bone tools happened much earlier than previously thought — plus, how cells’ waste-disposal systems could help defend against infection.

rows.title: Eye problems cloud NASA’s vision of Mars
rows.summary: Mysterious syndrome remains a ‘red risk’ for long-term spaceflight.

rows.title: Designer cannabinoids could be the key to pain relief without adverse effects
rows.summary: Current approaches to pain relief are falling short. Chemically modifying a synthetic cannabinoid could enable scientists to capitalize on the body’s natural pain-killing pathway without evoking drug tolerance or psychoactivity.

rows.title: Human echolocation can be taught
rows.summary: Neuroscientist Lore Thaler explains why she thinks people with visual impairments should be taught to explore the world through mouth-click sounds.

rows.title: Sexual harassment allegations linked to drop in citations
rows.summary: But numbers remain steady for researchers who commit scientific misconduct.

rows.title: Daily briefing: PubMed blackout stokes fears about database’s future
rows.summary: A temporary blackout of PubMed has researchers concerned over the database’s future. Plus, a bird’s nest offers a time capsule of plastic rubbish.

rows.title: It’s time to shine for LEDs made using ecofriendly quantum dots
rows.summary: QLEDs — light-emitting diodes that rely on nanocrystals called quantum dots — are usually made with toxic heavy metals. A strategy has been developed to make QLEDs with a performance comparable to that of commercially available technologies but using a more environmentally friendly alloy of zinc, selenium, tellurium and sulfur, by improving the distribution of the tellurium atoms.

rows.title: How the brain decides when to stick at it, give up or try something new
rows.summary: To survive, animals must continually decide whether to persevere with their current goal, switch to a new one or disengage altogether. Three genetically defined types of neuronal cell in a small midbrain area called the median raphe nucleus are shown to control decisions about whether to persevere, explore or disengage.

rows.title: Little Shop of Dreams
rows.summary: A reality check.

rows.title: How AI could let us watch epic star collisions in real time
rows.summary: Locating sources of gravitational waves using artificial intelligence could enable astronomers to point telescopes at stellar mergers before they happen.

rows.title: Genus-wide plant pangenome could inform next-generation crop design
rows.summary: A compilation of genomes from species in the genus Solanum could help scientists to blend the best aspects of productive staple crops and genetically diverse but under-studied indigenous crops.

rows.title: ‘Silence is complicity’ — universities must fight the anti-DEI crackdown
rows.summary: Higher-education establishments must not be bullied into abandoning their mission of diversity, equity and inclusion.

rows.title: Ancient reef-building corals had a little help from microbial friends
rows.summary: Nitrogen-isotope analysis provides geochemical evidence that, similar to modern corals, some extinct coral groups had a symbiotic association with photosynthetic microorganisms. This ‘photosymbiosis’ might have contributed to the high productivity of ancient reefs in low-nutrient environments and puts long-term ecological research on ancient reefs into a fresh perspective.

rows.title: Amazonian deforestation makes the wet season wetter, and the dry season drier
rows.summary: Clearing of Amazonian forest boosts rainfall during the wet season, but reduces it in the dry season, when the ecosystem needs water most — highlighting the need to prevent further clearance of a climate-regulating environment.

rows.title: How can treatment for eye disease be made easier?
rows.summary: Therapies currently in clinical trials could last longer and help to save more vision in people with age-related macular degeneration.

rows.title: Ancient humans used bone tools one million years earlier than thought
rows.summary: Objects discovered in Tanzania and dated to 1.5 million years ago help to rewrite human ancestors’ use of carved bone implements.

rows.title: Diversity in neuronal activity could be caused by differences in inputs
rows.summary: Different neuronal cells have a diverse range of activity patterns, but the cause has remained unclear. In mice, maps of brain-wide inputs to individual neurons that do or do not show activity modulation by the behavioural state has uncovered wiring rules that could help to explain this functional diversity.

rows.title: Artificial intelligence could boost eye care in low-income countries
rows.summary: Technology rivals ophthalmologists at detecting diabetic retinopathy, allowing more people to be screened globally.

rows.title: Protein waste turned into antibiotics as a defence strategy of human cells
rows.summary: As well as degrading proteins, the proteosome surprisingly also functions in human defence against bacterial infection. By changing how proteins are cleaved, this system generates antibiotic peptides on demand.

rows.title: Behind every great woman in science, there’s another great woman in science
rows.summary: To mark International Women’s Day on 8 March, six award-winning female scientists highlight women who have inspired them by pushing innovative research and creating opportunities for others.

rows.title: This key protein could be responsible for brain ageing
rows.summary: An amyloid protein targeted by Alzheimer’s disease therapies seems to be involved in normal mental decline.

rows.title: ‘Perfect potato’ designed thanks to unearthed genetic diversity
rows.summary: Potato genomes that contain the complete sequences from both sets of chromosomes uncover the deleterious variations previously hidden in genomes disclosed for only one set of chromosomes. An ideal set of genes was designed computationally by combining desirable sequences from different potato varieties. This ideal genotype could guide the breeding of hybrid potatoes.

rows.title: A supersolid made using photons
rows.summary: Supersolids are a unique phase of matter that combine the friction-free flow of superfluids with an ordered structure. They have previously been achieved only with condensates of ultracold atoms. The observation of the supersolid state in photons provides a new window through which to peer into its mysteries.

rows.title: Restoring vision with optogenetics
rows.summary: Trials of therapies that enhance the light-sensitivity of cells in the retina are returning surprisingly positive results in people with retinitis pigmentosa.

rows.title: How the brain decides whether to persist — and when to give up
rows.summary: Neuroscientists demonstrate how specific neurons in the brainstem control these behavioural strategies in mice.

rows.title: How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown
rows.summary: Researchers want firms to be more transparent about the electricity demands of artificial intelligence.

rows.title: Why women’s brains are more resilient: it could be their ‘silent’ X chromosome
rows.summary: Study in mice and human cadavers hints that a brain-protective gene in the chromosome becomes more active with age.

rows.title: The search for solutions to geographic atrophy of the retina
rows.summary: Momentum is building behind a variety of therapies that can slow, stop or even reverse the most advanced form of the eye condition age-related macular degeneration.

rows.title: AI algorithm helps telescopes to pivot fast towards gravitational-wave sources
rows.summary: Fast electromagnetic follow-up observations of gravitational-wave sources such as binary neutron stars could shed light on questions across physics and cosmology. A machine-learning approach brings that a step closer.

rows.title: Superconductivity and quantized anomalous Hall effect in rhombohedral graphene
rows.summary: Rhombohedral tetralayer graphene aligned to a hexagonal boron nitride substrate hosts gate-tunable superconductivity and quantized anomalous Hall states, and thermodynamic compressibility measurements further show a fractional Chern insulator at zero magnetic field, paving the way for new hybrid interfaces between superconductors and topological edge states.

rows.title: Aspirin prevents metastasis by limiting platelet TXA 2 suppression of T cell immunity
rows.summary: Inhibition of cyclooxygenase 1 releases T cells from immunosuppression by platelet-derived thromboxane A 2 , thereby enhancing the immune response against metastasis.

rows.title: Homogeneous ZnSeTeS quantum dots for efficient and stable pure-blue LEDs
rows.summary: By suppressing compositional heterogeneities in cadmium-free quantum dots, environmentally friendly pure-blue-light-emitting diodes with enhanced efficiencies, lifetimes and spectral purity are achieved, rivalling state-of-the-art cadmium-based blue quantum-dot light-emitting diodes.

rows.title: Real-time inference for binary neutron star mergers using machine learning
rows.summary: Analysis of gravitational waves from merging binary neutron stars was accelerated using machine learning, enabling full low-latency parameter estimation and enhancing the potential for multi-messenger observations.

rows.title: TIR1-produced cAMP as a second messenger in transcriptional auxin signalling
rows.summary: cAMP produced by the TIR1/AFB receptors of the main endogenous developmental plant hormone auxin acts as a true second messenger, revising the established paradigm of transcriptional auxin signalling.

rows.title: Systematic bone tool production at 1.5 million years ago
rows.summary: Bone tools shaped by knapping found within Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania precede any other evidence of systematic bone tool production by more than 1 million years.

rows.title: Evolutionary fingerprints of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition
rows.summary: Malignant cells with mesenchymal features display increased chromatin accessibility, particularly in the pericentromeric and centromeric regions, in turn resulting in delayed mitosis and catastrophic cell division.

rows.title: Fingerprinting the recovery of Antarctic ozone
rows.summary: Pattern-based detection and attribution methods that make use of trend pattern information as a function of month and height provide evidence that reduction of ozone-depleting substances has resulted in the beginning of Antarctic ozone recovery.

rows.title: Sensory input, sex and function shape hypothalamic cell type development
rows.summary: Paired transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility profiling are used to examine the developmental trajectories of neuronal populations in the hypothalamic preoptic region, including cell types with key roles in physiological and social behaviour functions have been identified.

rows.title: Prohormone cleavage prediction uncovers a non-incretin anti-obesity peptide
rows.summary: Computational drug discovery is used to identify a 12-mer peptide derived from BRINP2 with potent anti-obesity effects that are independent of leptin, glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor and melanocortin 4 receptor.

rows.title: 10,000-h-stable intermittent alkaline seawater electrolysis
rows.summary: Construction of a phosphate passivation layer on the surface of a cathode to withstand fluctuating operation in alkaline seawater is proposed following understanding the mechanism behind the dynamic evolution and degradation of cathode in intermittent electrolysis.

rows.title: Cell-autonomous innate immunity by proteasome-derived defence peptides
rows.summary: Proteasomal degradation of cellular proteins generate defence peptides constitutively and in response to bacterial infection. Such peptides might provide a source of natural antibiotics that could lead to biotechnology applications and therapeutic interventions.

rows.title: A mixed-precision memristor and SRAM compute-in-memory AI processor
rows.summary: A mixed-precision heterogeneous memristor combined with a compute-in-memory artificial intelligence (AI) processor allows optimization of the precision, energy efficiency, storage and wakeup-to-response time requirements of AI edge devices, which is demonstrated using existing models and datasets.

rows.title: Structure of mitochondrial pyruvate carrier and its inhibition mechanism
rows.summary: Structural findings define the architecture of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, delineate its substrate-binding site and translocation pathway, and reveal its major conformational states, providing the molecular basis for understanding its function and inhibition.

rows.title: Vulnerability of amphibians to global warming
rows.summary: A 4 °C global temperature increase would push 7.5% of amphibian species beyond their physiological limits.

rows.title: A subcortical switchboard for perseverative, exploratory and disengaged states
rows.summary: Behavioural experiments in mice demonstrate that GABAergic (γ-aminobutyric acid-expressing), glutamatergic and serotonergic neurons in the median raphe nucleus have distinct and complementary functions in regulating decision-making resulting in flexible behavioural strategies.

rows.title: A cryptic pocket in CB1 drives peripheral and functional selectivity
rows.summary: A peripherally restricted CB1 agonist (VIP36) targeting a cryptic receptor pocket was developed, showing high efficacy in mouse pain models with minimal side effects and tolerance, potentially revolutionizing chronic pain treatment and GPCR drug design.

rows.title: Fine-scale patterns of SARS-CoV-2 spread from identical pathogen sequences
rows.summary: The analysis of pairs of identical SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences enables characterization of transmission patterns between geographies and age groups.

rows.title: Impact of Amazonian deforestation on precipitation reverses between seasons
rows.summary: Reversed precipitation responses to Amazon deforestation show that deforestation leads to precipitation increases in the wet season and decreases in the dry season.

rows.title: Genome duplication in a long-term multicellularity evolution experiment
rows.summary: In the Multicellularity Long Term Evolution Experiment, diploid yeast evolve to be tetraploid under selection for larger multicellular size, revealing how whole-genome duplication can arise due to its immediate benefits, persist under selection, and fuel long-term innovations via aneuploidy.

rows.title: Clonal dynamics and somatic evolution of haematopoiesis in mouse
rows.summary: Isolating and studying haematopoietic stem cells in young and aged mice demonstrates evolutionary processes related to blood production and provides a framework for interpreting future work using laboratory mice to study stem cell ageing.

rows.title: Canopy functional trait variation across Earth’s tropical forests
rows.summary: Data from a variety of sources—including satellite, climate and soil data, as well as field-collected information on plant traits—are pooled and analysed to map the functional diversity of tropical forest canopies globally.

rows.title: Chanoclavine synthase operates by an NADPH-independent superoxide mechanism
rows.summary: The unique structure and mechanism of chanoclavine synthase (EasC), a haem catalase that uses superoxide for substrate transformation in ergot alkaloid biosynthesis, are revealed in this study, challenging established catalase mechanisms.

rows.title: Emerging supersolidity in photonic-crystal polariton condensates
rows.summary: Experimental evidence is presented for a new implementation of supersolidity in a driven-dissipative, non-equilibrium context realized in a photonic-crystal waveguide, demonstrating the breaking of translational symmetry with exceptionally low losses.

rows.title: Evolution of temperature preference in flies of the genus Drosophila
rows.summary: A study using flies of the genus Drosophila adapted to life in diverse thermal environments shows how evolution has shaped temperature preference by acting on both molecular heat receptors and thermosensory circuits in the flies.

rows.title: Solanum pan-genetics reveals paralogues as contingencies in crop engineering
rows.summary: Gene duplication and subsequent paralogue diversification are major obstacles to genotype-to-phenotype predictability.

rows.title: Elon Musk has some supporters in science
A name for the study of life in the Universe
rows.summary: An argument for introducing the word ‘cosmobiology’, and accounts of the human side of science, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: AI hallucinations are a feature of LLM design, not a bug
Should scientists ditch the social-media platform X?
AI must be taught concepts, not just patterns in raw data
China’s supreme court calls for crack down on paper mills
rows.summary: China’s top court says businesses that write bogus manuscripts for payment should be punished.

rows.title: The science of shopping addiction: what makes people buy loads of stuff?
rows.summary: From China to Brazil to Germany, huge numbers of people are addicted to shopping, driven in part by companies that use gaming strategies.

rows.title: ‘Omg, did PubMed go dark?’ Blackout stokes fears about database’s future
rows.summary: A brief outage has focused attention on scientists’ reliance on the US-government-funded website.

rows.title: Three AI-powered steps to faster, smarter peer review
rows.summary: Tired of spending countless hours on peer reviews? An AI-assisted workflow could help.

rows.title: Train clinical AI to reason like a team of doctors
rows.summary: As the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act takes effect, AI systems that mimic how human teams collaborate can improve trust in high-risk situations, such as clinical medicine.

rows.title: Meet the ‘woolly mouse’: why scientists doubt it’s a big step towards recreating mammoths
rows.summary: De-extinction company Colossal mixed mammoth and mouse mutations in a single strain to create a shaggy-haired rodent.

rows.title: I want to ensure that Africans take part in the AI revolution
rows.summary: Vukosi Marivate learnt that communities, not just superstar individuals, can open doors in artificial intelligence.

rows.title: How AI can achieve human-level intelligence: researchers call for change in tack
rows.summary: A survey finds that most respondents are sceptical that the technology underpinning large-language models is sufficient for artificial general intelligence.

rows.title: Daily briefing: US scientists rise up against Trump’s efforts to dismantle federal science
rows.summary: US scientists are ramping up protests against the policies of President Donald Trump. Plus, scientists unveil the ‘woolly mouse’.

rows.title: We moved a conference halfway around the globe to avoid visa discrimination
rows.summary: Event organizers often overlook the visa-related difficulties that researchers in low- and middle-income countries face. This must change.

rows.title: Tracking gulls to prevent a bird flu pandemic
rows.summary: Sölvi Rúnar Vignisson observes species of sea bird as they gather and mix in Iceland.

rows.title: Use your research to beat health inequities: four strategies from experts
rows.summary: Scientists must commit to engaging with the communities they want to help at all stages of the research process — from planning to dissemination.

rows.title: ChatGPT for students: learners find creative new uses for chatbots
rows.summary: The utility of generative AI tools is expanding far beyond simple summarisation and grammar support towards more sophisticated, pedagogical applications.

rows.title: US science is under threat ― now scientists are fighting back
rows.summary: Researchers are organizing protests and making their voices heard as Trump officials slash funding and lay off federal scientists.

rows.title: Against the odds: 12 women who beat bias to succeed in science
rows.summary: A book deftly highlights how women have been considered unsuitable as researchers for reasons other than their ability and commitment.

rows.title: Boosting science: ‘Give foreign STEM students ten-year visas’
rows.summary: Alongside nurturing entrepreneurial skills in mathematicians, Ewan Kirk lobbies to keep scientific talent in the United Kingdom.

rows.title: Daily briefing: What another round of layoffs means for US science
rows.summary: A second tsunami of layoffs is set to strike US federal agencies. Plus, a commercial spacecraft has become the first to ace a landing on the Moon.

rows.title: Private spacecraft nails Moon landing: first images of Blue Ghost on the lunar surface
rows.summary: The touchdown is a much-needed win for NASA’s partnerships with commercial space companies.

rows.title: China research on next-generation computer chips is double the US output
rows.summary: Leading efforts in fields such as optical physics could stymie US export controls designed to stifle the country’s microchip industry.

rows.title: Constitutively active glucagon receptor drives high blood glucose in birds
rows.summary: Hepatic expression of constitutively active glucagon receptor may have contributed to the glucose and lipid metabolism and the high metabolic rates that enabled the evolution of flight in birds.

rows.title: Just a smidgen of yellow-fever vaccine is enough
rows.summary: The standard protective dose is almost 14,000 units, but even 500 units raises antibody levels sufficiently to do the job.

rows.title: Audio long read: Why kids need to take more risks — science reveals the benefits of wild, free play
rows.summary: Evidence suggests that risky play provides a wide-range of benefits to children, despite opportunities to do it becoming more restricted than ever.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Trump administration policies create turmoil for NIH-funded researchers worldwide
rows.summary: Trump administration policies are creating turmoil for US PhD students and NIH-funded researchers abroad. Plus, the month’s best science images.

rows.title: Ukraine’s research sector is struggling — can Europe help?
rows.summary: Having access to funding through EU initiatives is a huge boon for Ukrainian researchers, but many are also hoping for cultural changes in their institutions.

rows.title: How academia’s ‘lone wolf’ culture is harming researcher mental health
rows.summary: Scientists who don’t consistently publish great papers and attract bumper funding are often overlooked, say campaigners for healthier lab environments.

rows.title: Trump team orders huge government lay-offs: how science could fare
rows.summary: Nature talks to scientists inside US agencies about what the latest directive could mean for their staff members and budgets.

rows.title: Lhasa ′ s rocks reveal an Australian birthplace
rows.summary: Granite from the chunk of Earth’s crust called the Lhasa terrane did not come from India, as had previously been thought, but from much further afield.

rows.title: Vesuvius volcano turned this brain to glass
rows.summary: Rare substance found in ancient skull reveals presence of a super-heated ash cloud.

rows.title: Our Galaxy’s central black hole puts on a fireworks show
rows.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope uncovered repeated flares from the supermassive object called Sagittarius A*.

rows.title: Four ways to power-up AI for drug discovery
rows.summary: Insights from artificial intelligence could eventually transform drug development, if the quality and quantity of biological and chemical data can be improved.

rows.title: US universities curtail PhD admissions amid Trump science funding cuts
rows.summary: Nature talks to prospective students left in limbo as some institutes withdraw offers and put applications on hold.

rows.title: Meet the ice-hunting robots headed for the Moon right now
rows.summary: Two US probes launched today, one laden with a drill and a hopper looking for lunar water.

rows.title: See snazzy slugs in all their luminous glory — February’s best science images
rows.summary: The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature ’s photo team.

rows.title: Author Correction: CTLA4 blockade abrogates KEAP1/STK11 -related resistance to PD-(L)1 inhibitors
Daily briefing: An unvaccinated child is first US measles death in a decade
rows.summary: An unvaccinated child has died of measles in the United States. Plus, a crucial ocean-current system is safe from the effects of climate change — for now.

rows.title: If your heart stops, this smartwatch-AI can call for help
rows.summary: The machine learning algorithm picks up sudden loss of pulse and automatically alerts emergency services — plus, the latest from the Nature Briefing .

rows.title: Take me home, country toads
rows.summary: Cane toads have remarkable navigation abilities, even when their sense of smell and magnetic-sensory systems are compromised.

rows.title: Causal claims, causal assumptions and protected area impact
Evolutionary flexibility to gain or lose tooth complexity sparks fish diversification
rows.summary: Why are some species more likely to diversify than others? For the largest group of vertebrates, ray-finned fishes, the ability to evolve by transitioning back and forth between simple and complex teeth fuelled their diversification.

rows.title: US pulls back from gold-standard scientific climate panel
rows.summary: Trump officials bar NASA climate scientist from international meeting, and the space agency shuts down a team supporting the next global climate assessment.

rows.title: Superelastic titanium alloy has potential for space missions
rows.summary: Metallurgists have designed an extraordinary titanium alloy that is light, strong and flexible, and which recovers its original shape after large amounts of deformation — even when as cold as liquid helium or hotter than boiling water.

rows.title: Can AI help beat poverty? Researchers test ways to aid the poorest people
rows.summary: Measuring poverty is the first step to delivering support, but it has long been a costly, time-intensive and contentious endeavour.

rows.title: Nursing-home residents’ skin is a source of transmitted harmful and drug-resistant microbes
rows.summary: Genomic sequencing has revealed that individual strains of life-threatening, antibiotic-resistant bacteria and Candida auris fungi reside on human skin and can be commonly transmitted between residents of nursing homes.

rows.title: Iconic ocean-current system is safe from climate collapse ― for now
rows.summary: But even a weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation could have grave consequences worldwide.

rows.title: Reply to: Causal claims, causal assumptions and protected area impact
Daily briefing: Nature denounces Trump’s attack on US research
rows.summary: Nature calls for the global community to stand united in defence of science in the United States. Plus, how AI might help researchers remedy poverty.

rows.title: ‘Slime’ keeps the brain safe ― and could guard against ageing
rows.summary: Slippery proteins in the brain’s blood vessels form a protective barrier that breaks down with age, studies in mice show.

rows.title: Combine AI with citizen science to fight poverty
rows.summary: Artificial-intelligence tools and community science can help in places where data are scarce, so long as funding for data collection does not falter in the future.

rows.title: Streamflow shifts with declining snowfall
Computational workflow limits need to ‘guess and check’ in the synthesis of complex molecules
rows.summary: For decades, chemists have tried to train computers to predict how different molecules can be synthesized, but existing approaches use ‘shortcut’ algorithms that are unreliable when the target is complex. Adding quantum-mechanical and statistical modelling at weak points in the algorithms can provide feedback to reroute the predictions towards successful chemical syntheses.

rows.title: How blowing the whistle on the Theranos scandal transformed Erika Cheung’s career
rows.summary: Cheung, a laboratory assistant straight from university, raised the alarm over dodgy science and a duplicitous boss.

rows.title: Revealing how fungi build planet-altering ‘road’ networks
rows.summary: Fungi made Earth’s land liveable by building networks that released nutrients locked in primordial rock and supplied those nutrients to plant roots. An imaging study now sheds light on how these fungal networks are constructed.

rows.title: NIH turmoil sparks anxiety over future of its global grants
rows.summary: Researchers are concerned about whether the US National Institutes of Health will continue to fund international projects.

rows.title: Atlantic circulation could be more resilient to global warming than was thought
rows.summary: A system of ocean currents called the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation strongly affects climate, but is showing signs of shutting down. An analysis now suggests that total collapse is unlikely this century.

rows.title: Quantum technologies need big investments to deliver on their big promises
rows.summary: Sustained investments can deliver quantum devices that handle more information, more rapidly and more securely than can classical ones.

rows.title: Choice
rows.summary: Selective pressure.

rows.title: Reply to: Streamflow shifts with declining snowfall
Spectroscopy of the fractal Hofstadter energy spectrum
rows.summary: High-resolution STM/STS visualizes the fractionalization of flat moiré bands into discrete Hofstadter subbands in moiré graphene near the predicted second magic angle, and experimentally establishes several fundamental properties of the fractal Hofstadter energy spectrum.

rows.title: Mass-spectrometry-based proteomics: from single cells to clinical applications
rows.summary: This Review summarizes advances in mass-spectrometry-based proteomics and explores the potential applications of these technologies in the clinic.

rows.title: A lightweight shape-memory alloy with superior temperature-fluctuation resistance
rows.summary: A Ti–Al-based shape-memory alloy adhering to the stringent criteria of lightness, functionality and extreme thermal fluctuation resistance is introduced, showing excellent superelasticity with a recoverable strain exceeding 7% and an ultra-wide temperature window from 4.2 K to 400 K.

rows.title: Programs, origins and immunomodulatory functions of myeloid cells in glioma
rows.summary: A study of myeloid cells in gliomas, a type of brain tumour, used a factor-based computational framework to reveal four immunomodulatory gene-expression programs that are expressed across myeloid cell types, driven by microenvironmental cues and predictive of therapeutic response.

rows.title: Macrophages recycle phagocytosed bacteria to fuel immunometabolic responses
rows.summary: Phagocytosed bacteria can serve as an alternative nutrient source for macrophages, influencing their metabolic and immune responses through the recycling of microbial components, with the process regulated by nutrient-sensing mechanisms and bacterial viability.

rows.title: Evolutionary lability of a key innovation spurs rapid diversification
rows.summary: A study shows that the rapid diversification of cichlids in African lakes is driven by their ability to evolve between having simple or complex teeth.

rows.title: Integrated analysis of the complete sequence of a macaque genome
rows.summary: A complete genome assembly of a crab-eating macaque, revealing 46% fewer segmental duplications and 3.83 times longer centromeres than those of humans, is presented, enhancing understanding of lineage-specific phenotypes, adaptation and primate evolution.

rows.title: Brain-wide presynaptic networks of functionally distinct cortical neurons
rows.summary: Behavioural-state-dependent pyramidal neurons have a distinct pattern of long-range glutamatergic inputs, with a larger proportion of thalamic versus motor cortex inputs compared with non-behaviour-dependent neurons.

rows.title: A hypothalamic circuit underlying the dynamic control of social homeostasis
rows.summary: New data on brain-wide circuits centred around two interconnected hypothalamic neuron populations provide significant mechanistic insights into the emergence of social need during social isolation and the satiation of social need during social reunion.

rows.title: Systems-level design principles of metabolic rewiring in an animal
rows.summary: Systems-level Worm Perturb-Seq of metabolic genes reveals design principles of transcriptional metabolic rewiring, many of which can be explained by a compensation–repression model.

rows.title: Glycocalyx dysregulation impairs blood–brain barrier in ageing and disease
rows.summary: Disruption of mucin-domain glycoprotein expression and function in the endothelial glycocalyx are associated with ageing and Alzheimer’s disease, leading to dysregulated blood–brain barrier function.

rows.title: The conserved HIV-1 spacer peptide 2 triggers matrix lattice maturation
rows.summary: A study reports that the structural maturation of the matrix domain of the Gag protein of HIV-1 is induced by the proteolytic release and binding of the spacer peptide SP2.

rows.title: Automated loss of pulse detection on a consumer smartwatch
rows.summary: A study reports the development and validation of a wrist-worn, consumer wearable-based system that identifies sudden loss of pulse events with a performance profile suitable for societal-scale use.

rows.title: Continued Atlantic overturning circulation even under climate extremes
rows.summary: Climate models suggest that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is unlikely to collapse this century, owing to stabilization from wind-driven upwelling in the Southern Ocean.

rows.title: Comparative characterization of human accelerated regions in neurons
rows.summary: The cis -regulatory functions of human accelerated regions of genomic loci and their potential contribution to human brain evolution are revealed.

rows.title: Clonal Candida auris and ESKAPE pathogens on the skin of residents of nursing homes
rows.summary: Analyses of strain-resolved metagenomics with isolate sequencing data of skin samples from residents at nursing homes suggest that skin is a reservoir for Candida auris and other multidrug-resistant bacterial species.

rows.title: Glacial isostatic adjustment reveals Mars’s interior viscosity structure
rows.summary: Emplacement of the north polar cap of Mars is investigated by combining viscoelastic deformation calculations and observations, showing that it formed over the last 1.7–12.0 Myr atop a stiff lithosphere and high-viscosity mantle (10 22 Pa s), and that glacial isostatic adjustment could be further constrained.

rows.title: Multiplexed entanglement of multi-emitter quantum network nodes
rows.summary: Multiplexed entanglement distribution in a quantum network, with each node comprising multiple solid-state emitters in nanophotonic cavities, enables scalable quantum communication.

rows.title: A compendium of human gene functions derived from evolutionary modelling
rows.summary: Evolutionary modelling and expert review are applied to integrate experimentally supported knowledge accumulated in the Gene Ontology knowledgebase to create a draft human gene ‘functionome’.

rows.title: A manufacturable platform for photonic quantum computing
rows.summary: A manufacturable platform for quantum computing with photons is introduced and a set of monolithically integrated silicon-photonics-based modules is benchmarked, demonstrating dual-rail photonic qubits with performance close to thresholds required for operation.

rows.title: Achieving kilowatt-scale elastocaloric cooling by a multi-cell architecture
rows.summary: An elastocaloric cooling platform is constructed based on shape memory alloys with a cellular architecture that enables cooling powers above 1 kW.

rows.title: A single-fibre computer enables textile networks and distributed inference
rows.summary: A textile fibre computer combining sensing, memory, processing and communication in a 5-g mass has been developed, enabling distributed computation on the human body through garments.

rows.title: Humans in Africa’s wet tropical forests 150 thousand years ago
rows.summary: The identification of tools dated to the time of Homo sapiens associated with microfloral evidence of wet tropical forests indicates that West African forests were occupied by humans much earlier in human evolution than previously thought.

rows.title: Genome-coverage single-cell histone modifications for embryo lineage tracing
rows.summary: Two new methods, target chromatin indexing and tagmentation (TACIT) and combined TACIT (CoTACIT), enabled single-cell profiling of the epigenome and lineage tracing from mouse zygotes to blastocysts.

rows.title: Orbital hybridization in graphene-based artificial atoms
rows.summary: Orbital hybridization in artificial atoms is achieved by altering their shape, and the anisotropy of the confining potential gives rise to the hybridization between quasibound states with different orbital quantum numbers within the artificial atom.

rows.title: Interplay of geometrical and spin chiralities in 3D twisted magnetic ribbons
rows.summary: The interplay between geometrical and spin chiralities in three-dimensional twisted magnetic ribbons can lead to new functionalities that could allow for innovative chiral spintronics.

rows.title: Disorder-assisted real–momentum topological photonic crystal
rows.summary: A real–momentum topological photonic crystal that harnesses real-space disorder is used to generate a Pancharatnam–Berry phase while preserving momentum-space topology.

rows.title: Latitudinal scaling of aggregation with abundance and coexistence in forests
rows.summary: A unified framework is presented that integrates observed spatial patterns of individual trees in forests with ecological processes into a novel coexistence theory.

rows.title:
Rare disease gene association discovery in the 100,000 Genomes
Project
rows.summary:
A rare variant burden analytical framework for Mendelian diseases was
developed and applied to data from the 100,000 Genomes Project, identifying 69
probable new disease–gene associations.

rows.title: A systems-level, semi-quantitative landscape of metabolic flux in C. elegans
rows.summary: A strategy is introduced that infers whole-animal metabolic flux wiring from transcriptional phenotypes in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans and several features in its adult metabolism are discovered that are validated by stable isotope tracing.

rows.title: Hardware-efficient quantum error correction via concatenated bosonic qubits
rows.summary: Bosonic qubits can be engineered to feature intrinsic protection against certain kinds of errors, which makes quantum error correction across many bosonic qubits possible with less overhead.

rows.title: A travelling-wave strategy for plant–fungal trade
rows.summary: Symbiotic fungi control network-level structure and flows to meet trade demands.

rows.title: Extensive mutual influences of SMC complexes shape 3D genome folding
rows.summary: Orthogonal acute inducible degradation cell lines are used to delineate the mechanisms of how extrusive cohesin, cohesive cohesin and condensin interact to remodel chromosome architecture from interphase to mitosis.

rows.title: Sharing benefits of research is key to effective science communication
Other countries should copy Nepal’s approach to tackling cervical cancer
National climate policies must address mental health
How to develop a good writing style
rows.summary: Tips for clear scientific communication, and news of efforts to kill the larvae that cause river blindness, in this week’s pick from Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: China’s low-altitude economy needs to grow with more caution
Daily briefing: Postdocs and PhD students hit hard by Trump’s crackdown on science
rows.summary: A junk-food splurge can change your brain activity. Plus, hear from US postdocs and PhD students hit hard by Trump’s crackdown on science.

rows.title: Author Correction: Neutralizing GDF-15 can overcome anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 resistance in solid tumours
We use 30 billion tonnes of concrete each year — here’s how to make it sustainable
rows.summary: Promising methods are emerging to reduce emissions, resource use and waste from construction industries.

rows.title: Move beyond ‘publish or perish’ by measuring behaviours that benefit academia
rows.summary: A standardized system to measure contributions in mentorship, collaboration and more could bring about systemic change in science.

rows.title: How quickly are you ageing? What molecular ‘clocks’ can tell you about your health
rows.summary: Armed with an influx of cash and public enthusiasm, researchers are looking to improve how ageing is measured.

rows.title: My experience of speaking at a conference with a baby
rows.summary: Hannah Chance spent a day during her parental leave telling a group of postdocs about her science-policy work. Aidan, aged six months, came along too.

rows.title: PhD scientists who forged a career off the beaten track
rows.summary: These seven scientists escaped big-city life after completing their PhDs. Here’s how they make it work.

rows.title: Author Correction: A comprehensive spatio-cellular map of the human hypothalamus
Trump 2.0: an assault on science anywhere is an assault on science everywhere
rows.summary: US President Donald Trump is taking a wrecking ball to science and to international institutions. The global research community must take a stand against these attacks.

rows.title: Author Correction: The Ronne Ice Shelf survived the last interglacial
Chasing wildcats with my daughter
rows.summary: Mariola Sánchez-Cerdá works to track the elusive European wildcat’s movements and habits.

rows.title: Ancient apex predator tore into hippos with hyena-like teeth
rows.summary: Newly discovered species of leopard-sized carnivore lived some 30 million years ago in what is now Egypt.

rows.title: Author Correction: HIV-1 Env trimers asymmetrically engage CD4 receptors in membranes
How scientists can drive climate action: celebrate nature and promote hope
rows.summary: After years of storytelling and running classes and festivals, I’ve seen first-hand how a love of nature makes people want to protect it.

rows.title: Will AI jeopardize science photography? There’s still time to create an ethical code of conduct
rows.summary: Generative artificial-intelligence illustrations can be helpful, but fall short as scientific records.

rows.title: Daily briefing: What science photos do that AI-generated images can’t
rows.summary: Breast cancer is on the rise, and people in low- and middle-income countries face the heaviest burden. Plus, what science photography does that AI-generated images can’t.

rows.title: Trekking across Nepal to bridge its gender gap in the sciences
rows.summary: Biochemist Babita Paudel strives to change Nepal’s standing as the Asian country with the lowest participation of women in science.

rows.title: The racial injustice laid bare by COVID must not be forgotten
rows.summary: A methodical analysis of pandemic policies in Chicago, Illinois, reveals why short-term interventions are unable to tackle systemic inequities that affect marginalized communities.

rows.title: Breast cancer is on the rise: data reveal drastic gap in survival rates
rows.summary: Lack of screening and limited treatment options mean that low- and middle-income countries face higher death rates despite having fewer cases than wealthier nations.

rows.title: Postdocs and PhD students hit hard by Trump’s crackdown on science
rows.summary: As US federal grants remain frozen and budget cuts loom, anxiety and fear grip early-career researchers.

rows.title: UK PhD students welcome 8% pay boost, but demand more to meet rising living costs
rows.summary: Minimum stipends will rise from October in line with living-wage levels, says the country's main funding agency.

rows.title: Stories of people, past, present and future: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: Tropical forest’s last old growth is being toppled — illegally
rows.summary: Satellite imagery helps to identify two hotspots of deforestation in the Atlantic Forest along Brazil’s eastern coast.

rows.title: How AI is revealing the language of the birds
rows.summary: Crows make a huge number of different sounds; Artificial Intelligence could help us understand what they mean.

rows.title: What sparked the COVID pandemic? Mounting evidence points to raccoon dogs
rows.summary: More than five years on, studies suggest the animal is the most likely culprit, but other candidates haven’t been ruled out.

rows.title: How a junk-food splurge can change your brain activity
rows.summary: A short bout of indulgence in fatty, sugary snacks leads to lingering brain-activity changes ― even if it does not cause weight gain.

rows.title: Putting early cancer detection to the test
rows.summary: Identifying tumours using blood samples is possible, but researchers are still working out how to validate and deploy multi-cancer tests.

rows.title: Cancer evolution could inform targets for personalized anticancer vaccines
rows.summary: Through comprehensive genomic and immune analyses, mechanisms of lung cancer resistance after treatment with EGFR inhibition and vaccine therapy were investigated. This case report, together with data from the longitudinal lung cancer study TRACERx, highlight the importance of understanding when targeted variants are acquired during the cancer’s evolutionary history.

rows.title: How to bring health and happiness to your lab
rows.summary: Can mindfulness, meditation and other tools designed to boost well-being make a difference? Adam Levy investigates.

rows.title: Asteroid 2024 YR4 now unlikely to hit Earth — but scientists are ready for future threats
rows.summary: Objects that could strike the planet will be spotted more regularly as new asteroid-hunting telescopes come online.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Where did COVID-19 come from? Evidence points to raccoon dogs
rows.summary: Where did the virus that causes COVID-19 come from? The number one suspect is the raccoon dog. Plus, what the brain can teach us about urban planning.

rows.title: Author Correction: The genetic origin of the Indo-Europeans
Trump’s siege of science: how the first 30 days unfolded and what’s next
rows.summary: The breakneck pace and devastating impact of the administration’s policy changes has shocked researchers.

rows.title: How leading a postdoc network boosted my career prospects
rows.summary: Tracy Wietecha says the experience swallowed up evenings and weekends, but taught her budgeting, networking and conflict-management skills.

rows.title: Daily briefing: First in-womb treatment for motor-neuron condition is a success
rows.summary: A motor-neuron condition has been successfully treated in the womb. Plus, how has one month of Donald Trump’s second presidency affected science?

rows.title: AI tool diagnoses diabetes, HIV and COVID from a blood sample
rows.summary: ‘One-shot’ approach that uses machine learning to screen immune cells could help to detect conditions with overlapping symptoms.

rows.title: Revealed: NIH research grants still frozen despite lawsuits challenging Trump order
rows.summary: The Trump administration is exploiting a loophole to keep a funding freeze in place, leaving researchers in limbo.

rows.title: Rare genetic disorder treated in womb for the first time
rows.summary: The child, who is now almost three years old, shows no signs of the often fatal motor neuron disease.

rows.title: Structural dynamics of human fatty acid synthase in the condensing cycle
rows.summary: A study examines functional human endogenous fatty acid synthase and characterizes its structural dynamics using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, providing insights into its dynamics during the fatty acid synthesis condensing cycle.

rows.title: Snapshots of acyl carrier protein shuttling in human fatty acid synthase
rows.summary: Using cryo-electron microscopy, the structures of mammalian fatty acid synthase reveal how the acyl carrier protein dynamically shuttles intermediates between selected active sites.

rows.title: Newfound bat virus that uses notorious receptor poses ‘spillover’ risk
rows.summary: The virus is related to the pathogen that causes Middle East respiratory syndrome and capitalizes on the same ‘entry receptor’ used by SARS-CoV-2.

rows.title: Low-iridium device speeds progress towards green hydrogen
rows.summary: A catalyst that reduces usage of an expensive rare metal could help to make hydrogen fuel affordable.

rows.title: Publisher Correction: Skin autonomous antibody production regulates host–microbiota interactions
Insufficient evidence for natural selection associated with the Black Death
Bespoke vaccines can elicit long-lived immune activity against pancreatic cancer
rows.summary: Cancer vaccines must induce immune cells, called CD8 + T cells, that can recognize cancer cells over the long term.
