rows.title: Copper-dependent halogenase catalyses unactivated C−H bond functionalization
rows.summary: A halogenase enzyme uses the copper in its active site to catalyse iterative chlorinations on multiple unactivated carbon−hydrogen bonds, enabling carbon−hydrogen functionalization that is not achievable with an iron-based halogenase.

rows.title: Signatures of longitudinal spin pumping in a magnetic phase transition
rows.summary: Longitudinal spin pumping is experimentally demonstrated using the magnetic phase transition of iron–rhodium, and the observed inverse spin Hall signal indicates that longitudinal spin pumping is driven by quantum fluctuations.

rows.title: Degradable thermosets via orthogonal polymerizations of a single monomer
rows.summary: Degradable thermoset multimaterials can be synthesized from a commercially accessible, biosourced monomer using orthogonal polymerizations in a single pot; after selective degredation, the resulting small molecules can be repolymerized.

rows.title: Maize monoculture supported pre-Columbian urbanism in southwestern Amazonia
rows.summary: Remote sensing, field survey and microbotanical analyses show that the pre-Columbian Casarabe culture in the Bolivian Amazon invested heavily in landscape engineering, constructing a complex system of drainage canals and newly documented savannah farm ponds.

rows.title: Contrasting drought sensitivity of Eurasian and North American grasslands
rows.summary: Eurasian grasslands have high production sensitivity to extreme drought compared with North American grasslands.

rows.title: Bat genomes illuminate adaptations to viral tolerance and disease resistance
rows.summary: A systematic analysis of 115 mammalian genomes, including 10 new bat genomes, reveals prevalent positive selection in immune genes in bats and shows key adaptations in the antiviral gene ISG15 that aid disease resistance in bats, including to coronaviruses.

rows.title: Expanding the human gut microbiome atlas of Africa
rows.summary: A cross-sectional study from four African countries shows the importance of investigating the gut microbiome in previously under-represented populations and provides a framework for equitable microbiome research.

rows.title: An evaporite sequence from ancient brine recorded in Bennu samples
rows.summary: Samples from the asteroid (101955) Bennu, returned by the OSIRIS-REx mission, include sodium-bearing phosphates and sodium-rich carbonates, sulfates, chlorides and fluorides formed during evaporation of a late-stage brine.

rows.title: The Ronne Ice Shelf survived the last interglacial
rows.summary: Sea salt data from an ice core record show that Antarctica’s Ronne Ice Shelf survived the last interglacial, the last period of enhanced and sustained global warmth about 125,000 years ago.

rows.title: CARD domains mediate anti-phage defence in bacterial gasdermin systems
rows.summary: Caspase recruitment domains (CARDs) are present in defence systems that protect bacteria against phage, where the bacterial CARD domain is essential for protease-mediated activation of bacterial gasdermins that promote cell death.

rows.title: Fine-tuning gibberellin improves rice alkali–thermal tolerance and yield
rows.summary: Precise regulation of the phytohormone gibberellin to optimal levels may not only confer alkali–thermal tolerance to Green Revolution rice varieties but may also further enhance their yield, and ATT2 , by enabling the fine-tuning of gibberellins, is expected to be a potential new post-Green Revolution gene.

rows.title: Global meta-analysis shows action is needed to halt genetic diversity loss
rows.summary: A comprehensive meta-analysis of global terrestrial and marine genetic diversity covering more than three decades of research demonstrates rapid loss of genetic diversity and identifies conservation interventions that could mitigate this process.

rows.title: Enhanced energy storage in antiferroelectrics via antipolar frustration
rows.summary: This study reports that incorporating non-polar nanodomains into antiferroelectrics greatly enhanced the energy density and efficiency.

rows.title: Nectar-robbing bees commit floral larceny
rows.summary: Our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive features progress in radiotherapy for cancer treatment a century ago, and bumblebees cheating to beat their competition.

rows.title: What lies beneath Europa’s icy surface? Perhaps a heart of metal
rows.summary: One of Jupiter’s biggest moons has the potential to harbour life in a subsurface sea. The nature of its core will provide information about that ocean.

rows.title: Canada’s postgraduate funding gap is still yawning even after budget increases
Author Correction: Continental influx and pervasive matrilocality in Iron Age Britain
Industrial projects in Chile threaten clear views of the Universe
India’s ‘One Nation’ publishing agreement is transformational — but beware inequities
No parent–child conflicts about when young cichlid fish leave home
rows.summary: Behavioural experiments in shell-dwelling cichlid fish reveal evolutionary adaptations in parents and offspring that control the timing of emergence from the nest.

rows.title: Author Correction: An RNA-dependent RNA polymerase formed by TERT and the RMRP RNA
Withdrawing funds from US vaccination programmes will worsen crisis of trust in public-health science
Did giant ice age beasts carve these vast caves in South America?
rows.summary: Researchers are investigating who — or what — cut ancient tunnels in sandstone in Brazil and nearby nations.

rows.title: Breaking up clusters of circulating tumour cells to halt cancer spread
rows.summary: A drug that limits the clustering of malignant breast-cancer cells that are moving through the bloodstream to distant organs might open avenues to block the lethal spread of a tumour.

rows.title: Chaos erupts in US science as Trump’s team declares freeze on federal grants
rows.summary: The freeze’s effect on research is still unclear, but scientists fear ‘incalculable’ damage.

rows.title: James Fraser Stoddart obituary: chemist and nanotechnology pioneer who built molecular machines
rows.summary: An early love of construction toys led the Scottish chemist to thread molecules together, opening up a new field of chemistry.

rows.title: Author Correction: Lithocholic acid phenocopies anti-ageing effects of calorie restriction
Daily briefing: The infinite optimism of polymath Gottfried Leibniz
rows.summary: Extreme heat will kill millions of people in Europe without rapid action on climate change. Plus, the tireless polymath who ‘couldn’t stop dreaming up ways to make the world better’.

rows.title: Our remote fieldwork taught us how to band together as scientists
rows.summary: Three early-career researchers thrown together on Sable Island, a treeless island in the North Atlantic, think others can learn from their experiences.

rows.title: Why more drilling doesn’t need to mean more harm to the environment
rows.summary: Looking at energy systems from resource extraction to end-use, not just individual components, can help.

rows.title: Ancient human genomes offer clues about the earliest migrations out of Africa
rows.summary: Analyses of 45,000-year-old bones from Europe allow scientists to pin down when modern humans interbred with Neanderthals, shedding light on the histories of populations with no present-day descendants.

rows.title: Why farmers are beginning to take their government to court over climate change
rows.summary: How a Swiss lawsuit is recasting agriculture’s role in climate policy.

rows.title: Humanity needs to diversify its lithium sources
rows.summary: The low-carbon transition needs batteries. And those need lithium. Fortunately, the metal is abundant, and science is getting better at finding, extracting and processing it.

rows.title: Author Correction: Gut microbiota strain richness is species specific and affects engraftment
How I find and explain plant fossils in Romania
rows.summary: From mines to metro stations, Mihai Emilian Popa analyses traces of the distant past.

rows.title: Even at one month, a baby’s brain shows an aptitude for smell
rows.summary: Brain regions linked to the sense of smell in adults were activated in infants exposed to the odours of petrol, strawberry and more.

rows.title: Retraction Note: A mechanism for the suppression of homologous recombination in G1 cells
Author Correction: Synthetic GPCRs for programmable sensing and control of cell behaviour
Four tips for writing the perfect ‘cold e-mail’ in job applications
rows.summary: These strategies can transform your unsolicited applications from forgettable to fabulous.

rows.title: Daily briefing: How a boy from the Bronx unearthed the workings of the Universe
rows.summary: Discover how to craft the perfect ‘cold e-mail’ job application. Plus, the swashbuckling memoir of physicist Steven Weinberg.

rows.title: Electric Dreams : exhibition reveals how artists can illuminate the unfolding AI revolution
rows.summary: Artwork created between 1945 and the 1990s captures a world in the throes of sweeping technological change.

rows.title: ‘Stamp out paper mills’ — science sleuths on how to fight fake research
rows.summary: A group of scientists who are experts at spotting fraudulent research outline five essential steps to combat industrialized scientific misconduct.

rows.title: Will bird flu spark a human pandemic? Scientists say the risk is rising
rows.summary: H5N1 is adapting to new mammalian hosts, raising the possibility of the virus spreading between humans.

rows.title: Four lessons COVID taught us about the immune system
rows.summary: Amid pandemic upheaval, researchers have gained fundamental insights about how the body fends off infections.

rows.title: Extreme heat will kill millions of people in Europe without rapid action
rows.summary: Climate models predict that the number of heat-related deaths could soar in cities over the coming century, even when efforts are made to keep people safe.

rows.title: How a boy from the Bronx unearthed the workings of the Universe
rows.summary: Nobel laureate Steven Weinberg’s posthumously published memoir details a swashbuckling life in physics.

rows.title: Daily briefing: What went wrong at 23andMe
rows.summary: Scientists are defecting to Bluesky from X en masse. Plus, the bumps in the road that led to 23andMe’s downfall.

rows.title: Star ecologist accused of misconduct loses university post
rows.summary: Tree researcher Thomas Crowther is seeking to move his laboratory from ETH Zurich, which says it will not renew his contract.

rows.title: Bluesky’s science takeover: 70% of Nature poll respondents use platform
rows.summary: Roughly 6,000 readers answered our poll, with many declaring that Bluesky was nicer, kinder and less antagonistic to science than X.

rows.title: ‘Do I need to lead this lifestyle to succeed?’ The mental health crises that forced faculty members to change tack
rows.summary: The pressures faced by lab leaders to be excellent researchers, teachers, managers, accountants and mentors can exact a heavy toll.

rows.title: The surprising link between muscle and the reproductive system
rows.summary: Myostatin, which blocks muscle development, unexpectedly has an effect on ovulation in female mice.

rows.title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Telomere dysfunction and Atm deficiency compromises organ homeostasis and accelerates ageing
Pioneering CERN scheme will pay publishers more if they hit open-science targets
rows.summary: The particle-physics funder will provide financial incentives to encourage practices such as data sharing and transparent peer review.

rows.title: What went wrong at 23andMe? Why the genetic-data giant risks collapse
rows.summary: At-home DNA testing is no longer in high demand — and critics have raised concerns about unreliable tests and privacy.

rows.title: China’s cheap, open AI model DeepSeek thrills scientists
rows.summary: DeepSeek-R1 performs reasoning tasks at the same level as OpenAI’s o1 — and is open for researchers to examine.

rows.title: ‘Never seen anything like this’: Trump’s team halts NIH meetings and travel
rows.summary: In an unprecedented move, research-grant reviews have been suspended indefinitely at the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research.

rows.title: Microplastics block blood flow in the brain, mouse study reveals
rows.summary: Real-time imaging shows how plastic-stuffed cells form clumps that affect mouse movement.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Cancer ‘poisons’ the immune system by giving it faulty machinery
rows.summary: Microplastics are piling up “like a car crash” in the brains of mice. Plus, cancer ‘poisons’ immune cells to deactivate them.

rows.title: Seaweed farms dish up climate benefits
rows.summary: First estimate of its type shows that cultivated seaweed beds can accumulate as much carbon as some natural ecosystems.

rows.title: Cancer cells ‘poison’ the immune system with tainted mitochondria
rows.summary: Immune cells lose their cancer-fighting prowess after taking tumours’ organelles on board.

rows.title: Mitochondrial swap from cancer to immune cells thwarts anti-tumour defences
rows.summary: Immune cells can destroy cancer, but tumours often evade such responses. The bidirectional transfer of mitochondria between cancer and immune cells is a newly discovered mechanism that thwarts anticancer defences.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Scientific serendipity is everywhere
rows.summary: The chance of a lucky break in biomedical research increases with bigger funding grants. Plus, the changing landscape of menopause treatments.

rows.title: Want to become a professor? Here’s how hiring criteria differ by country
rows.summary: Huge analysis identifies regional variations in the criteria that institutions use to move researchers up the ranks.

rows.title: Menopause research is globally underfunded. It’s time to change that
rows.summary: Nature asked the world’s largest health-research funders what they are doing to study a life stage experienced by half of humanity. Here is what some of them told us.

rows.title: From trainee to trainer: how I’m empowering imaging scientists in Latin America
rows.summary: A lack of experienced imaging trainers in her native Uruguay put Marcela Díaz on the path towards mentorship.

rows.title: A scalable system using mini-organs to test personalized RNA therapy
rows.summary: A rapid and efficient method developed to create stem-cell-based 3D mini-organs derived from the cells of patients offers a way to evaluate personalized treatments using RNA therapies for rare genetic diseases.

rows.title: Large study broadens view of the genetic landscape of bipolar disorder
rows.summary: A multi-ancestry genome-wide study of 158,036 people with bipolar disorder and 2,796,499 control individuals identified 298 genomic regions associated with the disease. Variations in 36 genes were linked to the condition, and this variation was enriched in certain neuronal cell populations. The genetic architecture underlying bipolar disorder varied with subtype and how cases were identified.

rows.title: US scientist cleared of hiding ties to China sues university that fired him
rows.summary: Feng ‘Franklin’ Tao says that the University of Kansas violated its own policies after he was wrongly arrested under the China Initiative.

rows.title: The new science of menopause: these emerging therapies could change women’s health
rows.summary: Researchers are exploring how to prolong ovarian life and revisiting hormone replacement therapy — a once routine treatment that has fallen out of favour.

rows.title: Mass testing of mutant enzymes involved in photosynthesis
rows.summary: Rubisco is the enzyme responsible for carbon fixation in plants, algae and many bacteria. A screen of a comprehensive library of rubisco variants (each with a different single-amino-acid mutation), expressed in engineered bacteria, identifies several mutations that improve the enzyme’s affinity for carbon dioxide.

rows.title: A quantum material governed by emergent Weyl fermions
rows.summary: In certain crystals, quasiparticles called Weyl fermions emerge from the collective quantum behaviour of electrons. However, these quasiparticles typically coexist with undesired conventional electronic states. After a decade-long search, physicists have engineered a crystal without conventional electronic states and with quantum properties governed entirely by Weyl fermions. Such materials could be useful for detecting and generating terahertz light.

rows.title: Multimodal cell mapping with optimal transport
rows.summary: Moscot is a cell-mapping framework based on the concept of optimal transport. It can analyse large-scale single-cell data, enabling mapping of the developmental trajectories of individual cells in and across organs. Moscot is scalable to millions of cells, and can track several cell characteristics simultaneously in space and time.

rows.title: X chromosome passed from mother to daughter influences brain ageing
rows.summary: Older female mice show poor spatial memory when their paternal X chromosome is inactive and only the maternal copy is active. This phenomenon could be responsible for variation in age-related cognitive decline among women.

rows.title: Please listen carefully because our menu options have recently changed
rows.summary: We’re here to help.

rows.title: What’s the best way to become a professor? The answer depends on where you are
rows.summary: Huge study highlights global discrepancy in hiring requirements — plus, how cancer cells palm-off misfiring mitochondria to help avoid destruction.

rows.title: Chirping chorus rings out from an unexpected part of outer space
rows.summary: Bursts of electromagnetic radiation that share similarities with birdsong have long been observed close to Earth. A detection farther out in space confirms a key part of the theory of their origin, but also poses questions.

rows.title: A map of parental-DNA exchanges charts course for studies of human evolution
rows.summary: Human genetic diversity and evolution rely on new mutations and exchange of DNA between chromosomes during the generation of sex cells, in a process called recombination. Recombination manifests as large-scale crossovers, and as short-scale transitions called non-crossovers. A map of where recombination occurs throughout the human genome now includes both types of variation.

rows.title: Neuromorphic computing at scale
rows.summary: Approaches for the development of future at-scale neuromorphic systems based on principles of biointelligence are described, along with potential applications of scalable neuromorphic architectures and the challenges that need to be overcome.

rows.title: Extended quantum anomalous Hall states in graphene/hBN moiré superlattices
rows.summary: New topological states have been observed in rhombohedral graphene/hBN moiré superlattices, including fractional and extended quantum anomalous Hall effects, at ultra-low temperatures, demonstrating the rich quantum phenomena emerging from correlated electrons in topological flat bands.

rows.title: Resolving native GABA A receptor structures from the human brain
rows.summary: Cryo-electron microscopy structures of native type A GABA receptors from human brain reveal diverse subunit compositions, protein binding partners and binding sites for antiepileptic drugs.

rows.title: Genomics yields biological and phenotypic insights into bipolar disorder
rows.summary: Using multi-ancestry genome-wide association study and fine-mapping, 298 loci and 36 credible genes are identified in the aetiology of bipolar disorder.

rows.title: Experience-dependent dopamine modulation of male aggression
rows.summary: Dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area have a role in modulating aggression in adult male mice, and this effect of dopamine depends strongly on fighting experience.

rows.title: Superconductivity in 5.0° twisted bilayer WSe 2
rows.summary: We report superconductivity, in a limited region of displacement field and density, in 5.0° twisted bilayer WSe 2 with a maximum critical temperature of 426 mK, establishing that moiré flat-band superconductivity extends beyond graphene structures.

rows.title: Tissue-resident memory CD8 T cell diversity is spatiotemporally imprinted
rows.summary: Profiling of the location and transcriptome of tissue-resident memory CD8 T cell formation at single-transcript resolution finds regionalized signalling as the basis of immune diversity in the intestine and provides a conceptual framework for the study of tissue immune networks.

rows.title: Field–particle energy transfer during chorus emissions in space
rows.summary: Whistler-mode chorus waves have been observed in the tail region of the terrestrial magnetosphere, where the magnetic field is not dipolar so that chorus waves were not expected, and their generation mechanisms have been tested with state-of-the-art observations.

rows.title: Global 3D model of mantle attenuation using seismic normal modes
rows.summary: Using whole-Earth oscillations to constrain a 3D global model of attenuation for the whole mantle, low attenuation correlates with low velocity in the lower mantle, suggesting long-lived deep-mantle provinces.

rows.title: The maternal X chromosome affects cognition and brain ageing in female mice
rows.summary: The maternal X chromosome in female mice impairs cognition through the silencing of certain genes and accelerates ageing of the hippocampus.

rows.title: RELMβ sets the threshold for microbiome-dependent oral tolerance
rows.summary: RELMβ mediates a gut immune–epithelial circuit regulating tolerance to food antigens, offering targetable candidates for the prevention and treatment of food allergies.

rows.title: A map of the rubisco biochemical landscape
rows.summary: A massively parallel assay developed to map the essential photosynthetic enzyme rubisco showed that non-trivial biochemical changes and improvements in CO 2 affinity are possible, signposting further enzyme engineering efforts to increase crop yields.

rows.title: Precise modelling of mitochondrial diseases using optimized mitoBEs
rows.summary: A study reports optimized mitochondrial base editors with reduced off-target effects to facilitate the generation of mouse models of human mitochondrial diseases.

rows.title: Multiscale footprints reveal the organization of cis -regulatory elements
rows.summary: We developed PRINT, a computational method that identifies footprints of DNA–protein interactions from bulk and single-cell chromatin accessibility data across multiple scales of protein size.

rows.title: Rapid and scalable personalized ASO screening in patient-derived organoids
rows.summary: A scalable platform for generating patient-specific organoids for testing personalized oligonucleotide therapeutics is described.

rows.title: Leveraging a phased pangenome for haplotype design of hybrid potato
rows.summary: A phased pangenome of potato constructed from 60 wild and cultivated haplotypes shows that substantial hybridization occurred during domestication and enables identification of many putative deleterious variants, providing a basis for the design of improved inbred lines.

rows.title: Immune evasion through mitochondrial transfer in the tumour microenvironment
rows.summary: Mitochondria with mutations in their DNA from cancer cells can be transferred to T cells in the tumour microenvironment, which leads to T cell dysfunction and impaired antitumour immunity.

rows.title: Complete human recombination maps
rows.summary: Complete human recombination maps are presented that enable exploration of both cross-over and non-cross-over events during meiosis, with the potential to provide insight into the causes of aneuploidies and pregnancy loss.

rows.title: Synthesis of a semimetallic Weyl ferromagnet with point Fermi surface
rows.summary: Van der Waals (Cr,Bi) 2 Te 3 , synthesized by non-equilibrium molecular beam epitaxy, is characterized by magnetotransport measurements and shown to be a semimetallic Weyl ferromagnet, with Fermi surface composed of two Weyl points and no irrelevant electronic states.

rows.title: Mapping cells through time and space with moscot
rows.summary: Moscot is an optimal transport approach that overcomes current limitations of similar methods to enable multimodal, scalable and consistent single-cell analyses of datasets across spatial and temporal dimensions.

rows.title: Ultrabroadband integrated electro-optic frequency comb in lithium tantalate
rows.summary: An integrated electro-optic frequency comb that combines microwave integrated circuits with a photonic circuit based on lithium tantalate leads to broadband operation with low power requirements.

rows.title: Regional and institutional trends in assessment for academic promotion
rows.summary: Analysis of policies for promotion criteria to full professor from academic institutions and government agencies worldwide reveals considerable variation in assessment practices, particularly between the Global North and South.

rows.title: CD45-PET is a robust, non-invasive tool for imaging inflammation
rows.summary: A non-invasive in vivo positron emission tomography imaging approach detects inflammatory disease using various preclinical models.

rows.title: Moiré-driven topological electronic crystals in twisted graphene
rows.summary: We report signatures of a generalized version of the anomalous Hall crystal in twisted bilayer–trilayer graphene, whose formation is driven by the moiré potential.

rows.title: Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer
rows.summary: A proof-of-principle study reports a complete photonic quantum computer architecture that can, once appropriate component performance is achieved, deliver a universal and fault-tolerant quantum computer.

rows.title: Rubbish under the floorboards exposes secret snacking in colonial Australia
rows.summary: Seeds, fruit stones and other remnants hidden in a Sydney barracks in the nineteenth century show residents’ deviation from the standard diet.

rows.title: Africa can’t wait for pandemic preparedness
For open communication, give researchers a permanent e-mail alias
All together now: chimps engage in contagious peeing
rows.summary: If one animal urinates, others are likely follow, according to a study of captive apes.

rows.title: Why AI will never be able to acquire human-level intelligence
The Doppler effect explained with steam trains
rows.summary: Our weekly peek at Nature ’s archive features musings on knowledge, and a physical phenomenon exemplified by the toot of a passing train.

rows.title: Faced with funding cuts, collaborate to define research priorities
Beyond black and white: an ecologist applies racial-justice principles to predators and their ecosystems
rows.summary: Tyus Williams harnesses his lived experiences to inform his research — and shares it all on social media.

rows.title: AI hallucinations can’t be stopped — but these techniques can limit their damage
rows.summary: Developers have tricks to stop artificial intelligence from making things up, but large language models are still struggling to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

rows.title: How I use data to highlight complex and overlooked work in health-care systems
rows.summary: Workforce modeller Alison Leary says that nursing and academia face similar gender-based challenges to recruit and retain staff.

rows.title: Build a DNA database to help identify children stolen in conflicts
rows.summary: The secure and ethical use of genetic testing can assist family reunifications in Ukraine and other settings for humanitarian disasters.

rows.title: Why we still don’t know the mounting health risks of climate change
rows.summary: Persistent exposure to heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and more will take a toll on people’s bodies. We must learn how this will manifest.

rows.title: Quantum stock whiplash: what’s next for quantum computing?
rows.summary: Despite stock-market jitters, firms in the sector continue to make progress — and to score hundreds of millions of dollars in investments.

rows.title: Octopuses changing colour rapidly incur a high metabolic cost
rows.summary: Colour change in animals can occur over different timescales and aids communication and camouflage. Direct evidence of the associated energetic costs has been lacking, but now an experimental study of octopuses fills this gap.

rows.title: More than 40% of postdocs leave academia, study reveals
rows.summary: Publishing highly cited papers helps postdoctoral researchers to land a faculty job.

rows.title: How often do unexpected scientific discoveries occur? More often than you might think
rows.summary: A study assessed 1.2 million biomedical publications and measured the ‘unexpectedness’ of their findings.

rows.title: What Trump’s flurry of executive orders means for science
rows.summary: The new president has signed decrees designed to shift the US government’s stance on climate and public health.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Huge study highlights new health risks of obesity drugs
rows.summary: Blockbuster weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic could raise a person’s likelihood of developing arthritis. Plus, how to reimburse young people for their participation in research.

rows.title: Sharing is caring and other moving stories: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: I explore the impact of wildfires on Hawaii’s coral reefs
rows.summary: Oceanographer Andrea Kealoha studies how the devastating Lahaina wildfire of 2023 affected the coral systems of Maui.

rows.title: Young people are crucial to research — how can they be paid fairly?
rows.summary: Children and teenagers bring unique value to research as advisers and participants — raising ethical and practical issues about how best to compensate them.

rows.title: Paralysed man flies virtual drone using brain implant
rows.summary: Device that links neural signals to fine movements provides unprecedented control over speed and direction in a video-game obstacle course.

rows.title: How to navigate uncertainty in an unpredictable world
rows.summary: A statistician offers a masterful guide to embracing the unknown.

rows.title: Martin Karplus obituary: theoretical chemist who first simulated proteins using molecular dynamics
rows.summary: The Nobel prizewinner used quantum and molecular mechanics to model the dynamics of complex chemical systems.

rows.title: Self-driving laboratories, advanced immunotherapies and five more technologies to watch in 2025
rows.summary: Sustainability and artificial intelligence dominate our seventh annual round-up of exciting innovations.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Who are Trump’s science advisers
rows.summary: A type of microRNA seems to revitalize old mice. Plus, the influence of US president Donald Trump on science in the United States, and on health and climate globally.

rows.title: How hosting Ukrainian scientists offers a template for supporting other scholars at risk
rows.summary: Ahead of the third anniversary of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, displaced academics describe their experiences settling into UK universities.

rows.title: Author Correction: R-loop-dependent promoter-proximal termination ensures genome stability
‘Publish or perish’ culture blamed for reproducibility crisis
rows.summary: Survey of more than 1,600 biomedical researchers also flagged small sample sizes and cherry-picking of data as leading causes of reproducibility problems.

rows.title: Obesity drugs: huge study identifies new health risks
rows.summary: Weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic might raise a person’s likelihood of developing conditions including arthritis.

rows.title: Science on the go: bringing labs into the field
rows.summary: ‘Lab vans’ and other facilities can bring researchers closer to what they study.

rows.title: Methane oxidation to ethanol by a molecular junction photocatalyst
rows.summary: Mechanistic insights into a photocatalyst with an intramolecular junction and two different active sites could inspire further exploration of ‘intramolecular heterojunctions’ as the basis of selective and stable photocatalysts for C–H activation and C–C coupling.

rows.title: Mines for a clean-energy metal have a surprise climate effect
rows.summary: Vegetation clearing to extract nickel, which is used in renewable technologies, leads to greater carbon emissions than realized.

rows.title: RNA molecule rejuvenates ageing mice by restoring old cells
rows.summary: Mice injected with a microRNA molecule lived longer and had fewer markers of ageing, but it’s not yet known if the treatment would work in people.

rows.title: Why fires spread quickly in modern cities — and how to slow them down
rows.summary: In the aftermath of deadly blazes in Los Angeles, researchers also suggest ways to make homes more resilient.

rows.title: Trump’s science advisers: how they could influence his second presidency
rows.summary: The president-elect quickly nominated confidantes with a focus on AI, but their recommendations for the rest of science remain unclear.

rows.title: How to be a brilliant ally to your neurodivergent lab mate
rows.summary: Two researchers, one with bipolar disorder and ADHD, the other with autism, discuss supportive workplaces, building networks, and how and when to disclose diagnoses.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The brickbats hurled at scientists researching tobacco’s harms
rows.summary: The science behind urban firestorms, and how to fight them. Plus, how public-health researchers are targeted for focusing on tobacco, alcohol and ultra-processed foods.

rows.title: Revealed: Why the fatal Huntington’s gene takes so long to cause harm
rows.summary: A mutation in neurons grows for decades before it reaches a deadly limit.

rows.title: How to trick the immune system into attacking tumours
rows.summary: Lab-grown viruses make cancer cells resemble pig tissue, provoking an organ-rejection response.

rows.title: Trump will weaken climate action — the rest of the US must not follow suit
rows.summary: Researchers, governments and others can all play a part in ensuring climate policies remain in the interest of all.

rows.title: Championing queer scientists of colour: ‘I don’t think we’ve scratched the surface on systemic exclusion’
rows.summary: Arachnologist Lauren Esposito develops community platforms to share LGBTQ+ voices and wants to shed light on the overlooked intersectional barriers affecting queer people of colour.

rows.title: Daily briefing: AI-designed proteins offer lifeline for treating snake bites
rows.summary: Artificial intelligence-designed proteins could block the deadly effects of snake venom. Plus, who are science’s winners and losers under Trump 2.0?

rows.title: Brain-wide neuronal circuit connectome of human glioblastoma
rows.summary: A study leveraging transsynaptic tracing demonstrates rapid and extensive integration of human glioblastoma organoids into the mouse brain.

rows.title: A generative model for inorganic materials design
rows.summary: MatterGen is a model that generates stable, diverse inorganic materials across the periodic table and can further be fine-tuned to steer the generation towards a broad range of property constraints.

rows.title: Author Correction: An endosomal tether undergoes an entropic collapse to bring vesicles together
AI-designed antivenoms could help treat lethal snakebites
rows.summary: Proteins made using machine learning successfully bind snake toxins — plus, Earth’s temperature breaks a significant climate threshold for the first time.

rows.title: Hidden tattoos on mummy skin emerge under a laser’s light
rows.summary: Blurry markings more than 1,000 years old become clear again thanks to scanning method.

rows.title: Got flu? Promising drug shortens symptoms
rows.summary: Influenza viruses have not evolved resistance to suraxavir marboxil, which relieves cough, fever and other symptoms.

rows.title: Women were at the centre of social networks in Iron Age Britain
rows.summary: Evidence from 2,000-year-old DNA reveals that women in Celtic society stayed in their ancestral communities after marriage, whereas men were mobile, and that the southern coast of Britain was a hotspot for cultural exchange.

rows.title: Will Europe ramp up defence research? War prompts major rethink
rows.summary: Nations consider increasing universities’ involvement in military research.

rows.title: Two companies launch Moon missions together: will they make history?
rows.summary: A pair of spacecraft developed by private firms blast off on a single rocket on the risky voyage to the lunar surface.

rows.title: Author Correction: Evolution of immune genes is associated with the Black Death
Road trip
rows.summary: Winner takes all.

rows.title: The road to CAR-T-cell therapy for lethal childhood brain tumours
rows.summary: A phase I clinical trial of GD2-CAR T cells (immune cells engineered to target the molecule GD2) in children and young adults with diffuse midline gliomas — incurable cancers of the central nervous system — shows promising results. Several trial participants exhibited substantial improvements, and one child’s tumour has been undetectable for more than three years.

rows.title: A mutation makes plant roots more welcoming to beneficial microbes
rows.summary: Promoting mutually beneficial relationships between plants and soil microbes that enhance nutrient acquisition by plants could improve crop production without increasing inorganic-fertilizer use. A mutation that causes an amino-acid substitution in a channel called CNGC15 in the plant cell’s nucleus boosts the formation of such endosymbiotic relationships.

rows.title: Striving for open-source and equitable speech-to-speech translation
rows.summary: US technology company Meta has produced an AI model that can directly translate speech in one language to speech in another. Two scientists discuss the technical feats and ethical questions that underpin this advance in machine translation.

rows.title: Meta AI creates speech-to-speech translator that works in dozens of languages
rows.summary: Machine-learning system can process words spoken in 101 languages, spitting out voice-synthesized translations in 36 target languages.

rows.title: What Trump 2.0 means for science: the likely winners and losers
rows.summary: The incoming US president is expected to gut support for research on the environment and infectious diseases, but could buoy work in artificial intelligence, quantum research and space exploration.

rows.title: Imaging reveals how plants cope with salt
rows.summary: A groundbreaking imaging method for tracking salt inside plant cells has rewritten knowledge of how roots handle toxic levels of sodium ions. The findings might aid efforts to boost plant resilience to stress driven by high levels of salt.

rows.title: Dear Donald Trump: A letter from Nature on how to make science thrive
rows.summary: The US federal government can harness science to secure the health, prosperity and safety of Americans and the world.

rows.title: Daily briefing: New obesity definition sidelines BMI to focus on health
rows.summary: Researchers offer a more nuanced definition of obesity. Plus, two private Moon missions launch at the same time.

rows.title: Gene drives development of brain’s emotional centre and its connections
rows.summary: A brain structure called the amygdala, and its connections with another region, the prefrontal cortex, shape people’s experiences and social interactions. The discovery of a key molecular mechanism that controls the development of these structures uncovers principles about how cortico-amygdala circuits form, and shows how this connectivity might be altered in neuropsychiatric disorders.

rows.title: Two eighth-century communities near Vienna shared culture but not ancestries
rows.summary: An interdisciplinary analysis of ancient DNA obtained from 722 individuals who lived in the region during the Avar period (between about ad 650 and ad 800) shows that two neighbouring communities had strikingly different genetic ancestries. Two family trees comprising six generations and some 500 related individuals reveal that different marriage networks kept these communities genetically distinct despite their shared culture.

rows.title: AI-designed proteins tackle century-old problem — making snake antivenoms
rows.summary: Machine learning has supercharged the field of computational protein design.

rows.title: Episodic and associative memory from spatial scaffolds in the hippocampus
rows.summary: A neocortical–entorhinal–hippocampal network model based on grid cell states recapitulates experimental results and reconciles the spatial, associative and episodic memory roles of the hippocampus.

rows.title: All-solid-state Li–S batteries with fast solid–solid sulfur reaction
rows.summary: By using lithium thioborophosphate iodide glass-phase solid electrolytes in all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries, fast solid–solid sulfur redox reaction is demonstrated, leading to cells with ultrafast charging capability, superior cycling stability and high capacity.

rows.title: Continental influx and pervasive matrilocality in Iron Age Britain
rows.summary: An analysis of ancient mitochondrial and nuclear DNA shows evidence of matrilocal communities in Iron Age Britain.

rows.title: Targeting protein–ligand neosurfaces with a generalizable deep learning tool
rows.summary: A computational deep learning approach is used to design synthetic proteins that target the neosurfaces formed by protein–ligand interactions, with applications in the development of new therapeutic modalities such as molecular glues or cell-based therapies.

rows.title: Prolonged persistence of mutagenic DNA lesions in somatic cells
rows.summary: Persistent DNA lesions can occur throughout the human lifespan and can remain in the genome of affected cells for several years and generate a substantial proportion of the mutational burden.

rows.title: The human and non-human primate developmental GTEx projects
rows.summary: The developmental Genotype-Tissue Expression (dGTEx) projects will catalogue and integrate gene expression, regulation and genetics data across 120 human donors from birth to adulthood with developmentally matched non-human primates, including 126 rhesus macaques and 72 common marmosets.

rows.title: GZMK-expressing CD8 + T cells promote recurrent airway inflammatory diseases
rows.summary: Comparing T cells in nasal polyps from repeated surgeries shows that effector memory-like persistent clones colonize the mucosal tissue during disease recurrence and promote inflammation by producing Granzyme K, a complement-activating tryptase, which is a potential therapeutic target.

rows.title: Massively parallel characterization of transcriptional regulatory elements
rows.summary: Lentivirus-based reporter assays for 680,000 regulatory sequences from three cell lines coupled to machine-learning models lead to insights into the grammar of cis -regulatory elements.

rows.title: Structural insights into RNA cleavage by PIWI Argonaute
rows.summary: After target binding, PIWI proteins undergo a conformational change from ‘open’ to ‘locked’, facilitating base pairing and enhancing target cleavage efficiency, providing insights into how dynamic conformational changes from PIWI coordinate cofactors to safeguard gametogenesis.

rows.title: Targeting FOXM1 condensates reduces breast tumour growth and metastasis
rows.summary: The transcription factor FOXM1 forms functional condensates, the formation of which can be targeted with a specific peptide to suppress breast cancer growth and metastasis.

rows.title: IL-33-activated ILC2s induce tertiary lymphoid structures in pancreatic cancer
rows.summary: IL-33 induces tertiary lymphoid structures.

rows.title: Long-lived entanglement of molecules in magic-wavelength optical tweezers
rows.summary: By engineering an exceptionally controlled environment using rotationally magic optical tweezers, long-lived entanglement between pairs of molecules using detectable hertz-scale interactions can be achieved.

rows.title: De novo designed proteins neutralize lethal snake venom toxins
rows.summary: Deep learning methods have been used to design proteins that can neutralize the effects of three-finger toxins found in snake venom, which could lead to the development of safer and more accessible antivenom treatments.

rows.title: Ensemble reactivations during brief rest drive fast learning of sequences
rows.summary: In macaques, motor cortex activity associated with motor learning tasks is reactivated during brief breaks between learning blocks and predicts subsequent performance gains.

rows.title: Bilayer nanographene reveals halide permeation through a benzene hole
rows.summary: Halide permeation through a single benzene-sized defect in a molecular nanographene shows the permeability of fluoride, chloride and bromide, whereas iodide is impermeable.

rows.title: Autoactive CNGC15 enhances root endosymbiosis in legume and wheat
rows.summary: Nuclear calcium oscillations initiate plant–arbuscular mycorrhiza and nitrogen-fixing bacteria symbioses for nutrient acquisition, with a newly discovered autoactive CNGC15 mutant enhancing these partnerships, potentially improving crop nutrition and reducing inorganic fertilizer dependence.

rows.title: Engineered enzymes for enantioselective nucleophilic aromatic substitutions
rows.summary: A biocatalytic approach to enantioselective nucleophilic aromatic substitution (S N Ar) was achieved through laboratory evolution of highly efficient and selective S N Arase biocatalysts.

rows.title: Methane emissions from the Nord Stream subsea pipeline leaks
rows.summary: Modelling of the evolution of atmospheric methane emissions from the 2022 Nord Stream subsea pipeline leaks shows that the event emitted the largest recorded amount of methane from a single transient event.

rows.title: Illuminating the multidimensional contributions of small-scale fisheries
rows.summary: A study aimed at revealing the role of small-scale fisheries in sustainable development shows they provide at least 40% of the global fishing catch and affect the livelihoods of 1 in 12 people in the world, among other important contributions.

rows.title: Widespread occurrence and relevance of phosphate storage in foraminifera
rows.summary: Phosphate storage in foraminifera is found to be widespread, indicating that these organisms are probably relevant for marine phosphorus cycling and potentially buffer anthropogenic eutrophication in coastal environments.

rows.title: Elemental cryo-imaging reveals SOS1-dependent vacuolar sodium accumulation
rows.summary: This study demonstrates that cryo nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (CryoNanoSIMS) enables direct multi-elemental imaging at subcellular resolution of macro- and micronutrients or trace elements in plants and may provide insights into the in vivo roles of many transporters.

rows.title: Transducing chemical energy through catalysis by an artificial molecular motor
rows.summary: A cross-linked polymer gel driven by artificial molecular motors transforms chemical energy into mechanical force, achieving powered contraction and re-expansion, demonstrating a considerable advance in understanding energy transduction mechanisms and informing nanotechnology design principles.

rows.title: Clouds reduce downwelling longwave radiation over land in a warming climate
rows.summary: Results derived from an optimal spectral fingerprinting method applied to reanalysis and satellite datasets show that low cloud cover in warming climates caused a reduction in downwelling longwave radiation over land, which is not site specific.

rows.title: Pathogenesis of bovine H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b infection in macaques
rows.summary: Routes of infection with bovine highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in cynomolgus macaques are investigated, and in contrast to orogastric inoculation, intranasal or intratracheal inoculation could cause systemic infection resulting in mild and severe respiratory disease, respectively.

rows.title: Joint speech and text machine translation for up to 100 languages
rows.summary: SEAMLESSM4T is a single machine translation tool that supports speech-to-speech translation, speech-to-text translation, text-to-speech translation, text-to-text translation and automatic speech recognition between up to 100 languages.

rows.title: Specification of claustro-amygdalar and palaeocortical neurons and circuits
rows.summary: A conserved gene regulatory network involving SOX4 , SOX11 and TFAP2D shapes the development of excitatory neurons in ventrolateral pallium and their connectivity with the prefrontal cortex.

rows.title: Cationic peptides cause memory loss through endophilin-mediated endocytosis
rows.summary: Elucidation of the mechanism by which zeta inhibitory peptide erases memories, involving endocytosis of AMPA receptors on potentiated synapses, provides insight into more general mechanisms of memory maintenance and response to traumatic brain injury.

rows.title: Ancient DNA reveals reproductive barrier despite shared Avar-period culture
rows.summary: Ancient genome-wide data of 722 individuals and interdisciplinary analysis of large seventh- to eighth-century ce neighbouring cemeteries near Vienna are used to address the impact of the encounter between Eastern Asian Avars and Europeans.

rows.title: Philanthropic foundations must step in to shield science from Trump’s cuts
Has Bluesky replaced X for scientists? Take Nature ’s poll
rows.summary: The research community has flocked to the social-media platform Bluesky. Tell us about your experience.

rows.title: Advising policymakers can’t be taught — researchers must learn by doing
The scientific reason to cook with simmering rather than vigorously boiling water
rows.summary: An energy-efficient lesson for the kitchen that is still relevant 150 years later, and the automation of long-distance communication by telephone or text gathers pace, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: AlphaFold 3 is great — but it still needs human help to get chemistry right
Remove subsidies to solve India’s fertilizer-overuse problem
Social-media bans won’t work — there are better ways to keep kids safe
rows.summary: Planned bans — such as in Australia — should be replaced with research and resources to educate parents and carers about the best ways to manage their children’s use of social media.

rows.title: How science recruiters and job applicants can get on the same page
rows.summary: Nature ’s survey of hiring in science has revealed a gulf between the expectations of people looking for jobs in science and those who hire.

rows.title: How should we test AI for human-level intelligence? OpenAI’s o3 electrifies quest
rows.summary: Experimental model’s record-breaking performance on science and maths tests wows researchers.

rows.title: Retractions caused by honest mistakes are extremely stressful, say researchers
rows.summary: A survey highlights the emotional toll of retractions for authors and what could be done differently.

rows.title: How to sustain scientific collaboration amid worsening US–China relations
rows.summary: Researchers need to define ‘safe zones’ for joint work in which the benefits outweigh the political risks. Here’s how.

rows.title: Harsh criticism and unreasonable expectations worsen PhD students’ mental health
rows.summary: Research and teaching pressures can exacerbate anxiety and depression, causing many young scientists to consider quitting, a survey finds.

rows.title: AI-powered contract automation helps research managers level up
rows.summary: Laura Arfi and Shannen Lau are automating routine tasks to free up time for more strategic work.

rows.title: New obesity definition sidelines BMI to focus on health
rows.summary: Fresh approach to diagnosing the condition looks at how excess body fat affects the body.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Pluto-Charon duet started with a gravitational ‘kiss-and-capture’
rows.summary: Pluto might have caught its largest moon with a ‘kiss’. Plus, is air pollution messing with our minds?

rows.title: The astonishing scientists who starved to protect plants during the Second World War
rows.summary: The trials and tribulations of the world’s first seed bank reveal botanists’ enormous generosity and sacrifice during the siege of Leningrad.

rows.title: Do you need extra training before graduate school? Consider a post-baccalaureate position
rows.summary: Many US graduates seek short-term positions to enhance their CVs in an increasingly competitive landscape for graduate admissions.

rows.title: Air pollution and brain damage: what the science says
rows.summary: Epidemiological studies have linked dirty air to dementia and other brain disorders. Now researchers are trying to determine how pollutants do their damage, and how much harm they cause.

rows.title: My work on quantum computing aims to solve the world’s most complex problems
rows.summary: Sang-Wook Han hopes that the technology will spark innovations in materials science, drug development, finance and defence.

rows.title: Pictograms, comics and other illustrations: Books in brief
rows.summary: Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

rows.title: Did Pluto ‘kiss and capture’ its largest moon?
rows.summary: Cutting-edge simulations reveal a new potential mechanism by which Pluto trapped its biggest satellite, Charon.

rows.title: PhD parents: the pros and cons of having a child during your doctorate
rows.summary: Early-career researchers describe how they juggled workloads, emotions and finances after having children.

rows.title: A new vision for how evolution works is long overdue
rows.summary: The idea that evolution is driven by an organism’s development — not just the natural selection of its genes — challenges a dearly held orthodoxy among evolutionary biologists.

rows.title: ‘Expansion microscopy’ turns ten: how a tissue-swelling method brought super-resolution imaging to the masses
rows.summary: A decade in, expansion microscopy is unlocking insights across biology and medicine.

rows.title: Daily briefing: The science behind the deadly Los Angeles firestorm
rows.summary: Just ten bacterial species account for half of all publications, leaving the majority ignored. Plus, the complex reasons driving the deadly Los Angeles wildfires.

rows.title: ‘Nicotine Nazis’: the brickbats hurled at scientists researching tobacco’s harms
rows.summary: A study highlights how public-health researchers are targeted for focusing on tobacco, alcohol and ultra-processed foods.

rows.title: Why a silly-sounding name suits the serious mission of our biotech spin-off
rows.summary: How do you choose what to call your company? Wobble Genomics’s chief executive, Richard Kuo, explains.

rows.title: Voter turnout drives margins of victory ― if elections are fair
rows.summary: Model that predicts the spread of winning margins could be used to detect electoral interference.

rows.title: How the brain cleans itself during deep sleep
rows.summary: Blood vessels in the brain rhythmically constrict and dilate to drive waves of cleansing fluid through the organ.

rows.title: Rising stars in AI use robotics and automation to accelerate their work
rows.summary: These three scientists are pushing boundaries in their fields.

rows.title: Mind matters: investigating academia’s ‘mental health crisis’
rows.summary: Adam Levy discusses some of the systemic changes needed to make the academic workplace both a happier and healthier place.

rows.title: These are the 20 most-studied bacteria — the majority have been ignored
rows.summary: Model microbes such as Escherichia coli hog scientists’ attention, leaving most known bacteria with few publications devoted to them.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Earth breaches 1.5 °C climate limit for the first time
rows.summary: A grim milestone of climate heating, the public-health legacy of former US president Jimmy Carter and a possible problem with tennis balls.

rows.title: Does fact-checking work? What the science says
rows.summary: Meta’s planned shift away from third-party fact-checking on Facebook in favour of a crowdsourced approach has perplexed those who study the spread of misinformation.

rows.title: Jimmy Carter obituary: former US president who dedicated his life after office to peace, human rights and global health
rows.summary: The Nobel prizewinner worked tirelessly with wife Rosalynn Carter to eradicate Guinea-worm disease.

rows.title: Earth breaches 1.5 °C climate limit for the first time: what does it mean?
rows.summary: The threshold has been exceeded for only one year so far, but humanity is nearing the end of what many thought was a ‘safe zone’ as climate change worsens.

rows.title: Male spiders smell with their legs
rows.summary: Sensory organs on the walking legs of the male wasp spider can catch the scent of a female in a mood for romance.

rows.title: Why the last cases of sleeping sickness will be the hardest to eliminate
rows.summary: Pharmaceuticals and vector-control programmes have greatly diminished the once-widespread disease, but sustained effort will be needed to stamp out infection for good.

rows.title: Author Correction: Progressive plasticity during colorectal cancer metastasis
Who’s quitting academia? Data reveal gender gaps in surprising fields
rows.summary: Even in scientific areas in which women are well represented, they are up to 40% more likely than men to leave research within 20 years.

rows.title: Revealed: the fatty cells that are the ‘bubble wrap’ of the body
rows.summary: Previously undescribed cells look like fat cells, but function to provide cushioning and support in cartilage.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Meet Punk and Emo , the 430-million-year old mollusc fossils
rows.summary: We learn how the brain ‘washes’ itself while asleep and meet two fossils that are changing our understanding of mollusc evolution.

rows.title: Repurposing of a gill gene regulatory program for outer-ear evolution
rows.summary: A study on the evolutionary origin of the mammalian outer ear finds that it shares genetic programs with the gills of fishes and amphibians, indicating that elements of an ancestral gill have been reused.

rows.title: Author Correction: Common and rare variant associations with clonal haematopoiesis phenotypes
Cosmic carnage: planetary rubble spotted at a dying star
rows.summary: Dust cloud is thought to be the first debris disk to be seen around a planetary nebula.

rows.title: Author Correction: A deep catalogue of protein-coding variation in 983,578 individuals
How quantum mechanics emerged in a few revolutionary months 100 years ago
rows.summary: It began with concerns about the orbits used to explain the motion of electrons in atoms — but quantum theory ended up upending reality itself.

rows.title: Graduate-student stipends in Canada below the poverty line
rows.summary: Students struggle to make ends meet despite recent boosts to federal scholarships, study finds.

rows.title: Electrochemical synthesis goes wireless
rows.summary: Electrochemical reactions for organic synthesis typically require intricate, specialized equipment, slowing progress in this field. Minuscule electric generators now enable faster reaction discovery and development.

rows.title: Reply to: Amino acids and KLHL22 do not activate mTORC1 via DEPDC5 degradation
Physicists describe exotic ‘paraparticles’ that defy categorization
rows.summary: Theoretical study predicts the existence of particles that are neither bosons nor fermions — and hints at applications in quantum computing.

rows.title: Circadian rhythms are set by epigenetic marks in neurons
rows.summary: Chemicals derived from neurotransmitter molecules in the brain can act as epigenetic marks on histone proteins to regulate gene expression. These marks control circadian clock genes and influence behaviour.

rows.title: Why kids need to take more risks: science reveals the benefits of wild, free play
rows.summary: Studies reveal how risky play can benefit child development. But encouraging it can be a challenge for parents.

rows.title: Quantum mechanics 100 years on: an unfinished revolution
rows.summary: A century ago, physics had its Darwinian moment — a change in perspective that was as consequential for the physical sciences as the theory of evolution by natural selection was for biology.

rows.title: Spiky fossils Punk and Emo change our understanding of molluscan evolution
rows.summary: The early evolutionary history of molluscs has long been controversial, and remains imperfectly understood. Two exceptionally preserved 3D fossils dating to about 430 million years ago highlight previously unknown diversity in the physical form and ecology of the molluscs, and the evolutionary plasticity inherent to the group.

rows.title: AI learns from chromatin data to uncover gene interactions
rows.summary: An artificial-intelligence model trained on data about where DNA is tightly packaged and where it is open to regulators can predict gene expression and interactions between transcription factors that regulate key genes.

rows.title: A new-year round-up of the science stories you may have missed
rows.summary: We highlight some Nature Briefing stories from the end of 2024, including the retraction saga of a controversial COVID study, the skin’s surprise immune-system and the running ability of our ancient relatives.

rows.title: Amino acids and KLHL22 do not activate mTORC1 via DEPDC5 degradation
The AI tool that can interpret any spreadsheet instantly
rows.summary: Artificial intelligence is already used extensively to infer outcomes from tables of data, but this typically involves creating a model for each task. A one-size-fits-all model just made the process substantially easier.

rows.title: We need to talk about human genome editing
rows.summary: In a few decades, gene-editing technologies could reduce the likelihood of common human diseases. Societies must use this time to prepare for their arrival.

rows.title: Human embryo editing against disease is unsafe and unproven — despite rosy predictions
rows.summary: Mathematical modelling suggests that it is theoretically possible to reduce risk of common diseases using heritable genome editing. Scientists argue that the technology involves considerable risk and uncertain benefits.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Why kids need to take more risks: science reveals the benefits of adventurous play
rows.summary: We learn that lead in the air of ancient Rome might have lowered IQs and discover why children need risky play.

rows.title: Paper stars
rows.summary: A good day.

rows.title: What will viruses do next? AI is helping scientists predict their evolution
rows.summary: Forecasts of viral variation could improve vaccine and antiviral treatments ahead of time.

rows.title: β-C−H bond functionalization of ketones and esters by cationic Pd complexes
rows.summary: Diverse methyl β-C−H functionalizations of ketones and esters are enabled by cationic Pd(II) complexes with MPANA ligands, offering access to spirocyclic and fused ring systems through enhanced catalyst–substrate affinity.

rows.title: How a small but mighty protein protects a life-sustaining enzyme
rows.summary: The enzyme nitrogenase ‘fixes’ nitrogen gas to form bioavailable ammonia, a vital process for life. Two studies solve a long-standing mystery: how a small protein saves nitrogenase from destruction by oxygen.

rows.title: Heritable polygenic editing: the next frontier in genomic medicine?
rows.summary: We discuss the potential consequences and ethical concerns of polygenic genome editing of human embryos to alter specific variants associated with polygenic diseases, highlighting the possibility of reducing disease susceptibility while exacerbating health inequalities.

rows.title: Hippocampal neuronal activity is aligned with action plans
rows.summary: Using high-density electrophysiological recordings, how internally generated cell assemblies are updated by action plans to meet external goals is explored.

rows.title: Precursors of exhausted T cells are pre-emptively formed in acute infection
rows.summary: T cell exhaustion was thought to be strictly associated only with chronic infections and tumours, but it turns out that acute infections also generate a subset of precursor T cells with exhaustion-like phenotypes.

rows.title: Bidirectional histone monoaminylation dynamics regulate neural rhythmicity
rows.summary: TG2 functions as an eraser and exchanger of H3 monoaminylations, including histaminylation of Gln5 of histone H3.

rows.title: Janus graphene nanoribbons with localized states on a single zigzag edge
rows.summary: Janus graphene nanoribbons with localized states on a single zigzag edge are fabricated by introducing a topological defect array of benzene motifs on the opposite zigzag edge, to break the structural symmetry.

rows.title: An early precursor CD8 + T cell that adapts to acute or chronic viral infection
rows.summary: Stem-like CD8 + T cells specific for lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus are generated early during chronic infection, suggesting that this crucial fate commitment occurs irrespective of the infection outcome.

rows.title: Conformational protection of molybdenum nitrogenase by Shethna protein II
rows.summary: A small ferredoxin (Shethna protein II) of Azotobacter vinelandii can provide protection from O 2 stress that may be crucial for the maintenance of recombinant nitrogenase in food crops.

rows.title: A rare PRIMER cell state in plant immunity
rows.summary: The development of a molecularly defined spatiotemporal atlas of pathogen-infected Arabidopsis thaliana leaves reveals specific cell states that have distinct roles in plant immunity.

rows.title: Satellite DNA shapes dictate pericentromere packaging in female meiosis
rows.summary: Divergent satellite DNA shapes influence architectural protein binding and chromatin organization in two mouse species so that the satellites can be packaged and centromere function maintained, mitigating the evolutionary cost of satellite DNA expansion.

rows.title: Functional evaluation and clinical classification of BRCA2 variants
rows.summary: Results from a comprehensive evaluation of the function of BRCA2 variants, particularly variants of uncertain significance, provide a useful resource to improve the clinical management of individuals who carry such genetic variants.

rows.title: How frictional ruptures and earthquakes nucleate and evolve
rows.summary: Experimental and theoretical evidence shows that incorporating finite interface widths extends fracture mechanics to include crack (and earthquake) nucleation; slow steady creep occurring at a well-defined stress threshold.

rows.title: Meta-analysis reveals global variations in plant diversity effects on productivity
rows.summary: A meta-analysis of biodiversity effects on plant productivity found that complementarity effects increased over time whereas selection effects decreased, and both remained consistent across global variations in climate.

rows.title: Dynamic supramolecular snub cubes
rows.summary: Left- and right-handed snub cubes show photocontrollable elasticity and hardness, in addition to the ability to encapsulate different small molecules in distinct compartments simultaneously, with potential applications in the development of advanced biomimetic materials.

rows.title: Host metabolism balances microbial regulation of bile acid signalling
rows.summary: A family of host-derived bile acid–methylcysteamine conjugates functions as FXR antagonists, forming part of a microbiota-dependent metabolic network that regulates FXR-dependent physiology.

rows.title: Li 2 ZrF 6 -based electrolytes for durable lithium metal batteries
rows.summary: Adding excess m -Li 2 ZrF 6 (monoclinic) nanoparticles to a commercial LiPF 6 -containing carbonate electrolyte forms a stable interphase rich in t -Li 2 ZrF 6 (trigonal), enhancing Li-ion transfer, suppressing dendrite growth and considerably improving the cycling stability of high-rate lithium metal batteries.

rows.title: The sequence–structure–function relationship of intrinsic ERα disorder
rows.summary: Serine 118 phosphorylation drives conformational changes through the disruption of hydrophobic interactions between aromatic-rich clusters, showing how hydrophobic mutations can restore oestrogen receptor-mediated transcription.

rows.title: RNA control of reverse transcription in a diversity-generating retroelement
rows.summary: This study presents cryogenic electron microscopy structural analysis of a diversity-generating retroelement (DGR) reverse transcription system from Bordetella bacteriophage, with results indicating that RNA surrounding the template controls reverse transcription through mechanisms that are conserved across distant taxa.

rows.title: Longitudinal strain enhancement and bending deformations in piezoceramics
rows.summary: We find that if the thickness of a polycrystalline piezoceramic is reduced such that a large fraction of the grains are in the triaxial–biaxal crossover regime, the longitudinal strain is enhanced and the piezoceramic bends.

rows.title: Saturation genome editing-based clinical classification of BRCA2 variants
rows.summary: CRISPR–Cas9-based saturation genome editing in a humanized mouse embryonic stem cell line was used for comprehensive functional characterization of single nucleotide variants in a region of BRCA2 , and shows good agreement with existing variant classifications and high predictive power.

rows.title: Complex rearrangements fuel ER + and HER2 + breast tumours
rows.summary: A study identifies three dominant genomic archetypes of breast cancer induced by discrete mutational processes, describing a continuum of genomic profiles and detailing the mechanisms underlying the progression of breast cancer.

rows.title: Computational microscopy with coherent diffractive imaging and ptychography
rows.summary: This review highlights transformative advancements in computational microscopy, encompassing coherent diffractive imaging and ptychography, which unify microscopy and crystallography to achieve unparalleled resolution, precision, and large fields of view, enabling diverse applications and driving breakthroughs across multidisciplinary sciences.

rows.title: Structural basis for the conformational protection of nitrogenase from O 2
rows.summary: Cryo-electron microscopy of Azotobacter vinelandii FeSII–nitrogenase reveals a core complex of molybdenum–iron proteins (MoFePs), iron proteins (FePs) and FeSII, in which FeSII mediates interactions with MoFeP and FeP to position their FeS clusters in catalytically inactive but O 2 -protected states.

rows.title: A foundation model of transcription across human cell types
rows.summary: A foundation model learns transcriptional regulatory syntax from chromatin accessibility and sequence data across a range of cell types to predict gene expression and transcription factor interactions, with generalizability to unseen cell types.

rows.title: Sulfide-rich continental roots at cratonic margins formed by carbonated melts
rows.summary: Examination of the sulfur and copper contents of global cratonic peridotites combined with new high-pressure experiments shows that the migration of carbonated melts towards cratonic margins explains the co-location of magmatic metal deposits with carbonatites.

rows.title: Molecular and cellular dynamics of the developing human neocortex
rows.summary: Tripotential intermediate progenitor cells are responsible for the local production of GABAergic neurons, oligodendrocyte precursor cells and astrocytes in the human neocortex.

rows.title: Site-saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains
rows.summary: Large-scale experimental analysis of Human Domainome 1, a library containing more than 500,000 missense mutation variants across more than 500 human protein domains, reveals that 60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce stability of protein domains.

rows.title: Accurate predictions on small data with a tabular foundation model
rows.summary: Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network, a tabular foundation model, provides accurate predictions on small data and outperforms all previous methods on datasets with up to 10,000 samples by a wide margin.

rows.title: Two-dimensional non-Hermitian skin effect in an ultracold Fermi gas
rows.summary: A two-dimensional non-Hermitian topological band is created in an ultracold system of fermions, which exhibits the non-Hermitian skin effect.

rows.title: One-quarter of freshwater fauna threatened with extinction
rows.summary: A global multi-taxon extinction risk assessment of freshwater fauna for The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species finds one-quarter of species to be at high risk of extinction.

rows.title: Proximity ferroelectricity in wurtzite heterostructures
rows.summary: Proximity ferroelectricity is reported in wurtzite heterostructures, which enables polarization reversal in wurtzites without the chemical or structural disorder that accompanies elemental substitution.

rows.title: Light-harvesting microelectronic devices for wireless electrosynthesis
rows.summary: A method to produce wireless microelectronic devices powered by light using standard nanofabrication techniques is described to convert any traditional 96-well or 384-well plate into an electrochemical reactor that can drive reactions in high throughput.

rows.title: Excitons in the fractional quantum Hall effect
rows.summary: Excitonic pairing in fractional quantum Hall states shows two new quantum phases, including a fractional exciton condensate and an unusual type of exciton that obeys fermionic or anyonic quantum statistics.

rows.title: Reinventing type 2 immunity in cancer
rows.summary: This Review addresses the roles of type 2 immunity in cancer and the potential for cancer immunotherapies targeting this pathway.

rows.title: A vision–language foundation model for precision oncology
rows.summary: Trained on unlabelled, unpaired image and text data, the Multimodal transformer with Unified maSKed modeling excelled in outcome prediction, image-to-text retrieval and visual question answering, potentially improving cancer diagnosis and therapy precision.

rows.title: Crypt density and recruited enhancers underlie intestinal tumour initiation
rows.summary: Mouse models of colorectal cancer show that adenoma formation following deletion of Apc is dependent on a proximity effect of mutant crypts and increased chromosome accessibility at specific enhancers.

rows.title: Particle exchange statistics beyond fermions and bosons
rows.summary: By developing a second quantization of paraparticles and constructing exactly solvable quantum spin models with emergent paraparticles, new theoretical evidence shows that non-trivial parastatistics inequivalent to either fermions or bosons can exist in physical systems.

rows.title: New Silurian aculiferan fossils reveal complex early history of Mollusca
rows.summary: Fossils of two new worm-like aculiferan species add to the diversity of this group, showing that evolution in early aculiferans generated unusual forms comparable to other crown-group molluscs.

rows.title: To ensure trust, AI weather-forecast models still need training in physics
Science communication has a problem — communication
Biodiversity credits are more problematic than carbon credits
Particle accelerators get an assist from AI co-pilots
rows.summary: Large language models can propose fine-tuning adjustments for an electron accelerator in Germany.

rows.title: What do people eat and why do they eat it?
rows.summary: A 1975 report sparks a debate about the place of sociology in human nutrition research, and a crystal-clear lecture on chemical morphology, in our weekly dip into Nature ’s archive.

rows.title: Researchers: concentrate on bread-and-butter issues to get political buy-in
Daily briefing: Why did Europe’s first cities disappear? Uncovering the mysterious Cucuteni–Trypillia culture
rows.summary: We examine evidence that global warming might be speeding up and ask what happened to the egalitarian Cucuteni–Trypillia culture.

rows.title: The structure of bad cholesterol comes into focus
rows.summary: Insights into how cholesterol-carrying low-density lipoproteins are structured, and how they interact with receptors to enter cells, could help to clarify the role of these particles in cardiovascular disease.

rows.title: Who built Europe’s first cities? Clues about the urban revolution emerge
rows.summary: Around 6,000 years ago, a group known as the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture developed egalitarian settlements north of the Black Sea and created the region’s earliest urban centres. Then, after two millennia, they vanished.

rows.title: NASA still has no plan for how to bring precious Mars rocks to Earth
rows.summary: The US$2.7-billion Perseverance rover collected the samples looking for evidence of past life, but NASA is dithering about how to get them off the red planet.

rows.title: The trill of the chase: recording birdsong in Ireland’s disappearing wilderness
rows.summary: Seán Ronayne’s quest is to record all common bird species in Ireland, sharing both happy and sad stories about wildlife.

rows.title: Earth shattered heat records in 2023 and 2024: is global warming speeding up?
rows.summary: Nature examines whether the temperature spike is a blip or an enduring — and concerning — trend.

rows.title: Spacecraft makes closest-ever fly-by of Sun: what the trip will tell us
rows.summary: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe could solve the mysteries of the solar wind and test Einstein’s theory of relativity.

rows.title: ‘WithdrarXiv’ database of 14,000 retracted preprints launches
rows.summary: A trove of data is providing insights into the main reasons studies are pulled from the arXiv preprint platform.

rows.title: ‘One of the last taboos’: breaking the stigma of substance-use disorders in academia
rows.summary: Those recovering from drug or alcohol misuse speak up — and say they wish more researchers could do so freely at work.

rows.title: Daily briefing: Sleeping mice hint at why new memories don’t overwrite old ones
rows.summary: We see evidence in mice of why new memories don’t overwrite existing ones and explore how AI tools are helping decipher previously unreadable ancient texts.

rows.title: Author Correction: Ab initio characterization of protein molecular dynamics with AI 2 BMD
Why don’t new memories overwrite old ones? Sleep science holds clues
rows.summary: Research in mice points towards a mechanism that avoids ‘catastrophic forgetting’.

rows.title: ‘Precocious’ early-career scientists with high citation counts proliferate
rows.summary: Researchers have questions about how so many authors have racked up a large number of citations so quickly, although some of those authors are honest overachievers.

rows.title: Fancy birds decorate nests with a natural pattern: snakeskin
rows.summary: The use of shed skins might help to ward off predators, experiments suggest.

rows.title: Author Correction: Oxidative cyclization reagents reveal tryptophan cation–π interactions
Climate engineering faces hostility — here’s how scientists say it might move forwards
rows.summary: Questions about effectiveness, risks and regulation must be answered before Sun-dimming technology can be developed, according to researchers.
